llm_summary: Cytomegalovirus, a common virus that causes serious infections in people who receive organ transplants, is difficult to treat and can come back even after medication. Researchers studied 145 organ transplant patients who developed significant cytomegalovirus infections between 2010 and 2016, tracking which patients had infections that didn't respond to treatment, developed resistance to antiviral drugs, or experienced the infection returning. They found that patients with lower immune cell counts early after transplant were more likely to have infections that didn't respond to initial treatment, while those with very high levels of virus in their blood were more likely to develop drug-resistant infections. About one in five patients experienced the infection returning within six months, though surprisingly, having a difficult-to-treat infection did not directly increase the risk of death in this group. These findings suggest that doctors should monitor immune cell counts and virus levels closely in transplant patients to better predict and prevent serious cytomegalovirus infections.

title: Intra-Articular Purified Exosome Product and Hyaluronan Attenuate Osteoarthritis Progression in a Minimally Invasive Turkey Model.
abstract: Our study aimed to develop a novel, reproducible, minimally invasive turkey knee osteoarthritis (OA) model and evaluate whether intra-articular hyaluronan (HA) alone or combined with purified exosome product (PEP) attenuates OA-related functional and structural deterioration. OA was induced arthroscopically by transection of the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments with resection of the anterior horn of the medial meniscus. Animals received intra-articular injections of saline, HA, or PEP + HA at postoperative 2-5 weeks. Gait was assessed at 4, 8, and 12 weeks, and cartilage degeneration, subchondral bone sclerosis, osteophyte formation, synovial fibrosis, heterotopic ossification, and meniscal integrity were evaluated by quantitative CT and histology at week 12. Compared with saline, HA improved lameness, preserved cartilage glycosaminoglycan content, and reduced meniscal rupture, subchondral bone sclerosis, and periarticular heterotopic ossification. PEP + HA provided additional benefits, including prolonged stance phase, reduced synovial fibrosis, and greater chondroprotection than HA alone, while plantar pressure variables, subchondral bone remodeling, and patellar osteophytes did not differ between HA and PEP + HA. This turkey model reliably produces human-like OA changes and enables longitudinal functional and structural assessment. Intra-articular HA mitigated OA progression, and the addition of PEP conferred incremental joint protection.© 2026 Orthopaedic Research Society.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether two injectable treatments could slow down knee damage in turkeys with artificially induced osteoarthritis, a condition where the protective cartilage in joints breaks down over time. They created a new surgical method to damage turkey knees in a way that mimics how human knees deteriorate, then injected some birds with salt water, some with hyaluronan (a slippery substance naturally found in joints), and others with hyaluronan combined with purified exosomes (tiny particles from cells that may reduce inflammation). After twelve weeks, the birds that received hyaluronan alone showed improved walking ability and less cartilage damage compared to those given salt water, while the group receiving both hyaluronan and exosomes experienced even greater benefits including reduced inflammation in the joint lining. These findings suggest that injecting hyaluronan into damaged knees can help protect cartilage and improve movement, and that adding exosomes provides additional protection beyond hyaluronan alone. title: Deriving target exposure indices for common radiography exams based on automatic exposures of flat-field phantoms.
abstract: The IEC exposure index (EI), deviation index (DI), and target exposure index (EIT), represent critical standardized metrics for the evaluation of exposure and quality in radiographic imaging.This work develops and validates a systematic procedure to estimate the EIT for eight of the most common radiography imaging protocols utilizing automatic exposure control (AEC) from measurements acquired under reference conditions.A model was developed to define the relationship between a systems AEC logic, and an estimation of the EI under flat-field conditions (EIFFC). Separately, clinical data and acquisition protocol information for resultant EI during patient studies were also collected for the eight protocols studied: Chest posteroanterior (PA), Chest lateral, Abdomen anteroposterior (AP), Pelvis AP, L-Spine AP, C-Spine AP, T-Spine AP, and Ribs AP. Data were collected from 41 x-ray units spanning seven institutions. For each protocol on each unit the EIFFC was computed based on the acquisition protocol, as well as median EI from clinical exams to produce a scaling factor (SF). Kruskal-Wallis statistical tests were used to compare SF's between vendors and AEC cell configurations.SFs for eight radiographic imaging protocols have been produced per vendor and per AEC cell selection. A workflow has been established for end-users to follow to apply these SFs to flat-field measurements taken at their own locations to establish local EIT.The study results show that in seven of the eight imaging protocols, the SFs for most units included in the study report SFs within 1 DI (± 25%) of their respective final vendor reported SF (218/228). The ribs protocol is the exception to this finding (n = 26). SFs have high utility for establishing EIT values on individual x-ray units and normalizing EI value distributions for quality assurance purposes.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined how to establish standard exposure targets for common chest and spine X-ray procedures, which is important because consistent radiation exposure helps ensure good image quality while protecting patients from unnecessary radiation. The team developed a systematic method to estimate target exposure levels by testing eight common radiography protocols across forty-one X-ray machines at seven different hospitals, using flat-field phantoms (uniform test objects) and automatic exposure control systems that adjust radiation dose during imaging. They collected data on how much radiation was actually used during patient exams and compared it to measurements taken under controlled laboratory conditions to create scaling factors that could predict proper exposure levels for each machine and imaging type. The results showed that for seven out of eight imaging protocols tested, most machines produced scaling factors that were within acceptable ranges, meaning the method worked reliably for establishing appropriate exposure targets at individual hospital locations. This workflow provides a practical tool for hospital staff to use their own equipment to set proper exposure standards and monitor radiation quality, though the ribs imaging protocol showed more variability and may need additional investigation.

title: AMCP Market Insights: Getting to the heart of hard-to-control hypertension in managed care.
abstract: Hard-to-control hypertension, comprising uncontrolled and resistant hypertension, is highly prevalent, meaning many patients with hypertension remain at risk of adverse outcomes despite treatment. To discuss the role of managed care in addressing hard-to-control hypertension, AMCP Market Insights virtually convened an expert panel of managed care stakeholders in November 2025. This article provides a qualitative summary of the panel discussion. Key insights were that despite multiple effective, low-cost pharmacotherapy options, a significant proportion of patients have blood pressure above recommended goals because of confounding factors at both the micro and macro levels; and managed care-specific challenges in hard-to-control hypertension include competing organizational priorities, data gaps, and lack of integration of existing resources. Opportunities to advance care in hard-to-control hypertension include focusing on prevention and providing additional patient and clinician support such as with education and enhancing use of digital technologies. Other insights were that top payer priorities in hypertension include reducing cardiovascular events and other complications and meeting quality goals, and that current clinical guidelines and provider input are important elements of payer decision-making. These findings can support informed clinical and coverage decisions, can offer practical actions for payers, and may inform future work.

llm_summary: Many people with high blood pressure remain at risk for serious health problems like heart attacks and strokes even though they are taking medications, which is why understanding how to better manage this condition is important. A group of managed care experts, meaning people who work for health insurance companies and make decisions about patient care, met together in November 2025 to discuss the challenges of treating hard-to-control high blood pressure. The experts found that even though there are many affordable medications available to treat high blood pressure, many patients still have readings above the healthy target because of various personal and system-wide factors that get in the way of good treatment. The panel identified several opportunities to improve care, including focusing on preventing high blood pressure before it develops, giving patients and doctors more education and support, and using digital tools like apps and remote monitoring to help manage the condition better. These insights can help health insurance companies make better decisions about which treatments to cover and what actions they can take to help more patients achieve healthy blood pressure levels.

title: Melatonin improves postprandial hypoglycemia: an unusual presentation of insulinoma.
abstract: Insulinoma is the most prevalent neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas, presenting with a spectrum of neuroglycopenic symptoms. This case report describes a 64-year-old woman with primarily postprandial hypoglycemia, resulting in altered consciousness and confusion occurring several hours after meals. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) was used to establish the postprandial pattern of the patient's hypoglycemia, and this facilitated the confirmatory biochemical evaluation by a single blood draw done at the time of symptoms, without performing a 72-hour fast. Imaging demonstrated an 11-mm tumor in the pancreas, which was removed and confirmed to be a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor on histopathology. While awaiting pancreatic surgery, the patient began taking melatonin for sleep and reported an improvement in the frequency and severity of hypoglycemia symptoms, which was supported by CGM data and a robust expression of melatonin receptors on the excised tumor. This case raises interest in the role of melatonin receptor signaling in counteracting hyperinsulinemia and corresponding hypoglycemia in patients with insulinoma.© The Author(s) 2026. llm_summary: Insulinoma is a rare tumor of the pancreas that causes dangerously low blood sugar levels, which can lead to confusion and loss of consciousness, especially after eating meals. Doctors treated a 64-year-old woman by using continuous glucose monitoring, a device that tracks blood sugar throughout the day, to confirm her low blood sugar pattern and then found an 11-millimeter tumor in her pancreas that was surgically removed. While waiting for surgery, the patient started taking melatonin as a sleep aid and noticed that her low blood sugar episodes became less frequent and less severe, which was confirmed by her glucose monitoring device. The tumor tissue showed high levels of melatonin receptors, which are special proteins that respond to melatonin, suggesting that melatonin might help reduce the excessive insulin production that causes the dangerous low blood sugar. This case suggests that melatonin could potentially be a helpful treatment for insulinoma patients, though more research is needed to understand exactly how melatonin works against this condition.

title: 2025 Consensus Clinical Management Guidelines for Niemann-Pick Disease Type C.
abstract: In 2018, the International Niemann-Pick Disease Alliance (INPDA) and the International Niemann-Pick Disease Registry (INPDR) developed and published comprehensive clinical management guidelines to support inclusive and standardized care pathways in Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC)-an ultra-rare, autosomal recessive, neurovisceral lysosomal disorder. Since then, advances in diagnostics, care, and the approval of two novel disease-modifying agents have underscored the need to revise these guidelines to ensure safe, consistent, and high-quality care for those affected by NPC. In response, the INPDA and INPDR convened a multidisciplinary Guidelines Development Group (GDG) comprising individuals with NPC expertise from 14 countries across five continents, representing a broad range of specialties, as well as patients and families involved in NPC care. Informed by a comprehensive literature review and two meetings, the GDG systematically reviewed, revised, and updated the 2018 guideline statements, re-evaluating the level of evidence, strength of recommendations, and expert agreement for each. The resulting 2025 consensus clinical management guidelines constitute a timely, up-to-date, and internationally applicable resource for the diagnosis, treatment, and holistic management of individuals with NPC. These guidelines serve as a critical resource for specialist centers, hospital-based medical teams, staff involved in NPC patient care, family physicians and other primary caregivers, and, importantly, patients and their families.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Niemann-Pick disease type C is a rare inherited disorder that damages the nervous system and organs, and doctors needed updated guidelines because new treatments and diagnostic tools have become available since 2018. A team of medical experts from fourteen countries, including doctors, patients, and families affected by the disease, reviewed all available scientific research and met together to create improved care instructions. The group carefully examined and updated every recommendation from the previous guidelines, checking the strength of evidence behind each suggestion and making sure all experts agreed on the best approach. These new 2025 guidelines provide clear, standardized instructions for diagnosing and treating Niemann-Pick disease type C that doctors, hospitals, and families can use around the world to ensure consistent and high-quality care. The guidelines serve as an important resource for specialist centers and primary care doctors, helping them deliver the best possible treatment and support to patients and families dealing with this serious genetic condition.

title: Sociocultural Aspects of the Pathophysiology, Clinical Presentation, and Management of Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction.
abstract: Sociocultural determinants such as cultural norms, diet, and environmental factors, along with their effects on the gastrointestinal microbiome, can modify the risk to develop disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI). These factors also shape symptom perception and health care-seeking behaviors, and how society and health care providers respond to patients with DGBI. This document summarizes the knowledge about the role of sociocultural factors in the manifestation of DGBI and the management of these patients. Symptom expression and societal response to DGBI varies across different cultural settings, influencing individual patient outcomes and the overall societal burden of disease. Patients with DGBI are often stigmatized, leading to a bias toward conditions with visible abnormalities and underfunded services for DGBI. Recognizing the role of sociocultural factors for DGBI outcomes presents an opportunity to refine pathophysiologic concepts and improve patient outcomes. llm_summary: Researchers examined how cultural beliefs, eating habits, and living conditions affect disorders of gut-brain interaction, which are conditions where the stomach and intestines don't work properly due to problems with how the brain and digestive system communicate. The study found that these sociocultural factors influence not only whether people develop these digestive disorders but also how they experience symptoms and whether they seek medical help. The research revealed that symptoms and how society responds to these conditions vary greatly depending on cultural background, which affects how well patients do and how much the disease impacts entire communities. Patients with these disorders often face unfair treatment and stigma because their conditions don't show obvious physical signs like broken bones or visible wounds, which leads to less funding and fewer resources for research and treatment. The authors conclude that understanding and addressing these cultural and social factors could help doctors better understand these conditions and improve outcomes for patients, which requires greater attention and fair distribution of money for studying and treating these disorders.

title: Patient Experience, Gender, Age, Race, and Social Determinants of Health.
abstract: Women are disproportionately affected by disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI), including esophageal, gastroduodenal, bowel, and anorectal conditions, and frequently experience overlapping pain syndromes. This review synthesizes clinical and preclinical evidence on sex- and gender-related differences in DGBI, highlighting alterations in central pain processing, autonomic regulation, stress, microbiota composition, epithelial permeability, motility, genetic and epigenetic factors, and immune responses that may underlie observed disparities. Emerging data indicate that gonadal hormones, interacting with environmental stressors across the lifespan, modulate symptom severity and disease course. Social determinants of health, inadequate patient-provider communication, and disorder-associated stigma further exacerbate inequities in diagnosis and care. Research remains limited by lack of standardized definitions of sex and gender, under-representation of men and gender minorities, and insufficient consideration of hormonal changes and exogenous hormone exposure. Addressing these gaps is essential to advance our understanding of DGBI and guide gender-informed diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for DGBI management.Copyright © 2026 AGA Institute. llm_summary: Women experience gut-related disorders, which are conditions affecting the digestive system and the connection between the brain and stomach, much more often than men, and these conditions frequently occur together with overlapping pain problems. Researchers reviewed existing scientific evidence to understand why these differences exist, looking at factors like how the brain processes pain, stress responses, the bacteria living in the digestive system, and how hormones affect symptoms throughout a person's life. The review found that female and male hormones interact with life stressors to influence how severe symptoms become and how the disease progresses over time, while social factors like poverty, poor communication between patients and doctors, and shame about having these conditions make diagnosis and treatment even harder. The findings suggest that doctors need to develop better diagnostic and treatment approaches that take into account a patient's gender and life circumstances rather than using one-size-fits-all methods. Future research must include more diverse groups of people in studies, use consistent definitions of sex and gender, and pay closer attention to how hormones affect these conditions so that healthcare providers can offer more personalized and effective care.

title: Pharmacological, Pharmacokinetic, and Pharmacogenomic Aspects of Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction.
abstract: We conducted a literature review of preclinical, animal and human pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacogenomics related to disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI). This article reviews animal models of visceral pain, abnormal motility, and epithelial transport, and human models of motility and sensation and their utility in drug development for DGBI with focus on colorectal and gastric biomarkers. We highlight preclinical studies related to pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, and toxicology required for development of novel therapeutic agents, and principles of pharmacogenomics based on drug metabolism and the few examples of pharmacogenetics related to targets in treatment of IBS. Finally, we summarize the human pharmacology of medications used for treatment of DGBI based on the individual indications - specifically psychopharmacologic and nonpsychotropic agents for DGBI associated with dyspepsia, constipation, diarrhea, and visceral pain, as well as introduction of biomarkers for individualizing therapy for IBS and recommendations for future research.Copyright © 2026 AGA Institute. llm_summary: Disorders of gut-brain interaction, which are conditions where the brain and digestive system don't communicate properly, affect many people and require better treatment options. Researchers reviewed scientific literature on how medications work in the body, how the body processes these drugs, and how genetic differences affect drug response in patients with these digestive disorders. The review examined animal studies and human studies that test new treatments for problems like stomach pain, abnormal digestion, constipation, and diarrhea, while also looking at specific markers in the colon and stomach that could help doctors choose the right medicine for each patient. Understanding how different medications work and how individual genetic differences influence drug effectiveness could help doctors personalize treatment plans and develop new therapies that work better for people with these gut-brain disorders. The researchers recommend that future studies focus on using genetic testing and biomarkers to match patients with the most effective medications for their specific type of gut-brain disorder.

title: Fundamentals of Neurogastroenterology: Basic Science.
abstract: This review highlights major advances in neurogastroenterology since Rome IV, offering a condensed summary of a comprehensive document to appear in the forthcoming Rome V book. Prepared by an international team of experts, it emphasizes pivotal studies that have deepened understanding of the physiological and pathophysiological mechanisms underlying disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI). These disorders are inherently complex and multifactorial, shaped by interactions among neuronal, epithelial, immune, smooth muscle, interstitial, and microbial populations. The review outlines cutting-edge technologies advancing the field and explores key themes, including brain-gut interactions, neurobiology, and neuroplasticity of the enteric nervous system, neuroimmune function, microbiome influences, and abnormalities of the gut-brain axis in DGBI. Risk factors for DGBI are considered, with serotonergic signaling presented as a conceptual framework for linking symptomatology and pathophysiology. Finally, we discuss how these scientific advances can translate into novel therapeutic strategies to improve patient care.Copyright © 2026 AGA Institute. Published by Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: An international team of experts created this review to explain how the brain and gut communicate with each other and how problems with this communication can cause digestive disorders that affect millions of people. The researchers summarized major scientific discoveries made since the previous Rome IV guidelines, focusing on how the nervous system in the gut, immune cells, bacteria in the digestive tract, and the brain all work together to influence digestive health. They found that digestive disorders involving brain-gut interaction are complex conditions caused by multiple factors, including problems with nerve signals, immune system dysfunction, changes in gut bacteria, and how the brain processes signals from the stomach and intestines. The review highlights how serotonin, a chemical messenger in the body, plays an important role in these disorders and could help doctors understand why patients experience their symptoms. These scientific advances could lead to new treatments that work better than current options and improve the quality of life for people suffering from these common digestive conditions.

title: A proof-of-concept study of multitask learning for cranial synthetic CT generation across heterogeneous MRI field strengths.
abstract: Accurate synthesis of computed tomography (CT) images from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is clinically valuable for cranial applications such as attenuation correction, radiotherapy planning, and image-guided interventions. However, the heterogeneity of MRI data across magnetic field strengths and pulse sequences limits the generalizability of existing methods, posing a barrier to clinical translation.This study aims to reformulate cranial CT synthesis as a modular, structurally coupled problem using a deep learning approach, enhancing adaptability across heterogeneous MRI conditions, including different field strengths and sequence protocols.We implemented a cascaded multitask pipeline that jointly models skull segmentation and Hounsfield Unit (HU) regression in anatomically targeted regions. A 3D patch-based training paradigm shifts the modeling focus from global image translation to localized bone feature extraction. The backbone leverages a residual Mamba-based state space model within a 3D U-Net structure to improve spatial representation, while a Transformer U-Net serves as a widely recognized reference baseline comparison. The model was trained and evaluated in terms of multi-modal (T1-weighted and T2-FLAIR) and cross-domain transferability from a public 1.5 Tesla brain dataset (n = 37) to an independent 7 Tesla clinical brain dataset (n = 44). Performance was assessed using Dice and Jaccard indices for segmentation accuracy and mean absolute error (MAE) for HU regression.Quantitative analysis showed that our multitask pipeline, incorporating both morphological and HU map prediction stages, significantly outperformed conventional direct MRI-to-CT mapping across all metrics on the public 1.5T dataset (p < 0.05). Consistent performance on an external 7T clinical dataset (p < 0.001) further demonstrated the method's robustness and adaptability across field strengths.These findings support that task-structured training for modality transformation markedly improves both accuracy and generalizability of cranial CT synthesis across heterogeneous MRI conditions. The observed consistency across field strengths validates the robustness of the proposed methodology.© 2026 American Association of Physicists in Medicine.

llm_summary: Researchers examined a new artificial intelligence method to convert brain MRI scans into CT scans, which are important for cancer treatment planning and surgical guidance, because current methods struggle when hospitals use different types of MRI machines with varying strengths. The team created a computer learning system that breaks down the conversion task into two related steps: first identifying the skull bones in the MRI image, and second predicting the density values that would appear in a CT scan, using a specialized neural network architecture designed to process three-dimensional medical images. When tested on brain scans from a standard 1. 5 Tesla MRI machine and then on scans from a more powerful 7 Tesla clinical machine, the new method significantly outperformed traditional direct conversion approaches, showing it could accurately handle different MRI equipment and imaging techniques. These results suggest that structuring the conversion task into smaller, connected steps helps artificial intelligence systems work reliably across different hospital equipment and imaging protocols, which could speed up the adoption of this technology in real clinical settings.

In rare cases, this procedure can trigger an unusual immune response where the body forms small clusters of immune cells called granulomas, which can resemble a condition called sarcoidosis that typically affects the lungs and other organs.

title: Systematic Review of Kidney Transplant Outcomes in Monoclonal Ig Deposition Disease.
abstract: Historical case series of monoclonal Ig deposition disease (MIDD) after kidney transplantation (KTx) reported unfavorable outcomes. Recent case series support more acceptable outcomes in selected patients.We performed a pooled analysis of case series and case reports using available individual participant data (IPD). We searched MEDLINE, Web of Science, SCOPUS, Cochrane Library, and gray literature. Recurrence-free survival, graft survival, and overall survival from the time of KTx were analyzed. Sensitivity analyses were performed according to publication type, hematologic response before KTx, exposure to novel agents, and era.Eighty-seven kidney allografts were included from case series and case reports between 1986 and 2023. During the median follow-up of 46 months, recurrence occurred in 47 allografts (54%), at a median of 30 months after KTx. The estimated median recurrence-free survival was significantly longer in patients who achieved a very good partial response (VGPR) hematologic response or better. Graft survival at 5- and 10-years was 67.1% and 45.9% respectively. Recurrence was the main cause of the graft loss in the majority. Among the patients who faced recurrence, the median time from recurrence to graft failure was longer in those who received clone-directed therapies (62 vs. 11 months, P = 0.02). Overall survival rates at 5 and 10 years were 83.8% and 47.4%, respectively.More recent outcomes of patients with MIDD after KTx are favorable. Clone-directed therapies in recurrent disease appear to prolong graft survival.© 2026 Published by Elsevier, Inc., on behalf of the International Society of Nephrology.

llm_summary: Researchers examined kidney transplant outcomes in patients with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease, a condition where abnormal proteins build up in the kidneys and can damage transplanted organs. The study pooled together data from eighty-seven kidney transplant cases reported between 1986 and 2023 to understand how often the disease came back and how long the transplanted kidneys lasted. About half of the transplanted kidneys experienced disease recurrence at a median of thirty months after transplantation, though patients who achieved strong responses to treatment before transplant had better outcomes without recurrence. The five-year survival rate for transplanted kidneys was sixty-seven percent, and patients who received targeted therapies designed to attack the abnormal cells had significantly longer graft survival after disease recurrence compared to those who did not receive these treatments. These findings suggest that modern treatment approaches, particularly clone-directed therapies that specifically target the disease-causing cells, offer more hope for kidney transplant patients with this condition than older historical data indicated.

title: Identification of genetic risk loci associated with aquaporin 4-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder: a genome-wide association study.
abstract: Little is known about the causes of serum aquaporin 4 (AQP4) antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4-positive NMOSD) or how its pathophysiology differs from other demyelinating autoimmune diseases, which limits therapeutic and preventative opportunities despite available diagnostic biomarkers. By performing a pan-ancestry genome-wide association study (GWAS), we aimed to deepen our understanding of the genetic architecture of AQP4-positive NMOSD and to explore shared heritability with other autoimmune diseases.We performed a pan-ancestry GWAS in 2833 individuals, including 1573 AQP4-positive NMOSD cases and 1260 controls (comprising non-affected relatives, healthy non-relatives, and those with other autoimmune diseases). Samples were collected from the International NMOSD Genetics Consortium, comprising 36 hospitals and research facilities across the world. All individuals with AQP4-positive NMOSD fulfilled the 2015 international consensus diagnostic criteria for NMOSD, including positive AQP4-IgG status. We also performed a second GWAS with only the 1857 samples of European ancestry (803 cases and 1054 controls). We then compared our GWAS findings to those from other autoimmune diseases.We found three independent associations with AQP4-positive NMOSD that reached genome-wide significance: two within the MHC and a third within an intron of the STAT4 gene. In the pan-ancestry study, we identified a complement C4A-associatied variant, rs1150753 (chr6:32092090:A>G, p=1·61 × 10-29, odds ratio [OR] 2·95, 95% CI 2·44-3·56), rs607929 (chr6:32619221:C>G, p=2·87 × 10-24, OR 1·93, 95% CI 1·70-2·20), and a STAT4-associated variant, rs35593987 (chr2:191051800:AC>A, p=8·49 × 10-14, OR 1·75, 95% CI 1·51-2·03). In Europeans, we identified variants that were either in linkage disequilibrium with or the same as those from the pan-ancestry study: rs1270942 (chr6:31951083:A>G, p=2·52 × 10-28, OR 3·01, 95% CI 2·47-3·66), rs607929 (p=1·12 × 10-20, OR 1·99, 95% CI 1·72-2·30), and rs3821236 (chr2:191038032:G>A, p=1·20 × 10-10, OR 1·74, 95% CI 1·47-2·06). rs1270942 is in linkage disequilibrium with rs1150753 (r2=0·96) as well as two AQP4-positive NMOSD-associated HLA alleles, HLA-DRB1*03:01 (p=2·80 × 10-26, OR 2·79, 95% CI 2·30-3·37) and HLA-B*08:01 (p=1·02 × 10-24, OR 2·68, 95% CI 2·22-3·24). A priori testing of the P1104A variant (rs34536443, chr19:10352442:G>C) within the TYK2 gene, which acts upstream in the STAT4 pathway, found it to be protective (p=0·0008, OR 0·52, 95% CI 0·35-0·76 in the pan-ancestry study). Genetic sharing was observed with several comorbid autoimmune diseases for both the complement C4A-associated and STAT4-associated variants, including Sjögren's syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus.AQP4-positive NMOSD is more genetically similar to systemic autoimmune diseases than to multiple sclerosis, despite sharing overlapping clinical phenotypes. Specifically, a polymorphism associated with reduced complement C4 was identified as the biggest disease genetic risk factor, which has been shown to facilitate the development of autoantibody-producing B cells. Our findings also support a pathogenic role of HLA-restricted CD4+ T cells, owing to both a genome-wide significant association of HLA-DRB1*03:01 as well as heritable risk within the TYK2-STAT4 signalling pathway. Having already been shown to be a successful target for treating psoriatic arthritis and, potentially, systemic lupus erythematosus, we propose the TYK2-STAT4 pathway as a possible therapeutic target in AQP4-positive NMOSD.The OAK Foundation, The Guthy Jackson Charitable Trust Foundation, and the UK Medical Research Council.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined a rare autoimmune disease called aquaporin 4-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which damages the nervous system and causes vision loss and paralysis, to understand what genetic factors make people vulnerable to developing it. The study involved analyzing the DNA of nearly 2,800 people from around the world, including over 1,500 patients with the disease and more than 1,200 healthy controls, to identify genetic variations linked to disease risk. The researchers discovered three main genetic risk factors: two related to immune system genes in a region called the MHC and one in a gene called STAT4, with the strongest risk factor being a variation that reduces levels of a protein called complement C4 that normally helps control the immune system. The findings suggest that this disease is more similar genetically to other systemic autoimmune diseases like lupus than to multiple sclerosis, and that the STAT4 pathway could be a promising target for new treatments since drugs targeting this pathway have already shown promise in other autoimmune conditions. These genetic discoveries could help doctors better understand why some people develop this serious disease and may lead to new preventive treatments or therapies in the.

title: Correlation of sonographic posterolateral rotatory stress test and posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow.
abstract: Posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) of the elbow is challenging to diagnose using physical examination alone. This study aims to describe preliminary sonographic criteria for diagnosing PLRI using stress ultrasound to assess ulnohumeral joint instability in clinically unstable patients.This retrospective cohort study included 40 elbows from 28 patients (mean age, 45 ± 14 years), divided into 3 groups: symptomatic with clinical instability [elbow pain with a positive posterolateral rotatory drawer or lateral pivot shift test on physical exam] (n = 16); symptomatic with no clinical instability [elbow pain without positive physical exam tests above, eg, common extensor tendinopathy] (n = 13); and asymptomatic controls (n = 11). A sonographic posterolateral rotatory stress test assessed lateral ulnohumeral joint (L-UHJ) laxity by subtracting the L-UHJ measurement at rest from L-UHJ measurement under stress (stress delta). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to determine the optimal threshold for stress delta predictive of PLRI.The L-UHJ stress delta was significantly greater in clinically unstable elbows (2.2 ± 1.1 mm) compared to stable symptomatic (0.9 ± 0.7 mm) and asymptomatic elbows (0.6 ± 0.5 mm), P < .001. ROC analysis identified a threshold stress delta of ≥1.6 mm as optimal for distinguishing clinically unstable elbows, with an area under the curve of 0.90, sensitivity of 75%, and specificity of 91%.Sonographic posterolateral rotatory stress test findings for PLRI in clinically unstable patients may be smaller than previously shown in cadaveric models. An L-UHJ stress delta ≥1.6 mm demonstrates high sensitivity and specificity in the assessment of L-UHJ laxity in the diagnosis of PLRI. Further research is needed to validate these findings across larger, more diverse patient populations and clinical settings.© 2026 The Author(s).

llm_summary: Posterolateral rotatory instability, which is when the elbow joint becomes unstable and moves abnormally, is difficult for doctors to diagnose using only physical examination and touch. Researchers studied forty elbows from twenty-eight patients by using ultrasound imaging combined with stress tests, which involve applying pressure to the joint while taking pictures to measure how much the joint moves. They found that unstable elbows showed significantly more movement when stress was applied, measuring about two point two millimeters of extra movement compared to only zero point nine millimeters in painful but stable elbows and zero point six millimeters in healthy elbows. Using statistical analysis, doctors determined that a measurement of one point six millimeters or more of extra movement under stress was the best threshold for identifying truly unstable elbows, with a seventy-five percent chance of correctly identifying the problem and a ninety-one percent chance of correctly ruling it out. Although these findings show promise for using ultrasound as a diagnostic tool, researchers emphasize that larger studies with more diverse groups of patients are needed to confirm these results before this method can be widely used in clinical practice.

title: Clinical Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Epilepsy.
abstract: Functional MRI (fMRI) is a noninvasive imaging technique used to map areas of the brain important for language, motor, and visual function before surgery. Language lateralization with fMRI has proven useful as a surrogate for direct memory testing in patients with epilepsy to help predict postoperative morbidity, with Wada testing remaining useful if at risk for global amnesia. Task-based and resting-state fMRI can play a role in the evaluation of patients with generalized epilepsy before disconnective surgery or neuromodulation.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Functional MRI, which is a brain imaging technique that shows which parts of the brain are active during specific tasks, can help doctors plan surgery for patients with epilepsy, a condition that causes seizures. Researchers examined how this noninvasive imaging method could map important brain areas related to language, movement, and vision before patients undergo surgery. The study found that functional MRI was particularly useful for determining which side of the brain controls language, and this information helped doctors predict whether patients might have memory problems after their surgery. For patients at high risk of severe memory loss, doctors may still use an older test called Wada testing alongside functional MRI to get the most complete picture before operating. Both task-based functional MRI, where patients perform activities during scanning, and resting-state functional MRI, where patients simply rest in the scanner, can help evaluate patients with generalized epilepsy who are considering surgery or other brain treatments.

title: The Clinical Characteristics and Outcomes of Multiple Myeloma Patients With Oligo or Non-Secretory Relapse-A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Oligo-secretory and non-secretory MM present a clinical challenge due to the difficulties in initial diagnosis, response to treatment assessment, and relapse detection. They are excluded from most clinical trials, which typically require measurable disease. We describe the characteristics and outcomes of 86 patients with secretory myeloma at diagnosis who developed an OSR, matched 1:1 to a cohort with secretory relapse (SR). With a median follow-up of 9.3 years, 16.6% (48/289) of evaluable patients developed an OSR. Lower levels of light chains at presentation, and younger age are predictive of an OSR. The median OS since relapse of the OSR group was 4.01 (95% CI 1.625-6.395) versus 3.25 (95% CI 2.255-4.245) years in the SR control group (p = 0.4). A third of our OSR cohort had a subsequent SR. We did not find any predictive factor for SR after OSR. The median OS of the subgroup of patients who developed a SR after OSR was 3.35 years (95% CI 1.541-5.159), versus 5.8 years (95% CI 2.072-9.528) in the group that remained oligo-secretory (p = 0.336). The median TTNT of the SR after OSR group was 1.68 years (95% CI 0.341-0.919) versus 4.58 (95% CI not reached-not reached) in the group that remained oligo-secretory (p < 0.001).© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined a challenging type of blood cancer called multiple myeloma that sometimes stops producing detectable proteins in the blood during relapse, making it harder to track the disease and assess treatment response. The study followed 86 patients who initially had detectable disease markers but later developed what doctors call oligo-secretory or non-secretory relapse, meaning their cancer was still present but produced little to no measurable proteins, and compared them to 86 matched patients whose cancer continued producing detectable proteins. Patients who were younger at diagnosis and had lower protein levels initially were more likely to develop this harder-to-detect type of relapse, and about one-third of these patients eventually went back to producing detectable proteins again. The survival time after relapse was similar between the two groups, though patients whose disease switched back to producing detectable proteins needed new treatment sooner than those who remained in the harder-to-detect state. This research highlights the need for better ways to monitor and treat multiple myeloma patients whose cancer stops producing measurable markers, since current clinical trials typically exclude these patients and doctors lack clear guidelines for managing their care.

title: Nuclear Imaging of Epilepsy.
abstract: For epilepsy, brain single-photon emission computed tomography and PET are noninvasive nuclear medicine studies that can guide complex management decisions and surgical intervention. Due to seizure-related changes in cerebral blood flow and glucose utilization during the ictal and interictal period, these nuclear medicine studies can localize epileptogenic regions and assess broad functional changes in epilepsy. Advanced quantitative and computational techniques can increase the yield of these studies and assist with interpretation. Future developments in PET radiopharmaceuticals targeted inflammation, synaptic density, or various neurotransmitter systems may provide additional diagnostic capabilities for epilepsy.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Nuclear imaging techniques that take pictures of the brain's activity are important tools for helping doctors understand and treat epilepsy, a condition where people have repeated seizures. Brain scans using single-photon emission computed tomography and PET imaging, which are types of nuclear medicine studies that show how the brain is functioning, can help doctors find where seizures are starting and plan surgical treatment when needed. These imaging methods work because seizures cause changes in blood flow and how the brain uses glucose, or sugar for energy, which the scans can detect during and between seizure episodes. By using advanced computer analysis techniques to study these scans more carefully, doctors can get better information to guide treatment decisions and improve outcomes for people with epilepsy. Future developments in imaging technology that can target inflammation, measure connections between brain cells, or track brain chemicals may give doctors even more powerful tools to diagnose and understand epilepsy in the years ahead.

title: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation for maternal cardiac arrest secondary to amniotic fluid embolism during external cephalic version: a case report.
abstract: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a rare complication of pregnancy with high morbidity and mortality. A healthy 33-year-old G4P2012 woman at 39 + 2 weeks presented for an external cephalic version (ECV). During ECV attempts, the patient experienced sudden onset cardiac arrest. Emergent resuscitative delivery was performed followed by emergent application of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation via peripheral veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) due to profound maternal hemodynamic instability. The patient developed postpartum hemorrhage and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, necessitating massive transfusion. Post-delivery, a posterior circulation stroke was discovered, possibly due to paradoxical emboli in the setting of a previously undiagnosed patent foramen ovale. Both the patient and the neonate recovered and discharged home. This case highlights successful intervention of VA-ECMO with favorable maternal and neonatal outcomes following maternal cardiac arrest that was highly suspicious for amniotic fluid embolism. Prompt delivery, early ECMO activation, and multidisciplinary care were pivotal in the favorable outcomes.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: A rare but life-threatening condition called amniotic fluid embolism, where fluid from the pregnancy sac enters the mother's bloodstream, can cause sudden heart failure during childbirth or pregnancy procedures. Doctors reported the case of a healthy 33-year-old pregnant woman who suffered sudden cardiac arrest while undergoing an external cephalic version, which is a procedure to turn a breech baby into the correct head-down position for delivery. When the mother's heart stopped, the medical team immediately delivered the baby and connected the mother to an extracorporeal membrane oxygenation machine, a device that takes over the work of the heart and lungs by pumping blood outside the body. The mother developed serious complications including severe bleeding and blood clotting problems that required massive blood transfusions, and she also had a stroke affecting the back of her brain, but both she and her newborn eventually recovered and went home. This case demonstrates that using advanced life support technology quickly, delivering the baby immediately, and coordinating care among multiple medical specialists can save lives when amniotic fluid embolism causes cardiac arrest during pregnancy.

title: OCTA in age-related macular degeneration: consensus on practical guidelines for optimal imaging strategies across different clinical scenarios.
abstract: To provide expert-driven, practical guidelines for the optimal use of optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) in the clinical management of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Given the heterogeneity of AMD and the versatility of OCTA, clinicians require scenario-specific recommendations to navigate imaging strategies effectively across various stages and phenotypes of the disease.An expert panel from the European Young Retinal Imaging and Retina Study Group conducted a consensus-based review integrating the latest evidence and extensive clinical experience. The panel focused on developing OCTA-based protocols tailored to distinct clinical scenarios in AMD, including neovascular subtypes, geographic atrophy, non-exudative neovascularization, and ambiguous fluid accumulations. Recommendations emphasize appropriate scan sizes, slab selections, and strategies for interpreting flow signals across disease presentations.The expert panel delineated structured OCTA protocols for a range of AMD phenotypes to enhance diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making. In neovascular AMD, OCTA enables detailed characterization of macular neovascularization (MNV) subtypes—types 1, 2, and 3—through high-resolution, depth-resolved imaging. Recommendations include the use of cross-sectional OCTA to localize flow and appropriate selection of en face slabs to optimize lesion visualization. In geographic atrophy (GA), while structural OCT remains the primary modality, OCTA may assist in identifying subclinical or complicating MNV and in assessing choriocapillaris perfusion in the peri-atrophic zone, which may have prognostic implications. In cases of early and intermediate AMD, OCTA plays a critical role in detecting non-exudative MNV—particularly type 1 and type 3 lesions—providing valuable prognostic information given the risk of exudative conversion. Additionally, OCTA contributes to the differential diagnosis of pseudovitelliform lesions, detection of deep retinal age-related microvascular anomalies (DRAMAs), and exclusion of neovascularization in cases presenting with atypical intraretinal or subretinal fluid.This expert consensus offers a pragmatic framework for applying OCTA in AMD clinics, advocating for individualized imaging approaches based on lesion type and anatomical complexity. By enhancing diagnostic precision and enabling tailored monitoring strategies, OCTA integration into clinical workflows may significantly improve patient outcomes across the AMD spectrum.

llm_summary: Eye doctors need better guidance on how to use a special imaging technology called optical coherence tomography angiography, or OCTA, which takes detailed pictures of blood vessels in the eye to diagnose and monitor age-related macular degeneration, a common cause of vision loss in older adults. A group of European eye specialists reviewed the latest research and their own clinical experience to create practical recommendations for using OCTA in different situations involving macular degeneration, including cases where abnormal new blood vessels grow, areas where the retina wastes away, and situations where fluid buildup is unclear. The experts found that OCTA is particularly helpful for identifying and classifying different types of abnormal blood vessel growth in the wet form of macular degeneration, and it can also detect early warning signs of disease progression in patients with dry macular degeneration by showing subtle changes in blood vessel patterns. These new guidelines give eye doctors a clear framework for choosing the right imaging settings and techniques based on each patient's specific type of macular degeneration, which should help them make better treatment decisions and monitor patients more effectively. While this expert consensus provides valuable practical guidance for clinics, doctors will need to continue learning.

title: Neuroimaging-Based Deep Learning Applications for Lesion Detection and Predicting the Outcome Following Epilepsy Surgery.
abstract: Neuroimaging studies are essential for evaluating patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and determining their candidacy for epilepsy surgery. The past decade has seen the emergence of neuroimaging-based deep learning models, which have been developed to both detect epileptogenic lesions on MR imaging and predict post-surgical seizure outcome. Large, multi-center studies have demonstrated promise for epileptogenic lesion detection; however, neuroimaging-based surgical outcome prediction models remain exploratory. Translation of such models into routine epilepsy surgery clinical workflows will require transparent, interpretable, and prospectively validated model designs.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Neuroimaging studies, which are detailed brain scans, are crucial for helping doctors identify which patients with hard-to-treat epilepsy might benefit from surgery. Over the past ten years, researchers have developed artificial intelligence computer programs that can analyze these brain scans to find the specific areas causing seizures and predict whether surgery will stop a patient's seizures. Large studies involving multiple hospitals have shown that these computer programs work well at finding the problem areas in the brain on MRI scans. However, the computer programs that predict whether surgery will actually help patients are still in early testing stages and not yet ready for everyday use in hospitals. To use these tools in regular patient care, doctors will need computer programs that are transparent and easy to understand, and these programs must be tested ahead of time on new groups of patients to prove they work reliably.

title: Adherence to and tolerance of low-dose tamoxifen versus standard-dose tamoxifen in women at increased risk of breast cancer.
abstract: Tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 5 years decreases breast cancer (BC) risk by 49% in women with a family history of the disease and by up to 85% in women with a personal history of high-risk lesions. The TAM-01 study demonstrated that patients with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS), atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) or atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH) had a 50% reduction in cancer events with 5 mg daily for 3 years. We aimed to determine whether the use of low-dose tamoxifen (LDT) leads to better adherence and tolerance than standard-dose tamoxifen (SDT).A retrospective chart review of women with DCIS, LCIS, ADH/ALH, increased risk due to family history of breast cancer, or high-risk gene mutation was performed. Patients were grouped as SDT or LDT. Patients who declined medications were the control.Among 256 patients, 46% (N = 117) initiated LDT, 21% (N = 55) SDT and 33% (N = 84) declined tamoxifen. 59% of patients on LDT completed 3 years of therapy compared with 47.3% of SDT patients. Five women (2.0%) developed recurrent cancer, and 4 women (1.6%) developed a new malignancy. Vasomotor symptoms were the most commonly reported adverse events, affecting over 40% of patients in both tamoxifen groups.LDT was well tolerated, with a trend toward increased likelihood of completion of therapy. Patients with more than one indication for tamoxifen were more likely to complete therapy. Side-effects were similar in the two treatment groups, although severity was not able to be assessed due to the retrospective study design.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Tamoxifen is a medication that can significantly reduce breast cancer risk in women who have a family history of the disease or have had precancerous changes in their breast tissue, but doctors wanted to know if using a lower dose might help women stick with the treatment better. Researchers looked back at medical records of 256 women who were prescribed either a standard dose of tamoxifen or a low dose, comparing how many completed their treatment and what side effects they experienced. Women taking the low dose were more likely to finish the full three years of treatment, with 59 percent completing therapy compared to only 47 percent of those on the standard dose. Both groups experienced similar side effects, with hot flashes and night sweats being the most common problem affecting over 40 percent of patients in each group. The study suggests that using a lower dose of tamoxifen may help more women complete their cancer prevention treatment, though researchers note that because they reviewed old medical records rather than conducting a controlled experiment, they could not fully measure how severe the side effects were for each patient.

title: The role and effects of metabolic and bariatric surgery on endometrial cancer care.
abstract: Obesity has become one of the most prevalent chronic diseases in the United States, contributing to various obesity-related medical conditions and affecting women's health. It has been shown to be a major modifiable risk factor in the development of menstrual cycle disorders, anovulation, and infertility. It remains the second leading cause of cancer in general, and its increasing incidence has been associated with an increased risk of female- and hormone-specific cancers, especially endometrial cancer. Various mechanisms have been implicated in the relationship between adiposity and endometrial proliferation, which include but are not limited to hormonal pathway disruptions and hyperinsulinemia. This well-established connection has necessitated interventions that target weight loss. Bariatric surgery remains one of the most sustainable and effective long-term treatments, which not only leads to successful weight loss, but also restores the physiologic hormonal pathways, contributing to improved women's health, fertility and pregnancy outcomes. Most importantly, weight-loss surgery has been proven to reduce the incidence and mortality of endometrial cancer and to mediate other obesity-related medical conditions that impact overall survival in patients with endometrial cancer. With more studies evaluating the effects of bariatric surgery on endometrial cancer over the long-term, it can increasingly be advocated as a potential adjunct treatment in this regard.Copyright © 2026 American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery. llm_summary: Obesity is a major health problem in the United States that increases the risk of endometrial cancer, which is cancer of the uterine lining, by disrupting hormones and causing high insulin levels in the body. Researchers reviewed how bariatric surgery, which is weight loss surgery that reduces stomach size or changes how food is digested, affects endometrial cancer outcomes in obese patients. The evidence shows that bariatric surgery successfully reduces weight over the long term and restores normal hormone levels, which in turn lowers both the chances of developing endometrial cancer and the death rate from this disease. These findings suggest that weight loss surgery could be used alongside standard cancer treatments to improve survival and overall health in patients with endometrial cancer. Future studies with longer follow-up periods are needed to fully understand how bariatric surgery can be best incorporated into endometrial cancer care.

title: Evaluation of Otolaryngology Provider Bias in Portal Messaging.
abstract: Patient messaging portals are widely used in clinical practice and are linked to improved patient outcomes, but they are also associated with provider burnout, a phenomenon that is understood to exacerbate implicit bias. This study evaluates provider bias in responses to patient portal messages within an academic otolaryngology practice.A total of 167,866 patient messages and provider responses were extracted from May 2018 to April 2023 within the Otolaryngology department, along with patient demographic and surgical data. Provider response length and response time were calculated as surrogates for implicit bias and compared across patient populations by demographics and economic class (estimated by zip code and using insurance type), with and without adjusting for surgical and message factors.Of the total messages, 32,447 initial patient messages that received a provider reply were included in the analysis. In unadjusted comparisons, response time and length did not differ significantly by gender, ethnicity, or income. Medicare patients received 3% shorter replies (p = 0.009). White patients had a faster response time than those with unknown race (420.0±5.8 vs 469.0±37.7 minutes, p = 0.01). In adjusted models, provider responses varied significantly by message category and patient status. Compared with postoperative questions (reference), paperwork/insurance messages had 41.5% shorter response delays, imaging 26.9% shorter, and appointment/scheduling 21.2% shorter (all p<0.001). Nonsurgical patients had 12.7% longer adjusted response delays (p<0.001).When controlling for relevant patient and message factors, surrogates of provider bias in portal messages showed limited associations and no relationship with patient demographics.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. llm_summary: Patient messaging portals, which are online systems that let patients communicate with their doctors, are becoming common in hospitals and clinics and help improve patient care, but they can also make doctors feel burned out and stressed, which may lead them to treat some patients differently than others. Researchers examined over 167,000 messages sent through an ear, nose, and throat department's patient portal between 2018 and 2023 to see if doctors were responding differently to patients based on their race, gender, income level, or insurance type. When looking at the raw data without adjusting for other factors, doctors' response times and message lengths were mostly similar across different patient groups, though Medicare patients received slightly shorter replies and white patients got faster responses than patients with unknown race. After accounting for the type of message and whether the patient had surgery, the researchers found that differences in how doctors responded were mainly based on what the patient was asking about rather than who the patient was, suggesting that implicit bias, or unconscious unfair treatment, was not significantly affecting the doctors' responses. These findings suggest that when doctors' workload and message type are considered, patient demographics like race and income do not appear to influence how otolaryngologists.

title: BPHL promotes TNBC stemness by resolving R-loops via POLR2A lactylation inhibition and BARD1-mediated ubiquitination.
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) poses a formidable clinical challenge due to its aggressive behavior and limited therapeutic avenues. Here, we delineate a novel pathway wherein BPHL governs R-loop homeostasis to sustain cancer stem cell (CSC) stemness in TNBC. Through single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of 26 breast cancer samples, we identified low R-loop scores as a defining feature of TNBC CSCs, marked by elevated chromosomal instability and stemness signatures. Extensive cohort analysis further confirmed that this low R-loop profile significantly correlates with poor patient prognosis and advanced tumor staging. Bioinformatics interrogation pinpointed BPHL as the pivotal regulator, a finding corroborated by the strong positive correlation between BPHL expression and lactylation markers in clinical specimens. Functional studies across multiple TNBC models revealed that BPHL overexpression expanded the CSC compartment, bolstered sphere formation, and accelerated tumor growth in vitro and in vivo. Consistent with the low R-loop phenotype, genes enriched in low R-loop TNBC cells and CSCs were linked to cell cycle progression, DNA replication/checkpoint control, and p53-associated pathways.Mechanistically, BPHL engages POLR2A, curtailing its lactylation while augmenting BARD1-mediated ubiquitination to resolve R-loops and enable β-catenin nuclear translocation, thereby perpetuating Wnt signaling. Beyond intrinsic tumor programs, low R-loop states were also associated with enhanced intercellular communication (notably MIF/MK signaling) and elevated immune checkpoint gene expression (e.g., PDCD1, CTLA4, TIGIT, LAG3). Intriguingly, in vivo BPHL depletion curbed tumorigenesis-an effect partially mitigated by RNase H overexpression but reinstated by β-catenin blockade. These insights position BPHL as a compelling target for eradicating TNBC CSCs.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Triple-negative breast cancer is an aggressive form of cancer that is difficult to treat because cancer cells can develop stem cell properties, which allow them to survive and regrow even after treatment. Researchers examined tissue samples from twenty-six breast cancer patients using advanced genetic sequencing technology to identify which genes and cellular features were most common in the most dangerous cancer stem cells. They discovered that a protein called BPHL controls how cells manage structures called R-loops, which are tangles of genetic material, and that cancer stem cells with low R-loop levels grew faster, formed more tumors, and had worse patient outcomes. The study showed that BPHL works by changing how another protein called POLR2A is modified, which allows cancer cells to activate a growth pathway called Wnt signaling that keeps stem cells alive and dividing. These findings suggest that blocking BPHL could be a new treatment strategy to eliminate cancer stem cells and prevent triple-negative breast cancer from returning.

title: Is More Better? Evaluating Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy Cycles Before Surgery for High-Risk Upper Tract Urothelial Carcinoma.
abstract: Recent prospective trials and retrospective studies have supported the use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) in upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC); however, the optimal number of NAC cycles remains undefined. We investigated the impact of the number of NAC cycles on pathological response and survival outcomes using a multi-institutional cohort of clinically nonmetastatic high-risk UTUC patients treated surgically.We performed a retrospective analysis of the UTUC Collaborative Network (UCAN) database, comprising 2,276 patients who underwent radical nephroureterectomy (RNU) across seven high-volume tertiary care centers in the United States (2000-2021). We identified patients who received cisplatin-based NAC before surgery. Primary endpoints included pathologic complete response (pCR: ypT0N0) and noninvasive stage (≤ypT1N0) at surgery. Secondary endpoints included bladder cancer-free survival (BCFS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), cancer-specific survival (CSS), and overall survival (OS). Outcomes were assessed using multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models.Total 187 patients received between 1 and 4 cycles of cisplatin NAC for clinically node-negative (cN0) disease and were eligible for inclusion. 128, 49, and 10 patients received 4, 3, and 1 to 2 cycles of NAC, respectively. No patients who received 1 to 2 cycles achieved pCR, whereas 14% of patients who received 3 to 4 cycles achieved pCR. No significant difference in pCR was observed between 3 and 4 cycles (11% vs. 15%, P = 0.49). On multivariable logistic regression analysis, the number of NAC cycles received was not significantly associated with pCR rates between 3 vs. 4 cycles (OR = 1.38, 95% CI = 0.39-6.51, P = 0.6). In comparing oncologic outcomes on multivariable Cox regression analysis, 4 cycles of NAC were significantly associated with improved OS compared to 3 cycles (HR = 0.34, 95% CI = 0.17-0.69, P = 0.003), but this survival benefit did not extend to MFS, BCFS, or CSS.pCR rates and cancer-specific oncologic outcomes are similar between patients receiving 3 versus 4 cycles of cisplatin-based NAC prior to RNU for high-risk, clinically nonmetastatic UTUC. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether giving more rounds of cancer-fighting drugs before surgery helps patients with a serious type of kidney and ureter cancer called upper tract urothelial carcinoma. The study looked back at records from 187 patients treated at seven major medical centers between 2000 and 2021 who received chemotherapy before having surgery to remove their affected kidney and ureter. The results showed that patients receiving three or four rounds of chemotherapy had similar rates of complete cancer elimination, with about 11 to 15 percent achieving no remaining cancer cells, while those who received only one or two rounds had no complete responses. Surprisingly, while four rounds of chemotherapy led to better overall survival compared to three rounds, this extra treatment did not improve cancer-specific survival or prevent cancer from spreading to other parts of the body. The researchers concluded that three and four rounds of chemotherapy appear equally effective for controlling the cancer itself, suggesting that future studies should test whether three rounds might be sufficient to balance treatment benefits against potential side effects.

title: Con: All Cardiac Arrest Patients Should Be Transferred to a Cardiac Arrest Center.
abstract: Cardiac arrest centers (CACs) provide important critical expertise and advanced resources for select out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients, and their role within regional systems of care is both intuitive and necessary. However, a universal transport strategy for all cardiac arrest patients to CACs is neither evidence-based nor system-efficient. Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is a heterogeneous syndrome, and outcomes are driven predominantly by prehospital factors, patient characteristics, and arrest etiology. Existing data suggest that benefits associated with treatment at CACs are concentrated within specific subgroups, while indiscriminate transfer may delay stabilization, increase transport-related risk, preclude candidacy for advanced therapies, exacerbate rural-urban disparities, and strain finite critical care resources. A selective, triage-based approach to regionalization, prioritizing patients most likely to benefit from specialized care at CACs, may better optimize outcomes while preserving system resilience and equitable access to care.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Cardiac arrest centers are specialized hospitals equipped to handle patients who experience sudden heart failure, but sending every cardiac arrest patient to these centers may not be the best approach for all situations. The authors argue that cardiac arrest is a complex condition with many different causes and patient characteristics, meaning that outcomes depend more on what happens before patients reach the hospital and their individual health factors rather than simply being at a specialized center. Research shows that the benefits of treatment at cardiac arrest centers are mainly seen in certain groups of patients, while automatically sending all patients there could actually cause problems like longer delays in treatment, increased risks during transport, and worsening of care gaps between rural and urban areas. Instead of a one-size-fits-all approach, the authors recommend using a selective strategy that identifies which patients would benefit most from specialized care and directs only those patients to cardiac arrest centers while treating others at nearby hospitals. This targeted approach could lead to better overall outcomes while also making sure that critical care resources are used fairly and efficiently across the entire healthcare system.

title: Diagnostic Utility of Expression Imbalance in the Idylla GeneFusion Assay for Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: The Idylla GeneFusion Assay detects gene fusions with fusion-specific and expression imbalance methods. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic utility of detecting fusions with expression imbalance alone in non-small-cell lung cancer. Results of ALK, ROS1, and RET fusion detection with expression imbalance were compared with results of orthogonal testing. Of 1982 cases reviewed from October 2022 through August 2024, 63 (3.2%) had fusions detected with the expression imbalance method alone, including 47 ALK, 10 ROS1, and 7 RET fusions. One case had ALK and RET fusions. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) confirmation for 51 cases revealed 8 positive (15.7%), 3 equivocal (5.9%), and 40 negative (78.4%) results. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) immunohistochemistry performed for 22 ALK-detected cases revealed 3 positive (13.6%) and 19 negative (86.4%) results that were concordant with ALK FISH results. The positive predictive value of expression imbalance detection alone varied by gene (12.5% for ALK, 16.7% for ROS1, and 33.3% for RET). RNA next-generation sequencing results for seven select cases (three ALK, two ROS1, and two RET) showed six novel fusions (eg, STRN::ALK, SQSTM1::ROS1, and ERC1::RET) and had 100% concordance with FISH results. One case showed an NOL10::ALK out-of-frame fusion with negative ALK immunohistochemistry and equivocal ALK FISH results. Because the expression imbalance method can detect novel fusions, its implementation with confirmation testing is recommended.Copyright © 2026 Association for Molecular Pathology and American Society for Investigative Pathology. llm_summary: Researchers examined a diagnostic tool called the Idylla GeneFusion Assay that detects gene fusions, which are abnormal combinations of genes that can cause lung cancer, using a method that looks for imbalanced gene expression patterns in nearly two thousand patient samples collected over two years. The study compared results from this expression imbalance detection method alone against other standard confirmation tests like fluorescence in situ hybridization, which uses colored markers to highlight specific genes under a microscope, and immunohistochemistry, which uses special stains to identify proteins in tissue samples. When the researchers confirmed the results with these other tests, they found that the expression imbalance method alone correctly identified only about thirteen to thirty-three percent of the fusions depending on which gene was being tested, meaning most results were false positives or incorrect detections. However, when researchers used advanced genetic sequencing on seven selected cases, they discovered that the expression imbalance method could identify novel or previously unknown gene fusion combinations that the standard tests confirmed as real. The researchers concluded that while the expression imbalance method shows promise for finding new types of gene fusions, it should always be used together with confirmation testing to ensure accuracy.

title: Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor/KIT-Linked Proliferative Bias in Normal Breast Lobules from Matched Non-Hispanic Black and White Women Is Rapidly Reversible by Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Inhibition.
abstract: Basal-like/triple-negative breast cancers occur disproportionately at younger ages among non-Hispanic Black women (NHBW), but whether normal breast epithelium shows measurable, reversible differences in proliferative signaling is unclear. Histologically normal lobules from parity-, age-, and body mass index-matched NHBW and non-Hispanic White women (NHWW) donors (10 versus 10) were profiled using targeted transcriptomics (IO360/BC360) and whole-slide quantitative immunohistochemistry for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), KIT, and cytokeratin-5. Eighty-nine transcripts differed between groups at false discovery rate < 0.10, with EGFR and KIT elevated in NHBW lobules and enrichment of basal/receptor tyrosine kinase-linked programs. Quantitative immunohistochemistry confirmed higher protein in NHBW tissue; in lobule-level models, the group effect (NHBW - NHWW) was EGFR β = 0.055, P = 0.010; KIT β = 0.093, P = 0.0027; and cytokeratin-5 β = 0.126, P = 0.027. In prestasis human mammary epithelial cells, 24-hour treatment with EGFR (lapatinib) or KIT (ripretinib) inhibitors increased cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, decreased cyclins/cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6, and enforced G1 arrest; EGFR inhibition also increased apoptosis. Together, these data identify a coordinated EGFR/KIT-linked proliferative bias in NHBW epithelium that is rapidly reversible in vitro, supporting validation in larger cohorts and pharmacodynamic window studies.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s).
