llm_summary: Researchers examined whether normal breast tissue shows differences in growth-promoting signals between non-Hispanic Black women and non-Hispanic White women, since Black women develop certain aggressive breast cancers at younger ages. The study compared breast tissue samples from ten matched pairs of women, using genetic testing and protein imaging to measure levels of two growth-promoting molecules called EGFR and KIT. They found that normal breast tissue from Black women had higher levels of these growth-promoting molecules and showed patterns linked to faster cell division compared to White women's tissue. When the researchers tested drugs that block these growth molecules in laboratory cells, the drugs successfully stopped cell division and triggered cell death within 24 hours. These findings suggest that differences in breast tissue growth signals may help explain why Black women develop certain breast cancers more often, and that these differences could potentially be controlled with existing medications, though larger studies are needed to confirm these results.

title: Neuropsychological assessments in a large cohort of pediatric palliative epilepsy surgery patients.
abstract: Pediatric patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) are often referred for evaluation to consider epilepsy surgery. Neuropsychological testing is recommended for all patients undergoing surgical evaluation. Prevalence and factors affecting testing of neuropsychological testing in palliative epilepsy surgery are unknown.Data was collected from the PERC surgical database, a collaboration of pediatric epilepsy centers prospectively enrolling pediatric patients undergoing epilepsy surgery evaluation. Pediatric patients with DRE who sought care at PERC centers, underwent first-time palliative epilepsy surgery, and had neurocognitive data collected were included.569 patients had complete data with some form of neuropsychological assessment documented. Patients with focal motor (0.42 [CI 95% 0.28, 0.62] < 0.01) or cognitive delays (0.20 [CI 95% 0.13, 0.31] < 0.01) were less likely to receive neuropsychological testing, as were those with genetic etiology (0.5x, [CI 95% 0.33, 0.75] p < 0.01). The number of domains evaluated within corpus callosotomy (CC) (median 3, (1-9) < 0.01) and hemispherectomy (median 4 (1-9) <  0.01) groups was significantly lower than testing in other surgical groups. In addition the cognitive IQ and adaptive IQ were lower in patients undergoing CC and compared to other groups.All types of patients undergoing palliative epilepsy surgery had some neuropsychological testing. However, those with lower IQ and those undergoing CC or hemispherectomy were less likely to undergo testing. Reduced rates of testing in certain groups indicates room for improvement, especially given recommendations to use testing to help determine surgical success.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether children with drug-resistant epilepsy, which means seizures that do not stop with medication, were receiving recommended brain testing before surgery to help control their seizures. The study looked at information from 569 children at multiple epilepsy centers who had some type of neuropsychological testing, which is a detailed evaluation of how the brain works and how well a person can think and learn. The researchers found that while most children undergoing palliative surgery, a procedure meant to reduce seizures rather than cure epilepsy, did receive some testing, certain groups of children were less likely to be tested, including those with lower intelligence scores and those having specific types of surgery like corpus callosotomy or hemispherectomy, which involve cutting connections in the brain. Children who already had obvious motor problems or learning delays were also tested less often, even though these children might benefit most from understanding their brain function before surgery. The findings suggest that hospitals should improve their testing practices for all children before epilepsy surgery, since these evaluations help doctors understand whether the surgery will be successful.

title: Corpus Callosotomy or Focal Surgery in Children Presenting With Generalized Tonic Seizures: Findings From the Pediatric Epilepsy Research Consortium.
abstract: To elucidate the clinical profiles and surgical outcomes of patients with generalized tonic seizures (GTSs) undergoing corpus callosotomy (CC) or focal surgery (FS).Subjects with GTS undergoing CC or FS were identified using the Pediatric Epilepsy Research Consortium surgery database. Between-group comparisons were performed to assess differences in presurgical epilepsy characteristics and postsurgical seizure outcomes.Fifty-four patients (CC: 40 and FS: 14) included. Patients in the CC group had seizure onset at an older age (median = 1 year vs 0.4 years; P = 0.022), and were older at referral for phase-1 evaluation (median = 11.2 years vs 4.85 years; P = 0.026), and at time of surgery (median = 14 years vs 5.6 years; P = 0.008). The CC group showed higher rates of developmental delay (90% vs 57%; P = 0.013) and greater number of antiseizure medications attempted before surgery (median = 6 vs 4; P = 0.049). Electroencephalography localization also differed (P = 0.002), being most commonly generalized (64%, CC group) and multifocal (45%, FS group). Structural magnetic resonance imaging abnormalities were more common in FS group (92% vs 48%, P = 0.008). Median follow-up duration was 13.2 months (interquartile range = 5-24) in the CC group and 13.5 months in the FS group (interquartile range = 8-18). At last follow-up, FS group had a higher rate of seizure freedom (80% vs 19%; P = 0.0006).Our findings demonstrate differences in baseline characteristics and postsurgical outcomes of patients with GTS referred for FS and CC. FS yielded high seizure-freedom rates in focal cases. llm_summary: Researchers examined children with a specific type of seizure called generalized tonic seizures to compare two different surgical approaches: cutting the corpus callosum (the main connection between the two sides of the brain) or performing surgery focused on a specific seizure location. The study included fifty-four children from multiple hospitals, with forty receiving the corpus callosum surgery and fourteen receiving focused surgery, and researchers tracked their seizure outcomes for about a year after surgery. Children who received focused surgery had much better results, with eighty percent becoming seizure-free compared to only nineteen percent of those who had the corpus callosum surgery. The children in each group had different starting conditions, with the corpus callosum group being older at surgery and having tried more medications before surgery, while the focused surgery group had more visible brain abnormalities on imaging scans. These findings suggest that when doctors can identify a specific seizure location in the brain, focused surgery is the better choice, but for children without a clear seizure focus, corpus callosum surgery may still be helpful even though it takes longer to decide on this option.

The carpus can be accessed through open and arthroscopic techniques, allowing both visualization and assessment of volar and dorsal wrist anatomy. llm_summary: Managing wrist arthritis, which is wear and tear of the wrist joint, in younger patients requires doctors to have a thorough knowledge of how the wrist is structured and organized. The authors reviewed different surgical approaches, meaning the different ways surgeons can access and operate on the wrist bones and tissues. Surgeons can reach the wrist through either open surgery, where they make a larger cut to see inside directly, or arthroscopic surgery, which uses a tiny camera and small tools inserted through small cuts. Both approaches allow doctors to see and evaluate the damage on both the palm side and the back of the wrist, depending on what needs to be fixed. The choice of which surgical method to use depends on what specific problem the patient has and how much of the wrist area the surgeon needs to see and work on during the operation.

title: Global, regional, and national burden of meningitis, its risk factors, and aetiologies, 1990-2023: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
abstract: Meningitis remains the leading infectious cause of neurological disabilities globally, disproportionately affecting children younger than 5 years and populations in the African meningitis belt. Whereas previous global estimates focused on ten pathogen categories, this study presents the most comprehensive analysis to date, assessing the meningitis burden attributable to 17 causative pathogens based on the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023 framework.GBD is a systematic, scientific effort aimed at quantifying the comparative magnitude of health loss caused by diseases, injuries, and risk factors across age groups, sexes, and geographical locations over time. We estimated meningitis mortality using the Cause of Death Ensemble model (CODEm) and morbidity using DisMod-MR 2.1, incorporating data from vital registration, verbal autopsy, surveillance, hospital data, and systematic reviews. Aetiology-specific estimates were generated with pathogen-linked case-fatality ratios and splined binomial regression models. Risk factor attribution was based on established risk-outcome pairs and population attributable fractions.In 2023, there were 259 000 (95% uncertainty interval 202 000-335 000) global deaths and 2·54 million (2·20-2·93) incident cases of meningitis. Children younger than 5 years accounted for more than a third of deaths (86 600 [53 300-149 000]). Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, non-polio enteroviruses, and other viruses were the leading causes of death, while non-polio enteroviruses caused the most cases. The four WHO-defined preventable meningitis pathogens of interest (S pneumoniae, N meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae, and Group B streptococcus) contributed to 98 700 deaths (77 000-127 000) and 594 000 cases (514 000-686 000). Low birthweight, short gestation, and household air pollution were the top risk factors for meningitis-related mortality.Although mortality and incidence have declined significantly since 1990, progress is insufficient to meet WHO 2030 targets. Despite marked progress in reducing bacterial meningitis via global vaccination campaigns, a substantial meningitis burden persists, attributable both to common pathogens such as S pneumoniae and N meningitidis and to emerging non-bacterial pathogens such as Candida spp and drug-resistant fungi. Achieving WHO goals will require sustained investment in surveillance, vaccination, maternal screening, and health-system strengthening, especially in high-burden settings.Gates Foundation, Wellcome Trust, and UK Department of Health and Social Care.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. llm_summary: Meningitis, an infection of the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, remains one of the most serious infectious diseases affecting children worldwide, particularly in Africa and in children under five years old. Researchers analyzed data from 1990 to 2023 using a systematic method called the Global Burden of Disease Study, which collects information from death records, hospital data, and medical research to understand how many people get sick and die from meningitis caused by 17 different germs. In 2023 alone, meningitis caused about 259,000 deaths globally and affected 2. 54 million people, with more than a third of the deaths occurring in children under five years old, and bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis being the leading causes. Although vaccination campaigns have successfully reduced some types of bacterial meningitis over the past three decades, the disease burden remains too high to meet the World Health Organization's goals for 2030, and new threats from fungi and drug-resistant germs are emerging.

title: 7 Tesla MR Imaging for Evaluation of Epilepsy.
abstract: In patients with medically intractable epilepsy, 7T MR imaging may identify epileptogenic lesions that remain occult at lower magnetic field strengths. The higher signal-to-noise ratio and spatial resolution available at 7T allow for improved detection of focal cortical dysplasias and other cortical malformations. Detection and characterization of hippocampal abnormalities and cerebral vascular lesions is also superior at 7T MR imaging compared to 3T. Nevertheless, obstacles to widespread adoption include cost, imaging artifacts, and safety concerns related to scanning children as well as individuals with metallic implants. As continued research and development lower these barriers, more seizure patients will benefit from ultrahigh field imaging.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Patients with epilepsy that does not respond to medication sometimes have brain abnormalities that cannot be seen with standard MRI machines, which use lower magnetic field strengths. Researchers evaluated whether a more powerful 7 Tesla MRI machine, which creates stronger magnetic fields and produces clearer images, could detect these hidden brain problems better than the standard 3 Tesla machines currently used in most hospitals. The 7 Tesla imaging was superior at finding focal cortical dysplasias, which are areas where the brain's outer layer did not develop normally, as well as other brain malformations and problems with the hippocampus and blood vessels. This improved ability to spot these abnormalities could help doctors identify which patients might benefit from brain surgery to stop their seizures. However, challenges like high cost, image quality problems, safety risks for children and people with metal implants in their bodies, and the need for more research currently prevent this advanced technology from being widely available to all epilepsy patients.

title: MR Imaging Protocols for Epilepsy.
abstract: MR imaging is the imaging modality of choice in epilepsy for detecting structural brain abnormalities, particularly those being considered for surgery. A dedicated epilepsy protocol typically includes high-resolution 3 dimensional (3D) T1-weighted imaging (eg, magnetization prepared rapid acquisition gradient echo) and 3D T2 fluid-attenuation inversion recovery (FLAIR) of the whole brain for anatomic detail and characterization of suspected malformations of cortical development including subtle focal cortical dysplasias. Coronal T2-weighted and/or T2/FLAIR sequences perpendicular to the hippocampus are critical for assessing the architecture of the hippocampus and evaluating for mesial temporal sclerosis and other temporal lobe pathologies.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Magnetic resonance imaging, a type of brain scan that uses magnetic fields instead of radiation, is the best tool doctors have for finding structural problems in the brains of people with epilepsy, especially when surgery might be needed to treat the condition. The standard epilepsy imaging protocol uses two main types of detailed three-dimensional scans of the whole brain to look for brain abnormalities and identify subtle malformations, which are areas where the brain's outer layer did not develop normally. Special scans focused on the hippocampus, a small structure deep in the brain important for memory, are particularly important because they help doctors detect mesial temporal sclerosis, a common condition where this structure becomes scarred and damaged. These detailed imaging protocols allow doctors to identify the exact location of brain problems that may be causing seizures, which helps them decide whether surgery could help stop or reduce a patient's seizures. By using these specialized scanning techniques, doctors can provide patients with epilepsy better information about their condition and make more informed decisions about the best treatment options available to them.

title: Autoimmune Causes of Epilepsy.
abstract: This article reviews the clinical, imaging, and pathologic features of autoimmune encephalitis, emphasizing the diagnostic and therapeutic relevance of antibody class and target location. Surface antibody syndromes, such as anti-NMDAR and antileucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 encephalitis, typically present with seizures, and psychiatric symptoms, and have good immunotherapy response. Intracellular antibodies, such as anti-Hu or Ma2, are often paraneoplastic and associated with irreversible neuronal damage. MR imaging and 18F-fludeoxyglucose PET serve as critical tools in identifying disease patterns and guiding early treatment. Timely recognition and intervention are essential for improving prognosis and seizure control in autoimmune-associated epilepsy.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Seizures can sometimes be caused by the immune system attacking the brain, a condition called autoimmune encephalitis, which is important to recognize because it can be treated differently than other types of epilepsy. This article reviews how doctors can identify autoimmune epilepsy by looking at different types of antibodies, which are proteins the immune system makes that attack the brain, and where those antibodies target in the brain tissue. The researchers found that antibodies attacking the surface of brain cells, like anti-NMDAR, tend to cause seizures and psychiatric problems but respond well to immune-suppressing treatments, while antibodies attacking inside brain cells, like anti-Hu or Ma2, are often linked to cancer and cause permanent brain damage that is harder to reverse. Brain imaging scans, including MRI and a special type of PET scan that shows how active different brain areas are, are critical tools that help doctors spot patterns of autoimmune epilepsy and start treatment quickly. Early recognition and quick treatment of autoimmune epilepsy are essential for helping patients control their seizures better and improving their overall outcomes.

title: Malformations of Cortical Development.
abstract: Malformations of cortical development are complex and diverse. They are an etiology for drug-resistant epilepsy, and their imaging presentation may be striking or quite subtle. There are multiple schemes to classify this pathology group. One of the most well known is to group disorders based on the type of embryologic error that leads to each malformation. They can also be grouped based on imaging appearance, with the morphology of the involved cerebral cortex acting as the first major distinction.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Malformations of cortical development, which are abnormal formations in the brain's outer layer, are complex conditions that vary widely and often cause seizures that do not respond well to medication. These brain abnormalities can appear very obvious or extremely subtle when doctors look at brain imaging scans, making them challenging to diagnose and understand. Researchers have created multiple classification systems to organize these different types of malformations, with one popular approach grouping them by the specific developmental error that occurred during fetal brain growth. Another useful classification method organizes these malformations based on how they look in imaging scans, using the shape and structure of the affected brain tissue as the main way to tell them apart. Understanding these different classification approaches helps doctors better identify and treat patients with cortical malformations and drug-resistant epilepsy.

title: General Introduction to Epilepsy.
abstract: Epilepsy is a common disease with significant impacts on patients. Evaluation and management can be dynamic over time. After an initial seizure, focus is on risk stratification to decide whether treatment is necessary. Once epilepsy is diagnosed, then management with antiseizure medications is first-line in treatment, with individual patient factors considered in treatment decision making. Surgical treatments and invasive neuromodulation may be used if patients fail at least 2 appropriate seizure medications.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Epilepsy is a common brain condition that causes repeated seizures and significantly affects the lives of people who have it. When someone has their first seizure, doctors must decide whether treatment is needed right away by assessing how likely the person is to have more seizures in the future. Once epilepsy is officially diagnosed, the main treatment approach is to use antiseizure medications, which are drugs designed to prevent seizures from happening. Doctors choose which medication to prescribe based on each patient's unique health situation and medical history. If a patient's seizures continue even after trying at least two different antiseizure medications that were prescribed correctly, doctors may consider more advanced treatments like surgery or special devices that stimulate the brain to reduce seizures.

title: Impact of age on outcomes after CD19 CAR T-cell therapy for large B-cell lymphomas.
abstract: Age may influence clinical outcomes after CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. Real-world data on the survival and toxicity outcomes of older patients receiving CAR-T therapy are limited. We used data from the Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research for adults with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma who received CAR-T therapy from May 2018 to June 2020. Cumulative incidence and severity of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) were reported. Efficacy and safety outcomes were assessed using age as a continuous variable and among 4 age groups: 18 to 54, 55 to 64, 65 to 74, and ≥75 years. Nearly half (44%) of 1916 total recipients were aged ≥65 years. Patients received either axicabtagene ciloleucel (75%) or tisagenlecleucel (25%). Overall rates of CRS and ICANS were 75% and 43%, and severe rates of CRS and ICANS were 9% and 21%, respectively. For all patients, 12-month overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and relapse rates were 62%, 42%, and 55%, respectively. As a continuous variable, older age did not affect OS, PFS, and CRS; however, the risk of ICANS increased with age (hazard ratio [HR], 1.03; P < .001). At age >64 years, risk for ICANS increases (HR, 1.65;95% confidence interval (CI), 1.33-2.1; P < .001). In a categorical analysis, the 65 to 74-year age group had lower relapse risk (HR, 0.77;95% CI, 0.64-0.93; P = .005) than younger patients. CD19 CAR-T therapy is effective for older adults, and older age does not worsen mortality. Older age is associated with higher ICANS risk and should guide patient selection.© 2026 American Society of Hematology. Published by Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether age affects how well a newer cancer treatment called CAR T-cell therapy works for patients with a type of blood cancer called large B-cell lymphoma, since older patients are often left out of early studies. The study looked at real-world data from nearly 1,900 adult patients treated between 2018 and 2020, dividing them into age groups ranging from 18 to 75 years old, with almost half of the patients being 65 years or older. The results showed that older age did not make the cancer treatment less effective at keeping patients alive or preventing the cancer from coming back, though older patients did experience higher rates of a serious side effect called immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, which affects the nervous system. These findings suggest that doctors should not avoid giving this treatment to older patients based on age alone, but they should be more prepared to monitor and manage the nervous system side effects that become more common with advancing age. Future treatment decisions for older adults with this type of cancer should take into account both the proven benefits of CAR T-cell therapy and the increased risk of neurological complications that require careful medical management.

llm_summary: Background:  Ductal carcinoma in situ, or DCIS, is a type of early-stage breast cancer that starts in the milk ducts and has not yet spread to surrounding tissue, and doctors currently grade its severity using traditional microscope examination of tissue samples. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, which is a special type of imaging that tracks how contrast dye moves through breast tissue over time, offers a newer way to evaluate these tumors by analyzing patterns and textures in the images rather than relying solely on what pathologists see under a microscope.

title: Screw-bone interface loads from rod bending: Development of an instrumented spinal fusion simulator.
abstract: During spinal fusion procedures, spinal rods are bent to match the current and desired curvature of a spinal segment. Following bending, the rods are attached to the heads of pedicle screws that have been driven into the vertebral pedicles. A mismatch between the curvature of the spine and the curvature of the rod can lead to increased loads at the screw-bone interfaces. These increased loads have been associated with screw loosening and pull-out. We have developed a novel and inexpensive spinal fusion simulation device to explore how variables such as surgical techniques, tools, and hardware designs affect the dynamic and residual loads on the screw-bone interfaces. In addition, our device can act as a training tool providing real time and post-trial feedback. Our design consists of a series of load sensing vertebral bone surrogates with modular heights and intervertebral spacing. The device and its included software are capable of synchronized video capture, real-time feedback of screw-bone interface loads, and the generation of interactive reports. We showed that the stiffness of the device is comparable to reported in vitro values. Additionally, we showed an acceptable alignment between the recorded and predicted loads on several test contours and demonstrated data collection on a simulated L1-S2 contour. The ability to record synchronized video and create interactive reports allows for unique contextual analysis. In addition to being used as a research tool, interactive reports and real-time feedback allow the device to provide quantitative insights into spinal fusion surgical training.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. llm_summary: During spinal fusion surgery, doctors bend metal rods to match the shape of a patient's spine and then attach them to screws inserted into the vertebrae, but when the rod's curve does not match the spine's curve perfectly, it can create extra pressure at the screw-bone connection points that may cause the screws to loosen or pull out. Researchers created a new training device that uses artificial vertebrae with sensors to measure the forces placed on screw-bone interfaces during simulated spinal fusion procedures, allowing surgeons to test different surgical techniques, tools, and hardware designs in a controlled setting. The device successfully recorded and measured the loads on the screw-bone interfaces with results that matched both real laboratory measurements and computer predictions, and it was able to collect data from a simulated spinal segment spanning from the lower back to the sacrum. Beyond serving as a research tool, the device provides surgeons with real-time feedback and detailed video recordings during practice procedures, which can help train new surgeons by showing them exactly how their techniques affect the forces on the screws. This affordable simulator offers a practical way to improve surgical training and develop better hardware designs that could reduce complications like screw loosening in.

title: The Management of Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection in an Era of Universal Newborn CMV Screening.
abstract: The most common infectious disease responsible for paediatric developmental disability is congenital infection with human cytomegalovirus (cCMV). Many serious sequelae are caused by cCMV, including microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, neuronal migration defects, seizure disorders, developmental delay, and sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). Although long-term neurodevelopmental impairment is clearly more common in newborns with clinically apparent disease at birth, more knowledge is needed about management in the era of universal cCMV screening, since screening identifies infants that, in the past, would not have been discovered during routine newborn care-infants that we reference in this review as having clinically inapparent cCMV (CICMV) infections. For newborns identified with CICMV infections by universal cCMV screening, longitudinal audiologic assessment is needed, but other necessary laboratory and neuroimaging studies, as well as indications for antiviral therapy, are uncertain. This review summarises current concepts about the approach to cCMV infections identified by universal screening, with emphasis on the CICMV infant. We identify areas for future research that should inform and direct future evaluation and management of these infants.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection, a viral disease passed from mother to baby before birth, is the leading infectious cause of developmental disabilities in children and can cause serious problems like brain damage, seizures, hearing loss, and developmental delays. With new universal screening programs that test all newborns for this virus, doctors are now identifying babies who have the infection but show no obvious symptoms at birth, a group previously missed by routine care. The challenge for healthcare providers is determining which tests, imaging studies, and antiviral treatments (medicines that fight viruses) are necessary for these newly identified babies, since the current guidelines are unclear and based mainly on babies who show obvious signs of illness at birth. This review summarizes what doctors currently know about managing cytomegalovirus infections found through universal newborn screening, with special focus on babies who appear healthy but carry the infection. The authors highlight important areas where more research is needed to guide doctors in deciding how to best evaluate and treat these infants moving forward.

title: Key Insights From the International ICU Diary Conference 2025.
abstract: We report on the 2025 International ICU Diary Conference that provided a comprehensive update on current knowledge, innovations and global practices related to ICU diaries. Held in a 6-week online format, the event featured 23 speakers and was attended by mean 69.7 (SD 20.5) participants per session. Topics included development of ICU diaries, use in special settings, digital diaries, survivors' and families' experiences, Post-Intensive-Care Syndrome and follow-up and implementation projects. Highlights were innovative solutions for digital diaries and the report of persons with lived and living experiences with diaries, changing the focus on humanising critical care. RELEVANCE FOR PRACTICE: ICU diaries support patient- and family-centred care and should be implemented more widely across healthcare systems. Their successful adoption requires contextual adaptation and policy support, with future development likely to be shaped by the increasing use of digital ICU diaries.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: The International ICU Diary Conference in 2025 brought together healthcare professionals to share knowledge about how keeping diaries during intensive care stays can help patients and families cope with their experiences. The conference was held online over six weeks and featured 23 speakers who discussed topics ranging from how to develop these diaries to using them in special medical situations and creating digital versions. On average, about 70 participants attended each session, and they learned about innovative digital diary solutions and heard directly from patients and families who had actually used these diaries during their critical care stays. The research shows that ICU diaries are an important tool for supporting patient and family-centered care, meaning care that focuses on what patients and their loved ones need and want. Healthcare systems should work to implement these diaries more widely, adapting them to fit their specific settings and using digital technology to make them more accessible to more people in the future.

title: National prevalence of postoperative opioid prescription following cleft palate repair.
abstract: The prevalence of postoperative opioid prescribing following palatoplasty is largely unknown. We queried the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program-Pediatric (NSQIP-P) 2023 database to evaluate opioid prescribing at discharge and perioperative factors associated with opioid use in children aged 0-36 months undergoing palatoplasty. A total of 2026 patients (mean age 13.5 ± 4.6 months) were included. Approximately half of the patients (52.6%) received an opioid prescription at discharge, most commonly oxycodone (73.7%). Multivariable analysis demonstrated that longer anesthesia duration (OR: 1.03 per 10 min, 95% CI: 1.01-1.04, P < 0.001) and higher ASA classification (OR: 1.26, 95% CI: 1.09-1.46, P = 0.002) were independently associated with increased odds of opioid prescription at discharge, whereas Black or African American race (OR: 0.42, 95% CI: 0.30-0.60, P < 0.001) and longer time to discharge (OR: 0.93, 95% CI: 0.86-0.996, P = 0.04) were associated with decreased odds. Opioid prescribing rates following palatoplasty are high; however, variation exists across demographic and perioperative factors. Black or African American patients had lower odds of receiving a prescription, consistent with previously documented disparities in pediatric pain management. Indicators of procedural complexity, including anesthesia duration and ASA class, were associated with higher odds of prescribing. These findings highlight opportunities to refine postoperative analgesia following cleft palate repair and underscore the need for standardized, opioid-sparing strategies to optimize pain control and reduce practice variability and overprescription.Copyright © 2026 British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons. llm_summary: Researchers examined how often children undergoing cleft palate repair surgery, which fixes a birth defect affecting the roof of the mouth, receive opioid painkillers like oxycodone when they go home from the hospital. The study looked at information from over two thousand children aged newborn to three years old who had this surgery, analyzing which factors influenced whether doctors prescribed opioids at discharge. About half of the children received an opioid prescription, with longer surgery time and sicker patients (measured by health status scores) being more likely to get these strong painkillers, while Black and African American children were prescribed opioids less often than other groups. These findings reveal that opioid prescribing practices vary widely depending on patient characteristics and surgery details, and they highlight concerning racial differences in pain management that have been seen in other areas of pediatric medicine. The researchers recommend developing standardized pain management approaches that reduce reliance on opioids while still effectively controlling pain after cleft palate surgery.

title: 3-Mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase regulates mitochondrial metabolism and epithelial differentiation in neonatal patient-derived airway cells.
abstract: Early-life airway epithelial development relies on tightly coordinated mitochondrial metabolic programs, yet the pathways that govern normal epithelial maturation during this vulnerable developmental window remain poorly defined. Hyperoxia disrupts airway epithelial maturation, contributing to lung injury and airway remodeling in infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), underscoring the need to identify mitochondrial pathways that regulate early epithelial differentiation. 3-Mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase (MPST), a mitochondrial sulfur metabolism enzyme, supports mitochondrial metabolic and bioenergetic function, but its role in human airway epithelial development is unknown. In this study, we used neonatal patient-derived tracheal airway epithelial cells (nTAECs) in a three-dimensional air-liquid interface (ALI) model to show that hyperoxia reduces MPST protein abundance. To determine how MPST loss alters early epithelial differentiation and metabolic homeostasis, we used RNAi to knock down MPST during ALI differentiation. MPST loss in nTAECs induced early (ALI day 3) transcriptomic shifts involving mitochondrial metabolic pathways, epithelial differentiation programs, and stress-response signature corresponding with decreased ciliated cell numbers during mid-differentiation phase (ALI day 7). Metabolic flux analysis revealed significantly reduced mitochondrial respiration without compensatory increase in glycolysis, indicative of disrupted metabolic flexibility. Together, these data show that MPST is essential for maintaining mitochondrial metabolic integrity necessary for normal airway epithelial development. Loss of MPST creates a developmental vulnerability that may contribute to hyperoxia-induced airway injury in neonates. Targeting MPST-dependent pathways could represent a new strategy to preserve airway health in infants at risk for BPD airway remodeling.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study identifies 3-mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase (MPST) as a previously unrecognized regulator of neonatal airway epithelial development. In our neonatal patient-derived three-dimensional organotypic model, hyperoxia reduces MPST, and MPST loss alters mitochondrial metabolism and epithelial differentiation programs. These findings indicate that MPST deficiency contributes to mitochondrial dysfunction under hyperoxic conditions and highlight MPST-linked pathways as potential therapeutic targets to mitigate early-life airway injury and remodeling relevant to infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD).

llm_summary: Researchers examined how a specific enzyme called three-mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase, which helps cells produce energy in their mitochondria (the powerhouses of cells), affects the development of airway cells in newborns. They used airway cells taken from newborn patients and grew them in a special three-dimensional model, then reduced the enzyme's levels to see what would happen during normal cell development. When the enzyme was reduced, the cells showed problems with their energy production and failed to develop properly into the specialized cells that line healthy airways, particularly losing ciliated cells that help clear mucus from the lungs. The findings suggest that this enzyme is critical for maintaining healthy airway development in newborns, and its loss may contribute to a serious lung disease called bronchopulmonary dysplasia that affects premature infants exposed to high oxygen levels. These results point to a new potential treatment approach that could protect newborn airways from injury by targeting this enzyme's related pathways.

title: Survival after intensive therapy or clofarabine in fit older adults with acute myeloid leukemia: E2906 phase 3 trial.
abstract: Clofarabine is a second-generation purine nucleoside analog with encouraging reported 30-day induction mortality (IM) and complete remission (CR) or CRi (incomplete platelet recovery) rates, and represents a lower-intensity therapy for older adults with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). We evaluated long-term outcomes in a prospective phase 3 study using a noninferiority design. Patients aged ≥60 years with newly diagnosed AML and normal renal and cardiac function were randomized to standard intensive daunorubicin and cytarabine or single-agent clofarabine. The primary objective was overall survival (OS) using a weighted analysis. We incorporated prospective central testing for measurable residual disease (MRD; ≥0.1%) at remission using multiparameter flow cytometry. Among 727 patients (standard, n = 363; clofarabine, n = 364), there was no difference in CR/CRi (50%) or IM (8.5%) rates. The median follow-up was 58.6 months. In the primary analysis, OS was inferior with clofarabine (median, 10.4 vs 12.4 months [standard]; P = .04), although not in patients aged ≥70 years, with secondary AML, or unfavorable cytogenetics. Allogeneic transplantation was strongly associated with OS on multivariate analysis (HR, 0.53; P < .0001). MRD-negative remission was achieved in 41% of patients and strongly associated with 5-year OS irrespective of treatment (MRD-positive, 48.8% vs 12.2%; P = .003). In contrast, MRD-positive patients assigned to clofarabine (vs high-dose cytarabine) consolidation had significantly inferior OS. Clofarabine is inferior to standard intensive therapy despite similar remission rates. Achieving MRD-negative remission is associated with high, sustained rates of OS regardless of therapy. Increasing MRD negativity and improving outcomes among MRD-positive patients remain pressing, ongoing challenges. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a newer cancer drug called clofarabine could work as well as standard intensive chemotherapy for older adults with acute myeloid leukemia, a serious blood cancer. In this large study involving 727 patients aged 60 and older, half received standard chemotherapy and half received clofarabine, and researchers tracked their survival over nearly five years while also testing for remaining cancer cells using special blood tests. Both treatments worked equally well at first, producing the same rates of cancer remission and similar numbers of early deaths, but patients who received standard chemotherapy lived longer overall than those who received clofarabine. The most important finding was that patients whose blood tests showed no remaining cancer cells after treatment had much better long-term survival regardless of which drug they received, suggesting that eliminating all detectable cancer is crucial for better outcomes. The results show that while clofarabine is a gentler option, standard intensive therapy remains more effective for most older adults with this disease, though finding ways to help more patients achieve complete cancer elimination and improving outcomes for those with remaining cancer cells remain important goals for future research.

title: The Society for Vascular Surgery clinical practice guideline on the management of blunt thoracic aortic injury: Focused update.
abstract: Blunt thoracic aortic injury (BTAI) remains a devastating and potentially fatal complication of major trauma that requires expedient diagnosis and management by a collaborative team of trauma and vascular specialists. Trauma patients with BTAI commonly have multiple associated injuries, including intracranial or truncal hemorrhage, that increase the complexity of factors related to timing and conduct of repair. Optimal outcomes for these patients require consideration of these factors and updated knowledge of the available evidence by all stakeholders of care in a collaborative fashion. In 2011, the Society for Vascular Surgery published its clinical practice guidelines on the management of BTAI. Based on the available evidence from published research at the time, seven specific key questions were formulated spanning areas including patient selection, timing and conduct of repair, considerations in the setting of specific high-risk associated injuries, and surveillance. A systematic review and evidence synthesis of each question was conducted by a dedicated methodology team. The Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach was used to describe the strength of each recommendation and the level of certainty of evidence. The review identified major gaps in evidence across most of the questions posed, highlighting opportunities for additional research. Since that publication in 2011, the cumulative experience in the diagnosis and management of BTAI has grown significantly. This provided an opportunity for a focused update based on the current evidence. We assembled a panel of experts who identified seven specific areas of investigation and commissioned a systematic review of the published literature. Thirteen recommendations are provided in the current update. They address indications for and timing of definitive treatment, use of perioperative anticoagulation, management of the left subclavian artery, and imaging surveillance. In addition, we discuss the use of anti-impulse therapy for medical management as well as BTAI management for patients with concomitant injuries such as traumatic brain injury and solid organ injury. The collaborative engagement of all stakeholders in care of these complex patients is considered fundamental to optimal care. Significant unmet research needs in the field are also outlined.Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: Blunt thoracic aortic injury, which is severe damage to the main artery in the chest caused by trauma, is a life-threatening condition that requires quick diagnosis and treatment by teams of trauma and vascular doctors working together. The Society for Vascular Surgery, a professional organization of doctors who specialize in blood vessel treatment, originally published guidelines in 2011 on how to best manage these injuries, but medical knowledge has grown significantly since then. The expert panel reviewed all published research on seven key areas including when to perform surgery, how to use blood thinners safely, how to manage related injuries to the brain or organs, and how to monitor patients after treatment. The updated guidelines now include thirteen recommendations that address important questions about the timing of treatment, use of medications to reduce stress on the aorta, management of a specific artery called the left subclavian artery, and long-term imaging follow-up. The researchers emphasize that caring for these complex patients requires all healthcare team members to work closely together and identify that significant gaps in research still exist, meaning doctors need more studies to fully understand the best ways to treat these injuries.

llm_summary: Older adults often experience delirium, which is a sudden state of confusion and disorientation, and this condition can make it difficult for them to swallow food and liquids safely, a problem called oropharyngeal dysphagia. Researchers examined case reports to understand how delirium and swallowing problems create a harmful cycle where each condition makes the other worse in elderly patients. The study found that when older adults develop delirium, their ability to swallow properly decreases, and this swallowing difficulty can then worsen their confusion and disorientation. These findings suggest that healthcare providers need to recognize and treat both delirium and swallowing problems together rather than focusing on just one condition, since addressing both may help patients recover more effectively. Future research should explore better ways to prevent and manage this dangerous combination of symptoms in older adults to improve their safety and quality of life.

title: National trends in prescription drug expenditures and projections for 2026.
abstract: To report historical patterns of pharmaceutical expenditures, to identify factors that may influence future spending, and to predict growth in drug spending in 2026 in the United States, with a focus on the nonfederal hospital and clinic sectors.Historical patterns were assessed by examining data on drug purchases from manufacturers using the IQVIA National Sales Perspectives database. Factors that may influence drug spending in hospitals and clinics in 2026 were reviewed-including new drug approvals, patent expirations, and potential new policies or legislation. Focused analyses were conducted for biosimilars, cancer drugs, endocrine drugs, generics, specialty drugs, and vaccines. For nonfederal hospitals, clinics, and overall (all sectors), estimates for growth of pharmaceutical expenditures in 2026 were made based on a combination of quantitative analyses and expert opinion.In 2025, overall pharmaceutical expenditures in the US grew 12.7% compared to 2024, for a total of $915.2 billion. Utilization (a 9.3% increase) drove this increase, while growth due to new drugs (0.9%) and price increases (1.2%) had a modest impact. Tirzepatide was the new top drug in 2025, followed by semaglutide and apixiban. Drug expenditures were $42.9 billion (a 9.6% increase) and $190.5 billion (a 19.0% increase) in nonfederal hospitals and in clinics, respectively. In clinics, volume drove drug expense growth, contributing with a 13.6% increase, while price and new drugs each contributed with a 2.7% increase. In nonfederal hospitals, expenditure growth was driven by increases in volume (4.6%), new products (3.7%), and prices (1.5%). Several new drugs that will influence spending are expected to be approved in 2026. Specialty, endocrine, and cancer drugs will continue to drive expenditures.For 2026, we expect overall prescription drug spending to rise by 10.0% to 12.0%, whereas in clinics and hospitals we anticipate increases of 14.0%-16.0% and 4.0%-6.0%, respectively, compared to 2025. These national estimates of future pharmaceutical expenditure growth may not be representative of any health system because of the myriad of local factors that influence actual spending.© American Society of Health-System Pharmacists 2026. title: Factors influencing accelerated progression in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia.
abstract: This study aimed to identify neuropsychiatric, motor, and cognitive features associated with accelerated disease progression in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD).192 participants were classified as having mild or moderate disease severity based on CDR + NACC FTLD global scores, with scores of 0.5 or 1.0 defined as mild (n = 106) and 2.0 as moderate (n = 86). Participants were further categorized as having accelerated (mild: n = 35; moderate: n = 32) or non-accelerated (mild: n = 71; moderate: n = 54) progression rates based on change in CDR + NACC FTLD-SB sum of boxes (SB) scores (≥ 3.5 points) between Visit 1 and 2. Random forest modeling and logistic regression identified features most predictive of accelerated progression within each group.In mild bvFTD, episodic memory impairment and presence of frontal-behavioral neuropsychiatric symptoms were predictive of accelerated progression, whereas in moderate bvFTD, language impairments and motor signs were the strongest predictors. Identified features improved prediction of accelerated progression beyond demographic and clinical factors in mild (∆R2 = .22, p < 0.001) and moderate bvFTD (∆R2 = 0.11, p = 0.08) but did not achieve statistical significance in the moderate group.Distinct clinical profiles predict accelerated progression in mild versus moderate bvFTD, underscoring the importance of stage-specific clinical markers for prognosis and care.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined what signs and symptoms predict whether people with behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, a rare brain disease that affects behavior and thinking, will get worse quickly or slowly. The study followed 192 patients with this disease, dividing them into groups based on how severe their condition was and how fast it was progressing, then used computer analysis to identify which specific symptoms were most predictive of rapid decline in each group. In patients with early-stage disease, memory problems and behavioral changes were the strongest signs of faster progression, while in patients with more advanced disease, language difficulties and movement problems were better predictors of how quickly they would decline. These findings show that doctors should look for different warning signs depending on what stage of the disease a patient is in, which could help them better predict how the disease will progress and plan care accordingly. The study suggests that having stage-specific markers, or specific symptoms to watch for at different points in the disease, is important for helping doctors give patients and families more accurate information about what to expect.

title: Early ctDNA stratifies survival in locally advanced and oligometastatic lung cancer treated with radiotherapy.
abstract: Circulating tumor fraction estimate (ctFE) is a machine learning-derived composite metric of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) burden. We hypothesized that pre- and early on-treatment ctFE could robustly risk-stratify patients with locally advanced and oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with radiotherapy.In a prospective phase II clinical trial (NCT03916419), 26 patients with unresectable stage IIB-III NSCLC received MR-guided hypofractionated chemoradiation (chemoRT) followed by immunotherapy. Plasma ctDNA was profiled at baseline and mid-treatment (day 10-14) to derive ctFE and maximum variant allele frequency (Max VAF). A burden-based ctFE threshold derived from baseline samples was applied unchanged to mid-treatment samples and validated in two external cohorts: locally advanced NSCLC treated with chemoRT (LA-RW; n = 94) and oligometastatic NSCLC treated with radiotherapy (OM-RW; n = 309).Pre- and mid-treatment ctFE burden strongly stratified overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), markedly outperforming Max VAF and ctFE detectability. Baseline ctFE was prognostic for OS (HR 5.93, p = 0.005) and PFS (HR 11.08, p < 0.001) and remained significant at mid-treatment (OS: HR 7.08; PFS: HR 12.06; both p < 0.001). Early ctFE dynamics defined three molecular response groups with striking OS separation (median OS 60.8 vs. 13.0 vs. 2.9 months; p < 0.001). ctFE remained associated with survival in both validation cohorts.Early ctFE derived from a clinically available, tumor-naïve ctDNA assay enables noninvasive risk stratification in locally advanced and oligometastatic NSCLC treated with radiotherapy, supporting its use as a practical biomarker for precision treatment adaptation.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a blood test measuring tumor DNA could help predict which lung cancer patients would survive longer after receiving radiation therapy combined with chemotherapy and immunotherapy. In a clinical trial, they collected blood samples from 26 lung cancer patients before treatment and again about two weeks into treatment, measuring the amount of cancer DNA circulating in the blood using a machine learning method. Patients with higher levels of circulating tumor DNA at the start of treatment had much worse survival outcomes, and those whose tumor DNA levels did not drop significantly during early treatment had the poorest prognosis, with some surviving only a few months compared to others who survived over five years. The researchers validated these findings in two larger groups of lung cancer patients treated at other hospitals, confirming that the blood test results remained reliable predictors of survival across different patient populations. This simple blood test could help doctors identify which patients need more aggressive treatment or closer monitoring, potentially allowing for personalized treatment adjustments early in the course of therapy.

title: How should myelodysplastic neoplasms with isolated deletion 5q and TP53 multihit alterations be classified?
abstract: Myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS) with TP53 multihit alterations are associated with dismal outcomes. MDS with isolated del(5q) present favorable prognosis but is defined by the absence of TP53 multihit alterations. However, whether TP53 multihit alterations exert the same adverse impact in this genetic context remains uncertain. We retrospectively analyzed the characteristics and outcome of 43 patients with MDS with isolated del(5q) harboring TP53 multihit alterations (MDS-del(5q) TP53 multihit) and compared with 68 patients with low-blast MDS with TP53 multihit and without isolated del(5q) (MDS-LB TP53 multihit). Patients with MDS-del(5q) TP53 multihit showed significantly higher platelet counts, more frequent SF3B1 mutations, were less often classified as high-risk by IPSS-R or IPSS-M, and had significantly better outcomes than patients with MDS-LB TP53 multihit: overall survival of 70.2 vs 13.9 months, and time to acute myeloid leukemia progression (AML) of 31.9 vs 7.2 months, respectively. Moreover, the superior outcomes of MDS-del(5q) TP53 multihit patients persisted significant even when compared with MDS-LB TP53 multihit cases without complex karyotype (survival of 70.2 vs 39.9 months; time to AML progression of 31.9 vs 11.4 months). These findings indicate that, in MDS-del(5q) the adverse impact of TP53 multihit alterations may be less important than in other MDS subtypes.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined a group of blood cancer patients with a specific genetic condition called myelodysplastic neoplasm with isolated deletion 5q, which normally has a good outlook, to understand what happens when these patients also have multiple harmful changes in a gene called TP53. The study looked back at medical records for 43 patients with this rare combination and compared them to 68 patients who had the TP53 gene damage but without the deletion 5q condition. Patients with both the deletion 5q and TP53 damage lived much longer (about 70 months compared to 14 months) and took much longer to develop acute myeloid leukemia, a more serious blood cancer (about 32 months compared to 7 months). These results suggest that the harmful effects of TP53 gene damage may not be as severe when patients also have the deletion 5q condition, which could change how doctors classify and treat these patients. The findings indicate that current classification systems may need to be updated to account for this genetic combination, though more research is needed to confirm these results and understand why this protective effect occurs.

title: Age-Related Changes in Respiratory System Mechanics and Lung Morphometry.
abstract: Aging leads to degenerative changes in lung structural and mechanical properties that may impact breathing. Relatively little is known about how age-related alterations in lung mechanical properties impact expiratory duration (TE) and residual volume (RV). The present study tested three hypotheses: 1) alveolar airspace increases with age due to alveolar wall breakdown, 2) lung elastic recoil decreases, slowing expiratory flow (E-flow), and 3) airway compliance (Caw) decreases, promoting air trapping reflected by increased RV. To test these hypotheses, we evaluated changes in alveolar size using histological assessments, mechanical properties using forced oscillation perturbations with a programmable mechanical ventilator and breathing parameters using plethysmography in young (6 months) and old (24 months) Fischer 344 rats. Mean linear intercept (Lm) was higher in old (65 ± 10 µm) compared to young (55 ± 5 µm) rats, indicating alveolar airspace increase. In old rats, decreased elastic recoil was indicated by increased parameter K (0.178 ± 0.010 vs. 0.167 ± 0.013 in young) and higher V₁₀/TLC (80.7 ± 1.2% vs. 78.5 ± 2.5% in young). In addition, RV was higher in old rats (0.41 ± 0.10 mL vs. 0.27 ± 0.05 mL in young), consistent with air trapping. These mechanical changes were associated with increased E-flow (~30%) in old rats, attributable to increased tidal volume (2.08 ± 0.41 mL vs. 1.53 ± 0.36 mL in young) as TE was unchanged. These results indicate important changes in the lung parenchyma, causing alteration in passive and active properties of the respiratory system in aging rats.

llm_summary: Aging causes the lungs to lose their ability to work properly, which can make breathing harder and less efficient. Researchers studied young and old rats to understand how the lungs change with age by measuring the size of air sacs in the lungs, testing how well the lungs can stretch and contract, and tracking breathing patterns. They found that older rats had larger air sacs due to breakdown of the lung tissue, less elastic recoil meaning the lungs could not spring back as well, and more air getting trapped in the lungs after breathing out. The older rats also breathed out faster and took bigger breaths, even though the time spent exhaling stayed the same, suggesting their bodies were compensating for the weaker lung function. These findings show that aging causes important changes in lung structure and how the breathing system works, which could help explain why older people often experience breathing difficulties.

title: SETD2 Deficiency Drives Mitochondrial DNA Leakage and Creates a Druggable Dependency on BCL-XL in Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: SETD2 is frequently mutated or deleted in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). Loss of SETD2 could create synthetic lethal dependencies that confer therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, we demonstrated that SETD2 deficiency promotes cytoplasmic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) leakage, leading to basal activation of cGAS-STING inflammatory signaling and increased apoptotic priming. This inflammatory state upregulated the BH3-only protein NOXA, constrained MCL-1 function, and enforced a synthetic lethal dependency on the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-xL. Pharmacological inhibition of BCL-xL further amplified cGAS-STING signaling in SETD2-deficient cells through sublethal mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, resulting in increased mtDNA release and robust NOXA induction. Elevated NOXA neutralized the compensatory MCL-1-mediated survival signaling, triggering apoptosis. In contrast, SETD2 proficient ccRCC cells exhibited minimal cGAS-STING activation and failed to induce NOXA following BCL-xL inhibition, rendering them resistant. Genetic ablation of cGAS, STING, IRF3, or NOXA rescued sensitivity to BCL-xL inhibition, confirming that mtDNA-driven innate immune signaling is required for this dependency. In vivo, BCL-xL inhibition suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in SETD2-deficient xenograft models. Collectively, these findings establish a mechanistic link between SETD2 loss, mtDNA-driven innate immune activation, and enforced BCL-xL dependence in ccRCC, revealing a therapeutically targetable vulnerability in SETD2-deficient tumors.

llm_summary: Researchers examined a common genetic mutation in kidney cancer called SETD2 deficiency, which occurs frequently in patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a serious form of kidney cancer. The study found that when the SETD2 gene is lost or damaged, it causes mitochondria (the energy-producing structures inside cells) to leak their DNA into the cell's main compartment, triggering the cell's natural alarm system and making cancer cells more likely to die. This leakage activates a survival protein called BCL-xL that the cancer cells become dependent on to stay alive, creating a potential weakness that could be exploited with drugs. When researchers used a drug to block BCL-xL in cancer cells lacking SETD2, it caused even more mitochondrial DNA to leak out, ultimately triggering cell death, while cancer cells with normal SETD2 were resistant to this treatment. These findings suggest that BCL-xL inhibitor drugs could be an effective new treatment specifically for kidney cancer patients whose tumors have SETD2 mutations, though further clinical testing in human patients would be needed to confirm this approach works in real-world treatment.

title: Climate, geography and socioeconomic vulnerability and emergency care accessibility in Nepal, 2022: a high-resolution geospatial analysis of inequalities.
abstract: Strengthening emergency care systems could reduce death and disability in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet many struggle to provide timely, high-quality care. LMICs also face growing risks from climate-related shocks and mass casualty events. This study identifies unmet emergency care needs in Nepal-one of the world's most climate-vulnerable countries-using high-resolution geospatial data to estimate socioeconomic and climate-related inequalities.We conducted a cross-sectional geospatial analysis using data from the 2022 Nepal Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), the 2021 DHS Service Provision Assessment and publicly available climate vulnerability data. Government hospitals were classified into three emergency care levels using World Health Organzation criteria: A (basic 24-hour services), B (A plus resuscitative capabilities) and C (B plus ≥50 beds and a surgeon). Household location and injury data were obtained from the DHS. Accessibility was defined as the proportion of the population within 1-hour and 2-hour travel times, estimated using AccessMod 5.8, incorporating road networks, rivers, land cover and elevation.Most public hospitals (77.7%) met Level A criteria but only 49.3% met Level B and 10.8% met Level C. Nationally, 78.7% of households had 1-hour access to Level A care, 71.8% to Level B and 44.6% to Level C. Adjusted logistic regression showed rural, poorer and climate-vulnerable households had significantly lower 1-hour access compared with urban households, rural households had lower odds of access: Level A OR: 0.33 (95%CI 0.30 to 0.37), Level B OR: 0.33 (95%CI 0.30 to 0.36), Level C OR: 0.56 (95%CI 0.51 to 0.61). Households in high climate vulnerability areas had reduced access across all levels.Substantial gaps and inequities in timely access to high-quality emergency care exist in Nepal. Rural, poorer and climate-vulnerable populations experience markedly lower access. Targeted, decentralised strengthening of emergency care capacity is essential both in Nepal and in other LMICs facing similar constraints.© Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined emergency care accessibility across Nepal, a country highly vulnerable to climate-related disasters, because strengthening emergency services could save lives in low- and middle-income countries that currently struggle to provide timely care. The study used detailed geographic data from 2022 to map where hospitals offering different levels of emergency care were located and measured how many people could reach these facilities within one or two hours of travel time. They found that while most public hospitals offered basic 24-hour emergency services, far fewer had advanced capabilities like resuscitation equipment or surgical teams, and only about 45 percent of the population could reach the most advanced emergency centers within an hour. Rural households, poorer families, and people living in areas at high risk from climate disasters had significantly lower access to quality emergency care compared to urban and wealthier populations. The researchers concluded that Nepal and other similar countries need to build stronger emergency care systems in rural and remote areas to reduce the dangerous gaps in care that currently exist for the most vulnerable populations.

title: Mitigating CT number variability between scanners, tube potentials, and patient sizes using spectral CT virtual monoenergetic imaging.
abstract: This study assessed CT number consistency in different materials and tissues as x-ray tube potential, scanner model and manufacturer, and phantom size were varied. We investigated using virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMIs) to improve CT number consistency compared to single-energy (SE) images. Approach: Four clinically-relevant material inserts (calcium, adipose, iodine, soft tissue) were placed into two phantom sizes (28-cm and 40-cm width) and scanned at each available tube potential on three CT scanners with distinct methods of spectral data collection. SE images and VMIs were reconstructed for each scan. The average CT number of each insert was calculated for each image series, and the consistency of this average value across different combinations of scan parameters was compared between VMIs and SE images using coefficient of variation (COV), median, range and a linear model estimating scanner-based CT number differences.Main results: The COV for calcium, adipose, iodine and soft tissue inserts decreased from 10.1%, 9.7%, 28.8%, and 6.2% in SE images to 1.6%, 3.1%, 2.9%, and 5.7% in VMIs, respectively. When only tube potential was changed, the median standard deviation in insert average CT number decreased in VMIs compared to SE images in all materials. VMIs decreased the range of insert values between phantom sizes. VMIs decreased CT number variation due to scanner in both phantom sizes for iodine and in the calcium, 28-cm phantom. Inter-manufacturer differences in VMI CT numbers were observed in low density materials and the 40-cm phantom. Significance: Scan parameter variation affects CT numbers, negatively impacting quantitative imaging consistency and downstream patient metrics. This limits measurement standardization in serial studies, diverse cohorts, and between hospitals with data collection differences. VMIs from spectral CT can reduce this variability by providing more consistent material CT numbers relative to changes in tube potential, scanner model, and patient size.© 2026 Institute of Physics and Engineering in Medicine. llm_summary: Researchers examined how CT scans, which are medical imaging tools that take detailed pictures inside the body, produce different numbers for the same materials depending on which machine is used, how powerful the machine is set, and the size of the patient being scanned. The team tested four common materials found in the body on three different CT scanners of varying sizes and power settings, then compared traditional scan images with a newer type called virtual monoenergetic imaging, which adjusts the data to simulate images taken at a single energy level. The results showed that virtual monoenergetic imaging dramatically reduced inconsistencies in the numbers assigned to materials, with improvements ranging from cutting calcium variability from ten percent down to one point six percent and iodine variability from nearly twenty-nine percent down to under three percent. This improvement matters because doctors rely on consistent CT numbers to track changes in patients over time, compare results between different hospitals, and make accurate diagnoses, so reducing these inconsistencies could help ensure patients receive more reliable care regardless of which scanner or hospital they visit. The findings suggest that virtual monoenergetic imaging from spectral CT technology could become an important tool for making medical imaging measurements more standardized and trustworthy across.

title: Measurable residual disease is not a universally reliable surrogate for progression-free survival in clinical trials of new chronic lymphocytic leukemia therapies.
abstract: Several recent trials of new chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) therapies used results of measurable residual disease (MRD)-testing as a primary endpoint assuming it is an accurate surrogate for progression-free survival (PFS) which is, itself, a surrogate endpoint for survival. But whether MRD-testing results accurately correlates with PFS following Bruton tyrosine kinase-inhibitor (BTK-i) therapy with or without venetoclax or for fixed duration therapy regimens is controversial. We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library up to February 8, 2025, identifying 43 trials involving 9628 subjects to assess MRD's accuracy in predicting PFS. At the individual-level subjects with detectable MRD (dMRD) had a significantly higher risk of progression or death than those with undetectable MRD (uMRD; Hazard Ratio [HR] = 3.67; 95% Credibility Interval [CrI] 3.34, 4.03; P < 0.01). In contrast, MRD-testing results and PFS were weak at the trial-level (Spearman rho [R] = -0.33; Determination Coefficients [R² ] = 0.06), especially for BTKi- therapy (R = -0.05, R² = 0.03) and venetoclax-based therapies (R = -0.28, R² = 0.02). Correlations were stronger for therapies involving drugs such as chemoimmunotherapy and/or monoclonal antibodies, where MRD tests of bone marrow (R = -0.94; R2 = 0.86) were more accurately predicted PFS than blood. In sensitivity analyses stratified by treatment approach we found a correlation of treatment-effect in fixed-duration therapy approaching the pre-specified validity threshold (R = -0.80 [-0.93, -0.53]; R² = 0.43, P < 0.01). Our data indicate the accuracy of MRD-testing results to surrogate PFS is context-dependent, influenced by treatment approach, therapy type, and the sampling source, and should be interpreted cautiously when informing clinical or regulatory decisions.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a blood test called measurable residual disease testing, which detects leftover cancer cells after treatment, could reliably predict how long patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia would survive without their cancer getting worse. The team reviewed 43 clinical trials involving nearly 10,000 patients to compare results from the blood test with actual patient outcomes over time. While individual patients with detectable cancer cells had a much higher risk of their disease returning compared to those without detectable cells, the blood test results did not reliably predict outcomes when comparing results across different trials, especially for newer drug treatments like BTK inhibitors and venetoclax. The accuracy of the blood test varied greatly depending on the type of treatment used, where the cancer cells were sampled from, and how long patients took their medications, meaning doctors cannot always trust this test alone to make important treatment decisions. These findings suggest that blood tests for leftover cancer cells should be used cautiously in clinical trials and medical decisions, and researchers need to develop better ways to predict which patients will benefit most from new leukemia treatments.

title: Comparative Effectiveness of Azithromycin Versus Doxycycline in Hospitalized Patients With Community-Acquired Pneumonia Treated With Beta-Lactams: A Multicenter Matched Cohort Study.
abstract: Doxycycline is a frequently used alternative treatment for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in hospitalized patients; however, the evidence base is limited. We aimed to compare outcomes in CAP patients treated with doxycycline or azithromycin in combination with beta-lactams.We evaluated patients with CAP admitted to Mayo Clinic hospitals from May 2018 to September 2022 and treated with either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with a beta-lactam. Patients who received both antibiotics or were on either antibiotic as chronic therapy prior to admission were excluded. The primary outcome was mortality. Patients were 1-to-1 matched according to the presence of congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, human immunodeficiency virus infection, recent immunosuppressant use, and pneumonia severity index class.Among 8492 patients (5810 for azithromycin, 2682 for doxycycline), 2671 doxycycline-treated patients were matched with azithromycin-treated patients. In-hospital mortality was significantly lower in the azithromycin group than in the doxycycline group (odds ratio, 0.71; 95% confidence interval [CI], .56-.9), as was 90-day mortality (hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% CI, .73-.95). Patients on azithromycin also had significantly more hospital-free days (HFDs) than those on doxycycline (estimate, 1.37; 95% CI, .99-1.74).Among hospitalized patients with CAP, azithromycin was associated with lower mortality and more HFDs compared with doxycycline in combination with beta-lactams. llm_summary: Researchers examined which antibiotic works better for hospitalized patients with community-acquired pneumonia, which is a serious lung infection that people catch in everyday settings rather than in hospitals. The study compared outcomes in patients who received either azithromycin or doxycycline, both common antibiotics, combined with beta-lactams, which are another class of antibiotics that fight bacterial infections. After carefully matching patients with similar health conditions and disease severity, the researchers found that patients treated with azithromycin had lower death rates both during their hospital stay and within 90 days after admission, and they also spent more days out of the hospital compared to those treated with doxycycline. These results suggest that azithromycin may be a more effective choice than doxycycline when combined with beta-lactams for treating hospitalized pneumonia patients. However, the researchers note that larger, carefully controlled experiments are still needed to confirm these findings and to better understand the side effects of each treatment option.

title: Out of sight, hiding in plain clues.
abstract: A 76-year-old man with advanced non-small cell lung carcinoma undergoing treatment with carboplatin and paclitaxel plus pembrolizumab presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of rapidly progressive, severe bilateral visual loss and pain on eye movement. Ocular movements were full, with no other neurological deficits noted. Visual acuity was reduced bilaterally: 20/63 right eye, 20/200 left eye. Color vision testing was borderline normal, bilateral visual fields were constricted, while both funduscopy and optical coherence tomography were unremarkable. Urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed patchy FLAIR hyperintensities in both optic nerves and faint post-contrast enhancement. By the time of neurological assessment one week later, the patient had experienced partial spontaneous improvement in vision. A comprehensive neuro-oncological differential diagnosis was performed, prompting the request for further diagnostic tests. This case illustrates the evolving landscape of neuro-oncology, where advances in diagnostic approaches and the use of immunotherapies such as pembrolizumab may alter immune tolerance, leading to immune-related adverse events such as myelin oligodendrocyte glycoporotein antibody-associated disease.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc.
