llm_summary: When cells copy their DNA, the machinery that does the copying sometimes runs into the machinery that reads genes and makes proteins, which can damage the genetic code and cause problems. Researchers discovered that a protein called KCTD10 acts like a traffic controller that detects when these two processes are moving in the same direction along the DNA strand. This KCTD10 protein works by adding special chemical tags called ubiquitin to another protein called TCEA2, which temporarily changes the shape of the gene-reading machinery to let the copying machinery pass through safely. This discovery shows that cells have an active system for managing these collisions rather than just letting them happen randomly, which helps keep our genetic information stable and protected. Understanding how cells resolve these conflicts could eventually help researchers develop better treatments for diseases caused by DNA damage, such as cancer.

title: A lifecycle governance and learning health system framework for trustworthy, generalizable, and sustainable human-ai partnership in clinical practice: Lessons from the asthma-guidance and prediction system (A-GPS).
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical decision support (CDS) holds promise for proactive, personalized, and precision care. However, current understanding of how to establish trustworthy human-AI partnerships is in its infancy, despite its critical importance for implementing AI in healthcare. We present the Asthma-Guidance and Prediction System (A-GPS) as a case study of a practice-integrated AI platform that demonstrates how trustworthy, generalizable and sustainable AI can be developed, evaluated, and implemented in real-world asthma care. We describe major challenges and solutions based on our real-world experience during the process and offer the practical framework, approaches, tools and workflow for implementing trustworthy, generalizable and sustainable AI in frontline practices. While A-GPS is an asthma-specific AI tool, it was built on top of a disease-agnostic electronic health record (EHR)-integrated clinical decision support (CDS) platform based on an Application Programming Interface (API)‑first backbone of reusable services. It was designed to reduce chart-review/processing burden and enable proactive, guideline-concordant asthma management by synthesizing fragmented longitudinal multimodal data into a clinical decision-relevant summary at the point of care. A-GPS platform integrates multiple natural language processing (NLP) algorithms to leverage free texts info in EHRs, machine learning model to offer risk stratification, and remote patient monitoring (RPM) approaches to capture real-time data from patients, enabling remote asthma (chronic disease) care. The platform has been deployed via Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies-on-Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (SMART-on-FHIR) to ensure in-workflow delivery and maintainable governance making it flexible and interoperable across different EHRs systems and different chronic diseases. The translational maturity of A-GPS as an AI-powered CDS tool for pediatric asthma was demonstrated and sustained through engagement and co-design with diverse community and care team partners, including adult and pediatric Community Advisory Board, pediatric patients and their parents, clinicians (primary care providers and specialists), nurses, schedulers, as well as bioethicists and regulatory experts. Moreover, the tool was evaluated in two randomized clinical trial (RCT)s. The first trial showed a 67% reduction in clinicians' EHR review time, high clinician satisfaction, potential healthcare cost savings, fairness in model performance, and no adverse events. Trustworthiness was further assessed and supported through fairness evaluation by participant socioeconomic status (SES) using the HOUsing-based SocioEconomic Status (HOUSES) index, human-centered user interface/user experience (UI/UX) analysis, clinician workflow optimization, transparent governance practices, and best practices for regulatory science. The A-GPS experience operationalizes a reproducible, lifecycle-governed framework for generating decision-grade evidence on safety, effectiveness, usability, fairness, and workflow integration, directly addressing the translational gap between AI model development and trustworthy, sustainable deployment in real-world clinical environments. These efforts led to national recognitions, including invitation to the inaugural American Medical Informatics Association (AMIA) AI Showcase, and AI evaluation use case for a national health AI coalition. The second RCT evaluated the feasibility of integrating a remote patient monitoring (RPM) device (home spirometry) into the A-GPS platform, with a published RCT protocol that serves as a framework for RCT for evaluating AI models under the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) guidelines for RCTs that evaluate AI tools, offering the practical framework, approaches, tools, and workflow for trustworthy, generalizable and sustainable AI tools in asthma care. This work illustrates how team science, community engagement, implementation science, and learning health system principles can be operationalized to establish a human-AI partnership model to advance translational science and clinical care, with the goal of improving health for all.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. title: An X-linked long non-coding RNA, PTCHD1-AS, and the core features of autism.
abstract: There are around 100 genes or copy-number variations used in genetic testing for autism spectrum disorder (ASD)1,2. The established genes are protein coding, and the associated phenotypes usually extend beyond sociobehavioural traits seen in autism, including cognitive/medical complexities and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)3,4. We examined whole-genome sequencing data in cases of ASD (9,349) and controls (8,332) and identify 27 male individuals with ASD with X-chromosome microdeletions that implicate the long non-coding RNA PTCHD1-AS as an ASD-susceptibility gene (odds ratio = 2.56, P = 0.01). Two Ptchd1-as-knockout mouse models, which were created by disrupting/deleting the evolutionarily conserved exon 3, show ASD-like features in male mice, including increased repetitive behaviours and impaired social behaviour and communication without cognitive comorbidities or ADHD-like behaviours. Hippocampus-dependent synaptic function, complex learning and locomotor activity are unaffected in knockout mice. Native nuclear-enriched mouse Ptchd1-as showed sustained expression from postnatal day 7 onwards in the dorsal striatum, a predominantly GABAergic brain region that is implicated in ASD5. Multi-omics analysis revealed transcriptomic alterations in striatal oligodendrocytes, astrocytes and neurons impacting myelination and synaptic plasticity. Disrupting Ptchd1-as led to reductions in conventional protein kinase C (cPKC) isoforms, altered SRC and GSK-3α/β phosphorylation and enhanced striatal synaptic plasticity (long-term potentiation and long-term depression). Together, these findings implicate striatal molecular and circuit-level dysregulation through PTCHD1-AS in ASD aetiology.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Researchers examined genetic data from thousands of people with autism spectrum disorder and healthy controls to identify new genes that might cause autism, which is a developmental condition affecting how people communicate and interact socially. They discovered that a long non-coding RNA called PTCHD1-AS, which is a type of genetic instruction that does not make proteins but helps control other genes, was linked to autism in 27 male individuals who had deletions on their X chromosome. When scientists created mice without this gene, the male mice showed autism-like behaviors such as repetitive movements and difficulty with social interaction, but they did not have the learning problems or attention difficulties that often accompany autism in humans. The researchers found that the missing gene caused changes in the striatum, a brain region involved in movement and behavior, affecting how brain cells communicate through a process called synaptic plasticity. These findings suggest that problems with the PTCHD1-AS gene in the striatum may be an important cause of autism in some people, opening new possibilities for understanding and potentially treating the condition.

title: The Scarlet Letter of the Unmatched Neurosurgery Reapplicant: Trends, Opinions, and Guidance from a Nationwide Survey.
abstract: Increasing interest in neurosurgery residency has led to a growing number of unmatched applicants, who often struggle to find appropriate guidance for their next steps. The authors examined trends, opinions, and options available to unmatched neurosurgery residency reapplicants.Demographic data of US applicants from MD programs obtained from the National Resident Matching Program (2009 to 2024) were analyzed using 1-way ANOVA analysis of time-interval averages. Opinions about reapplicants were assessed via an online survey of national neurosurgery leaders, including residency program directors and chairpersons (N = 356).All application trends showed greater change over time; however, the rate of accepted reapplicants showed no significant change among early (2009 to 2013: 4.8 ± 1.8), mid (2014 to 2018: 7.6 ± 4.8), and recent periods (2019 to 2024: 9.8 ± 2.5; p = 0.068). The survey had a 23.0% response rate (82 of 356). Commonly indicated reasons for failure to match included poor interview skills, weak recommendation letters, and personality issues. Although most survey respondents supported candidates reapplying, dual applications (applying to more than 1 specialty) were not widely encouraged. For those reapplying, pursuing a preliminary general surgery or research fellowship, obtaining new letters of recommendation from new subinternships, and publishing higher-quality research were the most endorsed uses of time before reapplying. However, most programs reported interviewing reapplicants sometimes to rarely and matching a reapplicant rarely to never.The number of reapplicants successfully matching into neurosurgery has not changed significantly during the past 15 years. Surveys indicate that leaders view reapplicants unfavorably, despite reapplicants' efforts to improve their applications. These results suggest that neurosurgery mentors may do a disservice to potential reapplicants based on how residency program leadership considers reapplications. Candid guidance is needed for reapplicants in the residency matching process.Copyright © 2025 by the American College of Surgeons. Published by Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined why some medical students fail to match into neurosurgery residency programs, which are highly competitive training positions that doctors need to complete their specialty education. The study analyzed fifteen years of application data from the National Resident Matching Program and surveyed over eighty neurosurgery program leaders across the country to understand their views on students who reapply after not matching the first time. The results showed that while more students are applying to neurosurgery each year, the actual number of reapplicants who successfully secure positions has remained flat and unchanged over the entire fifteen-year period. Program leaders identified poor interview skills, weak recommendation letters, and personality issues as the main reasons students fail to match, yet most leaders rarely interview reapplicants or accept them into their programs despite supporting the idea of reapplication in theory. The findings suggest that neurosurgery mentors may be giving students misleading advice about how to improve their chances, and clearer, more honest guidance is needed to help reapplicants understand the realistic challenges they face in the matching process.

title: Translating ctDNA into cutaneous melanoma care: An international expert survey.
abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising biomarker in melanoma, with higher sensitivity for tumor burden detection than conventional diagnostics. While well established in research, clinical routine implementation remains pending. Key global questions concern optimal clinical applications and barriers to adoption.A web-based survey of 116 members of the Melanoma World Society Study Group assessed international expert opinions on ctDNA utility across predefined clinical scenarios. The questionnaire included 18 general questions on ctDNA use and 5 clinical vignettes with de-identified patient data and retrospectively obtained ctDNA results.ctDNA was rated most valuable for detecting minimal residual disease (mean score 3.63), surveillance of recurrent disease (3.85), and stage IV melanoma (3.82), with limited utility in early stages. Experts considered ctDNA superior to S100 and LDH for early relapse detection and identifying progressive disease. Most participants (80%) agreed that ctDNA correlates with radiographic response, and 82% favored its integration into routine follow-ups. In urgent high-tumor-burden settings, 82.8% would initiate BRAFi/MEKi therapy based on ctDNA if tissue analysis was pending, and 93.9% if unavailable. For central nervous system lesions, 62% did not support blood ctDNA, while 66% considered cerebrospinal fluid valuable. Pragmatic approaches with small to mid-size targeted panels and short turnaround times were preferred. Major barriers included the need for prospective trials (85%), standardized guidelines (83%), and reimbursement policies (82%).Key opinion leaders regarded ctDNA as a valuable adjunct selected melanoma scenarios. Validation through prospective studies, guideline development, and reimbursement frameworks are essential for broader clinical implementation.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd.. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether circulating tumor DNA, which is genetic material from cancer cells found in the bloodstream, could become a useful tool for detecting melanoma skin cancer earlier and more accurately than current methods. The study surveyed 116 international melanoma experts through an online questionnaire that asked about the best ways to use this blood test and presented them with five realistic patient scenarios to evaluate. Experts agreed that the blood test was most valuable for detecting leftover cancer after treatment, monitoring patients for cancer return, and tracking advanced melanoma, though it was less helpful for early-stage disease. The survey found that most experts believed this blood test should be added to routine patient follow-up care and that doctors would feel confident starting cancer treatment based on the blood test results when tissue samples were not immediately available. The main obstacles to using this test in regular medical practice are the need for large-scale studies to prove its effectiveness, clear medical guidelines on when to use it, and insurance companies agreeing to pay for the test.

title: Diffuse Extra-Thoracic Vascular Disease in Nonsyndromic Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection.
abstract: Patients with nonsyndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection (nsTAAD) may have systemic arterial involvement, but the distribution and clinical correlates of extrathoracic disease remain poorly defined. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with nsTAAD at Mayo Clinic (2018-2024). Trained reviewers manually confirmed thoracic aortic dilation and all extrathoracic vascular lesions; syndromic, congenital, and fibromuscular dysplasia-related cases were excluded. Cross-sectional imaging availability was abstracted for the head or neck, chest, and abdomen or pelvis. Detection frequencies of nonthoracic aneurysm (nTA-A) were calculated among patients imaged in ≥1 extrathoracic territory, while nonaortic dissection (nTA-D) frequencies used the full cohort denominator. Group differences were assessed using Chi-square or t Tests, and logistic regression identified predictors of nTA-A. Among 3,989 patients (28.6% female), 82.0% had CT or MRI of ≥1 extrathoracic territory. nTA-A was detected in 443/3,270 (13.5%) and increased with age (7.4% at 18-30 years, 8.4% at 31 to 50 years, 18.3% at ≥51 years; p <0.001), with the greatest detection burden in the abdomen or pelvis followed by the head/neck. nTA-D occurred in 136/3,989 (3.4%) and also rose with age (0.7%, 2.2%, 4.9%; p <0.001). Hypertension and hyperlipidemia were independently associated with nTA-A (p ≤0.05). Patients with nTA-A or nTA-D had higher rates of heart failure, myocardial infarction, stroke, and mortality (all p ≤0.01). In conclusion, extrathoracic aneurysms and dissections are common in nsTAAD and increase with age, supporting careful clinical assessment with vigilant symptom monitoring and risk factor optimization, and providing a foundation for future studies to determine when broader vascular evaluation improves longitudinal risk stratification and outcomes.Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether patients with thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, which are serious conditions involving weakening and tearing of the main artery in the chest, also develop similar problems in blood vessels elsewhere in their bodies. The study looked back at nearly four thousand patients treated at Mayo Clinic between 2018 and 2024, reviewing their medical imaging scans to find aneurysms (bulges in blood vessel walls) and dissections (tears in blood vessel walls) outside the chest area. The researchers found that aneurysms occurred in about thirteen and a half percent of patients and dissections in about three and a half percent, with both conditions becoming more common as patients got older, particularly in the belly and pelvis region. Patients who had these extra blood vessel problems experienced higher rates of heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, and death compared to those without them. The findings suggest that doctors should carefully monitor patients with chest aortic disease for similar problems in other parts of the body and manage risk factors like high blood pressure and high cholesterol to improve long-term health outcomes.

title: The outcome of patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation by body mass index.
abstract: Body mass index (BMI) is an independent, predictor of adverse outcomes among patients with cardiovascular diseases. Our aim was to evaluate how BMI modifies the association of severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) with poor survival.Consecutive echocardiographic reports linked to clinical data from a tertiary medical center (2007-2021) were reviewed. BMI was stratified to underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obesity with cutoffs of 18.5, 25, and 30 Kg/m2. Multivariable Cox regression models were applied to calculate adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) for all-cause mortality.The study population included 111,830 patients with a median age of 65 (IQR 52-76) years (58% males), 3436 (3.1%) patients had severe TR. There were 2398 (2%), 40,393 (36%), 43,790 (39%), and 25,249 (24%) individuals with underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obesity, respectively. During a median follow-up of 6 (3-10) years, 29,921 (27%) patients died. There was an interaction between BMI and TR with the outcome (p < 0.01). Severe TR was associated with mortality for patients with normal weight, overweight, and obesity, with an HR of 1.29 (95% CI 1.20-1.39), 1.26 (1.16-1.37), and 1.28 (1.15-1.43), respectively. This association was not evident among patients with underweight with an HR of 0.88 (0.64-1.22). Sub-analysis of hospitalized patients, with adjustment of the model to baseline comorbidities, including frailty, yielded similar point estimates to the main analysis.The association of severe TR with mortality is modified by BMI group. llm_summary: Researchers examined how body weight relative to height, measured as body mass index or BMI, affects survival outcomes in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation, which is a condition where a heart valve does not close properly and allows blood to leak backward. The study reviewed medical records and heart imaging tests from over 111,000 patients at a hospital between 2007 and 2021, tracking which patients died during an average follow-up period of six years. They found that severe tricuspid regurgitation was linked to higher death rates in patients who had normal weight, were overweight, or had obesity, but this harmful connection did not appear in patients who were underweight. The results suggest that body weight plays an important role in how dangerous this heart valve problem becomes, meaning that doctors may need to consider a patient's BMI when predicting health risks for those with this condition. Future research should investigate why underweight patients with this heart valve problem do not show the same increased death risk as other weight groups, which could help doctors better understand and treat this condition.

title: Psychiatric and obstetric outcomes among peripartum patients with bipolar disorder: A single-institution study.
abstract: Individuals living with bipolar disorder (BD) are at elevated risk for adverse obstetric and psychiatric outcomes in the peripartum period. This study aims to identify clinical correlates most associated with increased risk for poor psychiatric and pregnancy related outcomes.This retrospective review examined electronic health records (EHR) from January 2017 to June 2023 for individuals with a history of BD and ≥1 pregnancy seen at our institution.55 individuals were included. Data on demographics, psychiatric, medical, and obstetric history were abstracted and analyzed for associations with outcomes of interest including mood episodes during pregnancy or first year postpartum, gestational diabetes and hypertension.Pregravid obesity (BMI ≥ 30) was a risk factor for onset of a mood episode during pregnancy and postpartum. History of psychiatric hospitalization, comorbid anxiety disorder diagnosis, and any substance use during pregnancy were also associated with postpartum mood episodes. A history of self-harm, trauma, and pregravid obesity were associated with adverse obstetric outcomes (gestational diabetes mellitus and/or gestational hypertension). Among patients with BD, the specific diagnosis (type I, type II, or other specified bipolar disorder) was not significantly associated with psychiatric outcomes.Our study is limited by omissions from the medical record, single-institution nature of the study, and small sample size.This work is a step towards more individualized recommendations for perinatal patients with BD including the need to consider historical severity of illness as a predictor for mood episodes in pregnancy, noting that the specific BD subtype was not a predictor of mood course during pregnancy.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. llm_summary: Researchers examined medical records to understand which factors put pregnant women with bipolar disorder, a serious mood condition that causes extreme emotional swings, at higher risk for complications during pregnancy and after birth. The study looked at 55 women with bipolar disorder who had been pregnant and received care at one hospital between 2017 and 2023, collecting information about their medical history, psychiatric treatments, and pregnancy outcomes. The researchers found that women who were overweight before pregnancy, had been hospitalized for mental health reasons, had anxiety disorders, used substances during pregnancy, or had experienced trauma were more likely to have mood episodes during pregnancy or in the first year after giving birth. Additionally, women with a history of self-harm, trauma, or obesity before pregnancy were more likely to develop gestational diabetes (high blood sugar during pregnancy) or gestational hypertension (high blood pressure during pregnancy). The study suggests that doctors should pay close attention to a patient's past mental health severity and personal history rather than focusing only on the specific type of bipolar disorder when planning care for pregnant women with this condition.

llm_summary: Chronic neutrophilic leukemia is a rare blood cancer where the body makes too many immature white blood cells called neutrophils, and researchers have found that mutations in a gene called CSF3R are responsible for many cases of this disease. This study examined 44 patients with CSF3R-mutated chronic neutrophilic leukemia from two medical centers to better understand how the disease develops and progresses in people who carry this genetic change. The researchers collected information about the patients' medical histories, blood test results, and genetic characteristics to identify patterns in how the disease behaves and what treatments work best. Understanding the specific genetic cause of this rare leukemia helps doctors identify which patients have this particular type of disease and may eventually lead to better targeted treatments designed specifically for people with CSF3R mutations. This research provides important information that can guide future studies and help improve how doctors diagnose and care for patients with this uncommon form of blood cancer.

Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation circuits, which are machines that temporarily take over the work of the heart and lungs, are increasingly being used to keep donor lungs alive and functioning better before transplantation.

title: Photon-Counting Detector CTA for Localization of the Artery of Adamkiewicz.
abstract: Photo-counting detector CT is a relatively new technology that is becoming increasingly prevalent. In recent years, photon-counting CT has been shown to have benefits in numerous neuroradiologic clinical applications, including temporal bone imaging, detection of spinal CSF leaks, and CTA of the head, neck, and spine. New uses for photo-counting detector CT continue to emerge, capitalizing on the high spatial resolution and other advantages of this technology to improve patient care. One potential application in the spine is the detection and localization of the artery of Adamkiewicz, which provides the dominant supply to the inferior portion of the anterior spinal artery. Localization of this artery is sometimes needed before surgeries requiring ligation of the foraminal neurovascular complex. Traditional energy-integrating detector CT is useful but imperfect for the detection of this relatively small and transiently opacifying vessel. The improved spatial resolution and spectral information obtained with photon-counting CT may help improve the detection of the artery of Adamkiewicz. In this clinical report, we outline a protocol for imaging the artery of Adamkiewicz with photon-counting detector CT and describe a comparative analysis of 3 different reconstruction techniques in 6 consecutive patients who underwent this examination. We found that an intermediate sharp vascular kernel (Bv60) reconstructed with a low-energy threshold outperformed other conditions, including a sharper kernel and a low kiloelectron volt virtual monoenergetic reconstruction.© 2026 by American Journal of Neuroradiology.

llm_summary: Photon-counting detector CT is a newer imaging technology that takes very detailed pictures of the body and is becoming more common in hospitals for looking at the brain and spine. Researchers tested whether this advanced imaging could better locate the artery of Adamkiewicz, which is a small but important blood vessel that supplies the lower part of the spinal cord and sometimes needs to be identified before spine surgery. The team developed an imaging protocol and compared three different ways of processing the pictures from six patients, finding that a medium-sharpness filter combined with a specific image processing method worked best for seeing this small vessel. The results suggest that photon-counting detector CT could help doctors more reliably find this difficult-to-see artery before performing surgery, which could improve patient safety during spine procedures. Future studies with more patients will be needed to confirm whether this imaging method should become standard practice for surgeons planning spine operations.

title: Pan-neurodegeneration proteomics reveals disease subtypes and molecular signatures.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) pose clinical challenges due to their complexity and molecular heterogeneity. Here, we present a pan-neurodegeneration atlas (PanNDA) from multilayer, deep proteomic analysis of 2,279 human brain samples spanning 6 major NDs: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Lewy body dementia (LBD), frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology, progressive supranuclear palsy with tau pathology, vascular dementia, and Parkinson's disease. PanNDA integrates data from whole proteome, detergent-insoluble proteome, and posttranslational modifications (phosphorylation and ubiquitination), enabling intra- and inter-disease comparisons. Intra-disease analyses uncover distinct molecular subtypes (e.g., three in AD and four in LBD), reveal dysregulated pathways, and prioritize top-ranked proteins. Inter-disease comparisons identify shared alterations in NDs, such as GPNMB in microglial and lysosomal activation and NPTX2 in synaptic regulation, alongside disease-specific changes and hub regulators within protein networks. Overall, PanNDA provides a systems-level framework for understanding ND mechanisms and serves as a foundational resource that is accessible via an interactive website: https://penglab.shinyapps.io/pannda.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined brain tissue from nearly 2,300 people who had died from six major brain diseases that cause memory loss and movement problems, including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, to understand why these conditions affect people differently. The team performed detailed chemical analysis of the proteins in these brain samples, looking at both normal proteins and damaged versions, to create a comprehensive map showing how each disease changes the brain at a molecular level. They discovered that each major disease actually breaks down into several distinct subtypes with different protein patterns, meaning patients with the same diagnosis might have very different underlying causes for their symptoms. The researchers also found that while each disease has its own unique fingerprint, some proteins like GPNMB are abnormal across multiple diseases, suggesting that targeting these shared proteins might help treat several conditions at once. This new resource, which is available online for other scientists to use, provides a foundation for developing better ways to diagnose which subtype of disease a patient has and could eventually lead to more personalized treatments based on each person's specific protein patterns.

title: Advancing Perioperative Medicine: A Multistakeholder Perspective.
abstract: Perioperative medicine spans the entire surgical care continuum, improving patient outcomes while reducing morbidity and mortality. Anesthesiology is uniquely positioned to influence the continued development of perioperative medicine. Recognizing this opportunity, the American Society of Anesthesiologists (Schaumburg, Illinois) established the Center for Perioperative Medicine as an organizational framework to actively implement perioperative medicine. Whereas earlier efforts focused on why anesthesiology must evolve, the Center emphasizes how the specialty is advancing through rigorous, inclusive collaboration. Building on previous initiatives, the Center for Perioperative Medicine is a multidisciplinary partnership including anesthesiologists, surgeons, hospitalists, and other specialists, and incorporates both national and global perspectives. This article describes how perioperative medicine is characterized across clinical, educational, research, and leadership domains; summarizes key themes from discussions at the 2024 and 2025 Stakeholder Summits; highlights areas of convergence and variation across global viewpoints; and situates these perspectives within the evolving landscape of perioperative medicine practice worldwide today collectively.Copyright © 2026 American Society of Anesthesiologists. llm_summary: Perioperative medicine, which focuses on caring for patients throughout their entire surgical journey from before to after an operation, has the potential to improve patient outcomes and reduce serious complications and deaths. The American Society of Anesthesiologists created the Center for Perioperative Medicine to bring together anesthesiologists, surgeons, hospitalists, and other medical specialists from around the world to work collaboratively on advancing this field. The center examined how perioperative medicine is being developed and practiced across four main areas: actual patient care in hospitals, training of medical professionals, scientific research, and leadership in the field. Discussions at stakeholder summits in 2024 and 2025 revealed both common goals shared across different countries and some differences in how perioperative medicine is being implemented globally. This multidisciplinary approach represents an important shift toward more coordinated and comprehensive surgical care that brings together diverse medical experts to improve how patients are treated before, during, and after surgery.

title: Superficial siderosis in Marfan syndrome.
abstract: A 49-year-old woman presented with a dorsal column-predominant sensory myelopathy secondary to superficial siderosis. She had Marfan syndrome and was found to have dural ectasia. Superficial siderosis results from subpial haemosiderin deposition due to chronic subarachnoid space bleeding, often from a dural pathology, such as a tear. Dural ectasia is common in Marfan syndrome, but superficial siderosis is not. Gait ataxia, often with hearing impairment, is a common clinical presentation of superficial siderosis. Patients may develop myelopathy, here being a pure sensory myelopathy with predominant dorsal column deficit. Meningeal diverticulae and superficial siderosis are both associated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks. This patient had dural ectasia and meningeal diverticulae, but the CT myelogram found no CSF leak. Superficial siderosis should be considered in patients with sensory myelopathy. Lumbosacral dural ectasia, or less likely CSF leak, can cause superficial siderosis in people with Marfan syndrome.© Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2026. No commercial re-use. llm_summary: A 49-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome, a genetic condition affecting connective tissue, developed a serious spinal cord problem caused by iron deposits in the brain and spinal cord from chronic bleeding. The iron deposits, called superficial siderosis, occurred because she had dural ectasia, which is an abnormal widening of the membrane surrounding the spinal cord that is common in Marfan syndrome patients. Although doctors found signs of dural ectasia and small pouches in the membrane that typically leak fluid, they could not identify an active fluid leak on imaging tests. The patient experienced progressive weakness and loss of sensation in her legs, particularly affecting the dorsal columns, which are nerve pathways in the back of the spinal cord that carry sensory information. This case highlights that doctors should consider superficial siderosis as a possible cause when patients with Marfan syndrome develop sensory problems in their spinal cord, even when a clear fluid leak cannot be found.

title: Comparative Effectiveness of Individual Sodium Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors on Cardiovascular Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes With Moderate Cardiovascular Risk: Emulation of a Target Trial.
abstract: SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitors reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in type 2 diabetes. However, no direct comparison of individual SGLT2 inhibitor drugs has been conducted, particularly among adults with moderate cardiovascular risk who comprise most people with type 2 diabetes.We used data for commercial, Medicare Advantage, and Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries to emulate a target trial of adults (≥21 years) with type 2 diabetes and moderate cardiovascular risk who started canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, or empagliflozin between 2015 and 2020. We estimated propensity scores using the super learner ensemble method and incorporated them as inverse probability of treatment weights into Cox models, estimating risk of MACE, expanded MACE, and hyperglycemic and hypoglycemic crises through December 31, 2022.The weighted cohort, balanced on all baseline covariates, included 137 232 patients (mean age 65.7 years [SD, 8.1], 75.3% non-Hispanic White, 57.0% male, 81.9% on metformin, 11.4% on glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) starting canagliflozin (N=42 877), dapagliflozin (N=17 871), or empagliflozin (N=7648). The risk of MACE was lower among patients starting empagliflozin versus canagliflozin (hazard ratio [HR], 0.92 [95% CI, 0.87-0.97]), driven by reduced risk of all-cause mortality (HR, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.80-0.94]). There was no difference in MACE between empagliflozin versus dapagliflozin or dapagliflozin versus canagliflozin therapy. There was no difference in remaining outcomes between the three drugs.The 3 most used SGLT2 inhibitor medications demonstrate similar effectiveness on cardiovascular outcomes among patients with type 2 diabetes at moderate cardiovascular risk, with differences between these drugs small in magnitude. Clinicians and health systems should prioritize enhancing access to these cardioprotective therapies.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether three common diabetes medications called sodium glucose transporter 2 inhibitors, or SGLT2 inhibitors, work differently at protecting the heart in people with type 2 diabetes who have moderate heart disease risk. The study used health insurance records from over 137,000 patients who started taking one of three SGLT2 inhibitor drugs—canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, or empagliflozin—between 2015 and 2020, and followed them until the end of 2022 to track heart attacks, strokes, and deaths. The results showed that empagliflozin was slightly better than canagliflozin at preventing major heart problems and reducing death from any cause, but there were no meaningful differences between the other drug pairs. The findings suggest that all three medications are similarly effective at protecting the heart in patients with moderate cardiovascular risk, so doctors should focus on making sure patients can access whichever of these medications works best for their individual situation. Future research should continue monitoring these drugs to see if differences emerge over longer time periods or in patients with different levels of heart disease risk.

title: Risk Factors for Failure of Meniscal Repair.
abstract: Meniscal preservation is a cornerstone of modern knee surgery given the meniscus's essential role in load transmission, joint stability, and cartilage protection. As indications for meniscal repair have expanded, understanding the factors associated with repair failure has become increasingly important. The purpose of this review is to synthesize contemporary evidence regarding risk factors for failure of meniscal repair, clarify how failure is defined and evaluated, and outline current strategies for management of failed repairs to guide clinical decision-making.Recent literature supports meniscal repair as a joint-preserving procedure with superior long-term outcomes compared with meniscectomy, though failure and reoperation remain clinically relevant concerns. Failure risk is influenced by a combination of patient-related factors, including smoking status, limb alignment, and medical comorbidities; tear characteristics such as vascular zone, tear pattern, chronicity, and meniscal laterality; and surgical variables including isolated repair versus concomitant ligament reconstruction, repair technique, and postoperative rehabilitation. Advances in repair devices, imaging, and biologic augmentation have improved healing potential, and growing evidence supports revision meniscal repair in select patients with favorable tissue quality and tear morphology. Meniscal repair failure is multifactorial and cannot be attributed to surgical technique alone. Successful outcomes depend on appropriate patient selection, careful assessment of tear biomechanics, selection of an optimal repair strategy, and individualized rehabilitation. Revision meniscal repair remains a viable option for preserving meniscal function in appropriately selected patients. Future research should prioritize standardized definitions of failure, comparative studies of repair techniques, and biologic strategies to further improve healing and long-term joint preservation.© 2026. llm_summary: Meniscal repair, which is surgery to fix torn cartilage in the knee rather than remove it, is important because it helps preserve the knee's natural function and prevent long-term damage. Researchers reviewed existing studies to identify what factors make meniscal repair more likely to fail, including patient characteristics like smoking and overall health, features of the tear itself such as its location and pattern, and surgical choices like the repair technique used. The review found that meniscal repair generally works better than removing the damaged cartilage, but failure and the need for repeat surgery remain real concerns that depend on multiple factors working together. Success depends on choosing the right patients for surgery, understanding how the tear will behave mechanically, picking the best repair method, and providing proper recovery care tailored to each person's needs. Future research should focus on creating consistent ways to measure failure, comparing different repair techniques directly, and developing biological treatments to help the meniscus heal better and protect the knee long-term.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists and the Risk of Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy: A Consensus Statement by the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society and the American Academy of Ophthalmology.
abstract: Recent studies have reported a possible association between glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society and the American Academy of Ophthalmology provide consensus expert opinion and clinical guidance about this association. Currently available evidence primarily includes retrospective observational studies, many of which rely on analysis of electronic health record and administrative claims data and are subject to limitations. Although many report a small possible increased risk of NAION in patients taking GLP-1 RAs such as semaglutide, some studies report no correlation, and the overall magnitude of the risk of NAION remains low. Shared decision-making between each patient and their care team is warranted to decide whether to start, continue, or discontinue GLP-1 RAs. llm_summary: Recent reports have raised concerns that a popular diabetes and weight loss medication called glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, or GLP-1 RAs for short, might increase the risk of a serious eye condition called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, which occurs when blood flow to the optic nerve is suddenly blocked. Two major eye doctor organizations reviewed the available research on this possible connection and found that most studies were based on medical records and insurance claims data rather than carefully controlled experiments, which means the findings have some limitations. While several studies did report a small possible increase in eye problems among patients taking GLP-1 RAs like semaglutide, other studies found no connection at all, and the overall risk of developing this eye condition remains quite low. Doctors and patients should talk together about the benefits and risks of these medications before deciding whether to start taking them, keep taking them, or stop taking them. More research is needed to better understand whether these medications truly cause this eye problem or if other factors are responsible for the increased risk seen in some studies.

title: Malignant Mitral Valve Prolapse With Life-Threatening Ventricular Arrhythmias: A Multidisciplinary Team-Guided Stepwise Management.
abstract: A 45-year-old woman with long-standing bileaflet myxomatous mitral valve prolapse (MVP), mitral annular disjunction, and mild mitral regurgitation (MR) developed near-syncope and was found to have frequent polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on ambulatory monitoring. Despite medical therapy, she experienced recurrent ventricular fibrillation and multiple implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) shocks.Can malignant arrhythmogenic MVP occur in the absence of severe MR or detectable myocardial fibrosis on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging? Which combination of electrical and mechanical risk markers identifies patients at imminent risk for sudden cardiac death? Can early surgical correction of the mechanical substrate durably suppress ventricular arrhythmias?The patient underwent mitral valve repair. Since then, she has remained free of arrhythmias and ICD shocks.Malignant MVP can manifest with multifocal ventricular tachycardia independent of MR severity. llm_summary: A 45-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse, a condition where the heart valve doesn't close properly, developed dangerous irregular heartbeats that caused her to nearly faint and required multiple emergency shocks from an implanted heart device. Doctors discovered she had frequent abnormal heart rhythms despite being on medications and despite not having severe leaking from her valve or visible scarring on imaging tests of her heart. The research team asked whether this dangerous type of valve prolapse could cause life-threatening arrhythmias without severe valve leaking, which combination of warning signs could predict sudden cardiac death, and whether fixing the valve surgically could stop the dangerous rhythms. The patient underwent surgery to repair her mitral valve, and after the procedure she stopped having dangerous heart rhythms and no longer needed emergency shocks from her device. This case shows that dangerous heart rhythms from mitral valve prolapse can occur even without severe valve leaking, and that combining a heart device with surgical valve repair can effectively prevent sudden cardiac death in these patients.

title: Heart Rate and Vascular Responses to Spontaneous Arousals Following Experimental Sleep Restriction.
abstract: Study Objectives: Chronic short sleep duration is associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk, especially in females. The impact of biological sex on hemodynamic reactivity to spontaneous nocturnal arousals following experimental sleep restriction remains largely unknown. We therefore investigated the effect of nine-day four-hour sleep restriction on heart rate (HR) and pulse transit time (PTT) changes following spontaneous arousals in healthy males and females. We hypothesized that HR and PTT reactivity would be augmented following sleep restriction, and these responses would be more robust in females. Methods: Nineteen participants (8 females; 23±5 years) were enrolled into this study, which included two 16-day in-patient studies comprised of sleep restriction (four-hour sleep opportunity) and normal sleep (nine-hour sleep opportunity) study arms. Overnight polysomnography on days 2 (acclimation), 5 (early experimental), 11 (late experimental), and 14 (recovery) of each sleep intervention was used to analyze HR and PTT responses to spontaneous arousals. Results: Sleep restriction did not alter HR or PTT reactivity in males or females during the early experimental phase (Day 5; interaction: p>0.05). The HR response to arousal was altered in a sex-dependent manner following sleep restriction during the late experimental phase (Day 11, interaction: p=0.013). Continued sleep loss resulted in greater PTT reduction following spontaneous arousals in females, but not in males (Day 11, interaction: p=0.007) Conclusions: Sustained sleep curtailment disrupts nocturnal vascular responsiveness to spontaneous arousals, more evident in females than males. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the sex-specific relationship between shortened sleep duration and CVD risk in females.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how the body responds to sleep disruptions because getting too little sleep is linked to heart disease risk, especially in women. The study involved nineteen healthy young adults who participated in two separate sixteen-day hospital stays where they either slept only four hours per night or a normal nine hours per night, while researchers measured their heart rate and blood vessel responses during natural sleep interruptions. After nine days of severe sleep restriction, women showed greater changes in blood vessel tightness during sleep arousals compared to men, though heart rate responses took longer to appear. These findings suggest that prolonged sleep loss affects how women's blood vessels react to nighttime disturbances in ways that could increase their risk of developing heart disease. Future research should explore whether these differences between men and women help explain why women who sleep too little face higher cardiovascular disease risk.

title: Association between midazolam premedication and deep sedation following general anesthesia in pediatric patients: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: We examined if midazolam premedication via oral (PO) vs. intravenous (IV) route in pediatric patients was associated with risk for deep sedation in the postanesthesia care unit.Medical records from May 2018 to December 2023 of patients aged 2-17 years premedicated with midazolam were reviewed and stratified according to administration route. Sedation level was classified using the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale: deeply sedated (≤ - 4) or not (≥ - 3). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) analysis was performed to assess whether midazolam administration route was associated with postoperative deep sedation.Among 5245 pediatric patients, 608 (11.6%) experienced deep sedation. In unadjusted analyses, deep sedation occurred more frequently with PO than IV midazolam (13.7% vs. 5.3%, P < 0.001). After IPTW adjustment, this association remained significant (13.3% vs. 6.6%; OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.35-3.48; P = 0.001). The incidence of deep sedation decreased with increasing age and surgical duration. In IPTW-adjusted analyses, route-related differences were significant in patients aged 2-5 years (17.0% vs. 7.3%, P = 0.013) and 6-11 years (12.3% vs. 6.2%, P = 0.018), but not in adolescents (P = 0.632). Deep sedation rates were higher after procedures lasting ≤ 1 h (20.0% vs. 7.6%, P = 0.018), but not for longer procedures. No sedation-related adverse events were observed.Oral midazolam is a key driver of postoperative deep sedation in premedicated patients aged 2-11, especially following shorter procedures likely due to limited drug elimination time. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether the way doctors give a calming medicine called midazolam to children before surgery affects how deeply sedated, or sleepy, they become after the operation. They reviewed medical records from over five thousand children aged two to seventeen years who received midazolam either by mouth or through an IV injection, then tracked how sedated these children were in the recovery room using a standard measurement scale. Children who received midazolam by mouth became deeply sedated more often than those who received it through an IV, with this difference being especially noticeable in younger children aged two to eleven years and after shorter surgical procedures. The researchers believe that oral midazolam causes deeper sedation because the body has less time to break down and eliminate the drug when surgery is brief, but importantly, none of the deeply sedated children experienced any harmful side effects. These findings suggest that doctors should be aware that giving midazolam by mouth to younger children may lead to deeper sedation after surgery, though this deeper sedation did not cause any medical problems in this study.

title: Generative artificial intelligence for inpatient documentation summarization: mixed-methods quality assessment and early real-world experience.
abstract: We evaluated the quality and adoption of a large language model (LLM)-based summarization tool for ongoing hospital care.An AI summarization tool was created to provide a "Patient Story", specialty-specific "Recent Notes", and "Recent Events" over the previous 24 or 72 hours. We conducted a pragmatic mixed-methods quality assessment at three tertiary-care academic hospitals utilizing (1) Provider Documentation Summarization Quality Instrument (PDSQI-9), (2) utilization analytics, and (3) qualitative end user feedback. The PDSQI-9 included whether summaries were accurate, cited, comprehensible, organized, succinct, non-stigmatizing, synthesized, thorough, and useful. 512 users were given access, from whom 52 participants submitted 205 surveys (10.2% response rate).52 respondents submitted an average of 4.3 surveys (range 1-8). Users rated the tool favorably across all PDSQI-9 domains, with a combined average score of 4.68 (range 4.56-4.78, S.D. 0.67) across the eight domains scored on a 5-point modified Likert scale. Utilization metrics demonstrated strong uptake with frequent views. Positive qualitative feedback revealed cognitive offloading for complex patients and effective summarization of medical problems. Critical feedback showed a need to cross-reference narrative notes to current-state data and lack of detailed specialty-specific summarization.Generative artificial intelligence has emerged as a potentially transformative technology for generating succinct, verifiable summaries of ongoing care. In this pragmatic implementation, end-users indicated high perceived quality across PDSQI-9 domains.An LLM-based summarization tool for ongoing hospitalization care was rated of high quality by diverse clinicians in real-world settings, demonstrated a favorable safety profile, and showed sustained utilization.© The Author(s) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether artificial intelligence could help doctors quickly understand patient information during hospital stays, since doctors often spend significant time reading through lengthy medical records. The study tested an AI tool at three major teaching hospitals that automatically created short summaries of patient stories, recent medical notes, and recent events from the past day or three days, then surveyed over 50 doctors and nurses about the quality of these summaries using a nine-point checklist that measured accuracy, clarity, usefulness, and other important factors. Users rated the AI summaries very highly across all quality measures, giving them an average score of 4. 68 out of 5 points, and the tool was used frequently by the 512 clinicians who had access to it. Doctors and nurses reported that the summaries helped them understand complex patients more easily and saved them mental effort, though some noted that the summaries sometimes missed detailed specialty-specific information and needed better connections to current patient data.

title: Automated needle reconstruction for HDR prostate brachytherapy using a commercially compatible 3D-printed transrectal ultrasound sleeve with integrated EM tracking sensors.
abstract: Electromagnetic (EM) tracking can enhance the quality and efficiency of ultrasound-based HDR prostate brachytherapy by enabling automated digital needle reconstruction during treatment planning. This work integrates EM tracking sensors within a biocompatible, 3D-printed transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) sleeve engineered for compatibility with a commercially available probe and stepper to support clinical translation.A clinical TRUS probe was digitally scanned, and a conformal sleeve was designed in CAD and 3D-printed using sterilizable materials. The sleeve incorporated channels for EM sensors and snap-on mounting features to ensure reproducible positioning relative to the probe. Sensors were placed at the probe apex within the TRUS axial imaging plane to minimize uncertainties from mounting or EM field distortions. Multiple sleeves were fabricated to evaluate consistency and performance. EM tracking-based reconstruction accuracy was assessed in a water-tank phantom containing seven needles placed to approximate the peripheral needle positions of a typical HDR prostate implant.EM-tracked needle reconstruction showed close agreement with manual, image-based reconstruction, yielding median (interquartile range) errors of 0.60 (0.28-0.78) mm for needle depths and 0.64 (0.40-0.93) mm for needle shafts. Sleeve mounting reproducibility had 90% confidence intervals whose absolute bounds were below 0.17 mm (3D offset), 0.09° (pitch), 0.06° (yaw), and 0.51° (roll). A patient-specific calibration procedure was developed to correct potential variability in 3D printing and sensor placement. The potential net reduction in procedure time using EM-based reconstruction versus manual reconstruction was approximately 28 minutes.Integrating EM sensors into a 3D-printed TRUS sleeve provided automated needle reconstruction with sub-millimeter accuracy for HDR prostate brachytherapy. Future clinical implementation is supported by the use of sterilizable, patient-safe materials and compatibility with standard TRUS systems.Copyright © 2026 American Brachytherapy Society. llm_summary: Researchers examined a new way to improve prostate cancer treatment using a special ultrasound device that tracks needle positions during a minimally invasive procedure called brachytherapy, where radioactive seeds are placed directly into the tumor. The team designed and three-dimensional printed a custom sleeve that fits over a standard ultrasound probe and contains tiny electromagnetic sensors that automatically record where each needle is positioned during the procedure. When tested in a water tank with needles arranged like they would be in an actual patient, the electromagnetic tracking system accurately located the needles with errors smaller than one millimeter, which is precise enough for safe cancer treatment. This new technology could reduce the time doctors spend manually identifying needle positions by about twenty-eight minutes per procedure, making treatments faster and potentially more consistent across different patients. The researchers used sterilizable materials and designed the system to work with existing ultrasound equipment already found in hospitals, which means this innovation could realistically be used in clinical practice in the near future.

title: American Brachytherapy Society consensus guidelines for medical physics residency training endorsed by the American Association of Physicists in Medicine, Part I: High-dose-rate remote afterloader brachytherapy.
abstract: To provide recommendations on training guidelines for therapeutic medical physics residents, including standards for satisfaction of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Authorized Medical Physicist (AMP) high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy training and experience requirements.Following the Nominal Group Technique, an expert panel of 15 American Board of Radiology-certified medical physicists from 14 institutions, including academic centers and freestanding clinics, developed consensus recommendations that align with NRC form 313A (AMP).Training and experience requirements were defined at two levels. Level I addresses NRC training requirements and focuses on foundational HDR brachytherapy competencies. Trainees should understand quality assurance (QA) equipment needs, perform or describe all QA procedures, and demonstrate knowledge of shielding principles, regulatory dose limits, and emergency procedures. Clinical training should include at least 10 3D planned cases, 6 involving 2 or more channels. Level II addresses NRC work experience requirements. Trainees must meet all Level I standards and be capable of performing Level I clinical duties, providing QA and clinical guidance for new applicators or techniques, as well as emergency training for staff. Level II experience requires a minimum of 15 3D planned cases, including at least seven interstitial procedures (hybrid applicators allowed) and no more than five single-channel cases.Proper training and experience are essential for HDR brachytherapy. The two levels defined in this work offer a clear, structured pathway for trainees to achieve AMP status and ensure readiness for independent practice.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: A group of radiation therapy experts created training guidelines to ensure that medical physicists, who are scientists that work with radiation in hospitals, are properly prepared to safely use high-dose-rate brachytherapy, which is a cancer treatment that places radioactive sources directly inside or near tumors. The expert panel of fifteen certified physicists from different hospitals and clinics used a structured discussion method to develop two levels of training standards that meet requirements set by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the government agency that oversees radiation safety. The first training level focuses on teaching physicists the basic skills needed for this type of treatment, including understanding safety equipment, performing quality checks, and completing at least ten three-dimensional planned cases with at least six involving multiple treatment channels. The second training level requires physicists to master all the first-level skills plus gain experience with more complex procedures, including at least fifteen planned cases with seven or more being interstitial procedures, which means placing radiation sources inside body tissues. These clear training guidelines help ensure that physicists who work independently with this advanced cancer treatment have the knowledge and hands-on experience needed to protect patients and perform their jobs safely and effectively.

title: International expert consensus recommendations on standardised nomenclature of SSA/Ro (TROVE2/Ro60 and TRIM21/Ro52) autoantibodies in autoimmune diseases.
abstract: Autoantibodies directed against Telomerase RNA Ro y-RNAs and Vault RNAs Domain Family Member 2 (TROVE2)/Ro60 and Tripartite Motif 21 (TRIM21)/Ro52 are historically related to distinct SSA/Ro autoantigens. However, despite advances facilitating separate testing, these autoantibodies remain frequently confused resulting in a lack of clarity and precision in the literature. We conducted a systematic literature review to inform a Delphi process to achieve consensus on a clearer, harmonised nomenclature.The systematic review included primary publications in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and Sjögren disease (SjD) published between January 1, 2000 and May 26, 2025 that mentioned testing for anti-TROVE2/Ro60 and/or anti-TRIM21/Ro52 autoantibodies. This analysis contributed to a Delphi consensus exercise proposing preferred nomenclature by a group of 17 international expert physicians and laboratorians.Eight hundred ninety-one publications were included (301 SLE, 493 SjD, and 97 mixed SLE/SjD). Only 20.9% of studies tested and reported the autoantibodies separately; 75.0% did neither; and 4.2% tested but did not report them separately. There was considerable nomenclatural heterogeneity with 16 different terms used for anti-TROVE2/Ro60 and 11 terms for anti-TRIM21/Ro52 autoantibodies. After 2 rounds of voting, the Delphi panel reached a unanimous consensus on the terms anti-TROVE2/Ro60 and anti-TRIM21/Ro52 autoantibodies.The distinction of anti-TROVE2/Ro60 and anti-TRIM21/Ro52 autoantibodies was frequently unclear and imprecise throughout the literature. Their clinical associations also lacked clarity and precision. To clarify and strengthen the understanding of the clinical associations of these 2 important autoantibodies, the terms anti-TROVE2/Ro60 and anti-TRIM21/Ro52 are recommended for future studies and publications.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined a widespread problem in medical literature where two important autoantibodies, which are proteins the immune system mistakenly makes against the body's own cells, were being described using many different names and were often confused with each other. The team reviewed nearly nine hundred published studies about lupus and Sjögren disease, two autoimmune conditions where these antibodies are commonly found, and discovered that most studies either did not test for these antibodies separately or did not clearly report which one they were measuring. The analysis revealed that researchers used sixteen different terms to describe one antibody and eleven different terms for the other, creating significant confusion throughout the medical literature. To solve this problem, an international group of seventeen medical experts and laboratory specialists voted on the clearest and most accurate names for these antibodies and unanimously agreed that they should be called anti-TROVE2/Ro60 and anti-TRIM21/Ro52 autoantibodies. The experts recommend that all future medical studies and publications use these standardized names so that doctors and researchers can better understand how these antibodies relate to disease and can communicate more clearly with each other.

title: CHIP clinics: a practical overview of structure and function.
abstract: Modern knowledge about the principles of clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) has paved way for numerous clinical efforts aimed at managing this pre-malignant condition. The emergence of various CHIP clinics across the globe attests to collaborative attempts to formalize clinical management of CHIP and its entities. However, translational science in this field is limited to date, partly due to nascent therapeutic concepts with limited understanding of natural history and longitudinal follow up. Here, we explore the structure and function of existing CHIP clinics and propose a working model to materialize future CHIP clinics at academic and community health care systems. We discuss the critical elements in conceptualizing and operationalizing CHIP clinic workflows, including pinpointing unmet clinical needs, prospective and retrospective identification of patients with CHIP, and recruitment of key CHIP clinic personnel toward creation of an effective multidisciplinary team. We underscore the clinical utility of CHIP clinics with regard to value creation in preventive hematology, real-world risk assessment using evidence-based models, provision of clinical trial enrollment opportunities, establishment of curated research registries and tissue biorepositories, and development of community outreach efforts. Finally, we shed light onto prospects of continued multi-center participation in collaborative science related to emerging therapeutic options in CHIP. These concepts may have a favorable impact on previvorship in hematology in the coming years.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, which is a condition where blood-forming cells develop genetic changes that could potentially lead to blood cancer, has become important enough that hospitals around the world are now opening specialized clinics to manage it. These CHIP clinics, as they are called, bring together teams of doctors and researchers to identify patients with this condition, understand how it develops over time, and offer them opportunities to participate in new treatment studies. The authors of this paper examined how existing CHIP clinics are structured and operated, then proposed a practical model that other hospitals could use to start their own clinics by identifying patients early, assembling the right medical team, and creating research registries to track patient information. These clinics provide value by helping doctors catch blood cancer risks before they become serious, offering patients access to new clinical trials, and building research collections of patient samples and data that can lead to better treatments. The authors emphasize that by continuing to work together across multiple hospitals and sharing what they learn, the medical community can improve how people with this condition are cared for and potentially prevent serious blood cancers from developing.

title: A human-in-the-loop explanation framework for morphologically transparent AI predictions from whole-slide images.
abstract: Deep learning models enable the prediction of clinical endpoints from whole-slide images (WSIs), but many such models function as "black boxes", lacking transparency about whether and which histomorphological patterns drive their predictions, hindering interpretability and clinical adoption. Here we propose a human-in-the-loop explanation framework, MorphoXAI, which provides both local and global interpretability for deep learning models by incorporating human-expert interpretations. At the global level, it reveals the histomorphological patterns on which the model consistently relies to distinguish between classes of WSIs, as well as the patterns associated with confusion between classes. At the local level, it indicates which of these patterns are used in the prediction of an individual WSI and which regions within the slide correspond to such patterns. We validated our method across multiple deep learning-based WSI analysis tasks spanning different tissue types. The results show that our framework generates explanations that accurately reflect the histomorphology underlying the model's predictions at both global and local levels. For interpretability and clinical utility in diagnostic contexts, human evaluation results showed that our explanations were easy to interpret, rich in diagnostic features, and directly helpful for diagnostic decision-making, thereby enhancing pathologist-AI collaboration. Our work highlights that unifying global and local explanations and grounding them in expert-interpreted morphology enhances the interpretability and verifiability of deep learning models, thereby facilitating the transparent deployment of such models in clinical practice.© 2026. llm_summary: Deep learning models, which are computer systems trained to recognize patterns in medical images, can predict patient health outcomes from whole-slide images (detailed photographs of tissue samples), but doctors often cannot understand how these models reach their conclusions, which limits their use in real clinical settings. Researchers developed a new framework called MorphoXAI that combines artificial intelligence with human expert knowledge to explain what the computer model is looking at when it makes predictions about tissue samples. The framework works at two levels: it shows which tissue patterns the model generally relies on to tell different types of samples apart, and it also highlights which specific patterns and locations in an individual patient's sample influenced that particular prediction. When pathologists (doctors who study tissue samples) tested these explanations, they found them easy to understand, full of useful diagnostic details, and genuinely helpful for making medical decisions alongside the artificial intelligence system. This work demonstrates that making artificial intelligence models more transparent by grounding their decisions in actual tissue patterns that human experts can verify will help doctors trust and use these powerful tools more confidently in patient care.

title: Procedure duration predicts outcomes more than prehospital delay in endovascular stroke treatment.
abstract: Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) has transformed acute ischemic stroke (AIS) care, with onset-to-puncture (OTP) time widely recognized as a critical determinant of outcome. However, emerging evidence suggests that in-hospital procedure time (PT)-from arterial puncture to final recanalization-may have an equally or more significant impact. This study examines the relative contribution of PT versus OTP to functional outcomes in patients with AIS undergoing EVT.A retrospective analysis was conducted of 6644 patients with AIS treated at 44 international stroke centers from the Stroke Thrombectomy and Aneurysm Registry (STAR; 2016-2023). Multivariable regression, time-equivalence analysis, and marginal effects modeling were used to assess associations between PT, OTP, and 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) outcomes. Centers were stratified by procedural efficiency and compared using propensity score matching (PSM). Mediation analysis evaluated whether PT accounted for inter-center differences.PT and OTP were independently associated with functional outcomes; however, PT had a significantly stronger effect (adjusted OR for mRS 0-2: PT=0.56 vs OTP=0.96 per hour). Each 5 min increase in PT was equivalent to 78-100 min of additional OTP in outcome impact. Centers with faster average PT had higher rates of functional independence (number needed to treat (NNT)=10), fewer complications, and lower symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage rates. PT significantly mediated the relationship between center tier and outcomes (Sobel's P<0.001).While minimizing OTP remains important, PT exerts a greater influence on outcomes after EVT. Procedural efficiency should be emphasized in stroke systems of care and included in center performance metrics to improve patient outcomes.© Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether the time it takes to perform a stroke procedure matters more than the time patients wait before arriving at the hospital, since a new treatment called endovascular thrombectomy has dramatically improved outcomes for people having acute ischemic strokes, which occur when blood clots block brain vessels. The study analyzed information from over 6,600 stroke patients treated at 44 hospitals around the world between 2016 and 2023, using statistical methods to compare how procedure duration and prehospital delay each affected patient recovery at 90 days after treatment. The results showed that the time spent actually performing the procedure, from the moment doctors inserted a catheter into the artery until they successfully removed the clot, had a much stronger impact on outcomes than the time patients spent waiting before reaching the hospital. Hospitals that completed procedures more quickly had significantly better patient outcomes, with fewer complications and better rates of functional independence, suggesting that procedural efficiency should become a key measure of hospital performance in stroke care. These findings indicate that while reducing prehospital delays remains important, healthcare systems should focus equally or even more on training and organizing procedures to minimize the time spent in the operating room to improve survival and.

title: When Does Acceptable Become Unacceptable? Toxicities of Emerging Therapies.
abstract: Novel systemic anticancer therapies, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), bispecific antibodies, and next-generation targeted agents, have improved survival, expanded into earlier disease settings, and created a growing population of long-term survivors. However, these therapies introduce toxicity profiles that differ substantially from those of traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy, including differences in organs affected, timing of onset, management strategies, and long-term sequelae. Tailored approaches to monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment are therefore required, along with stronger evidence to guide strategies that reduce morbidity and mortality while maintaining antitumor efficacy. Importantly, patients' lived experiences of toxicity often do not align with clinician-graded Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events classifications. Nonobservable symptoms, daily functioning, and quality of life must also be taken into account. Here, ocular and cutaneous adverse events are used as illustrative examples of how toxicities that may appear mild can become unacceptable when they impair function, quality of life, or treatment sustainability. Interdisciplinary collaboration between oncologists and organ specialists is essential for optimal recognition and management. At the same time, the evidence base for toxicity risk and management must continue to evolve through registries such as Side Effect Registry Immuno-Oncology and prospective comparative studies. Better tailored treatment strategies, particularly for immune-related adverse events, are needed to preserve both tumor response and organ function while reducing reliance on corticosteroids and broad immunosuppression. Although these therapies are highly effective, their risks must be better understood and managed to maximize patient benefit.

llm_summary: New cancer treatments like immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help the body's immune system fight cancer, have saved many lives but cause side effects that are very different from older chemotherapy drugs. These newer therapies can affect different organs in the body, appear suddenly or gradually, and require special monitoring and treatment approaches that doctors are still learning about. A major problem is that doctors and patients often disagree about how serious these side effects are, since medical rating systems may miss invisible symptoms and the real impact on a patient's daily life and ability to continue treatment. The researchers used eye and skin problems as examples to show how side effects that seem minor on paper can actually become serious enough to stop treatment when they interfere with how someone sees, feels, or functions day to day. To better help patients, doctors from different specialties need to work together, hospitals need to collect more data about these side effects through registries, and researchers need to find ways to reduce harmful side effects while keeping the cancer-fighting benefits and avoiding overuse of steroids and strong immune-suppressing drugs.
