llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a popular diabetes and weight loss medication called GLP-1 receptor agonists might increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviors by reviewing forty-three existing studies on this topic. The team searched medical databases for observational studies, which are research projects that track what happens to people without controlling their treatment, and found that different types of studies produced different results. Some case reports suggested a possible link between the medication and suicidal thoughts, while other studies actually found the medication was associated with fewer suicide attempts, creating a confusing and mixed picture overall. The researchers concluded that the current evidence does not prove the medication causes suicidal thoughts or behaviors, but they recommend that doctors should still check on their patients' mental health before and during treatment with this medication. Importantly, having a history of mental health problems should not automatically prevent someone from using this medication, as doctors should make decisions based on each individual patient's unique situation and needs.

title: A National Cross-sectional Assessment of the Mayo Clinic Vestibular Schwannoma Quality of Life (VSQOL) Index by Tumor Management Strategy.
abstract: To compare disease-specific quality of life (QOL) among patients with sporadic vestibular schwannoma (VS) by tumor management strategy using the recently developed and validated Mayo Clinic VSQOL Index relative to established minimal important difference (MID) thresholds.Cross-sectional cohort.Acoustic Neuroma Association and tertiary care center.Adults with sporadic VS.Microsurgery, radiation, or observation.VSQOL Index scores were compared by tumor management strategy adjusting for age, sex, setting, tumor size at diagnosis, and duration of follow-up. Scores range from 0 to 100; higher scores indicate better QOL.Of the 652 patients included, 333 (51%) were managed with microsurgery, 175 (27%) with radiation, and 144 (22%) with observation. The mean (SD) duration of follow-up was 6.2 (2.7) years. Global QOL adjusted mean scores (95% CI) differed significantly (P<0.001) by management group: 70 (67-72) for microsurgery, 73 (70-77) for radiation, and 79 (75-83) for observation. Hearing Problems (P<0.001), Dizziness and Imbalance (P<0.001), Problems with Face or Eyes (P<0.001), and Difficulty with Thinking and Memory (P=0.03) domain scores also differed significantly by group. Pairwise comparisons that exceeded at least the lower bound of published MIDs included Global QOL scores (microsurgery versus observation) and Hearing Problems scores (microsurgery and radiation versus observation).At a mean follow-up of 6.2 years, several notable statistically and clinically significant differences in QOL were identified. These findings may be used to guide patient counseling regarding management options and require validation in future prospective studies.Copyright © 2026, Otology & Neurotology, Inc.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how quality of life differs for patients with vestibular schwannoma, which is a noncancerous tumor that grows on the nerve connecting the ear to the brain, depending on which treatment approach they chose. The study included 652 patients who were either treated with surgery to remove the tumor, radiation therapy to shrink it, or simply monitored over time without immediate treatment, and researchers measured their quality of life using a specialized questionnaire that scores results from zero to one hundred. Patients who chose observation without immediate treatment reported the best quality of life with an average score of seventy-nine, while those who had surgery reported the lowest score at seventy, with radiation patients falling in between at seventy-three. The differences were particularly noticeable in areas like hearing problems, dizziness and balance issues, and facial nerve problems, with surgery patients experiencing more of these complications than those who were simply observed. These findings could help doctors have better conversations with patients about the pros and cons of each treatment option, though researchers note that future studies are needed to confirm these results.

title: Exploring Qualitative Education Research: A Primer for Physiologists.
abstract: Determining how students perceive and navigate the physiology classroom is crucial for designing evidence-based pedagogy and a well-informed curriculum. As trained scientists, most physiology instructors are well versed in using quantitative research, a methodology that prioritizes statistical analysis to predict future outcomes. While these methods offer valuable insights into measurable trends, they often rely on assumptions that overlook the "why" and "how" of student learning which fall into the realm of qualitative research methodologies. This primer aims to help physiology educators to better understand qualitative research by providing an overview of qualitative research, some key questions to address while forming a qualitative research question and some of the main differences between qualitative and quantitative educational research. Finally, some examples of qualitative research in physiology are highlighted.

llm_summary: Understanding how students learn in physiology classes is important for teachers who want to create better learning experiences and design courses based on solid evidence. Most physiology instructors are trained as scientists and rely on quantitative research, which uses numbers and statistics to find patterns and make predictions about outcomes. However, this numerical approach often misses the deeper reasons why students learn the way they do, which is where qualitative research comes in by asking open-ended questions and exploring student experiences in detail. This primer serves as a guide to help physiology educators understand qualitative research methods, learn how to ask good research questions, and see the key differences between counting and measuring things versus exploring the stories and experiences behind learning. By highlighting real examples of qualitative research already being used in physiology education, the authors show instructors how these methods can complement traditional statistical approaches to create a more complete picture of student learning.

title: Evaluation of algorithms for predicting new baseline renal function after complex partial nephrectomy for multifocal renal tumors.
abstract: Partial nephrectomy (PN) for localized renal cancer is associated with favorable survival outcomes due to preservation of renal function. Approaches for predicting new-baseline-GFR (NBGFR) after PN have been proposed, including multivariable algorithms and a formula presuming that 90% of the renal parenchyma is preserved during PN. However, these models were developed from cohorts with sporadic single-tumor renal cancer. We evaluate these predictive models in patients undergoing PN for multifocal disease. Accurate prediction of NBGFR has major implications in these patients, as they may require multiple PN for metachronous kidney cancer.Patients who underwent PN for removal of ≥2 tumors from 2006 to 2024 and had available measurements of preop/postoperative GFR were considered. The final cohort included 453 patients, of whom 184 underwent multiple PN. Four predictive models were evaluated. Model performance was assessed using correlation-coefficient(r) and mean-squared-error (MSE).Approximately 30% of patients had sporadic, multifocal renal tumors, and 70% had hereditary renal cancer. The 90% formula had a higher r and lower MSE values compared to the multivariable models, and also showed improved accuracy, bias, and precision. In patients undergoing multiple PN, 85% to 91% of the GFR was preserved in each PN.Models for predicting NBGFR after PN showed strong performance in our cohort with multifocal renal tumors. The conceptually simple formula presuming 90% renal parenchymal preservation, and thus 90% GFR preservation, most accurately predicted NBGFR. The %GFR preserved with each PN remained stable across sequential PN. These findings suggest that preservation of renal parenchyma is a relevant determinant of NBGFR after PN for multifocal tumors.Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how well different mathematical formulas can predict kidney function after surgery to remove multiple tumors from the same kidney, which is important because patients with multiple kidney tumors may need repeated surgeries throughout their lives. The study included 453 patients who had surgery to remove two or more tumors between 2006 and 2024, and the researchers compared four different prediction methods to see which one most accurately forecast the patients' kidney function after surgery. The simplest formula, which assumed that 90 percent of the kidney tissue would be preserved and therefore 90 percent of kidney function would remain, performed better than more complex mathematical models at predicting actual kidney function outcomes. When patients needed multiple surgeries over time, the kidney preserved between 85 and 91 percent of its function with each operation, showing that the amount of kidney tissue saved stayed consistent across repeated procedures. These findings suggest that doctors can use the straightforward 90 percent preservation formula to reliably predict how much kidney function patients will have after surgery for multiple tumors, which helps guide treatment decisions for people who may require future kidney surgeries.

title: SAGES colorectal and metabolic bariatric surgery committee joint task force call to action for synchronized severe obesity and colorectal cancer management.
abstract: Severe obesity (body mass index ≥ 40 kg/m2 or ≥ 35 kg/m2 with obesity-related comorbidities) is increasingly prevalent and independently associated with elevated perioperative morbidity and inferior oncologic outcomes in patients with colorectal cancer (CRC). Despite these risks, intentional preoperative weight optimization is not routinely incorporated into CRC management, owing to concerns regarding treatment delay, absence of guideline endorsement, and limited supporting evidence.A literature review was conducted using PubMed and Embase to evaluate the impact of severe obesity on morbidity, mortality, and oncologic outcomes in CRC. Peer-reviewed English-language studies involving adult human subjects were included, while conference abstracts, non-English publications, and studies unrelated to obesity and CRC were excluded. In the absence of published reports describing synchronized weight loss and CRC management in patients with severe obesity, three novel retrospective case examples were included to demonstrate feasibility during neoadjuvant treatment, with institutional review board approval obtained for all cases.Severe obesity complicates CRC staging due to limitations in cross-sectional imaging and anatomic delineation. Furthermore, severe and particularly visceral obesity is associated with increased rates of anastomotic leak, surgical site infection, and conversion to open surgery. Current CRC guidelines do not incorporate structured weight-loss strategies into standard treatment algorithms. Metabolic bariatric procedures, such as sleeve gastrectomy, achieve rapid and clinically meaningful weight reduction, often resulting in improved operative exposure and technical conditions for subsequent resection. Pharmacologic therapies, while more broadly accessible and less invasive, typically yield more modest reductions in visceral adiposity. Task force members report early experience across three distinct cases of locally advanced CRC in patients with severe obesity, demonstrating successful preoperative visceral fat reduction through multidisciplinary coordination incorporating metabolic bariatric surgery or pharmacologic therapy during neoadjuvant windows, followed by definitive oncologic resection.Severe obesity adversely influences CRC staging, operative complexity, and perioperative outcomes. Intentional metabolic optimization-through bariatric surgery or pharmacologic therapy-may represent a viable adjunct within multidisciplinary, patient-centered CRC care pathways. However, the absence of prospective short- and long-term outcome data underscores the need for systematic investigation to define optimal timing, safety parameters, and oncologic efficacy of weight-loss interventions in this high-risk population.© 2026. llm_summary: Severe obesity, defined as having a body mass index of 40 or higher, makes colorectal cancer surgery more dangerous and leads to worse outcomes, yet doctors do not routinely help patients lose weight before cancer treatment. Researchers reviewed published studies and examined three real patient cases to understand how weight loss during cancer treatment could improve surgical results for severely obese patients with colorectal cancer. The study found that severe obesity makes it harder to see the cancer on imaging scans, increases the risk of serious surgical complications like infections and leaks at surgical connection sites, and makes surgery technically more difficult for doctors. The researchers discovered that weight loss procedures like sleeve gastrectomy, which reduces stomach size, or weight loss medications could help reduce dangerous belly fat and improve conditions for cancer surgery when done during the waiting period before definitive treatment. Although these early cases show promise for combining weight loss with cancer care, doctors need more research with long-term follow-up to determine the safest timing and best methods for helping severely obese cancer patients.

title: "Who's on Backup?"-Exploring Internal Medicine Residency Backup Coverage Systems: Findings from a National Survey.
abstract: Little is known about backup coverage systems for clinical coverage when resident physicians call in for acute absences.To define prevalence, core characteristics and explore challenges of backup coverage systems in Internal Medicine (IM) residency programs.A nationally representative, cross-sectional survey of US IM program directors (PDs) explored "backup" coverage systems.PDs of 466 IM residency programs accredited by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education responded during August-December 2023.Responses were analyzed using inferential statistics and thematic analysis of an open-ended question.Response rate was 57.1% (266 of 466). IM programs reported formal (92.9%, 247/266) or informal (6.4%, 17/266) backup systems. Most (64.3%, 169/263) felt use of the backup system had increased since the COVID-19 pandemic. Over 90% of programs listed acute illness, family emergencies, fatigue/impairment, and bereavement as reasons for backup coverage. Most programs (> 90%) provided coverage for absences from the inpatient ward, ICU services, and/or night float; however, 40.2% covered absences in primary care clinics. Most programs (87.4%, 229/262) had residents on backup during other clinical/educational rotations. Fewer than 20% of programs compensated residents for backup, namely time off and decreased likelihood of pull for future coverage. Only 15.4% (8/52) of programs provided monetary compensation. For long-term absences, 82.7% (220/266) of programs coordinated trades and 35.7% (99/266) used backup. Six themes characterized challenges of backup coverage: healthcare resources, call-ins culture change, balancing equity, patient care versus education, administrative burden, wellness/ burnout focus, parental/extended leave requirements. IM PDs expressed competing demands with backup systems.While backup systems are nearly ubiquitous in IM residency programs, PDs report significant strains in these systems including possible cultural shift in illness definition, workload imbalances post-COVID, and prioritization of inpatient coverage over primary care. System-level changes are needed to improve backup coverage systems.© 2026. This is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply.

llm_summary: When doctors in training need to call in sick or deal with emergencies, hospitals need backup plans to cover their patient care responsibilities, but little information existed about how these backup systems actually work across the country. Researchers surveyed program directors at 266 internal medicine residency programs across the United States between August and December 2023 to understand what backup coverage systems existed, how they operated, and what challenges they faced. Nearly all programs had some kind of backup system in place, with most programs covering absences in hospital wards and intensive care units but fewer programs covering absences in primary care clinics, and most programs reported that backup coverage needs increased after the COVID-19 pandemic. Program directors identified six major challenges with their backup systems, including concerns about fairness among residents, the burden on administrative staff, resident burnout and wellness, and the difficulty of balancing the need to care for patients with the need to provide educational opportunities for doctors in training. The researchers concluded that while backup coverage systems are nearly universal in internal medicine training programs, significant improvements are needed to address workload imbalances, cultural shifts in how illness is defined, and the prioritization of hospital coverage over clinic coverage.

title: Feedback loops between DNMT1 and autophagy as well as senescence promotes organ aging and canities.
abstract: Alternations of DNA methylation occur in aging, which is regulated by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs). In this study, we show that even though the transcription of DNMT1, the only enzyme that maintains DNA methylation in the mammalian genome, is reported to be decreased in an age-dependent manner, the decrease of Dnmt1 mRNA does not result in a decrease of its protein. Instead, DNMT1 protein is increased in aged mouse tissues, which is responsible for the methylation of genes related to macroautophagy/autophagy, senescence repression, and melanin synthesis and transport in aged organs, resulting in a decline of autophagy, an increase of senescence in those organs, and a decrease in melanin production in hair follicles (canities) in response to ionizing radiation (IR). Genetic deletion and inhibition of DNMT1 can reverse these processes. The interaction of DNMT1 with ATG7 through its CXXC domain is essential for its degradation, and treatment with senolytics also downregulates DNMT1 in aged organs, supporting two feedback loops between them.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how a protein called DNMT1, which controls how genes are turned on and off through a process called DNA methylation, changes as we age and contributes to aging and hair graying. They discovered that while the instructions for making DNMT1 decrease with age, the actual protein itself increases in older tissues, and this extra protein turns off genes related to autophagy, which is the body's natural cleaning system that removes damaged cells. This increase in DNMT1 protein leads to a buildup of old, damaged cells and a decrease in melanin production, the pigment that gives hair its color, resulting in gray hair and accelerated aging in organs exposed to radiation. When the researchers genetically removed DNMT1 or used drugs to block it, they were able to reverse these aging processes and restore the body's natural cleaning and repair functions. These findings suggest that controlling DNMT1 levels could be a promising strategy to slow aging and prevent age-related conditions like canities, though more research is needed to understand how to safely apply these discoveries to human patients.

title: Prepregnancy Care and Counseling: A Review.
abstract: Prepregnancy care and counseling optimize maternal health before conception to improve outcomes for mothers and infants. In the US, 66.4% of reproductive-aged women have at least 1 modifiable risk factor for adverse pregnancy outcomes.For all individuals desiring pregnancy, recommended interventions include folic acid supplementation; cessation of tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, and opioids; immunizations against hepatitis B virus, varicella, and rubella; and screening for syphilis and HIV. Folic acid use before pregnancy is associated with reduced fetal neural tube defects (relative risk [RR], 0.67; 95% CI, 0.52-0.87). Maternal tobacco smoking is associated with increased risks of stillbirth (summary RR [sRR], 1.46; 95% CI, 1.38-1.54), neonatal death (sRR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.14-1.30), and perinatal death (sRR, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.25-1.41). Screening for and treatment of syphilis and HIV prior to and during pregnancy decrease rates of fetal and neonatal infection. Prepregnancy immunizations against hepatitis B virus, varicella, and rubella decrease neonatal infection and mortality. Individuals using tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, and opioids should receive counseling and treatment prior to pregnancy (eg, buprenorphine or methadone for opioid use disorder). For individuals with chronic disease, routine health examinations and contraceptive care in the year before conception can optimize pregnancy timing and are associated with decreased risk of severe maternal morbidity. Compared with planned pregnancies, unintended pregnancies are associated with increased risk of postpartum depression (15.7% vs 9.6%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.51; 95% CI, 1.40-1.70), preterm birth (9.4% vs 7.7%; aOR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.12-1.31), and low infant birth weight (7.3% vs 5.2%; aOR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.02-1.21). Weight loss prior to conception is recommended for individuals with a body mass index of 25 or greater because overweight and obesity are associated with increased risk of gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, and cesarean delivery. Among patients with pregestational diabetes (type 1 or 2), hemoglobin A1c of less than 6.5% is associated with a decreased risk of fetal anomaly compared with hemoglobin A1c of 6.5% or greater. Cardiovascular complications such as hypertension and heart failure occur in 15% of pregnancies and are more common among those with preexisting cardiovascular disease. These patients should receive counseling on maternal and neonatal risk, monitoring, and medication management by specialists in cardiology and maternal fetal medicine.Prepregnancy counseling and care reduce maternal morbidity and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Primary care-based discussion of reproductive goals, immunizations, screening for infections and substance use, and risk-reducing interventions such as folate supplementation can optimize outcomes in individuals contemplating pregnancy.

llm_summary: Preparing for pregnancy before conception can significantly improve health outcomes for both mothers and babies, yet most women of childbearing age have at least one health risk factor that could be improved beforehand. The review examined evidence-based recommendations for prepregnancy care, including taking folic acid supplements to prevent birth defects of the brain and spine, quitting smoking and substance use, getting certain vaccinations, and screening for infections like HIV and syphilis. Key findings showed that folic acid use reduces neural tube defects by about one-third, smoking during pregnancy increases the risk of stillbirth and newborn death by 22 to 46 percent, and unintended pregnancies are associated with higher rates of depression after birth and premature delivery compared to planned pregnancies. Primary care doctors can help people planning to have children by discussing their reproductive goals, recommending vaccinations and health screenings, and suggesting lifestyle changes like weight loss and substance abuse treatment that reduce serious pregnancy complications. These prepregnancy interventions are practical steps that healthcare providers can offer during routine visits to help people achieve healthier pregnancies and better outcomes for their future children.

title: Changes in Upright Hemodynamics Preceding Heart Failure Events and Other Hospitalizations.
abstract: Trends in upright seated pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) with synchronous measurement of weight, blood pressure (BP), and heart rate (HR) have not been compared prior to heart failure events (HFE) and other causes of hospitalization during remote monitoring.We analyzed 24-month data from patients in PROACTIVE-HF trial. Participants (N=456) used the CordellaTM HF daily to measure seated PAP, weight, BP, and HR, all taken and transmitted within minutes. Events that were analyzed included HFE, those potentially related to HF treatment (HF-TRE) and others (non-HFE). Parameters were trended from 60-days before (D-60) to 30-days after (D+30) the day of event (D=0), and their concurrent changes were compared between D-60 and D=0, and D=0 and D+30 using mixed effects model.There were 196 HFE, 276 non-HFE and 66 HF-TRE. Prior to HFE, average mean PAP (mPAP) increased from 27.8±10.9mmHg at D-60 to 32.6±11.2mmHg at D=0 (p<0.001), and decreased to 30.0±12.4mmHg at D+30 (p=0.001). Kinetics of mPAP before HFE differed by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF); mPAP rose by 3.4±6.8mmHg in 2-weeks before HFE in those with LVEF>40%, whereas a similar magnitude (3.1±9.1mmHg) of mPAP rise occurred over 6-weeks before HFE in those with LVEF≤40%. No consistent changes in weight, SBP or HR prior to HFE were observed (p>0.05). Changes in vital signs but not mPAP were noted prior to HF-TRE and non-HFE.Seated mPAP increased weeks in advance of HFE and vital signs did not change consistently before HFE. Differential kinetics of mPAP prior to HFE by the LVEF suggest that an uptrend in seated mPAP may need to be addressed more rapidly in those with LVEF>40%. Changes in vital signs with non-HFE and HF-TRE need further validation.© The Author(s) 2026. Published by Oxford University Press on behalf of the European Society of Cardiology.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether changes in heart pressure measured while sitting upright could predict when heart failure patients would need to be hospitalized, since previous studies had not looked at this specific measurement pattern before hospital admissions. The study followed 456 heart failure patients over two years who used a special device called the Cordella to measure their seated pulmonary artery pressure (the pressure in the blood vessels of the lungs), along with weight, blood pressure, and heart rate, all recorded daily and sent to doctors automatically. The main finding was that average mean pressure in the lungs increased significantly in the weeks before a heart failure hospitalization, rising from about 28 millimeters of mercury sixty days before admission to about 33 millimeters of mercury on the day of admission, but this pattern did not appear before other types of hospitalizations. Importantly, the timing of this pressure increase differed depending on the patient's heart pumping strength, with patients who had stronger heart function showing the pressure rise more quickly over two weeks, while those with weaker heart function showed a similar rise spread over six weeks. title: A unifying model of stem cell dynamics explains age-related methylation patterns across mammals.
abstract: DNA methylation changes are reliable biomarkers of aging, but the driving mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we present SCARLET (Stem Cells and Age-ReLated Epigenetic Trajectories), a parsimonious mathematical model that describes how methylation changes in blood arise and propagate through hematopoietic stem cell divisions. Using a large human cohort, we demonstrate that seemingly distinct age-related methylation patterns can be explained by a unifying mechanistic model. We show that SCARLET captures known drivers of epigenetic aging, with accelerated individuals showing reduced ratios of stem cell pool size to division rate (N/s). Applying SCARLET to methylation data from 11 mammalian species reveals that N/s scales with maximum lifespan, suggesting that evolutionary adjustments to stem cell dynamics, rather than epigenetic maintenance efficiency, drive the previously observed relationship between methylation rates and lifespan. Our findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding epigenetic aging and suggest that stem cell dynamics may be a key driver of aging across mammals.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers have long known that DNA methylation, which is a chemical marking system on our genes that changes as we age, can be used to predict how old someone is, but scientists did not fully understand what causes these changes in the first place. To solve this mystery, a team of scientists created a mathematical model called SCARLET that explains how these age-related chemical markings appear and spread through blood-forming stem cells, which are special cells that divide to create new blood cells throughout our lives. By studying a large group of people and comparing their genetic data, the researchers found that people who age faster have fewer stem cells relative to how often those cells divide, suggesting that the balance between stem cell numbers and division rates is what drives aging at the molecular level. The scientists then tested their model on genetic information from eleven different mammal species and discovered that this stem cell balance ratio directly relates to how long each species naturally lives, meaning that evolution has shaped how quickly different animals age by adjusting their stem cell dynamics rather than improving how well they maintain their genes. These findings provide scientists with a new framework for understanding why we age at the genetic level and suggest that controlling stem cell behavior could be a promising target for future treatments aimed at sl.

title: American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy Technology Status Evaluation Report: tools for benign pancreaticobiliary dilation.
abstract: The American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE) Technology Committee provides reviews of existing, new, or emerging endoscopic technologies that have an impact on the practice of GI endoscopy. An evidence-based methodology is used, with a MEDLINE literature search to identify pertinent clinical studies on the topic and a Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (U.S. Food and Drug Administration Center for Devices and Radiological Health) database search to identify the reported adverse events of a given technology. Both are supplemented by accessing the "related articles" feature of PubMed and by scrutinizing pertinent references cited by the identified studies. Controlled clinical trials are emphasized, but in many cases, data from randomized controlled trials are lacking. In such cases, large case series, preliminary clinical studies, and expert opinion are used. Technical data are gathered from traditional and web-based publications, proprietary publications, and informal communications with pertinent vendors. Technology Status Evaluation Reports are drafted by 1 or 2 members of the ASGE Technology Committee, reviewed and edited by the committee as a whole, and approved by the ASGE Governing Board. When financial guidance is indicated, the most recent coding data and list prices at the time of publication are provided. For this review, the MEDLINE database was searched through March 2025 for articles related to pancreaticobiliary stricture management. Technology Status Evaluation Reports are scientific reviews provided solely for educational and informational purposes. They are not rules and should not be construed as establishing a legal standard of care or as encouraging, advocating, requiring, or discouraging any particular treatment or payment for such treatment.Copyright © 2026 American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. llm_summary: The American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy created this report to evaluate tools and techniques used to treat blockages in the pancreas and bile ducts, which are important tubes that help with digestion. The researchers searched medical databases and safety reports through March 2025 to find all published studies about treating these blockages, focusing on controlled trials when available but also including smaller studies and expert opinions when needed. They gathered information from scientific publications, manufacturer data, and conversations with medical device companies to understand both the benefits and risks of different treatment tools. This report serves as an educational guide to help doctors understand the current state of available technologies for treating pancreatic and bile duct problems, though it is not meant to establish rules or requirements for how doctors must treat patients. The findings provide doctors and patients with evidence-based information to make informed decisions about which treatment options might work best for benign pancreaticobiliary dilation, a condition where these important digestive tubes become abnormally widened.

title: Patterns of adjuvant intracavitary instillation and recurrence after endoscopic management of upper tract urothelial carcinoma.
abstract: Endoscopic management offers acceptable oncologic control in select patients with upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) while preserving renal function. Adjuvant intracavitary treatment with chemotherapy or Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) has been proposed to reduce recurrence risk. We aimed to evaluate the impact of adjuvant intracavitary treatment on ipsilateral UTUC recurrence following endoscopic management.We queried a multi-institutional cohort of patients who underwent endoscopic management for UTUC. Treatment groups were defined as no instillation, single post-operative instillation, or multiple instillations. Ipsilateral UTUC recurrence-free survival (RFS) was estimated using Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models evaluated factors associated with recurrence.A total of 599 renal units, of which 43 received single instillation and 86 multiple instillations, in 334 patients treated endoscopically for UTUC were analyzed. The median follow-up time for patients without recurrence was 12 months (IQR 4-33). Multiple adjuvant instillations of any intracavitary treatment were associated with a significantly improved RFS (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.34-0.79), whereas a single instillation was not associated with a significant reduction in recurrence (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.37-1.13). This association between multiple instillations and improved RFS remained significant after adjustment for clinical risk factors, including tumor grade (adjusted HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.16-0.81), and was confirmed in sensitivity analyses limited to patients with primary UTUC (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.26-0.85).Multiple intracavitary instillations of BCG or chemotherapy after endoscopic management of UTUC were associated with longer ipsilateral RFS. These findings suggest a potential benefit of repeated instillations and warrant prospective validation.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether giving patients repeated doses of cancer-fighting drugs or immune-boosting treatments directly into the kidney area after minimally invasive surgery could help prevent cancer from coming back in patients with upper urinary tract cancer, a type of kidney cancer. The study looked at nearly 600 kidney units from 334 patients across multiple hospitals who had undergone endoscopic management, which is a less invasive surgical approach that preserves kidney function, and tracked how many patients experienced cancer recurrence over time. Patients who received multiple instillations, meaning several rounds of treatment delivered directly into the surgical area, had significantly better outcomes with a 48 percent lower risk of cancer returning compared to those who received no treatment, while a single treatment dose did not show the same protective benefit. These findings suggest that repeating the instillation treatments after surgery may help patients with upper urinary tract cancer avoid having their cancer come back in the same kidney. The researchers emphasized that while these results are promising, larger prospective studies where patients are randomly assigned to different treatment groups are needed to confirm these benefits before changing standard medical practice.

title: Elasticity-guided tumor resection: applying biomechanical information to neurosurgical practice.
abstract: Tumor stiffness and adhesion are decisive factors in neurosurgical strategy, yet they remain absent from standard planning and navigation. Advances in biomechanics allow these properties to be measured and mapped across modalities: magnetic resonance elastography for preoperative stiffness and adhesion, intraoperative ultrasound elastography for real-time updates, and rheometry as biological ground truth. Emerging frameworks could integrate these measurements with artificial intelligence and multimodal neuroimaging to produce probabilistic maps of tumor consistency and brain-tumor interface quality. We define this concept as elasticity-guided neurosurgery: the incorporation of biomechanical parameters into surgical decision-making to improve safety, efficiency, and personalization. By transforming tactile impressions into actionable data, elasticity-guided neurosurgery could represent a paradigm shift toward more information-driven neurosurgical oncology.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Tumor stiffness and how well a tumor sticks to surrounding brain tissue are important factors that surgeons currently cannot measure before or during brain tumor operations, even though these properties affect how safely and completely a tumor can be removed. Researchers propose a new approach called elasticity-guided neurosurgery that uses advanced imaging and measurement tools to map out tumor stiffness before surgery using magnetic resonance elastography, update these measurements in real time during surgery using ultrasound elastography, and verify the accuracy of these measurements using laboratory testing. By combining these biomechanical measurements with artificial intelligence and other brain imaging techniques, doctors could create detailed maps showing exactly where the tumor is stiff or soft and how strongly it adheres to healthy brain tissue. This information-driven approach could help surgeons make better decisions during operations, reduce damage to healthy brain tissue, complete tumor removal more effectively, and personalize treatment plans for each patient based on their specific tumor characteristics. The next step is to integrate these biomechanical measurements into actual surgical practice and demonstrate that this new method improves patient outcomes compared to traditional surgery guided only by a surgeon's sense of touch and visual inspection.

title: Empiric and Trigger-Guided Superior Vena Cava Isolation in AF Ablation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Superior vena cava isolation (SVCI) is performed as an adjunct to pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) for atrial fibrillation, yet whether an empiric or trigger-guided strategy is preferable remains uncertain. Prior meta-analyses have been largely restricted to index procedures in paroxysmal AF and have not explicitly stratified by ablation strategy. We sought to address these gaps through a systematic review of available randomized evidence.Major databases were searched through November 2025 for RCTs comparing PVI+SVCI versus PVI alone. Trials were stratified by strategy: empiric SVCI (performed irrespective of SVC ectopy) or trigger-guided SVCI (performed only upon demonstrated SVC triggers). The primary outcome was atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence (≥30 s) beyond the blanking period. Random-effects models, pre-specified subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and GRADE certainty assessment were performed.Eight RCTs (n = 1231) were included; most enrolled paroxysmal AF, while two incorporated non-paroxysmal AF subtypes and one evaluated repeat ablation procedures. Overall, SVCI+PVI significantly reduced recurrence versus PVI alone (97/604 vs. 135/627; RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61-0.97; p = 0.03; I2 = 0%). On stratified analysis, empiric SVCI demonstrated a significant recurrence reduction (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53-0.92; p = 0.01; I2 = 0%), while trigger-guided SVCI did not reach statistical significance (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.37-1.74; p = 0.57; I2 = 52%). In paroxysmal AF (n = 1038), adjunctive SVCI significantly reduced recurrence compared with PVI alone (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.52-0.90; p = 0.01; I2 = 0%). Fluoroscopy time was longer with SVCI; total procedure duration was comparable. Major complications were infrequent but numerically higher with SVCI+PVI (15/604 vs. 7/627; RR 1.96, 95% CI 0.87-4.38; p = 0.10). Meta-regression identified no significant effect modifiers. GRADE certainty was high for overall and empiric analyses, and moderate for trigger-guided SVCI.Empiric SVCI significantly reduced AT/AF recurrence as an adjunct to PVI, while trigger-guided SVCI did not demonstrate a significant benefit. These findings suggest SVC isolation confers benefit independent of prior trigger documentation, supporting the role of empiric SVCI as an adjunct to AF ablation.© 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether adding superior vena cava isolation, which is a procedure that treats an extra source of irregular heartbeats in a vein near the heart, improves outcomes when combined with the standard pulmonary vein isolation procedure for atrial fibrillation, a common heart rhythm disorder. The team reviewed eight randomized controlled trials, which are the gold standard type of medical studies, involving 1,231 patients to compare two different approaches: performing the extra isolation procedure on all patients versus only performing it when doctors detected abnormal electrical activity from that vein. The results showed that adding the superior vena cava isolation procedure reduced the return of irregular heartbeats by about 30 percent overall, with the strongest benefit seen when the procedure was done routinely on all patients rather than only when triggered by detected abnormal activity. These findings suggest that doctors should consider performing superior vena cava isolation as a standard part of atrial fibrillation treatment rather than waiting to see if a patient shows signs of problematic electrical activity from that vein. While the procedure did require longer radiation exposure during the operation and showed a trend toward slightly more complications, the overall safety profile remained acceptable and the benefits appeared.

title: Arteriovenous fistula creation results in cardiac dysfunction and remodeling in a uremic pig model.
abstract: The arteriovenous fistula (AVF) is required for hemodialysis in end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). AVF creation results in compensatory cardiovascular hemodynamics, which are subsequently associated with cardiac remodeling. Relatedly, cardiovascular mortality and morbidity are elevated in ESKD patients, which worsens in dialysis patients. Currently, no suitable uremic large animal models exist to investigate the mechanisms of AVF-induced cardiac remodeling. This study aims to characterize cardiovascular changes secondary to AVF creation, supported by percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA), in a uremic pig model. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) was induced via renal embolization, followed by AVF creation 28 days later. AVF stenosis was alleviated 28 days thereafter via PTA, and cardiac MRI was performed at 14-, 28-, and 42-days post-PTA. Increased end-diastolic volumes were observed in both ventricles, while systolic function was preserved. LV stroke volume and blood flow through the aorta, pulmonary artery, and vena cava were also increased. In perivascular areas of the LV, senescence markers showed increased p16 expression and decreased p21 expression. The LV showed perivascular fibrosis, with increased cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area, reduced collagen-type IV expression, and MMP2 activity, possibly not driven by TGF-β/CTGF/pSMAD signaling. However, CD4+ or CD68+ cell LV infiltration or inflammatory polarization of resident macrophages were unchanged. In conclusion, AVF creation modified left and right ventricular function and increased peripheral flow, potentially mediated by cellular senescence and fibrosis, resulting in progressive cardiac remodeling. This model may be used to evaluate mechanisms of AVF induced cardiac disease and potentially investigate the efficacy of senolytics and anti-fibrotic agents.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how arteriovenous fistulas, which are surgically created connections between arteries and veins needed for kidney dialysis patients, affect the heart in a pig model of kidney disease. The study involved inducing chronic kidney disease in pigs through a procedure that blocked blood flow to the kidneys, then creating an arteriovenous fistula and treating any narrowing that developed with an angioplasty procedure, while monitoring heart function with imaging scans over six weeks. The researchers found that the fistula caused the heart's chambers to enlarge and the heart to pump more blood overall, while also triggering cellular aging and scarring in the heart tissue. These changes suggest that the increased blood flow demands from the fistula lead to progressive heart damage through mechanisms involving cellular senescence, which is when cells stop dividing and functioning properly, and fibrosis, which is excessive scar tissue formation. This pig model provides researchers with a valuable tool to test whether new treatments targeting cellular aging and scar tissue formation could prevent or reverse the heart damage that commonly affects dialysis patients.

title: Consensus Recommendations for CAR T-Cell Administration in Adult Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: a Modified Delphi Study.
abstract: The use of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is increasing in adult B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), with three commercially available CD19 CAR T cell products. Several key clinical questions related to best practices for CAR T cell administration in this population exist, and limited prospective randomized trials have been conducted to fill these knowledge gaps. Thus, to help guide clinical practice, we conducted a modified Delphi study to develop and validate consensus recommendations on the administration of commercially available CAR T cell therapy for adults with B-ALL. Consensus panelists (n= 9) included Principal Investigators (PIs) from Real World Outcomes Collaborative of CAR T Cell Therapy in Adult ALL (ROCCA) consortium sites and were selected based on expertise and CAR T center volume. Final panel consensus recommendations were distributed for rating by the remaining PIs from ROCCA consortium sites, which served as the validation group (n=27). Consensus topics included patient selection, bridging and pre-CAR T leukemia staging, lymphodepletion and CAR T treatment setting, specific toxicity prevention and management, post-CAR T response assessment and disease monitoring, and the role of consolidation and/or maintenance therapies following CAR T cell therapy. Initially, 58 recommendation statements were evaluated for consensus. After two panel meetings, a total of 34 statements achieved consensus rating among the expert panel. After rating by the validation group, all but one recommendation statement continued to meet consensus, for a total of 33 consensus recommendation statements on the administration of CAR T cell therapy in adult B-ALL.Copyright © 2026 American Society of Hematology.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how to best use a newer cancer treatment called CAR T cell therapy, which involves taking immune cells from patients, modifying them in a lab to fight leukemia, and putting them back into the body, because three different versions of this treatment are now available but doctors lack clear guidelines on how to use them. The study used a modified Delphi approach, which means experts answered questions in multiple rounds to reach agreement, with nine leading specialists from major cancer centers first developing recommendations and then twenty-seven additional doctors from similar centers rating and validating those recommendations. After two rounds of expert discussion, the panel agreed on thirty-three practical recommendations covering important topics like which patients should receive the treatment, how to prepare patients beforehand, how to manage side effects, and whether additional therapies should follow the initial CAR T cell treatment. These consensus recommendations provide doctors with evidence-based guidance to help them make consistent decisions about CAR T cell therapy for adult patients with a type of blood cancer called acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The study shows that even without large randomized trials comparing different approaches, experienced specialists can work together to create useful clinical guidelines that can help standardize care across different cancer treatment centers.

title: Post-dural Puncture Headache in Dural Puncture Epidural and Combined Spinal-Epidural Using 24- and 25-Gauge Needles Versus Conventional Epidural Labor Analgesia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract: Compared to standard labor epidurals, placement of a dural puncture epidural (DPE) has been shown to improve labor analgesia efficacy, speed onset of analgesia, and decrease failure rates. However, there is a concern of increased post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) risk. A 25-gauge or larger spinal needle is typically needed for a DPE to have improved efficacy over a standard epidural. A prior meta-analysis comparing combined spinal-epidurals (CSEs) with epidurals did not identify a difference in PDPH rates, but many of the included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) used smaller diameter (27-29 gauge) spinal needles. This systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs evaluates headache frequency following CSE or DPE labor analgesia techniques with 24- or 25-gauge spinal needles.Medline, EMBASE, Scopus, Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects, Web of Science Core Collection, and Cochrane databases were searched on May 7, 2024, for RCTs comparing either DPE or CSE techniques using 24- or 25-gauge spinal needles with epidural labor analgesia. The primary outcome was headache. The risk-of-bias 2 tool was used to assess bias. The odds ratio (OR) was the chosen effect size using binomial family Bayesian estimation. The reference category for estimation was the conventional epidural technique group.Encompassing 3278 patients, 1765 (53.8%) received labor epidurals, 971 (29.6%) received DPEs, and 542 (16.5%) received CSEs. The rate of headaches in both groups was low, with headache rates of CSE/DPE and epidural groups (0.59% vs 0.34%), respectively. Headache was a secondary outcome in all the RCTs. In 10 of the 16 RCTs (62.5%), no patients of 1428 (0%; 95% credible interval [CI], 0.00-0.25) reported a headache. A total of nine (0.6%) headaches were reported in the DPE/CSE patients (denominator 1513) and six (0.3%) headaches were reported in the traditional epidural patients (denominator 1765). The posterior distribution of the treatment effect (θ) showed that the log OR of 0.35 favored the control group as having fewer events, but the number of events was rare, and the 95% CI was wide (-0.49 to 1.22).Headache was a rare event in both groups. Although these results are reassuring that either technique is clinically safe, they should be interpreted cautiously. A large RCT examining PDPH as the primary outcome with long-term follow-up is needed to more precisely determine if placement of a DPE or CSE with a 24- or 25-gauge spinal needle increases the risk of PDPH.Copyright © 2026 International Anesthesia Research Society.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether certain labor pain relief techniques that involve puncturing the membrane around the spinal cord increase the risk of headaches compared to standard epidural anesthesia, which is a common pain relief method used during childbirth. The study analyzed data from sixteen previous clinical trials involving over three thousand patients to compare headache rates between two newer techniques called dural puncture epidural and combined spinal-epidural, which use slightly larger needles, against traditional epidural pain relief. The results showed that headaches were extremely rare in both groups, with less than one percent of patients experiencing headaches regardless of which pain relief method they received. Although these findings suggest that all three techniques are safe to use during labor, the researchers cautioned that the number of headaches was so small that it is difficult to draw firm conclusions about whether the newer techniques truly carry the same risk as traditional epidurals. The researchers recommend that a large, well-designed study specifically focused on measuring headaches as the main outcome is needed to provide clearer answers about the safety of these newer pain relief techniques.

title: Promises of reprogramming-induced rejuvenation.
abstract: Reprogramming-induced rejuvenation (RIR) reverses cellular aging by transiently engaging early reprogramming states without full dedifferentiation. This review examines current developments in the molecular mechanisms, technological advances, and tissue-specific applications of RIR. Recent mechanistic insights highlight persisting questions in timing, heterogeneity, and pathways engaged in the epigenetic response. New technological advances have expanded RIR modalities beyond traditional Yamanaka factors to include mRNA-based delivery, CRISPRa, and chemical cocktails, while high-throughput screening platforms are systematically identifying novel rejuvenation factors with improved safety profiles. Recent tissue-specific applications demonstrate functional restoration across brain, liver, intestine, cardiovascular, and epithelial systems through reversal of cellular senescence, reduction of DNA damage and epigenetic age, and enhanced regenerative capacity. However, clinical translation faces challenges including narrow therapeutic windows, incomplete mechanistic understanding, and limited biomarker standardization. We discuss how single-cell technologies, computational prediction tools, and systematic in vivo testing may advance RIR toward geroscience therapies for age-related diseases.Copyright © 2026. llm_summary: Researchers are studying a new approach called reprogramming-induced rejuvenation that aims to reverse aging in cells by briefly returning them to an earlier state without completely transforming them into different cell types. Scientists have developed several new methods to trigger this rejuvenation process, moving beyond the original techniques to include messenger RNA delivery, genetic editing tools called CRISPR, and chemical combinations that work together to restore youthful cell function. Early experiments show promising results across different body systems including the brain, liver, heart, and skin, where cells have regained the ability to repair damage, reduce signs of aging, and regenerate more effectively. While these findings are exciting, researchers still face significant obstacles before this approach can be used to treat patients, including understanding exactly how long the treatment window lasts, developing reliable ways to measure whether rejuvenation is working, and ensuring the process is safe enough for human use. Moving forward, scientists plan to use advanced cell analysis tools and computer prediction models to better understand how rejuvenation works and to test these approaches more thoroughly in living organisms before attempting to treat age-related diseases in people.

title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated lymphocytic colitis in a patient with metastatic melanoma.
abstract: We describe the case of a man in his 60s with metastatic melanoma on encorafenib/binimetinib and nivolumab/relatlimab, with a history of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-induced acute interstitial nephritis, who presented with acute-onset nausea, vomiting and profuse watery diarrhoea. Investigations excluded infectious causes, and flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy demonstrated lymphocytic colitis. His symptoms persisted despite discontinuation of Braftovi-Mektovi (BRAF-MEK) therapy and required escalation of corticosteroid therapy and budesonide initiation. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of differentiating ICI-mediated colitis from adverse events of targeted therapy and underscores the importance of endoscopic and histological confirmation in guiding treatment.© BMJ Publishing Group Limited 2026. llm_summary: A man in his sixties with advanced melanoma, a serious skin cancer that had spread to other parts of his body, developed severe stomach and bowel problems while being treated with multiple cancer drugs including immune checkpoint inhibitors, which are medications that help the body's immune system fight cancer. Doctors investigated his symptoms of nausea, vomiting, and severe watery diarrhea by ruling out infections and then using a camera to look inside his colon and take tissue samples for examination. The tissue samples showed that his colon was inflamed due to an accumulation of white blood cells, a condition called lymphocytic colitis that was likely caused by his cancer medications rather than an infection. Even after stopping one of his cancer drug combinations, his symptoms continued and required stronger doses of steroid medications, which reduce inflammation, along with a special anti-inflammatory medicine taken directly in the colon. This case demonstrates how important it is for doctors to use both camera examinations and tissue biopsies to correctly identify the cause of bowel problems in cancer patients, since similar symptoms can come from different sources and require different treatments.

title: Endoscopic Ultrasound-Guided Franseen Fine-Needle Biopsy for Solid Pancreatic Lesions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Accurate tissue acquisition (TA) of solid pancreatic lesions is essential for guiding treatment with endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy (EUS-FNB) being the preferred method. Among FNB designs, the three-pronged Franseen-tip needle demonstrates strong diagnostic performance, though direct head-to-head comparisons with other FNB designs remain limited.This meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251123856). Eligible studies enrolled patients with solid pancreatic lesions who underwent EUS-guided FNB, directly compared the Franseen-tip with other FNB needles. Six databases were systematically searched through July 2025, and study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment (QUADAS-2 tool) were performed independently by two reviewers. Pooled estimates were generated using random-effects and bivariate hierarchical models.Sixteen studies (2,010 Franseen vs. 2,811 comparator) were included. Bivariate analysis showed that sensitivity and specificity of the Franseen needle were comparable to newer-generation comparator needles (sensitivity 91.3% vs. 94.0%; specificity 99.99% vs. 99.15%), whereas older-generation needles demonstrated lower sensitivity (80.8%) and inferior discriminatory performance (Negative Likelihood Ratio [LR⁻] 0.19 vs. 0.09). Diagnostic accuracy was higher with the Franseen needle (RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01-1.14; I2 = 69%). Sample adequacy was similar overall (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.95-1.14) but superior to older-generation needles (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.02-1.41) and in lesions > 30 mm (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.02-1.28, I2 = 81.2%). The Franseen needle achieved nominally strong diagnostic performance (DOR 116.6), although small-study effects were observed. Primary procedural outcomes were comparable between Franseen and comparator needles, including technical success (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.98-1.02) and histological core procurement (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.92-1.17). The Franseen needle had fewer low-cellularity samples (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.45-0.69) and lower specimen bloodiness (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.25-0.90) but a slightly higher overall adverse event rate (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.06-1.57).The Franseen needle provides superior diagnostic accuracy and sample adequacy compared to older-generation FNB needles with comparable performance to newer-generation designs. llm_summary: Researchers examined a needle tool called the Franseen-tip needle, which doctors use during a special ultrasound procedure to collect tissue samples from pancreatic tumors to help diagnose cancer. They reviewed sixteen studies involving over four thousand patients to compare how well the Franseen needle worked compared to other needle designs used for the same purpose. The Franseen needle provided better accuracy than older needle designs and performed just as well as newer needles, while also producing cleaner tissue samples with less blood contamination. However, the Franseen needle was associated with slightly more side effects or complications during the procedure, though other main outcomes like success rates remained similar across all needle types. These findings suggest that the Franseen needle is a reliable choice for doctors collecting tissue samples from pancreatic lesions, though further research may help clarify the reasons for the increased complications.

title: Chronic PM2.5 Exposure Is Associated With Invasively Assessed Coronary Endothelial Dysfunction.
abstract: Coronary endothelial dysfunction (ED) represents an early stage of coronary artery disease (CAD). Several factors may induce ED. Air pollution, more specifically particulate matter <2.5 μm (PM2.5), has emerged as a major nontraditional cardiovascular risk factor contributing to early vascular injury, but its impact on coronary ED remains poorly defined.In this study, we sought to identify an association between chronic PM2.5 exposure and epicardial endothelial dysfunction (EED) determined by means of invasive coronary vasoreactivity testing, the criterion standard technique to assess EED.This observational study included prospectively enrolled patients with angina and nonobstructive CAD who underwent coronary reactivity testing at Mayo Clinic from 2000 to 2023. Residential addresses at the time of testing were geocoded to derive monthly PM2.5 exposure at a 0.01° × 0.01° spatial resolution, averaged over the 2 years preceding testing. EED was defined as percentage change of less than -20% in coronary artery diameter in response to acetylcholine infusion. Associations between continuous PM2.5 and EED were assessed according to a generalized propensity score with a gamma-distributed model to derive stabilized inverse probability weights, applied in multivariable logistic regression.A total of 1,485 patients with a median age of 51.7 years (Q1-Q3: 42.7-60.1 years) were included in the analysis. Individuals exposed to PM2.5 above environmental protection agency standards (9 μg/m3) were younger and had less cardiovascular comorbidities, although they had worse lipid profiles. In weighted multivariable logistic regression, each 1 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 was associated with increased odds of EED (OR: 1.078; 95% CI: 1.021-1.139; P = 0.007), adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and cardiovascular comorbidities.Chronic PM2.5 exposure is associated with epicardial coronary ED, suggesting a potential biological link between PM2.5 and CAD.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. title: Vedolizumab for stricturing Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum - an international multicenter cohort study.
abstract: Crohn's disease (CD) frequently progresses to stricturing complications. Anti-stricture therapies are lacking, and anti-inflammatory therapies are hence the mainstay of medical treatment. However, data on the efficacy of vedolizumab in stricturing CD are not available. We therefore aimed to assess outcomes of vedolizumab in this setting.We evaluated adult patients who received vedolizumab within 6 months of imaging-confirmed symptomatic ileal stricturing CD (CONSTRICT criteria) in a multicenter observational cohort study. Images were centrally read by an expert radiologist with experience in IBD imaging. Outcomes were rates of intervention (composite endpoint for endoscopic balloon dilation (EBD) or surgery during follow-up), EBD, surgery, obstructive symptoms, and vedolizumab persistence.Forty-four patients were included (61% female, median age 52 years); 64% had an anastomotic stricture; 84% had received prior biologics. Median follow-up was 17 months. Cumulative intervention rates were 23%, 44% and 50% of patients at 12, 24 and 48 months, respectively. 52% of patients reported symptom resolution, of whom 26% subsequently developed symptoms during follow-up. Vedolizumab persistence was 82%, 74% and 59% at 12, 24 and 48 months. Anastomotic stricture was inversely associated with intervention (HR0.21, P = 0.012) and surgery (HR0.11, P = 0.013). Higher obstructive symptom index (HR4.47, P = 0.040) and degree of prestenotic bowel dilatation (HR1.09, P = 0.030) were associated with recurrent obstructive symptoms. Elevated baseline CRP was associated with vedolizumab discontinuation (HR1.96, P = 0.014).Vedolizumab appears to be a treatment option in CD patients with terminal ileal strictures, especially in patients with anastomotic strictures, without obstructive symptoms or prestenotic bowel dilatation. llm_summary: Crohn's disease, a serious digestive condition that causes inflammation in the intestines, often develops strictures, which are narrow sections that can block food from passing through and cause painful symptoms. Researchers examined forty-four patients across multiple hospitals who received a medication called vedolizumab, which reduces inflammation in the digestive system, to see if it could help people with strictures in the terminal ileum, the last part of the small intestine. About half of the patients experienced relief from their obstructive symptoms, and most patients continued taking the medication, though over four years about half of the patients eventually needed procedures like balloon dilation or surgery to open up the strictures. The study found that vedolizumab worked better for patients whose strictures were at surgical connection sites and worse for patients who had severe swelling before the stricture or high levels of inflammation markers in their blood. While vedolizumab appears to be a helpful treatment option for certain patients with stricturing Crohn's disease, doctors need to conduct larger controlled studies to confirm these results before making it a standard recommendation.

title: Leading the Way: Cellular and Gene Therapies in Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Transforming Functional Outcomes Through Regenerative Innovation.
abstract: Regenerative rehabilitation combines rehabilitation science with regenerative medicine approaches to achieve synergistic and more effective outcomes. Within the field of regenerative medicine, there has been a growing number of cell and gene therapies (CGTs) that are either approved for clinical use or actively undergoing clinical trials. Many of these therapies-especially those targeting neurological and musculoskeletal disorders-use functional outcomes as primary or secondary endpoints, prompting discussion about how physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R) physicians can support the integration of CGTs into clinical care. In this perspective article, we explain why physicians specializing in PM&R could take a leading role in advancing the clinical translation of CGTs. Currently, CGTs are not confined to a single medical specialty, presenting a timely opportunity for PM&R-working collaboratively with neurology, hematology, and other disciplines-to assume greater leadership and influence the development and implementation of these transformative treatments. To our knowledge, this is the first publication within PM&R literature to emphasize the importance of our specialty serving as a leader and driving force in the adoption of these therapies.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. llm_summary: Regenerative rehabilitation combines physical therapy and rehabilitation science with regenerative medicine, which uses the body's own healing abilities to repair damaged tissues and organs, to create better treatment outcomes for patients. Physical medicine and rehabilitation physicians, who are doctors specializing in helping patients recover function and mobility, are well-positioned to lead the way in bringing cell and gene therapies, which are treatments that use living cells or genetic material to treat disease, into everyday clinical practice. Many of these cell and gene therapies are already approved for use or being tested in clinical trials, particularly for treating brain, nerve, and muscle disorders, and they measure success by looking at how well patients can move and function in daily life. The authors argue that rehabilitation specialists should take a leadership role in developing and implementing these new therapies by working together with other medical specialties like neurology and hematology, since no single medical field currently owns this area. This perspective article is the first in rehabilitation medicine literature to call for physical medicine and rehabilitation physicians to become the driving force behind adopting these transformative treatments that could significantly improve patient outcomes.

title: Cross-Vendor Validation of Proton Density Fat Fraction and T1 Mapping Using a Combined Proton Density Fat Fraction-T1 Phantom.
abstract: In chronic liver disease, fat and fibroinflammatory changes often coexist. However, their biomarkers, proton density fat fraction (PDFF) and T1, are typically assessed separately. Their reproducibility under mutual confounding remains unclear.To assess multicenter, multi-vendor reproducibility of confounder-corrected chemical shift-encoded (CSE)-MRI-based PDFF mapping and MOLLI-based T1 mapping using a combined PDFF-T1 phantom.Prospective phantom study.Commercial PDFF-T1 Phantom (Model 725) with varying PDFF (0%-30%) and T1 (200-1400 ms) values.1.5 T and 3 T multi-echo, three-dimensional spoiled-gradient-echo (SGRE) sequence for PDFF mapping, and MOLLI sequence (5(3)3 acquisition scheme) using two-dimensional SGRE readouts for T1 mapping across four centers and vendors.PDFF and T1 maps were acquired using standardized protocols. PDFF maps were reconstructed locally, while T1 maps were generated using a centralized algorithm. All maps were quantitatively analyzed by a single radiologist using standardized region-of-interest placement. Phantom temporal stability was assessed at one center across five sessions over 9 months (baseline, retest, 1 week, 6 and 9 months).Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), reproducibility coefficients (RDC), and linear regression analysis were used. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.PDFF showed overall excellent reproducibility (ICC = 0.987, RDC = 3.7%), with increased variability at higher T1 values (RDC up to 7.9% at T1 = 1400 ms). T1 mapping showed good reproducibility in the absence of fat (RDC 16-161 ms at PDFF = 0%), but moderate to poor reproducibility in the presence of fat, with RDC increasing up to 1553 ms at PDFF 30%. Temporal stability was excellent ICC ≥ 0.998 for both PDFF and T1, and RDC of 1.1%-1.3% for PDFF and 52-57 ms for T1.This phantom study demonstrated high reproducibility of PDFF, whereas T1 reproducibility deteriorated at higher fat and T1 levels, underscoring the need for fat-corrected T1 mapping for reliable assessment of fibroinflammatory changes.N/A.Stage 1.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined how well different hospital machines and manufacturers can measure two important markers of liver disease: fat content and tissue stiffness, which often appear together in patients with chronic liver problems. The team used a special test phantom, which is a standardized object designed to mimic liver tissue with known amounts of fat and stiffness, and scanned it across four different medical centers using machines from different vendors at two different field strengths. The results showed that measuring fat content was highly reliable across all machines with only small variations, but measuring tissue stiffness became less accurate when fat was present, with errors growing larger as both fat and stiffness levels increased. This finding is important because doctors need accurate measurements of both fat and stiffness to properly diagnose and monitor liver disease, and the current methods for measuring stiffness may not work well in fatty livers. The researchers concluded that while fat measurement is ready for clinical use, improved methods for measuring tissue stiffness that account for the presence of fat are needed before these tests can be reliably used to assess inflammation and scarring in patients with liver disease.

title: Risk Factors and Social Determinants of Health for Retinal Artery Occlusion in the National Institutes of Health All of Us Program.
abstract: Previous studies have identified inequities in stroke epidemiology. Given retinal artery occlusion (RAO) is a stroke equivalent, we investigated risk factors and social determinants of health (SDOH) associated with RAO.This was a retrospective case-control study. The case group consisted of all patients diagnosed with RAO in the National Institutes of Health All of Us database from November 1992 to November 2020. The control group consisted of all patients without a diagnosis of RAO during that time frame. Associations of predictors of RAO were estimated using logistic regression models.There were 384 patients with an RAO diagnosis and 328,639 participants in the non-RAO group. Median age at RAO diagnosis was 66 years (interquartile range [IQR] 57-72). Median age at study was 74 years (IQR 67-81) for the RAO group and 58 years (IQR 42-69) for the control group. Age- and sex-adjusted multivariable analysis revealed factors positively associated with RAO, including older age {odds ratio [OR]: 2.19 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.01-2.39), P < 0.001}, male sex (OR: 1.54 [95% CI: 1.25-1.89], P < 0.001), Black race (OR: 1.62 [95% CI: 1.24-2.09], P < 0.001), military/Veterans Affairs insurance (OR: 2.44 [95% CI: 1.61-3.66], P < 0.001), and Medicaid (OR: 1.51 [95% CI: 1.06-2.15], P = 0.022). Having a college/advanced degree (OR: 0.76 [95% CI: 0.59-0.98], P = 0.031), annual household income between $50,000 and $100,000 (OR: 0.72 [95% CI: 0.52-0.98], P = 0.035), and annual household income between $100,000 and $200,000 (OR: 0.48 [95% CI: 0.32-0.70], P < 0.001) were protective against RAO.These findings confirm previously described associations between RAO and cardiovascular comorbidities and identified novel associations between RAO and SDOH, including Black race and Medicaid insurance. llm_summary: Researchers examined why some people suffer from retinal artery occlusion, a serious eye condition caused by a blocked blood vessel in the retina that is similar to a stroke, because previous studies have shown that certain groups of people experience strokes at different rates. The study looked back at medical records from a large national database of over 328,000 people, comparing 384 patients who had been diagnosed with retinal artery occlusion to those who had not experienced this condition between 1992 and 2020. The results showed that older age, being male, being Black, and having Medicaid insurance or military insurance were all linked to a higher risk of retinal artery occlusion, while having a college degree or earning between $50,000 and $200,000 per year were protective factors that lowered the risk. These findings reveal that social and economic factors, not just medical conditions, play an important role in who develops this serious eye condition, suggesting that healthcare providers should pay special attention to patients from disadvantaged groups who may be at higher risk. Future research should explore why these social and economic differences exist and what steps can be taken to prevent retinal artery occl.

title: Vagal Nerve Stimulation in Patients With Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction: The ANTHEM-HFrEF Trial.
abstract: Vagal nerve stimulation (VNS) may reverse autonomic dysfunction in heart failure (HF). This paper describes results from a pivotal trial, while addressing challenges investigators face following premature trial termination.We report VNS actions in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction and investigators response to early discontinuation.Randomization was 2:1 to VNS or control. Entry required NYHA functional class II or III, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤35%, and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide ≥800 pg/mL. Primary efficacy endpoint was time to cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization. Secondary endpoints included LVEF, 6-minute walk distance, and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire. Adaptive sample sizing targeted ≤1,000 patients. P values are 1-sided.After randomizing 532 patients, the sponsor terminated enrollment, unrelated to futility or efficacy. The primary efficacy endpoint was not met (HR: 0.84; 95% CI: 0.62-1.12; P = 0.115). The primary safety endpoint achieved 96.7% freedom from procedure- or device-related serious adverse events. Autonomic engagement persisted long-term. Findings were favorable, although inconclusive, for the primary endpoint, HF hospitalization, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire, NYHA functional class, and 6-minute walk distance. LVEF was unchanged. The still-blinded investigators, seeking to extend data reporting while maintaining scientific integrity, had prespecified a single exploratory outcomes-symptoms win ratio. Results were favorable although merely hypothesis-generating, given primary endpoint neutrality, multiplicity, subjective bias, and marginal statistical significance.Early termination outside Data Monitoring Committee processes challenged investigators to maintain scientific and ethical integrity and transparency, while optimizing data reporting. The underpowered primary endpoint was neutral. Data documented feasibility, safety, and autonomic engagement. Trends favoring outcomes, symptoms, and function were inconclusive although hypothesis-generating, Importantly, we provide guidance for investigators facing trial discontinuation.
