llm_summary: Shoulder injury related to vaccine administration, or SIRVA, is a rare but serious condition where people experience persistent shoulder pain and limited movement that starts within two days of receiving a vaccine injection in the upper arm. This injury happens when the vaccine is accidentally injected into the wrong area of the shoulder, such as the space above the shoulder joint, which can trigger inflammation, tissue damage, or infection in that region. While most medical literature focuses on preventing SIRVA and catching it early through proper injection techniques, this study presents a case where a patient tried many non-surgical treatments without success and eventually needed surgery to find relief. The authors developed a systematic approach using detailed patient history and physical examination to help doctors diagnose SIRVA correctly and manage it effectively before complications become permanent. This case study highlights that surgery should be considered as a treatment option for patients with SIRVA who have exhausted all other treatment methods, even though very little medical information currently exists about surgical approaches to this condition.

title: A multisociety consensus statement on a new common definition and diagnostic criteria for PSVD or NCPF.
abstract: Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension has historically been described using heterogeneous and region-specific terminology, such as idiopathic portal hypertension (IPH), non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis (NCPF), obliterative portal venopathy, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia, leading to substantial variability in diagnosis, reporting, and international research collaboration. Differences in guideline definitions from major societies (AASLD, EASL, and APASL), together with the presence of characteristic histologic lesions in patients without clinically overt portal hypertension, have further complicated disease classification. To address these challenges, a large, multisociety, international initiative was convened to harmonize nomenclature and diagnostic criteria. Representatives from liver, pathology, and pediatric hepatology societies across the Americas, Europe, and Asia participated in a structured consensus process that included specialized working groups and external Delphi validation. The initiative produced a globally harmonized and implementable diagnostic framework. Consensus was reached that the terms porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder (PSVD) and NCPF may be used interchangeably when identical diagnostic criteria are applied, and that they should be written as PSVD or NCPF. The diagnosis was defined as fundamentally clinicopathological, requiring integrated assessment. Core principles include the need for a high-quality liver biopsy (≥10 mm), mandatory exclusion of cirrhosis, and systematic exclusion of specific alternative conditions. Importantly, the consensus recognizes that PSVD or NCPF may be diagnosed even without clinical portal hypertension and may coexist with other liver diseases, provided cirrhosis is excluded. Standardized major and minor histologic criteria were developed collaboratively by expert pathologists and externally validated. Features of portal hypertension were harmonized into specific and nonspecific categories applicable to routine clinical practice. An integrated diagnostic scoring system incorporating histology, clinical features, associated conditions, and concommitant etiologies was developed and validated using the Delphi method. This consensus provides the first internationally endorsed, unified framework for the diagnosis of PSVD or NCPF. Its global implementation is expected to reduce diagnostic variability, improve comparability across regions, and facilitate the development of robust, internationally harmonized clinical and translational research cohorts.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, a condition where blood pressure builds up in the liver's blood vessels without the liver being scarred, has been described using many different names and definitions across different countries, making it difficult for doctors to diagnose patients consistently and for researchers to collaborate internationally. A large group of liver specialists, pathologists (doctors who study tissue samples), and pediatric experts from around the world came together to create one unified definition and set of diagnostic rules that everyone could use. The group agreed that two terms, porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder and non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis, could be used interchangeably as long as doctors applied the same diagnostic criteria, and they established that diagnosis requires a high-quality liver tissue sample, confirmation that the liver is not scarred, and careful exclusion of other conditions. This new standardized framework means that doctors can now diagnose this condition more reliably, patients will receive more consistent care across different countries, and researchers can more easily compare results from studies conducted in different parts of the world. The consensus framework is expected to reduce confusion in medical practice and enable the development of stronger international research studies that will improve understanding and treatment of this liver.

title: An Evaluation of Pediatric Dermatology Fellowship Websites: Content Analysis and Perspectives of Fellows and Program Directors.
abstract: Prospective applicants for pediatric dermatology fellowships often use program websites as a source of information. This study evaluated the content of pediatric dermatology fellowship websites to identify potential areas of improvement including website accessibility and information found on websites. In addition, this study also surveyed current pediatric dermatology fellows and program directors (PDs) to determine priorities in website content across different stakeholders.Using the Society for Pediatric Dermatology's (SPD) list of fellowship programs, two independent evaluators assessed the same 40 total programs, with 29 of the same websites included for analysis, against 27 criteria across four domains. In addition, an electronic survey was disseminated via the SPD's mailing list to current pediatric dermatology fellows and fellowship PDs.On average between both evaluators, of the 29 included fellowship websites, 9 educational criteria were included 47.8% of the time across the websites, compared to 46.0% of 10 recruitment criteria, 30.7% of 5 social criteria, and 31.6% of 3 other criteria. Fellows were significantly more likely than PDs to consider several website components as highly valuable.These findings reveal variable and incomplete content across pediatric dermatology fellowship websites, as well as differing expectations for fellowship websites between pediatric dermatology fellowship applicants and PDs, which may help provide suggestions to optimize future website development to enhance applicant engagement.© 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

llm_summary: Prospective applicants for pediatric dermatology fellowships, which are specialized training programs for doctors who want to focus on skin conditions in children, often rely on program websites to learn about opportunities and make decisions about where to apply. Researchers examined the websites of 29 pediatric dermatology fellowship programs and surveyed both current fellows and program directors to evaluate what information was being shared and what content people thought was most important. The study found that fellowship websites were inconsistent in what they offered, with educational information appearing less than half the time, recruitment details appearing about 46 percent of the time, and social and other information appearing even less frequently. Interestingly, fellows applying to programs valued many website features significantly more than the program directors did, suggesting that applicants and program leaders have different ideas about what makes a good fellowship website. These findings suggest that pediatric dermatology programs should work to improve their websites by including more complete and consistent information that addresses what applicants actually want to know when choosing where to train.

title: ST8Sia6-dependent glycosylation restrains gut inflammation and pathogenic Th1 and Th17 programs.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), including ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD), are characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. Pathogenesis of IBD is multifactorial and incompletely understood. Here, we show that the sialyltransferase ST8Sia6 regulates gut inflammation and homeostasis. ST8Sia6-deficient mice spontaneously accumulate activated immune cells in the small intestine and exhibit enhanced sensitivity to dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis. ST8Sia6-knockout small bowel lamina propria T cells exhibit steady-state increases in Th1 and pathogenic Th17 programs and readily generate TNF-α upon in vitro stimulation. In addition, there are increased levels of inflammation-induced chemokines CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 in ST8Sia6-deficient immune and epithelial cells. ST8Sia6-deficient T cells show altered glycosylation of CD43 and CD45. ST8Sia6 heterozygous mice show an intermediate phenotype, demonstrating that gut immune homeostasis is sensitive to ST8Sia6 expression levels. This work thus establishes a role for immune cell glycosylation by ST8Sia6 in IBD.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis cause chronic inflammation in the digestive tract, and scientists still do not fully understand what causes them. Researchers studied a protein called ST8Sia6, which adds sugar-like molecules to immune cells, to see if it helps control gut inflammation by examining mice that lacked this protein and comparing them to normal mice. Mice without ST8Sia6 developed more inflammation in their intestines, accumulated more activated immune cells, and produced higher levels of inflammatory chemicals that trigger disease-fighting responses. The findings suggest that ST8Sia6 works by modifying the surface of immune cells in a way that prevents them from becoming too aggressive and causing damage to the gut. This discovery could lead to new treatments for inflammatory bowel diseases by targeting the way immune cells are modified with these sugar-like molecules.

title: Aortic valvar atresia with ventricular septal defect with well-developed mitral valve and balanced ventricles may mimic common arterial trunk.
abstract: Aortic valvar atresia is a congenital cardiovascular malformation in which there is no patency of the aortic valve, and thus no communication between aorta and either ventricle. A hypoplastic ascending aorta is a constant feature, usually in the context of a small left ventricle and mitral valve. A subset of this group is aortic atresia with a ventricular septal defect with well-developed mitral valve and balanced ventricles. This morphological variant is often misdiagnosed as common arterial trunk on echocardiography and computerised tomography. In the absence of coarctation or focal narrowing of the aortic arch, one can misdiagnose this entity as common arterial trunk with a single coronary artery from the brachiocephalic artery. Patients with this variant may have hypoplastic left heart physiology, but can potentially undergo a biventricular repair. Herein, we describe aortic valvar atresia with a large pulmonary trunk and ventricular septal defect, with balanced ventricles and a well-developed mitral valve. The patient was originally misdiagnosed as having a common arterial trunk. We emphasise the morphological differences, as well as the surgical importance, including technical considerations, conduction of cardiopulmonary bypass, and myocardial protection.

llm_summary: Aortic valvar atresia is a rare heart condition present at birth where the aortic valve, which normally allows blood to flow from the heart to the body, does not develop properly and blocks this flow. Doctors sometimes mistake this condition for a different heart defect called common arterial trunk because the two conditions can look similar on imaging tests like ultrasound and CT scans. This case study describes a patient with aortic valvar atresia who had a hole between the heart's two lower chambers, a well-functioning mitral valve, and balanced-sized heart chambers, which made the misdiagnosis more likely. The researchers emphasize that correctly identifying this specific type of aortic valvar atresia is important because patients may be candidates for biventricular repair, a surgical approach that uses both heart chambers to pump blood, rather than the more complex single-ventricle surgery typically used for similar conditions. Understanding the differences between these two heart defects helps surgeons plan the right operation and manage the patient's care during heart surgery, including how to protect the heart muscle during the procedure.

title: Fast Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing for Gram-Negative Bacteremia: The FAST Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Novel blood culture diagnostics provide rapid antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) results for bacteria causing bloodstream infections (BSIs) but have unclear clinical impact.To evaluate clinical outcomes of blood culture testing using a rapid AST method compared with standard AST in patients with BSIs caused by gram-negative bacilli in regions with high prevalence of antimicrobial resistance.Open-label randomized clinical trial that enrolled participants from December 2023 to May 2025 (final follow-up, June 18, 2025) at 7 medical centers in Greece (n = 2), India (n = 1), Israel (n = 3), and Spain (n = 1). Hospitalized patients (adults and children) with BSIs caused by gram-negative bacilli were eligible. Statistical analysis was conducted from August 2025 to January 2026.Patients were randomized to undergo blood culture evaluation using rapid, phenotypic AST directly from positive blood cultures plus standard susceptibility testing (n = 413) vs standard susceptibility testing alone (n = 437). Local antimicrobial stewardship teams reviewed all patients and provided treatment recommendations.The primary outcome was a desirability of outcome ranking (DOOR) at day 30, with 3 categories (alive without deleterious events, alive with deleterious events, and death). The difference between rapid and standard testing was summarized as the probability that the DOOR outcomes were more desirable in the rapid testing group. Superiority was concluded if the lower limit of the 95% CI exceeded 50%. Secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality, length of hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, acquisition of hospital-acquired infections, time to effective antibiotic therapy within 3 days, and time to antibiotic escalation or deescalation within 3 days.Of the 899 patients randomized, 850 were included in the primary outcome analysis (median [IQR] age, 72 [21] years; 43% female). The probability that DOOR outcomes were more favorable in the rapid testing group was 48.8% (95% CI, 45.3%-52.4%). Median time to effective antibiotic therapy was not different between the groups in the as-randomized population. Median time to antibiotic escalation or deescalation was faster in the rapid testing group by 14 hours (95% CI, 6-22) in the as-randomized population. There were no differences between the groups in other secondary outcomes. In the prespecified subgroup with carbapenem-resistant infections, median time to effective therapy was 9.5 hours in the rapid testing group vs 28 hours in the standard testing group (difference, -18 hours [95% CI, -42 to 6]).Among patients with gram-negative bacilli BSIs, rapid blood culture AST was not superior to standard testing by DOOR. When considered with other efficacy and safety outcomes, these findings may help inform the use of rapid susceptibility testing in clinical practice.ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06174649.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a new fast blood test method could improve treatment outcomes for patients with serious bloodstream infections caused by gram-negative bacteria, which are common germs that often resist antibiotics. The study randomly assigned 850 hospitalized patients across medical centers in Greece, India, Israel, and Spain to either receive rapid susceptibility testing (which quickly shows which antibiotics work against their infection) or standard testing that takes longer. The rapid testing method did not produce better overall patient outcomes at thirty days compared to standard testing, though it did help doctors make decisions about changing antibiotics about fourteen hours faster. The rapid testing showed more promise in patients with carbapenem-resistant infections, a particularly dangerous type of bacteria, where effective treatment was started about eighteen hours sooner with the fast method. These findings suggest that while rapid blood culture testing can speed up some treatment decisions, it may not significantly improve patient survival or recovery compared to standard testing methods in most cases.

title: Examining burnout, work-life balance, relocation and financial stress among UK resident doctors and medical students.
abstract: Burnout arises from prolonged, unresolved work-related stress and adversely affects professional performance and overall well-being. Resident doctors and medical students are particularly vulnerable because of the demands of balancing clinical, academic and related responsibilities.This study aimed to assess self-reported burnout and related stressors among UK resident doctors and medical students, and estimate the economic impact of burnout-related absenteeism among resident doctors.Self-report questionnaires assessing burnout and related stressors were distributed to UK resident doctors and medical students. A total of 2793 responses were received: 1439 (51.5%) from resident doctors and 1354 (48.5%) from medical students. Economic losses from absenteeism were calculated with a human capital approach.Burnout was reported by 70% (n = 1008) of resident doctors and 65.7% (n = 889) of medical students. Notably, 56.8% (n = 573) and 79.3% (n = 705) of resident doctors and medical students affected by burnout, respectively, were unaware of available support services. Relocation stress (85.1% of residents and 62.6% of students), financial stress (53.9% of residents and 57.8% of students) and poor work-life balance (32.1% of residents and 20.7% of students) were commonly reported. The annual economic burden of absenteeism related to burnout among resident doctors was estimated to reach £251.5 million.Burnout among UK resident doctors and medical students may reflect a combination of underlying factors, including financial strain, relocation stress and difficulties with work-life balance. These findings underscore the need for targeted interventions that support well-being and address financial and relocation challenges, which may, in turn, help prevent burnout and improve retention within the medical workforce. Reducing burnout and associated stressors may also help lessen its economic impact, allowing resources to be redirected towards patient care.

llm_summary: Researchers examined burnout, which is exhaustion from prolonged work stress, among doctors in training and medical students in the United Kingdom because these groups face intense pressure balancing clinical work, studies, and personal responsibilities. The team distributed questionnaires to nearly 2,800 resident doctors and medical students asking about their stress levels and related challenges like relocation, finances, and work-life balance. The results showed that about 70 percent of resident doctors and 66 percent of medical students reported experiencing burnout, yet most of those affected did not know about available support services to help them. Major stressors included having to relocate for work, struggling with money, and difficulty maintaining a healthy balance between work and personal life, with these problems being more common among resident doctors. The study estimated that burnout-related absences among resident doctors cost the healthcare system approximately 251.

These symptoms together often suggest conditions affecting the liver, heart, or lungs, and require careful medical investigation to determine the correct diagnosis and treatment.

title: Long-Term Outcomes of Leadless Pacemaker vs. Transvenous Pacemaker in End-Stage Renal Disease.
abstract: Patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) undergoing dialysis have an increased risk of pacemaker-related complications due to limited vascular access and increased susceptibility to infection. Leadless pacemakers (LPMs) may mitigate these risks compared with conventional transvenous pacemakers (TPMs), but long-term comparative data in this population remain limited.We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network, including adults (≥ 18 years) with ESRD on dialysis who underwent LPM or TPM implantation between May 2016 and December 2020. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using demographics and comorbidities. Outcomes assessed over up to 5 years included all-cause hospitalization, heart failure hospitalization, device re-intervention, device-related complications, infection-related hospitalization, pacemaker-induced cardiomyopathy, and all-cause mortality.After matching, 901 patients were included in each group with well-balanced baseline characteristics. LPM implantation was associated with a significantly lower risk of device re-intervention compared with TPM (4.1% vs. 9.3%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.44; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.28-0.69; p < 0.01). There were no significant differences between groups in all-cause hospitalization (65.5% vs. 68.3%; p = 0.22), heart failure hospitalization (26.9% vs. 30.2%; p = 0.13), all-cause mortality (37.5% vs. 35.3%; p = 0.34), device-related complications (14.5% vs. 14.3%; p = 0.94), infection-related hospitalization (1.6% vs. 2.1%; p = 0.35), or pacemaker-induced cardiomyopathy (9.0% vs. 8.6%; p = 0.66).In a large, propensity-matched cohort of patients with ESRD on dialysis, LPMs were associated with fewer device re-interventions and comparable long-term clinical outcomes compared with TPMs.© 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

llm_summary: Patients with end-stage kidney disease who need dialysis face serious risks when receiving pacemakers, which are devices that help the heart beat properly, because their damaged kidneys and limited blood vessel access make them more prone to infections and complications. Researchers compared two types of pacemakers in nearly two thousand kidney disease patients: leadless pacemakers, which are tiny devices placed directly in the heart without wires, and traditional pacemakers, which use wires threaded through blood vessels to reach the heart. The study found that patients who received leadless pacemakers needed fewer follow-up procedures to fix or replace their devices compared to those with traditional pacemakers, but both groups had similar rates of hospitalization, heart failure, infection, and death over five years. These results suggest that leadless pacemakers may be a safer option for kidney disease patients because they reduce the need for repeat surgeries while providing the same overall health benefits as traditional pacemakers. Future research should continue monitoring these patients long-term and explore whether leadless pacemakers might be the preferred choice for people with kidney disease who need pacemaker implants.

title: A Retrieval-Based Approach for Automatic Interpretation of Multi-Analyte Laboratory Profiles.
abstract: Interpretation of multi-analyte laboratory profiles, such as lupus anticoagulant (LAC) testing, requires integration of numerous test results and clinical information. However, this process is time-consuming, requires domain knowledge, and has limited scalability. Given that rule-based systems are rigid and difficult to maintain and large language models pose risks of "hallucinations," we developed and evaluated a novel retrieval-based approach to automate LAC profile interpretation to improve efficiency while maintaining fidelity and reliability for clinical use.Our method processes laboratory values through ensemble random forest (RF) models to retrieve the most similar expert interpretation from a curated database of 347 previously interpreted LAC profiles. The system's performance was assessed through technical accuracy metrics, a work flow efficiency timing study, and expert review of interpretation accuracy for held-out cases.Technical validation demonstrated high accuracy in retrieving correct interpretative elements (median: 93% accuracy, interquartile range [IQR]: 67% to 100%). Retrieval accuracy was highly correlated with the prevalence of a given element (ρ = 0.8307). In a timing study of 93 consecutive LAC profiles, ensemble-assisted interpretation achieved a median time of 22 s per report (IQR: 16 s to 31 s), representing a 78.6% total reduction compared to manual interpretation (median: 118 s, IQR: 96 s to 172 s; t = 18.61, P < 0.001). Furthermore, 92.5% of AI-assisted interpretations were completed within 60 s, exceeding the target of 85%. Expert review confirmed 100% concordance for LAC presence/absence.The proposed approach significantly improves efficiency of complex laboratory interpretation for LAC profiles, while maintaining consistency and high fidelity. Future studies will explore the method's inherent extensibility to the interpretation of other multi-analyte laboratory profiles.© The Author(s) 2026. llm_summary: Doctors often need to interpret complex laboratory test results that involve multiple measurements, a process that takes considerable time and requires specialized knowledge, which limits how quickly results can be delivered to patients. Researchers developed a new computer system that uses machine learning, a type of artificial intelligence that learns patterns from examples, to automatically match patient test results against a database of nearly 350 previously interpreted cases and retrieve the most similar expert interpretation. The system successfully identified the correct interpretation elements over 93 percent of the time and reduced the time needed to complete a report from about two minutes down to just 22 seconds, which is a 78. 6 percent improvement in speed. Expert doctors reviewed the computer-assisted interpretations and confirmed that the system was 100 percent accurate in determining whether a specific blood clotting condition was present or absent in patients.

title: Real-World Economic Burden Associated with Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in the US: An Administrative Claims Database Analysis.
abstract: Among patients with non-idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (non-IPF) interstitial lung disease (ILD), developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) is associated with increased economic burden, inpatient (IP) admissions, and mortality. However, little is known about the burden within specific payer types. This retrospective study assessed the economic burden of PPF and associated time to first IP admission among distinct cohorts of Medicare Advantage Prescription Drug (MAPD) beneficiaries and commercial enrollees in the United States (US).Medical and pharmacy claims were analyzed among patients diagnosed with non-IPF ILD between 1/1/2017 and 11/30/2023. Patients who developed PPF (cases) were matched with those who had not yet progressed (comparators) using 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) with replacement. The index date was the earliest PPF date for cases; the respective comparator was assigned an index date to create identical pre-index durations. Variable follow-up began on the index date and lasted for ≥ 3 months. Primary outcomes were all-cause and ILD-related healthcare resource utilization (HCRU) and costs (US dollars [USD] 2023) during follow-up. Outcomes were stratified by insurance type and weighted per patient per month (wPPPM). Multivariable models assessed all-cause costs and time to first IP admission, adjusting for covariates that remained imbalanced after PSM.A total of 60,171 matched pairs were analyzed: 50,683 MAPD and 9488 commercial. PSM generated well-balanced cohorts, except for race/ethnicity, ILD diagnosis year, unique pre-index medications filled (MAPD), and age group (commercial). For both insurance types, the PPF group was associated with significantly higher economic burden than the comparator group. All-cause costs averaged $3640 versus $1897 wPPPM (p < 0.001) in MAPD and $6164 versus $2741 (p < 0.001) in commercial. Differences were primarily driven by IP burden (MAPD: $1412 vs $507; commercial: $2094 vs $559; both p < 0.001). Mean length of IP stay was significantly longer among patients that developed PPF (MAPD: 0.9 vs 0.4 days; commercial: 0.5 vs 0.2 days; both p < 0.001). A generalized linear model showed that PPF was associated with higher adjusted all-cause costs (MAPD cost ratio [95% confidence interval {CI}]: 1.861 [1.807-1.916]; commercial: 2.096 [1.897-2.316]). Cox proportional hazards ratios (95% CI) showed a significantly higher hazard of first IP admission with PPF (MAPD: 2.060 [2.005-2.116]; commercial: 2.324 [2.133-2.532]). Notably, follow-up use of antifibrotics was low among patients with PPF (0.8% MAPD; 1.0% commercial).For MAPD and commercial cohorts, PPF was associated with significantly higher HCRU, costs, and hazard of IP admission. Differences in economic burden were primarily driven by IP utilization. These findings support the prioritization of treatments or strategies that attenuate the risk and rate of progression to mitigate downstream healthcare burden.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Researchers examined the financial and medical impact of progressive pulmonary fibrosis, a serious lung disease that worsens over time, on patients covered by two types of health insurance in the United States. The study compared medical and pharmacy claims from over 60,000 patients with lung disease, separating those whose condition progressed into pulmonary fibrosis from those whose condition remained stable, and tracked their hospital visits and healthcare costs over several years. Patients whose lung disease progressed to pulmonary fibrosis had significantly higher healthcare costs, with expenses nearly double those of patients whose condition did not progress, and these higher costs were mainly driven by more frequent and longer hospital stays. The findings show that preventing or slowing the progression of lung disease could substantially reduce the burden on patients and the healthcare system, though the study noted that very few patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis were actually receiving medications designed to slow lung scarring. These results suggest that doctors and health systems should prioritize strategies to prevent lung disease from worsening in order to reduce hospitalizations and overall healthcare expenses for patients with this serious condition.

title: Telemedicine Consultation : Lessons Learned from the Pararescue Experience.
abstract: Telemedicine is a critical military medicine capability in austere, remote, and denied environments where prolonged casualty care and knowledge gaps exist. Despite significant military investment in telemedicine, the literature lacks detailed lessons from real-world cases.U.S. Air Force Pararescue missions between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2020 that included telemedicine consultation were reviewed. Participating flight surgeons (FS) and Pararescuemen (PJ) were interviewed, and available after-action reports were analyzed. Mission parameters, outcomes, and technical or human factors affecting communication were evaluated.Across 13 telemedicine consultations, the 28 patients experienced: cave entrapment (13), trauma (7), burns (4), and illness (4). Consultations were from PJ to FS (11), U.S. Coast Guard to FS (1), and FS to neurosurgery (1). Secondary consultations (7) were from FS to dental (1), dermatology, burn/critical care, orthopedics (2), pediatric anesthesiology, and thoracic surgery specialists. Missions used voice over mobile or satellite phone, text, and email. Recommendations commonly involved medication selection (6), advisement against mission launch (3), and burn care (2). Consultation effectiveness was impacted by unclear directions (3) and degraded communications (2).Telemedicine is valuable to PJs during complicated cases and rarely performed procedures, but cannot replace pre-deployment medical exposure and training. Rehearsals may optimize telemedicine, and training should focus on synchronizing a shared mental model of the patient using well-understood patient report and evaluation tools (ATMIST and MARCH PAWS). Telemedicine may reduce human error, give medics the confidence to take action, and limit the psychological impact of difficult care decisions.2026.

title: Z-coded social determinants of health and cardiovascular risk among patients receiving dialysis.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death among patients with kidney failure on dialysis. Social determinants of health may worsen this risk but are seldom incorporated into prognostic models. ICD-10 Z-codes provide standardized documentation of social determinants of health, yet their prognostic value in dialysis populations remains uncertain. This study examined whether Z-coded social determinants of health are associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes and mortality among patients receiving dialysis for kidney failure.A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX Research Network (2010-2024), encompassing de-identified data from 103 institutions. Adults with kidney failure on chronic dialysis were stratified by the presence of ICD-10 Z-codes (Z55-Z65). Propensity score matching (1:1) balanced demographics, comorbidities, medications, and laboratory values. Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and hospitalization; secondary outcomes included acute heart failure, myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiac arrest, bradyarrhythmias, and ventricular tachycardia.After matching, mean age was 62 years, and 42.4% were female in the Z-code cohort versus 41.2% in controls. Over one year, mortality occurred in 12.5% versus 10.9% (hazard ratio [HR], 1.22; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.15-1.29) and all-cause hospitalizations in 57.3% versus 53.1% (HR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.19-1.26). Cardiovascular complications were consistently higher in Z-coded patients, including heart failure (24.3% vs 20.5%; HR, 1.29), myocardial infarction (8.0% vs 7.1%; HR, 1.19), stroke (6.6% vs 6.2%; HR, 1.13), cardiac arrest (3.8% vs 3.1%; HR, 1.29), and bradyarrhythmias (6.9% vs 5.5%; HR, 1.33).Among patients with kidney failure, documented Z-coded social risk factors were associated with greater mortality and cardiovascular morbidity. llm_summary: Cardiovascular disease, or heart and blood vessel problems, is the leading cause of death among patients with kidney failure who receive dialysis treatment, yet doctors rarely consider social factors like poverty or housing instability when predicting which patients are at highest risk. Researchers examined medical records from over 103 hospitals between 2010 and 2024, comparing dialysis patients who had documented social risk factors in their medical codes with those who did not, using statistical methods to ensure fair comparison between the two groups. Patients with documented social risk factors experienced significantly higher rates of death, hospitalization, heart attacks, strokes, and heart rhythm problems over one year compared to those without such documented factors. These findings suggest that recognizing and documenting a patient's social challenges in medical records could help doctors better identify which dialysis patients need extra support and targeted interventions to prevent serious heart complications. Future efforts to incorporate social determinant screening into routine kidney disease care may help improve outcomes and reduce preventable deaths among this vulnerable population.

title: Humility: The Essential Virtue Enhancing Patient Care, Education, Research, and Innovation.
abstract: The word humility is derived from the Latin word humus, meaning "ground" or "soil." Romans equated humility with being grounded. Perhaps because it contradicts our natural tendencies toward self-preservation, humility remains an often misunderstood and underappreciated virtue. It is foreign to many, especially in today's society, which is so focused on self-promotion. However, it is truly one of the most important and powerful virtues that a person can possess and practice. Humility is a just assessment of ourselves and the world around us. It is not thinking less of oneself; rather, it is actually thinking less about oneself. In looking beyond ourselves, we can obtain an honest estimate of our limitations and what is needed to remain patient-centered. In approaching our profession with humility, we more closely honor the privileges of caring for patients, teaching others, innovating, and advancing science. The aim of this article is to show how humility nurtures our development in all aspects of medicine. A humble clinician maintains a steadfast focus on their patient, a humble educator emphasizes the learner, a humble researcher respects science through their honesty and integrity, and a humble innovator does not let pride blind them, recognizing that innovation without humility is doomed to fail. In addition to being a superpower in medicine, humility blesses us with the wisdom and gratitude that come from experiencing, living for, and working for something bigger than ourselves. Gratitude has been considered the father of all virtues, and our ability to be truly grateful requires a core of humility.Copyright © 2026 by The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, Incorporated.

llm_summary: Humility, derived from the Latin word meaning "ground" or "soil," is an often misunderstood virtue that involves having an honest assessment of ourselves and our limitations rather than thinking less of ourselves. The authors argue that humility is essential in medicine because it helps doctors focus on their patients' needs, teachers emphasize learning in their students, researchers maintain honesty and integrity in their work, and innovators avoid letting pride interfere with creating better solutions. A humble approach to medicine means recognizing that we are part of something larger than ourselves and that our role is to serve patients and advance science with integrity. The authors contend that humility acts as a superpower in healthcare by fostering wisdom and gratitude, which come from dedicating ourselves to work that benefits others. By practicing humility in all aspects of medicine—patient care, education, research, and innovation—healthcare professionals can better honor the privilege of their profession and contribute more meaningfully to the wellbeing of those they serve.

title: Characterizing the Activity of Inflammasome-Related Genes and Their Association With Oncological Outcomes in Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Inflammation plays a critical role in cancer cell proliferation; however, the specific role of inflammasomes, multiprotein complexes that regulate inflammation-associated signaling pathways, in prostate cancer (PCa) remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to characterize the expression of inflammasome-related genes in PCa and evaluate their association with clinical outcomes.De-identified transcriptome data from the Decipher GRID RP, a cohort of 52,266 radical prostatectomy (RP) samples tested (2016-2024) with the Decipher prostate genomic classifier (Veracyte, San Diego, CA), were retrieved from the GRID registry (NCT02609269). Expression analysis of 34 genes involved in inflammatory pathways was conducted to associate their expression with clinical and genomic variables. Outcomes analyses were conducted on a retrospective cohort of 855 patients treated with RP (META855).Analysis of inflammasome gene expression in the GRID RP cohort revealed that most genes exhibit low baseline expression, whereas HSP90AB1, APP, TXN, and TXNIP demonstrate strong expression signals. Additionally, higher expression of most genes was associated with Gleason Grade Group 4-5 and very high Decipher scores. On survival analysis of the META855 cohort, higher expressions of AIM2 and HSP90AB1 were significantly associated with worse metastasis-free survival. Conversely, both high and low expression levels of NLRP3 were associated with better metastasis-free survival outcomes following RP compared to average expression. On multivariable Cox regression analysis, higher expressions of AIM2 (HR 1.75) and HSP90AB1 (HR 1.60) were significantly associated with shorter time to metastasis following RP.There is molecular heterogeneity within pro-inflammatory genes among patients with PCa. Our findings showed there is a potential association between the expression levels of certain inflammasomes, such as AIM2, HSP90AB1, and NLRP3, and oncological outcomes following RP.© 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

llm_summary: Inflammation, which is the body's response to injury or infection, plays an important role in cancer growth, but scientists have not fully understood how certain inflammatory proteins called inflammasomes affect prostate cancer development and outcomes. Researchers analyzed genetic information from over 52,000 prostate cancer patients who had surgery to remove their prostate glands, looking at 34 genes involved in inflammation to see which ones were active in cancer tissue and how their activity related to patient outcomes. The study found that four genes called HSP90AB1, APP, TXN, and TXNIP showed strong activity in cancer samples, and higher levels of two genes named AIM2 and HSP90AB1 were linked to cancer spreading to other parts of the body more quickly after surgery. In contrast, a gene called NLRP3 showed an unusual pattern where both very high and very low expression levels were associated with better outcomes compared to average expression levels. These findings suggest that measuring the activity levels of certain inflammasome genes could help doctors predict which prostate cancer patients are at higher risk for their cancer spreading and may lead to better treatment decisions in the future.

title: Predictive value of early pregnancy laboratory markers for recurrence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: A retrospective study.
abstract: Recurrence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) is linked to increased complications, but progress in reducing recurrence has been limited. Lasting vascular or metabolic changes after prior HDP may raise risk and could appear as subtle abnormalities in early pregnancy lab values. This study examined associations between early pregnancy labs and HDP recurrence or adverse perinatal outcomes in individuals with a history of HDP.We conducted a retrospective study of individuals with an index pregnancy complicated by HDP and a subsequent pregnancy with delivery >20 weeks within a single health system (2010-2022). Early pregnancy labs before 20 weeks including serum creatinine, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR), platelet count, and liver enzymes were collected. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations with HDP recurrence, preterm birth, and low birthweight. Models adjusted for HDP severity and gestational age at index delivery, maternal comorbidities among other factors. Receiver operating characteristic curves evaluated predictive performance.Among 2,499 pregnancies with HDP history, recurrence occurred in 40.6% of subsequent pregnancies; preterm birth in 11.5%, and low birthweight in 8.1%. Higher platelet count was associated with HDP recurrence (p < 0.01). UPCR and liver enzymes were associated with preterm birth (p < 0.01). Creatinine was not associated with any outcome. All markers showed limited predictive performance.In those with prior HDP, early pregnancy labs were associated with recurrence and adverse outcomes, possibly reflecting ongoing inflammation or metabolic disruption. While not strong predictors alone, these markers may contribute to broader risk stratification strategies to guide counseling in early pregnancy.Copyright © 2026 International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether simple blood tests taken early in pregnancy could predict which women with a history of high blood pressure during pregnancy would experience it again in future pregnancies. The study looked back at medical records from nearly 2,500 pregnancies between 2010 and 2022, measuring factors like platelet counts (cells that help blood clot), protein in urine, and liver enzymes in early pregnancy to see if these markers could forecast complications. They found that about 40 percent of women with previous high blood pressure in pregnancy experienced it again, and higher platelet counts were linked to recurrence while certain liver markers were connected to early delivery and low birth weight babies. Although these early pregnancy blood markers showed some connection to these serious outcomes, they were not strong enough on their own to reliably predict which women would have problems. The researchers concluded that while these simple blood tests alone cannot predict complications, they might be useful as part of a broader strategy to identify high-risk women early in pregnancy and provide them with better counseling and care.

title: A multisociety consensus statement on a new common definition and diagnostic criteria for PSVD or NCPF.
abstract: Noncirrhotic portal hypertension has historically been described using heterogeneous and region-specific terminology-such as idiopathic portal hypertension (IPH), noncirrhotic portal fibrosis (NCPF), obliterative portal venopathy, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia-leading to substantial variability in diagnosis, reporting, and international research collaboration. Differences in guideline definitions from major societies (AASLD, EASL, and APASL), together with the presence of characteristic histologic lesions in patients without clinically overt portal hypertension, have further complicated disease classification. To address these challenges, a large, multisociety, international initiative was convened to harmonize nomenclature and diagnostic criteria. Representatives from liver, pathology, and pediatric hepatology societies across the Americas, Europe, and Asia participated in a structured consensus process that included specialized working groups and external Delphi validation. The initiative produced a globally harmonized and implementable diagnostic framework. Consensus was reached that the terms porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder (PSVD) and NCPF may be used interchangeably when identical diagnostic criteria are applied, and that they should be written as PSVD or NCPF. The diagnosis was defined as fundamentally clinicopathological, requiring integrated assessment. Core principles include the need for a high-quality liver biopsy (≥10 mm), mandatory exclusion of cirrhosis, and systematic exclusion of specific alternative conditions. Importantly, the consensus recognizes that PSVD or NCPF may be diagnosed even without clinical portal hypertension and may coexist with other liver diseases, provided cirrhosis is excluded. Standardized major and minor histologic criteria were developed collaboratively by expert pathologists and externally validated. Features of portal hypertension were harmonized into specific and nonspecific categories applicable to routine clinical practice. An integrated diagnostic scoring system incorporating histology, clinical features, associated conditions, and concommitant etiologies was developed and validated using the Delphi method. This consensus provides the first internationally endorsed, unified framework for the diagnosis of PSVD or NCPF. Its global implementation is expected to reduce diagnostic variability, improve comparability across regions, and facilitate the development of robust, internationally harmonized clinical and translational research cohorts.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Noncirrhotic portal hypertension, a condition where blood pressure increases in the liver's blood vessels without the liver being scarred, has been described using many different names and definitions across different countries, making it difficult for doctors to diagnose patients consistently and for researchers to collaborate internationally. A large group of liver specialists, pathologists, and pediatric doctors from around the world came together to create one unified set of rules and criteria for diagnosing this condition, using a structured process that included expert committees and outside validation. The group agreed that two terms, porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder and noncirrhotic portal fibrosis, can be used interchangeably when the same diagnostic standards are applied, and they developed clear guidelines requiring a high-quality liver tissue sample, confirmation that the liver is not scarred, and systematic elimination of other possible causes. This new standardized framework means that doctors can now diagnose this condition more reliably whether or not patients show obvious signs of high blood pressure in the liver, and the condition can coexist with other liver diseases as long as cirrhosis is ruled out. The global adoption of these unified diagnostic criteria is expected to reduce confusion among healthcare providers.

title: Modulate Obesity and relateD metabolic complIcations For Yielding improvements in IBD outcomes (MODIFY-IBD): consensus on obesity and cardiometabolic comorbidities in inflammatory bowel disease using systematic reviews and the RAND/UCLA appropriateness method.
abstract: Obesity and related cardiometabolic comorbidities, including hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, are increasingly prevalent among individuals with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). These conditions influence disease activity, therapeutic response, surgical outcomes and overall quality of life, yet evidence remains fragmented. The Modulate Obesity and relateD metabolic complIcations For Yielding improvements in IBD outcomes (MODIFY-IBD) initiative aims to synthesise evidence and generate consensus recommendations to guide practice and future research in this area. This study describes a protocol for a structured evidence synthesis and Research ANd Development/University of California, Los Angeles (RAND/UCLA) Appropriateness Method (RUAM) consensus process.We will conduct three systematic reviews and a structured evidence synthesis organised into three domains: (1) the impact of obesity on IBD outcomes, (2) the burden of cardiometabolic complications in IBD and (3) the management of overweight, obesity and cardiometabolic comorbidities in IBD. A multidisciplinary international panel of gastroenterologists, surgeons, endocrinologists, hepatologists, cardiologists and dietitians will assess each statement using the RAND/UCLA appropriateness method. Panellists will rate the appropriateness of each statement (only those that fall within their area of expertise) on a 1-9 scale (1-3=inappropriate, 4-6=uncertain and 7-9=appropriate), with medians rounded up (eg, 6.5=appropriate). Agreement will be assessed using the RAND Disagreement Index (DI<1.0=agreement).This study will not involve direct patient participation, as it is based on evidence synthesis and expert consensus; therefore, formal research ethics committee approval will not be required. Patient representatives will contribute to the consensus process to provide contextual perspectives but no identifiable data will be collected.Findings will be disseminated through publication in peer-reviewed journals, presentation at major gastroenterology and IBD conferences and communication with professional societies. llm_summary: Obesity and related health problems like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, and heart disease are becoming more common in people with inflammatory bowel disease, a chronic condition affecting the digestive system, and these conditions can make the disease worse and harder to treat. Researchers created a project called MODIFY-IBD that will review all available scientific evidence and bring together experts from different medical fields to develop clear recommendations about how to manage weight and heart-related health problems in people with inflammatory bowel disease. The team will conduct three separate reviews of existing research to understand how obesity affects inflammatory bowel disease outcomes, how common heart and metabolic problems are in these patients, and what treatments work best for managing weight and related conditions. A diverse group of specialists including stomach doctors, surgeons, heart doctors, and nutritionists will rate whether specific recommendations are appropriate for clinical practice using a structured voting system that measures agreement among experts. The final recommendations will be shared through medical journals, conferences, and patient-friendly materials to help doctors improve care for people with inflammatory bowel disease who also struggle with obesity and related health complications.

title: Variants in genes regulating thiamine metabolism in children in the Lao Thiamine study.
abstract: The clinical symptoms of thiamine deficiency, or thiamine deficiency disorders (TDDs), present similarly in children with dietary thiamine deficiency and variants in genes of thiamine metabolism. In the rural north of Lao People's Democratic Republic there is a high incidence of TDDs, and the risk of TDDs differs with maternal ethnic group. While low dietary intake is a well-established risk factor for TDDs, the contribution of inborn errors of thiamine metabolism is unknown.This study was an adjunct to the Lao Thiamine study, a prospective cohort study of children aged ≥ 21 days to <18 months with and without symptoms of TDDs. Buffy coat samples were selected from 17 hospitalised children with clinical signs/symptoms of TDDs and both echocardiogram and cranial ultrasound changes consistent with thiamine deficiency, and 14 frequency-matched healthy children in the community. Genomic DNA was isolated, and samples underwent next-generation sequencing of genes involved in thiamine metabolism. Ultimately, 22 of 31 selected residual samples provided adequate material to complete gene sequencing.No pathogenic variants were identified in any of the 22 samples with completed gene sequencing. In a healthy infant, there was one variant of uncertain significance in LONP1, a gene implicated in an autosomal recessive disorder.Variants in genes of thiamine metabolism are unlikely to be a common aetiology of TDDs in a region at high risk of dietary thiamine deficiency. Differences between ethnic groups in the incidence of TDDs are probably related to culture-specific dietary practices and socio-economic risk factors.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether genetic mutations in genes controlling thiamine, a vital B vitamin, could explain why some children in rural Laos develop thiamine deficiency disorders, which cause serious health problems affecting the heart and brain. The study collected blood samples from 17 hospitalized children showing clear signs of thiamine deficiency and compared them to 14 healthy children from the same communities, then analyzed their genes using advanced sequencing technology to look for harmful mutations. The researchers found no disease-causing genetic mutations in any of the 22 samples that had enough material for testing, though one healthy child did have a variant of uncertain significance in a single gene. These results suggest that genetic problems in thiamine metabolism are not a common cause of thiamine deficiency in this high-risk region, meaning the health problems are more likely caused by not eating enough thiamine-rich foods rather than inherited genetic issues. The findings point to the importance of addressing cultural dietary practices and poverty-related factors to prevent thiamine deficiency in vulnerable populations rather than focusing on genetic screening.

title: Artificial intelligence-enhancement of flow cytometry data accelerates the identification of measurable residual chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
abstract: Flow cytometry (FC) is essential for detecting measurable residual disease (MRD) in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), but its use is limited by the expertise and time required for manual analysis. We developed an artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline, Clustering/Classification of All Events, Dimensionality reduction, Downsampling, and Aberrancy Scaling (CCADDAS), to automatically enhance raw FC files, streamlining CLL MRD detection using a single-tube 10-color panel. FC files from 166 MRD-positive and 61 MRD-negative cases were processed in a cloud environment. Automated steps included error correction (FlowCut), clustering (PARC), dimensionality reduction (UMAP), anomaly detection against negative controls, and cluster-informed downsampling that preserved rare MRD events. A deep neural network trained on expert-defined normal subsets enabled automated gating. AI-enhanced files were analyzed in standard FC software, yielding results highly concordant with conventional expert review (R² = 0.98). Downsampling reduced cellularity by 85% and file size by 78%, while retaining low-level MRD events. An AI-generated aberrancy scale distinguished CLL MRD from background B cells with excellent performance (AUC = 0.98). Manual analysis time decreased from 9.0 to 0.9 min per case (90% reduction). CCADDAS provides a largely unsupervised, software-agnostic method that accelerates and simplifies CLL MRD detection without compromising test performance compared to conventional analysis, enabling broader adoption of FC-based MRD testing.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined a major challenge in treating chronic lymphocytic leukemia, a blood cancer, where doctors need to detect tiny remaining cancer cells using a laboratory test called flow cytometry, which traditionally requires expert analysis and takes significant time. The team developed an artificial intelligence system called CCADDAS that automatically processes and analyzes flow cytometry data by correcting errors, organizing cell patterns, reducing file size, and identifying abnormal cancer cells without needing a human expert to manually review everything. When tested on samples from 227 patients, the AI system produced results that matched expert analysis nearly perfectly, reduced analysis time from nine minutes per case to less than one minute, and cut file sizes by 78 percent while still catching even very small numbers of remaining cancer cells. This breakthrough means that hospitals and clinics could more easily and quickly detect whether cancer is returning in leukemia patients, potentially allowing doctors to catch disease progression earlier and treat patients more effectively. The new method works with standard laboratory software and requires minimal human input, which could help many more hospitals adopt this important cancer detection test and improve care for patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

title: Natural history of asymptomatic moderate or severe aortic regurgitation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: The natural history of asymptomatic moderate or severe aortic regurgitation (AR) remains uncertain, with conflicting reports about its progression and surgical timing. We aimed to quantify adverse outcomes under conservative management and evaluate the association of aortic valve replacement/repair (AVR) with mortality.Systematic searches (inception-July 2025) identified cohort studies of asymptomatic moderate/severe AR. Random-effects models estimated pooled incidence rates of adverse events; fixed-effects models were used for hazard ratios (HRs) of AVR vs conservative management.Twenty-seven studies (4720 patients; mean age 49 years; mean follow-up 3.9 years) were included. Pooled incidence rates per 100 person-years were 1.75 (95% CI 1.27 to 2.41) for all-cause mortality, 1.29 for cardiac death, 0.29 for sudden death, 4.30 for new symptoms and 7.01 for AVR. Asymptomatic low left ventricular ejection fraction occurred in only 0.9 per 100 person-years. Mortality rates were more than double those of the general population across age groups-2.45 (1.90 to 3.18) per 100 person-years for cohorts with mean age ≥50 years versus 0.59 (0.29 to 1.21) for younger cohorts. Early AVR was associated with lower mortality (pooled HR 0.33; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.37).Asymptomatic moderate/severe AR carries significant excess mortality irrespective of age, contradicting its historically benign reputation. Given the rarity of asymptomatic LV dysfunction, earlier intervention guided by more sensitive markers of LV damage may improve outcomes, although heterogeneity and study quality warrant cautious interpretation.CRD42024522683.© Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined the long-term health outcomes of people with moderate to severe aortic regurgitation, a condition where the heart valve leaks blood backward, to better understand whether patients should have surgery early or wait and watch their condition. The team reviewed twenty-seven previous studies involving nearly five thousand patients and tracked what happened to them over an average of almost four years under regular monitoring without immediate surgery. They found that people with this condition died at rates more than twice as high as the general population, with about one to two deaths per one hundred patients per year, and that early surgical repair or replacement of the valve was linked to significantly lower death rates compared to waiting. The study challenges the old belief that asymptomatic aortic regurgitation, meaning people without symptoms, is harmless and suggests that doctors should consider operating sooner rather than later, possibly using better tests to detect early heart damage. However, the researchers note that the studies they reviewed varied in quality and methods, so doctors should interpret these findings carefully when making decisions about individual patients.

title: Decompression with or without Duraplasty for Chiari I and Syringomyelia.
abstract: In children with Chiari type I malformation and syringomyelia, neurosurgical posterior fossa decompression (PFD) provides clinical improvement, but whether duraplasty (incising the dura and placing a dural graft) improves outcomes is unclear.We conducted a multicenter, cluster-randomized, controlled trial of PFD with duraplasty (PFD-D) as compared with PFD alone. Persons 21 years of age or younger with cerebellar tonsillar ectopia of at least 5 mm and a maximum syrinx diameter of 3.0 to 9.9 mm were enrolled at 38 centers. Centers were cluster-randomized: all the participants within each center underwent the same intervention. The primary outcome was surgical complications within 6 months. Secondary outcomes were clinical improvement, syrinx reduction, and repeat decompression at 10 to 24 months and the change in overall health-related quality of life at 6 to 24 months.A total of 162 participants were included in the trial, of whom 78 were assigned to undergo PFD-D and 84 to undergo PFD alone. The percentage of participants with complications within 6 months was 14% with PFD-D and 6% with PFD (adjusted odds ratio, 2.59; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.86 to 7.84; P = 0.11). At 24 months, the percentage of participants with clinical improvement was 58% with PFD-D and 46% with PFD; the mean (±SD) syrinx reduction was 3.08±2.33 mm and 1.22±1.79 mm, respectively; and the percentage of participants with repeat decompression was 3% and 14%. Changes in health-related quality of life were similar in the two groups.The percentage of participants with surgical complications did not differ significantly between those who underwent PFD-D and and those who underwent PFD alone. Larger trials are needed to determine the relative benefits and risks of these two procedures. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether adding an extra surgical step called duraplasty, which involves cutting and patching the membrane surrounding the spinal cord, improves outcomes compared to decompression surgery alone in children with Chiari type I malformation, a condition where brain tissue extends into the spinal canal and causes fluid-filled cavities called syrinxes. The study involved 162 children at 38 medical centers who were randomly assigned to receive either decompression with duraplasty or decompression alone, and researchers tracked their complications, symptom improvement, syrinx shrinkage, and quality of life over two years. The results showed that adding duraplasty did not significantly reduce surgical complications within six months, though it did lead to greater syrinx reduction and slightly better clinical improvement at two years, while fewer children in the duraplasty group needed repeat surgery. Both groups experienced similar improvements in overall health-related quality of life, suggesting that the added complexity of duraplasty may not provide enough additional benefit to justify its use in all cases. Larger studies are needed to help doctors better understand which children would benefit most from the duraplasty procedure and which can safely have.

title: Polygenic scores for risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: evaluation of novel and published models.
abstract: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) may enhance risk stratification for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but existing models vary widely in design, predictive performance, and cross-ancestry transferability. We developed genome-wide PRSs using Bayesian methods (LDpred2 and PRS-CS) and p value thresholding (PRSice-2) and systematically evaluated these alongside 13 published PRSs to identify models with robust predictive performance across ancestries. Using GWAS summary statistics from 7531 cases and 10,631 controls, we derived the PRSs and tested associations in an independent sample of 4508 PDAC cases and 46,189 controls, with adjustment for well-established PDAC risk factors. Among all models, the genome-wide LDpred2-based PRS showed the strongest association with PDAC (OR = 1.57 per standard deviation increase; 95% CI: 1.51-1.62) and significantly improved discrimination beyond established risk factors alone (AUC = 0.74-0.76; p < 0.0001). Importantly, the genome-wide LDpred2 PRS demonstrated consistent associations across African, Admixed American, and European ancestry groups, whereas the best-performing published PRS was associated with PDAC risk only in individuals of European ancestry. These findings support genome-wide PRSs as a promising framework for multi-ancestry risk stratification for PDAC and to inform targeted early detection strategies.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether genetic risk scores, which are mathematical tools that combine information from multiple genes to predict disease risk, could help identify people at higher risk for pancreatic cancer before symptoms develop. The team tested different methods for creating these genetic risk scores using data from thousands of people with and without pancreatic cancer, then validated their findings in a separate group of patients to see which approach worked best. The most successful genetic risk score, created using a method called LDpred2, was significantly better at predicting pancreatic cancer risk than established risk factors alone and showed consistent results across people of African, mixed, and European ancestry. This finding is important because it suggests that genetic risk scores could eventually be used in clinical practice to identify people who should receive earlier screening or more frequent monitoring for pancreatic cancer. The researchers concluded that genome-wide genetic risk scores represent a promising approach for helping doctors identify high-risk patients across different populations and could inform strategies to catch pancreatic cancer earlier when treatment may be more effective.

title: Iron-addicted colorectal cancers exploit heme-complex II axis to resist oxidative cell death.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) cells are addicted to iron, which fuels nucleotide synthesis, mitochondrial respiration, and proliferation. Yet paradoxically, high intracellular iron is cytotoxic to most cells, raising the question of how CRC cells tolerate and exploit iron-rich environments. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, is thought to mediate iron toxicity. However, whether most ferroptosis regulators, identified through synthetic chemical screens or small molecule activators, play a role in modulating iron toxicity, particularly in vivo, remains unclear. Here, using multi-omics profiling, CRISPR screening, and in vivo models, we uncover a heme-succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-coenzyme Q (CoQ) axis that enables CRC cells to buffer iron-induced oxidative stress. Heme-dependent SDH reduces CoQ, which redistributes to mitochondrial and plasma membranes to detoxify lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS) as a radical-trapping antioxidant. llm_summary: Colorectal cancer cells need iron to grow and survive, but too much iron is normally poisonous to cells, which creates a puzzle about how cancer cells manage this dangerous situation. Researchers used advanced genetic screening tools and laboratory models to study how colorectal cancer cells protect themselves from iron poisoning, which is a type of cell death called ferroptosis. They discovered that cancer cells use a special pathway involving heme, a component of blood, and a protein called succinate dehydrogenase to reduce a molecule called coenzyme Q, which then moves around the cell to neutralize harmful molecules called reactive oxygen species that are created by excess iron. This finding shows that colorectal cancer cells have found a clever way to use the same iron that fuels their growth as a survival tool by activating protective mechanisms that prevent iron from killing them. These results could lead to new treatment strategies that target this iron-protection pathway to make colorectal cancer cells more vulnerable to death.

title: AI-Generated Avatar Videos for Postoperative Patient Education Among Health Care Workers: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Effective postoperative communication is vital for patient recovery, yet traditional text-based discharge instructions often lead to poor comprehension and adherence, particularly among patients with limited health literacy. Although educational videos improve understanding and retention, their widespread use has been hampered by high production costs. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers a scalable solution for creating engaging video content.The primary objective of this pilot study was to assess the feasibility of creating and deploying AI-generated, avatar-led videos for postoperative instruction delivery. Secondary objectives included comparing knowledge retention, engagement, perceived clarity, and user experience between AI-generated video and traditional text-based handout formats among health care workers.In this randomized pilot study, 38 health care worker volunteers were recruited as a convenience sample to pilot-test the intervention before patient implementation. Participants were assigned to either a text handout group (n=19, 50%) or an AI-generated video group (n=19, 50%). Both groups received information on 10 common postoperative topics. The primary outcome was objective knowledge, assessed via a 10-item quiz. Secondary outcomes, measured through surveys with 5-point Likert scales, included engagement time, subjective engagement, perceived clarity, usefulness, confidence in understanding, and information retention. Qualitative feedback was also collected.Objective knowledge quiz scores did not differ significantly between groups (mean 8.89, SD 1.20 for the AI-generated video group vs mean 8.21, SD 1.78 for the text handout group; P=.17; Cohen d=0.45). Participants in the AI-generated video group demonstrated significantly higher engagement time (mean 15.11, SD 7.78 minutes vs mean 8.84, SD 4.03 minutes; P=.004; Cohen d=1.04). They also rated instructions as significantly clearer (mean 4.63, SD 0.50 vs mean 4.00, SD 0.82; P=.007; Cohen d=0.93), more engaging (mean 4.05, SD 0.78 vs mean 3.32, SD 1.00; P=.02; Cohen d=0.81), and more effective for retention (mean 4.42, SD 0.84 vs mean 3.37, SD 0.68; P<.001; Cohen d=1.38). Qualitative feedback highlighted the engaging nature of AI-generated videos but noted areas for avatar refinement.In this pilot study with health care workers, AI-generated avatar videos did not improve objective knowledge scores but significantly enhanced engagement, perceived retention and perceived clarity (Cohen d=0.81-1.38). The study involved thirty-eight healthcare workers who were randomly assigned to either watch an AI-generated video about ten common postoperative topics or read a text-based handout with the same information, then both groups were tested on their knowledge and asked about their experience. The results showed that while both groups scored similarly on a knowledge quiz, the people who watched the AI videos spent significantly more time engaging with the material and reported that the instructions were clearer, more engaging, and better for remembering information. title: The Prevalence of Fibromyalgia in the General Population and At-Risk Subpopulations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Estimates of fibromyalgia prevalence vary widely worldwide due to differences in diagnostic criteria, study methodology, and population characteristics. Accurate estimates are essential to inform population-level surveillance, guide resource allocation, and highlight disparities in disease recognition and access to care. The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to determine the global prevalence of fibromyalgia in the general population, and secondarily to identify factors moderating prevalence variation and to assess prevalence in defined at-risk subpopulations. Pooled prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using the inverse variance heterogeneity model with Freeman-Tukey transformation. Subgroup analyses were performed by sex, diagnostic criteria, country, and other study characteristics, and meta-regression assessed moderators including publication year and Human Development Index (HDI). Of 21,645 records identified, 1,728 underwent full-text review and 882 studies were included in the final analysis. Across 38 countries and 30,070,032 individuals (188 studies), the pooled fibromyalgia prevalence in the general population was 1.40% (95% CI, 0.49-2.47), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 100%) and very low certainty of evidence. Among at-risk subpopulations (9,771,123 participants; 768 studies), prevalence was markedly higher in autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, such as chronic urticaria (37.1%), interstitial cystitis (30.8%), systemic sclerosis (20.6%), celiac disease (20.5%), and inflammatory bowel disease (19.9%), and elevated in chronic pain, rheumatologic, and post-infection cohorts. Meta-regression identified publication year (β = 0.008, P < .001) and HDI (β = 0.725, P = .002) as significant moderators of prevalence. In conclusion, fibromyalgia affects 1% to 2% of the global population, with substantially higher rates in at-risk subpopulations. llm_summary: Researchers examined how common fibromyalgia, a condition causing widespread pain and fatigue, actually is around the world, since different countries and doctors use different methods to diagnose it. They reviewed and combined information from 882 studies involving over 30 million people across 38 countries to get a clear picture of how many people have this condition. They found that fibromyalgia affects about one to two percent of the general population worldwide, but it is much more common in people who already have other diseases like autoimmune conditions, with rates reaching as high as thirty-seven percent in people with chronic urticaria, a skin condition. The researchers discovered that fibromyalgia diagnoses have increased over time and vary significantly depending on a country's wealth and development level, suggesting that differences in how doctors recognize and diagnose the disease play a major role in these variations. These findings highlight important gaps in how fibromyalgia is diagnosed and treated around the world, pointing to the need for more consistent diagnostic standards and better access to care for people suffering from this condition.

title: Development and Implementation of a Standardized Inpatient Fellow Hematology Curriculum: Enhancing Educational Experiences.
abstract: Inpatient hematology rotations are a cornerstone of fellowship training, although they often lack clear alignment of didactics with clinical duties and expectations. National surveys have highlighted heterogeneity in training environments and underscored the need for standardized educational frameworks. This education-focused quality-improvement project sought to establish and evaluate an inpatient Fellow Hematology Curriculum (FHC) at Mayo Clinic in Rochester. A baseline needs assessment survey of the fellowship trainees (n = 30) during the 2021-2022 academic year identified substantial variability in teaching quality, limited access to educational materials, inconsistent emphasis on evidence-based practice, and unclear learning objectives. In response, a structured, evidence-based inpatient FHC was developed using Kern's Six-Step Approach and implemented during the 2022-2023 academic year on the Lymphoma/Myeloma and Leukemia services. The curriculum incorporated weekly disease-focused themes, standardized lecture templates anchored to widely accepted resources, and fellow-generated faculty-vetted content distributed in advance of rotations. Post-implementation surveys demonstrated marked improvements across multiple domains. Fellows reported increased consultant engagement, improved access to educational materials (41% vs. 5% pre-implementation), stronger alignment of didactics with clinical duties (84% vs. 45%), and enhanced clarity of learning objectives (58% vs. 25%). Perceptions of evidence-based teaching rose from 15% to 58% and the quality of education was less dependent on the hematology consultants/attendings. Implementation of a structured inpatient FHC was feasible, well-received, and associated with substantial improvements in fellows' perceived educational quality. This scalable model offers a practical approach for programs seeking to enhance inpatient hematology training using systematic, learner-centered curriculum design.© 2026.
