llm_summary: More than one-third of surgery residents, particularly those from non-White backgrounds, report feeling unsupported by mentors at their own hospitals, which can affect their training and career development. Researchers created a national mentorship program that matched 123 resident doctors with 85 experienced surgeon mentors from different hospitals across the country, pairing them based on what qualities the residents were looking for in a mentor. After one year, about 77 percent of residents had actually met with their mentors, and nearly two-thirds said their mentor was a good fit, with some residents gaining opportunities they would not have had otherwise. The program showed promise in filling a real gap, especially for residents who wanted mentors who shared their background or identity, and most participating mentors found the experience meaningful and rewarding. To make the program work better in the future, organizers should send more reminders to keep people engaged and provide discussion guides to help mentors and residents have more productive conversations.

title: A Model for Clinician and Staff Education in the Engagement of American Indians in Genomic Research.
abstract: Despite notable differences in cancer incidence and outcomes, fewer American Indians have participated in cancer research and genomic testing relative to their population size. Contributing factors include historical scientific mistrust, lack of culturally appropriate research methodologies, and limited access. With the launch of a cancer genomic sequencing trial in American Indians from the Southwestern United States (US), clinicians and staff encountered challenges engaging patients, recognizing the complexity of research in this population. We describe a novel approach to educate study team members regarding genomic cancer testing and research in American Indian populations. Clinical faculty and staff investigators participated in (1) hands-on experiential workshops related to core beliefs and healthcare in American Indians and (2) the development of provider-facing educational materials. After participation in the workshops, investigators, including American Indian researchers, created two sets of provider-facing materials and implemented them in clinic. The first provided a summary detailing trial eligibility, procedures, and privacy safeguards. The second outlined topics fostering respectful engagement of American Indians in research, outlining core beliefs including the importance of family and community in decisions, a framework of inherent cycles in human life and nature, the importance of visual aids, and the complementary nature of traditional healing. An approach incorporating cultural training for clinicians and staff is feasible when engaging American Indians of the Southwestern US in genomic research. This methodology may serve as a model for future initiatives to engage with American Indians in cancer research and in both clinical and research related genomic testing.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: American Indian communities have experienced higher rates of cancer but have participated less often in cancer research and genetic testing compared to their population size, partly due to historical mistrust of science and lack of culturally appropriate approaches. Researchers created a training program for doctors and clinic staff working with American Indian patients in the Southwest who were participating in a cancer genomic sequencing trial, which is a study that examines a person's genes to understand their cancer risk. The training included hands-on workshops where staff learned about American Indian core beliefs and healthcare practices, and the team developed educational materials that explained the research in a respectful and culturally sensitive way. The educational materials highlighted important values like the role of family and community in medical decisions, the connection between human life and natural cycles, and the value of traditional healing practices alongside modern medicine. This approach shows that teaching clinicians and staff about cultural practices is practical and effective, and the same model could be used in future efforts to involve American Indian people in cancer research and genetic testing programs.

title: Neurological complications in microgravity and long duration spaceflight.
abstract: Long-duration spaceflight produces structural, functional, and hemodynamic brain changes driven by microgravity, radiation, elevated CO2, and isolation. Consequences include Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome, vestibular imbalance, orthostatic intolerance, and cognitive disturbance. We consolidate current evidence, present a cerebrovascular physiologic framework, and discuss emerging countermeasures-including lower body negative pressure, artificial gravity, advanced neuromonitoring, and synthetic torpor-needed to safeguard neurological health on exploration-class missions.© 2026. llm_summary: Long space missions expose astronauts to weightlessness and other harsh conditions that can cause serious changes in how the brain works and looks. Researchers reviewed all available evidence about the neurological problems that happen during extended spaceflight, including issues with vision and eye pressure, balance problems, difficulty standing up without fainting, and trouble thinking clearly. The study found that microgravity, radiation exposure, high carbon dioxide levels, and isolation all contribute to these brain and nervous system complications. The researchers proposed a framework based on how blood vessels in the brain function and suggested several new protective strategies such as applying pressure to the lower body, creating artificial gravity, using advanced brain monitoring technology, and inducing a sleep-like state called synthetic torpor. These findings are important for planning future long-distance space exploration missions and protecting astronauts' brain health during extended time away from Earth.

title: Reverberant wavefield characterization and directional filtering for penile vibro-elastography: a pilot feasibility study in post-prostatectomy erectile dysfunction.
abstract: Penile vibro-elastography is complicated by reverberant shear wavefields from the cylindrical geometry of the corpus cavernosum (CC), which bias shear wave speed (SWS) estimates. This study evaluated local phase velocity imaging with wavefield band-pass filtering (LPVI-WBF) for CC stiffness assessment in post-prostatectomy erectile dysfunction (ED), compared against phase gradient (PG) and time-of-flight (TOF) methods.Six patients with post-prostatectomy ED underwent penile vibroelastography at four longitudinal visits (902 acquisitions). SWS was estimated in flaccid and erect states at 100, 150, and 200 Hz using LPVI-WBF, PG, and TOF. Wavefield composition was quantified via the standing wave index. Simulations evaluated accuracy and frequency stability under clean and reverberant conditions.Reverberant components dominated penile acquisitions, with traveling wave energy absent in 59% of acquisitions and mean standing wave fraction of 57 ± 17%. LPVI-WBF was the only method producing physiologically consistent estimates, with erect SWS exceeding flaccid (3.59 ± 0.48 vs 3.25 ± 0.58 m/s, p < 0.0001). PG and TOF yielded reversed results (E < F, p < 0.0001). The dispersion exponent was near-zero for LPVI-WBF (α = 0.048, p = 0.21), consistent with weakly viscoelastic tissue, while PG (α = 0.184) and TOF (α = 0.321) showed significant frequency dependence from reverberant contamination. Simulations confirm PG accuracy in clean wavefields but collapse under reverberant ones.LPVI-WBF produced SWS estimates consistent with expected CC biomechanics across all patients and frequencies, a criterion PG and TOF failed to satisfy. llm_summary: Researchers examined a new imaging technique to measure tissue stiffness in the penis of men who developed erectile dysfunction after prostate removal surgery, since the standard methods were giving confusing results due to sound waves bouncing around inside the cylindrical penile tissue. Six patients underwent ultrasound vibration tests at four different visits where sound waves were sent into the tissue and the researchers measured how fast the waves traveled, using three different analysis methods to see which one worked best. The new method called local phase velocity imaging with wavefield band-pass filtering produced results that made biological sense, showing that erect tissue was stiffer than flaccid tissue, while the two older methods gave backwards results that contradicted what doctors would expect. This finding suggests the new technique could help doctors better understand and diagnose erectile dysfunction by accurately measuring how stiff the penile tissue becomes, which is important because tissue stiffness directly affects erectile function. The researchers acknowledge that more testing with artificial tissue models and additional wave direction studies are needed before this method can be fully trusted for routine clinical use.

title: SU056 potentiates SULF2 antibody in suppressing cholangiocarcinoma metastasis via SULF2-YBX1-CXCR4 signaling axis.
abstract: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), the second most common subtype of primary liver cancer around the world, is an aggressive neoplasm with high metastastic potential, which leads to a low rate of curative resections and dismal prognosis. In previous studies, Sulfatase 2 (SULF2) has been reported to regulate various important oncogenic signaling pathways and promote iCCA progression. Further research is needed to explore the role of SULF2 in iCCA metastasis. In this study, we verified the overexpression of SULF2 in iCCA tissues and its positive correlation with advanced stage and poor prognosis. Trans-well migration and invasion assay and mouse models explored the impact of SULF2 on iCCA metastasis in vitro and in vivo. We also demonstrated that SULF2 facilitated iCCA metastasis through upregulating CXCR4 transcription mediated by the transcription factor YBX1. Moreover, SULF2 could recruit USP7 to interact with YBX1 and inhibit Lys48-polyubiquitination of YBX1, stabilizing YBX1 and promoting a functional YBX1/CXCR4 axis. Combining SULF2 monoclonal antibody with SU056 had a synergistic effect in suppressing iCCA progression and metastasis of mouse models. In conclusion, SULF2 promotes iCCA progression and metastasis through an intracellular SULF2-YBX1-CXCR4 axis, and SULF2 monoclonal antibody combined with YBX1 inhibitor SU056 may be a potentially promising treatment strategy for iCCA.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, a type of liver cancer that spreads quickly and has a poor survival rate, is a serious disease that researchers are working to understand and treat more effectively. Scientists in this study examined how a protein called SULF2, which was found to be overproduced in cholangiocarcinoma tumors, helps cancer cells spread to other parts of the body by activating a chain reaction involving two other proteins called YBX1 and CXCR4. Using laboratory experiments with cancer cells and tests in mice, the researchers discovered that SULF2 stabilizes the YBX1 protein by preventing its natural breakdown, which then causes cancer cells to produce more CXCR4 and become more likely to migrate and invade surrounding tissues. The team found that combining a SULF2 antibody (a type of immune protein that targets SULF2) with a drug called SU056 (which blocks YBX1) worked together more effectively than either treatment alone to slow cancer growth and spread in mouse models. These findings suggest that using both treatments together could potentially become a new strategy to help patients with this.

title: Myelodysplastic Syndromes in VEXAS.
abstract: VEXAS syndrome is a clonal hemato-inflammatory disorder impacting older, predominantly male patients, characterized by systemic inflammation and progressive bone marrow failure. It is caused by somatic mutations in UBA1, an X-linked gene, essential for initiating cellular ubiquitination. Loss-of-function mutations, most commonly M41 missense variants, lead to decreased expression of the cytoplasmic isoform, UBA1b, resulting in accumulation of misfolded proteins and activation of the endoplasmic reticulum stress pathway. Patients classically present with systemic and often refractory inflammation, requiring chronic glucocorticoid treatment and targeted immunosuppressive therapies. A central hallmark of this syndrome is progressive bone marrow failure and associated cytopenia, with a diagnosis of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) being reported in approximately 30-50% of patients while only 1% of unselected MDS patients have UBA1 mutations. This review examines current literature on distinct MDS features reported in VEXAS syndrome. We first summarize the defects and alterations in the hematopoietic system from UBA1 mutations, including associated peripheral blood and bone marrow findings. Next, we describe the histological and molecular characteristics of patients with VEXAS syndrome, with and without MDS, and review potential treatment strategies, including responses to hypomethylating agents. Finally, we highlight that VEXAS-associated MDS is a challenging diagnosis but one with unique clinical, laboratory, and morphological features, including prognostic implications.Copyright © 2026 American Society of Hematology.

llm_summary: VEXAS syndrome is a rare blood disorder that primarily affects older men and causes both widespread inflammation and progressive bone marrow failure, a condition where the bone marrow gradually loses its ability to produce healthy blood cells. The disease is caused by mutations in a gene called UBA1, which normally helps cells break down and recycle damaged proteins, and when this gene malfunctions, harmful proteins build up inside cells and trigger stress responses. Researchers reviewed existing studies to understand how VEXAS syndrome affects the bone marrow and blood, finding that about 30 to 50 percent of VEXAS patients develop myelodysplastic syndromes, which are blood cancers characterized by abnormal blood cell production, compared to only 1 percent of typical blood cancer patients. The review identified that VEXAS-associated blood cancers have unique features in how they appear under a microscope and in their genetic makeup, and some patients respond well to certain cancer treatments like hypomethylating agents, which are drugs that change how genes are expressed. Understanding these distinctive characteristics of VEXAS-related blood cancer is important because it can help doctors recognize and diagnose the condition more accurately,.

title: Genomic features do not account for differences in multiple myeloma risk by ancestry.
abstract: Studies have reported conflicting findings regarding the contribution of germline variants or somatic genomic drivers to racial disparities in multiple myeloma (MM). To comprehensively investigate somatic drivers in relation to inherited genetics in MM, we combined newly sequenced whole-genome sequencing data with publicly available datasets (total n = 1,286). Overall, we did not identify germline or somatic genomic differences that explain the different risk of developing MM between patients with genetic similarity to African (AFR) or European (EUR) reference populations. A difference in the detectability and timing of APOBEC-associated and germinal center mutational activity was observed. Integrating epidemiological data and mutational signature-based temporal estimates, we challenge the assumption that individuals in the AFR group develop MM at a younger age. Finally, we demonstrate that, with equal access to efficacious therapies, patients in the AFR and EUR groups have equivalent clinical outcomes.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether genetic differences between people of African and European ancestry could explain why multiple myeloma, a blood cancer affecting bone marrow, occurs at different rates in these populations. The team combined new genetic sequencing data from patient tumors with existing datasets from nearly thirteen hundred patients to compare inherited genes and cancer-causing mutations between ancestry groups. They found no genetic differences in either inherited traits or tumor mutations that would account for the different risk of developing multiple myeloma between African and European ancestry groups. The study also showed that when patients from both ancestry groups had equal access to effective treatments, they experienced the same clinical outcomes and survival rates. These findings suggest that differences in multiple myeloma rates between populations are likely driven by factors outside of genetics, such as healthcare access or environmental influences, rather than by biological differences in the disease itself.

title: Aging Slows Maximum Shortening Velocity and Reduces Peak Power Output of Rat Diaphragm Muscle.
abstract: Sarcopenia is the age-related atrophy and weakening (decrease in force per cross-sectional area) of muscle fibers. In rat diaphragm muscle (DIAm), sarcopenia primarily affects type IIx/IIb fibers that generate greater specific force, have the fastest maximum shortening velocities (Vmax), but display greater fatigue with repeated activation. We hypothesized that because of the selective effect of sarcopenia on type IIx/IIb DIAm fibers, Vmax and peak power output of the DIAm decreases in old age, while endurance during repetitive isovelocity shortening is unaffected. Mid-costal DIAm strips were excised from 6-month (n=8; 4 female and 4 male) and 24-month (n=8; 4 female and 4 male) Fischer 344 rats. The DIAm was supramaximally stimulated using platinum plate electrodes to measure mechanical and endurance properties at 26oC. In 24- compared to 6-month old rats, maximum specific force of the DIAm decreased by ~35%, Vmax slowed by ~20%, and peak power output was reduced by ~35%. During repetitive isovelocity (~30% Vmax; approximating peak power output) contractions, endurance (the period during which power output was sustained) of the DIAm was not different between 6- and 24-month rats. The changes in DIAm mechanical properties corresponded to an age-related decline in the cross-sectional area of type IIx/IIb muscle fibers (~35%). We conclude that age-related atrophy of type IIx/IIb DIAm fibers underlies the changes in mechanical properties of the DIAm, which would only impact more forceful expulsive airway clearance and voiding behaviors of the DIAm. The resilience of type I and IIa DIAm fibers with aging ensures that force generation and endurance required for breathing is sustained in old age.

llm_summary: Muscles naturally weaken and shrink as people age, a condition called sarcopenia, which can affect how well the diaphragm (the main breathing muscle) works. Researchers studied young and old rats to see how aging changed the diaphragm's ability to contract quickly and generate power by removing muscle tissue and testing it in the laboratory. They found that older rats had a thirty-five percent decrease in maximum force, a twenty percent slowdown in how fast the muscle could shorten, and a thirty-five percent reduction in peak power output compared to younger rats. The good news is that the older rats' ability to keep working during repeated contractions stayed the same, meaning the basic breathing function was preserved even though the muscle lost some of its strength and speed. These findings suggest that aging primarily damages the fast-twitch muscle fibers that handle forceful actions like coughing, while leaving the slow-twitch fibers that control regular breathing relatively unharmed.

title: The Evolving Role of Clinical Anatomy: From Definition to Contribution.
abstract: The term "clinical anatomy" is widely used in education and research, yet its conceptual boundaries continue to be interpreted in various ways. Prior consensus-based efforts have emphasized integration, collaboration, and clinical relevance as central features of the field and have provided an important foundation for interdisciplinary engagement. At the same time, ongoing changes in academic structure, medical education, and interdisciplinary biomedical science raise important questions regarding how clinical anatomy can sustain its scientific identity and long-term relevance. Building upon prior discussions, this article argues that the continued maturation of clinical anatomy depends on the integration of conceptual frameworks with the sustained production of rigorous, reproducible, and clinically meaningful scholarly contributions. Historical and contemporary examples alike demonstrate that the influence of clinical anatomy has been shaped through contributions that directly advanced clinical science and practice. Accordingly, continued emphasis on methodological rigor, reproducibility, clinically meaningful contribution, and educational accountability may be essential to the field's future development and relevance.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Clinical anatomy, which is the study of human body structures and how they relate to medical practice, has become increasingly important in medical education and research, but experts have struggled to agree on exactly what it includes and how it should be defined. A group of leading anatomists and medical educators reviewed how clinical anatomy has evolved over time and examined what makes it most valuable to the medical field. They found that clinical anatomy's greatest impact comes from research and teaching that directly improves patient care and medical practice, rather than from abstract theoretical work alone. The authors argue that for clinical anatomy to remain relevant and respected in the future, it must focus on producing high-quality, trustworthy research that can be repeated by other scientists and that clearly benefits real-world medicine. Moving forward, the field should emphasize careful research methods, honest reporting of results, practical applications to patient care, and clear accountability in how anatomy is taught to medical students.

title: Risk Factors for Small Bowel Crohn's Disease Recurrence after Total Proctocolectomy.
abstract: Surgical management of Crohn's disease of the colon and rectum frequently requires total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy. There is limited data on the need for Crohn's disease-directed therapy and the prevalence of recurrence after surgery.To determine the risk of small bowel Crohn's disease recurrence and evaluate risk factors for postoperative recurrence after total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy.Retrospective cohort study.Multistate tertiary healthcare system.Adult patients with Crohn's disease undergoing total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy between 2014-2023.The primary outcome was small bowel Crohn's disease recurrence.A total of 193 patients with a median age of 45 years (IQR, 34-61) were included. Over half of the patients (n = 102, 52.9%) had a history of small bowel Crohn's disease and the majority (n = 134, 69.4%) received biologic therapy prior to surgery. The median follow-up time was 4.8 years (IQR, 2.0-7.6). Postoperatively, 30.6% of patients (n = 59) received biologic therapy. Thirty-five patients (18.1%) had small bowel Crohn's disease recurrence for an estimated 5-year recurrence-free rate of 80.2% (95% CI, 73.0-85.7). Seven patients (3.6%) developed small bowel Crohn's disease recurrence requiring surgery for an estimated 5-year surgical recurrence-free rate of 94.7% (95% CI, 89.0-97.5). On multivariable analysis, history of small bowel Crohn's disease (HR 2.17; 95% CI' 1.04-4.54) and diagnosis at age <18 years (HR 2.31; 95% CI'1.1-4.86) were associated with small bowel Crohn's disease recurrence.Retrospective design and non-standardized follow-up.Patients undergoing total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy for Crohn's disease have approximately a 20% risk of small bowel recurrence at 5 years but a low risk of requiring surgical intervention. Patients with a history of small bowel Crohn's disease and younger age at diagnosis have a higher risk of recurrence and may warrant consideration of more frequent surveillance and medical prophylaxis. This retrospective study, which means doctors looked back at medical records from 2014 to 2023, included 193 adult patients to determine how often the disease returned in the small intestine after surgery and what factors increased that risk. The results showed that about 18 percent of patients experienced a return of Crohn's disease in their small bowel within five years, though only about 3. 6 percent needed another surgery because of this recurrence. Patients who had previously experienced Crohn's disease in their small bowel or who were diagnosed with the disease before age 18 had roughly double the risk of recurrence compared to other patients.

title: Systematic review and meta-analysis: Stress ulcer prophylaxis in mechanically ventilated patients.
abstract: Studies have compared proton pump inhibitors (PPI) with Histamine 2 receptor antagonists (H2RA) and placebo for upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) prophylaxis in mechanically ventilated patients. We conducted this meta-analysis to compare PPI with H2RA or placebo for UGIB prophylaxis in these patients. Our outcomes of interest were clinically important UGIB, overall UGIB, mortality, ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and Clostridium difficile infection (CDI). We calculated pooled risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for all outcomes. We included eight RCTs comprising 32873 patients. Risk of clinically important UGIB was significantly lower in PPI group, RR (95%CI): 0.53 (0.32, 0.89). Risk of overall UGIB was also significantly lower in PPI group. There was no significant difference in mortality, VAP and CDI between groups. This meta-analysis demonstrates the superiority of PPI to H2RA and placebo for prophylaxis of UGIB in mechanically ventilated patients, without increasing the risk of adverse events.Copyright © 2026. llm_summary: Mechanically ventilated patients in intensive care units are at risk for upper gastrointestinal bleeding, which is bleeding in the stomach and upper digestive tract, so doctors often give medications to prevent this serious complication. Researchers reviewed eight randomized controlled trials involving nearly 33,000 patients to compare two types of preventive medications: proton pump inhibitors, which reduce stomach acid production, and histamine 2 receptor antagonists, which also reduce acid but work differently. The study found that proton pump inhibitors were significantly better at preventing both serious bleeding and overall bleeding compared to the other medication or no treatment at all. Importantly, using proton pump inhibitors did not increase the risk of other dangerous complications like pneumonia from the breathing machine or infections from the bacteria Clostridium difficile. These findings suggest that proton pump inhibitors should be the preferred choice for protecting mechanically ventilated patients from upper gastrointestinal bleeding without causing additional harm.

title: Disparities in Preoperative Weight Loss and Obesity Treatment Before Total Joint Arthroplasty.
abstract: Institutions often implement body mass index (BMI) cutoffs for offering total hip (THA) and knee (TKA) arthroplasty. The goals of this study were to determine disparities in preoperative obesity prevalence, obesity treatment utilization, and weight loss efficacy.Among 21,038 primary THAs and 23,726 TKAs performed between 2002 and 2019, we identified 6,128 patients who had preoperative BMIs ≥ 30 measured one to 24 months before surgery, including 4,953 with available Area Deprivation Index (ADI) information. The mean age was 67 years (range, 19 to 97) with 55% women. The mean BMI was 36 (range, 20 to 69). The ADI was used to analyze socioeconomic status. Univariable and multivariable analyses evaluated the use of nutrition services or bariatric surgery, the likelihood of weight loss, and ADI's potential association with weight loss.A few patients received preoperative weight loss medications (0.2%), nutrition services (1.6%), and/or bariatric surgery (2.6%). Compared to the best (least deprived) ADI quartile 1, the worse ADI quartiles 3 and 4 were associated with an increased odds of BMI ≥ 40 preoperatively (odds ratio (OR) 1.4, P = 0.01 and OR 1.9, P < 0.01, respectively). Women were associated with an increased odds of BMI ≥ 40 preoperatively (OR 1.6, P < 0.01) and were more likely to receive bariatric surgery (OR = 2.3, P < 0.01). Women had lower odds of losing ≥ five pounds (OR 0.9, P = 0.02).The BMI cutoffs of 40 before TJA may disproportionately affect women and patients who have lower socioeconomic status. Few patients received preoperative obesity treatment before TKA or THA via medications, nutrition services, or bariatric surgery. The study looked at over 44,000 patients who had these surgeries between 2002 and 2019, focusing on 6,128 patients who were overweight before their operations and analyzing whether their socioeconomic status (their income level and neighborhood resources) affected their care. The results showed that very few patients received help with weight loss before surgery, with less than three percent receiving weight loss medications, nutrition counseling, or weight loss surgery. title: Dysautonomia and Joint Hypermobility Reflect a Distinct Subtype in Eosinophilic Esophagitis.
abstract: Joint hypermobility (JH) and autonomic symptoms commonly co-exist and are associated with gastrointestinal symptoms and poor quality of life (QOL). Gastric and duodenal mast cells (MC) may be increased in these patients; however, their relevance to eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is unclear.We aimed to understand the relationship between autonomic symptoms and JH in EoE with symptoms, QOL, and MCs.Eighty EoE patients undergoing esophagogastroduodenoscopy at Lurie Children's Hospital (1/2021-3/2024) were prospectively enrolled. Patients/caregivers completed validated surveys assessing EoE symptoms (Pediatric Eosinophilic Esophagitis Symptom Survey [PEESS], QOL, and autonomic symptoms (Composite Autonomic Symptom Score [COMPASS-31]). JH was determined using a published survey and Beighton score. Tryptase immunohistochemistry was quantified in gastric and duodenal biopsies. COMPASS-31 was compared by disease activity and hypermobility and with a published control cohort. Associations with PEESS, PedsQL and MCs were assessed. Linear regression evaluated COMPASS-31 predictors.COMPASS-31 was higher in EoE patients than controls (P<0.001) and active EoE compared with Remission (P=0.02). COMPASS-31 correlated positively with PEESS scores, particularly Gastroesophageal Reflux, Nausea/Vomiting, and Pain domains, and inversely with QOL. 26% of EoE patients were hypermobile and had higher COMPASS-31 (P=0.003). llm_summary: Researchers examined whether people with eosinophilic esophagitis, a condition where the food pipe becomes inflamed due to immune cells called eosinophils, also experience problems with their nervous system that controls automatic body functions like heart rate and digestion, as well as joint flexibility issues. The study enrolled eighty patients with this esophageal condition who completed surveys about their symptoms, quality of life, and autonomic nervous system problems, while doctors also took tissue samples from their stomachs and small intestines to count immune cells. The researchers found that patients with active disease and those with loose, flexible joints had significantly higher levels of autonomic nervous system symptoms, and these two factors independently predicted how severe these symptoms were. title: Trial-design-aware funnel plot for publication bias assessment with non-inferiority or equivalence objectives.
abstract: Funnel plots are the most widely used graphical tool for assessing publication bias (PB) in meta-analyses of superiority trials. However, conventional funnel plots are not directly applicable to non-inferiority (NI) or equivalence (EQ) objectives, which are governed by distinct inferential frameworks and may be prone to inverse publication bias (IPB), a tendency for studies with results far from the null to be underreported. This pattern contrasts with classical PB, where studies with results close to the null are more likely to be suppressed.We propose trial-design-aware funnel plots, a design-aware visualization that incorporates inferential boundaries specific to NI and EQ objectives. By explicitly delineating regions corresponding to key decision thresholds, the proposed plots facilitate visual assessment of where PB or IPB is most likely to arise. For EQ objectives, the plot distinguishes regions supporting equivalence, inferiority, and superiority; for NI objectives, it highlights regions reflecting inferiority and non-superiority. The framework also accommodates meta-analyses comprising mixtures of NI, EQ, and superiority trials, enabling coherent bias assessment across heterogeneous study designs.We illustrate the proposed approach using three real-world meta-analyses: one EQ-only set, one NI-only set, and one mixed superiority-NI set. These examples demonstrate the flexibility and interpretability of the design-aware funnel plots across commonly encountered trial objectives.The trial-design-aware funnel plot offers a flexible and intuitive visualization tool for identifying between-study bias in meta-analyses with NI and EQ objectives. It may be particularly valuable for safety outcomes, where the bias mechanisms may differ from classic PB and carry substantial decision-making consequences. Conclusions regarding possible publication bias, however, may be strongly margin dependent and should be interpreted in light of the prespecified or clinically justified margin.Copyright © 2026. The team created a new visual tool called a trial-design-aware funnel plot that shows where bias or hidden studies are most likely to occur by marking different decision zones on a graph, making it easier to spot patterns that suggest some research results were never published. They tested their new method on three real examples from medical literature, including studies that mixed different types of trial objectives together, and showed that the tool could work across many different situations. This approach is especially important for safety studies where the reasons studies get hidden might be different from traditional research bias, and where these hidden studies could seriously affect medical decisions. However, researchers warned that conclusions about hidden studies depend heavily on the specific safety limits doctors set beforehand, so these findings should always be interpreted carefully alongside those predetermined limits.

title: Structural and functional changes in articulating joints during aging of male and female C57BL/6JN mice.
abstract: Define the natural history of articular joint changes in aging C57BL/6JN mice.Male and female C57BL/6JN mice of various ages were obtained from the National Institute on Aging (NIA). Male and female mice of different ages had their knee joints studied using three methods: a microscope that measures surface properties called atomic force microscopy, tissue examination under a regular microscope, and measurement of a protective protein called Proteoglycan 4 that lubricates joints. Male mice showed signs of cartilage damage and stiffness between 12 and 16 months of age, along with decreased levels of the protective lubricating protein, while female mice only showed stiffness changes at a later age and did not develop cartilage damage or meniscus problems. The atomic force microscopy method proved to be the most sensitive tool for detecting joint changes in both male and female mice, making it useful for future studies. These findings help scientists design better experiments and treatments for joint diseases in this common laboratory mouse strain.

title: Aortic Stenosis Progression: Lessons from Multimodality Imaging.
abstract: Calcific aortic stenosis primarily affects the aging population and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. The progression of aortic stenosis from sclerotic aortic valve to severe aortic stenosis is an active metabolic process that involves multiple signaling pathways. Multimodality imaging can assess aortic valve calcification and metabolic activity and quantify severity of disease. This review describes the clinical utility of echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, cardiac computed tomography, and nuclear imaging in the assessment of aortic stenosis. These imaging checkpoints may also serve as targets of clinical research trials aimed at halting the progression of aortic stenosis.Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: Calcific aortic stenosis, a condition where the aortic valve (the valve that controls blood flow from the heart) becomes thick and stiff due to calcium buildup, is a serious problem that affects many older people and causes significant health complications and deaths. Researchers reviewed how different imaging tools, including ultrasound of the heart, magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography scans, and nuclear imaging, can be used to see and measure the calcium buildup in the aortic valve and track how active the disease process is. The progression from a mildly damaged valve to severe aortic stenosis involves complex biological processes with multiple pathways that actively change over time, and multimodality imaging can help doctors assess both the amount of calcium present and the severity of the disease. These various imaging techniques can serve as checkpoints to monitor disease progression and may help researchers identify targets for new treatments designed to slow down or stop the worsening of aortic stenosis. Understanding how to use these imaging tools together could improve how doctors monitor patients and help guide future clinical trials testing new ways to prevent the disease from getting worse.

title: Mechanisms of Local CSF-Venous Fistula Persistence after Transvenous Embolization for Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension.
abstract: CSF-venous fistulas (CVF) are an important cause of spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) and are increasingly treated with transvenous embolization (TVE). Based on the current published literature, approximately 8% of patients experience symptomatic recurrence due to local CVF persistence at the same site and level of prior TVE. The mechanisms responsible for persistent local CVF after TVE are unknown. Among 10 patients with local CVF persistence/recurrence after TVE, we found two mechanisms: 1) CVFs that occur at the margin of the Onyx cast, typically within the external venous plexus or the basivertebral vein; and 2) CVFs that occur due to inadequate occlusion of the internal epidural venous plexus, though not necessarily at the distal end of the Onyx cast. These findings may facilitate technical optimization of TVE for CVF and may also enable localization of persistent CVF in patients with symptomatic recurrence after TVE.© 2026 by American Journal of Neuroradiology.

llm_summary: Cerebrospinal fluid leaks into veins in the spine, a condition called CSF-venous fistulas, are an increasingly recognized cause of low fluid pressure around the brain and spinal cord, and doctors have been treating them with a procedure called transvenous embolization where they block the problematic veins from the inside. However, about eight percent of patients treated with this procedure experience the problem returning at the same location, but doctors did not understand why this was happening. Researchers studied ten patients whose fistulas came back after treatment and discovered two main reasons for the failure: either the fistula reopened at the edges of the material used to block the vein, or the internal network of veins in the spine was not completely blocked even though the main blockage appeared successful. These findings help doctors understand what goes wrong during treatment and suggest ways to improve the procedure by being more thorough in blocking all the problematic veins. Understanding these failure patterns will help doctors better treat patients with this condition and predict where new fistulas might develop if symptoms return after an initial procedure.

title: A progeria syndrome links DNA hypermethylation to age-related pathology.
abstract: Declining tissue function and regenerative capacity underlie many chronic diseases. Experimentally establishing the mechanistic basis for such tissue aging presents substantial challenges, given decades-long timescales and multifactorial origins. Epigenetic alterations have been proposed to have a key etiological role, but whether they are correlative or causal remains a key unanswered question, as does their contribution to specific age-related pathologies. Here we describe an epigenetically driven accelerated aging syndrome. We demonstrate that DNMT3A gain-of-function mutations in Heyn-Sproul-Jackson syndrome recapitulate age-related gains in DNA methylation (DNAme), cause multilineage stem cell dysfunction, and phenocopy aspects of aging in humans and mice. We also show that region-specific DNA hypermethylation at lineage-specific genes can explain reduced stem cell output and lineage skewing. Hence, starting from a Mendelian disorder, we implicate DNAme-mediated stem cell dysfunction in the etiology of medically important age-related hematological, bone and metabolic pathologies, which might be targetable by future therapies.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined how changes in DNA chemical tags, called methylation, might cause the body to age faster and lead to age-related diseases like blood disorders and bone problems. They studied a rare genetic syndrome called Heyn-Sproul-Jackson syndrome, which is caused by mutations in a gene called DNMT3A that controls how these chemical tags are added to DNA. The team found that people and mice with this syndrome showed the same patterns of increased DNA methylation that normally happen during aging, and this caused stem cells (cells that can develop into different cell types) to stop working properly. These findings suggest that abnormal DNA methylation directly causes stem cell dysfunction and may explain why certain tissues lose their ability to repair and regenerate as we age. The research opens the door to developing new treatments that could reverse or slow down age-related diseases by targeting these harmful changes in DNA methylation.

title: ERO1a fosters glioblastoma aggressiveness and metabolic flexibility by regulating mitochondria-associated membrane dynamics.
abstract: Despite the wealth of data generated in the omics era to investigate molecular drivers, glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most incurable cancers with a poor median of survival. Here we unravelled the dynamic crosstalk between the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, known as mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs) and define how modulation of calcium fluxes and MAM structure influences GBM cell plasticity and metabolic flexibility. We identified ERO1α, whose expression is significantly associated with poor GBM patient survival, as a critical MAM protein that regulates MAM structure, dynamics and calcium-mediated functions. Our data demonstrate that ERO1α activity and expression promotes GBM aggressiveness in vitro and in vivo and enhances mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. By establishing a direct link between ERO1α-mediated MAM modulation and the antitumour effects of ERO1α inhibition, this work highlights a context-dependent, druggable vulnerability that can be exploited for GBM therapy.© 2026. llm_summary: Glioblastoma is one of the deadliest brain cancers with very poor survival rates, and scientists are searching for new ways to understand and treat it. Researchers studied how two cellular structures, the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, communicate with each other through special connection points called mitochondria-associated membranes, and how this communication affects cancer cell behavior and energy production. They discovered that a protein called ERO1 alpha plays a crucial role in controlling these connections and that high levels of this protein are linked to worse outcomes in glioblastoma patients. The team found that blocking ERO1 alpha activity slowed down cancer growth both in laboratory dishes and in living animals by reducing the cancer cells' ability to produce energy efficiently. This research suggests that targeting ERO1 alpha could be a promising new treatment strategy for glioblastoma patients in the future.

title: Emerging omics diagnosis of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract: Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (pCCA) frequently presents as an indeterminate perihilar biliary stricture. The diagnosis is often delayed or uncertain because of the limited sensitivity of conventional endobiliary sampling and blood-based markers, especially in patients with additional confounding conditions such as primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). This diagnostic ambiguity can significantly impact clinical outcomes as timely detection and accurate classification are critical for referral and curative-intent treatment. As such, research focused on advancing diagnostic methodologies is a priority. pCCA has a distinct proteomic signature, pattern of activated signaling cascades, epigenetic modifications, and metabolic interactions within its anatomic niche. Recent advances in omics-based diagnostics have leveraged these biological features to identify biomarkers for accurate pCCA diagnosis. In this review, we summarize emerging evidence for omics-based diagnostics in pCCA using clinically accessible samples, including biliary brushings, bile and serum/plasma samples. We discuss the key aspects of pCCA biology that form the foundation for development of novel techniques including glyco-/phospho-/proteomic, genomic, methylomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses as well as multiomic approaches. We conclude by outlining how artificial intelligence may help integrate the data into diagnostic algorithms and identifying areas requiring further investigation to advance these diagnostics into routine clinical practice.© 2026. llm_summary: Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma, which is a type of cancer that grows in bile ducts near the liver, is difficult to diagnose because current testing methods are not sensitive enough and the condition often looks similar to other bile duct problems, especially in patients with a related liver disease called primary sclerosing cholangitis. Researchers reviewed emerging diagnostic techniques based on studying the biological molecules and genetic material found in patient samples like bile fluid, blood, and tissue brushings collected during medical procedures. These new omics approaches, which involve analyzing proteins, genes, chemical markers, and metabolic patterns in cancer cells, have shown promise in identifying unique signatures that can accurately distinguish perihilar cholangiocarcinoma from other conditions. Finding better diagnostic methods is important because early and accurate detection allows doctors to refer patients for life-saving surgery and treatment before the cancer spreads. The review suggests that artificial intelligence computer programs could help combine all this biological data into practical diagnostic tools, though more research is still needed before these advanced tests become standard practice in hospitals and clinics.

title: Efficacy Outcomes of Fecal Microbiota, Live-jslm in Preventing Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection from Seven Clinical Studies.
abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is one of the most common healthcare-associated infections in the US, and recurrence remains a major clinical challenge, as standard-of-care antibiotics fail to prevent recurrence in up to one-third of cases. Fecal microbiota, live-jslm (RBL) is the first single-dose, microbiota-based product approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and Health Canada for the prevention of recurrent CDI (rCDI) following standard-of-care antibiotics. The RBL clinical development program is the largest to date for any microbiota-based product, encompassing seven studies and enrolling over 1700 participants to evaluate the safety and efficacy of RBL in preventing rCDI. Although the RBL development program consistently evaluated both efficacy and safety outcomes across all studies, this review summarizes the study designs, with a primary focus on the efficacy outcomes. The program consists of randomized controlled trials, open-label cohorts, retrospective analyses, and real-world data, each contributing unique insights across different patient populations and treatment settings. All studies enrolled adults aged ≥ 18 years with rCDI who received antibiotics for their enrolling CDI episode before RBL administration. Most studies administered RBL rectally, except for an open-label study and a retrospective study, which evaluated colonoscopic administration of RBL. Treatment success was evaluated at 8 weeks, and sustained clinical response was evaluated at 6 or 24 months after RBL and/or placebo administration, depending on the study design. Overall, the study designs for all seven studies were consistent, with slight differences between number of CDI episodes (specifically, 2 studies allowed enrollment after the first CDI recurrence), blinding, controls, and administration routes. Efficacy data of RBL reported across all studies consistently demonstrated RBL is efficacious for the prevention of rCDI in a broad adult population. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov. Researchers examined the safety and effectiveness of a new treatment called fecal microbiota, live-jslm, which is the first single-dose product made from healthy human gut bacteria that was approved by the Food and Drug Administration to prevent recurring infections after antibiotic treatment. title: Antigen Removal Approach to Murine Larynx Engineering Optimizes Extracellular Matrix Preservation.
abstract: To compare antigen removal processing with conventional sodium dodecyl sulfate decellularization for generating laryngotracheoesophageal scaffolds, focusing on preservation of extracellular matrix integrity and removal of immunogenic material.Laryngotracheoesophageal complexes were harvested from C57BL/6 mice and processed using either antigen removal or sodium dodecyl sulfate-based protocols. Scaffolds were analyzed for residual double-stranded DNA content, collagen preservation, glycosaminoglycan retention, and ultrastructural integrity via histology, quantitative image analysis, and scanning electron microscopy.Both antigen removal and sodium dodecyl sulfate protocols achieved effective decellularization, with comparable dsDNA removal relative to native controls (p = 0.001; p < 0.001). Antigen removal scaffolds demonstrated better collagen preservation compared to sodium dodecyl scaffolds, which exhibited marked collagen depletion (Muscle: Collagen I, p < 0.001; Collagen III, p < 0.01; Cartilage: Collagen I, p < 0.05; Collagen III, p < 0.01). Both antigen removal and sodium dodecyl sulfate groups showed significant glycosaminoglycan depletion compared with controls (p < 0.001). Scanning electron microscopy confirmed superior ultrastructural preservation in antigen removal-treated scaffolds, characterized by intact fibrillar architecture and lacunar morphology, while sodium dodecyl sulfate scaffolds demonstrated collapsed lacunae and irregular extracellular matrix organization.Antigen removal processing generates laryngotracheoesophageal scaffolds with enhanced extracellular matrix preservation compared with conventional sodium dodecyl sulfate decellularization, while maintaining equivalent levels of antigen elimination. Retention of collagen and ultrastructure suggests antigen removal scaffolds may provide superior biomechanical and biologic performance for laryngeal tissue engineering. Although glycosaminoglycan depletion remains a limitation in both approaches, antigen removal scaffolds represent a promising pathway toward clinically translatable alternatives to immunosuppression-dependent laryngotracheoesophageal repair.Preclinical.© 2026 The American Laryngological, Rhinological and Otological Society, Inc.

llm_summary: Researchers examined different ways to clean and prepare donated larynx tissue, which is the voice box, for use in transplants and tissue engineering to help patients with larynx damage. They compared two cleaning methods on mouse larynx tissue: one called antigen removal, which targets and eliminates immune-triggering substances, and another called sodium dodecyl sulfate decellularization, which is a more traditional chemical cleaning approach. Both methods successfully removed cellular material and immune-triggering substances from the tissue, but the antigen removal method preserved the tissue's structural proteins called collagen much better than the traditional method, which damaged these important proteins significantly. The antigen removal method also maintained the tissue's overall architecture and structure more effectively, as shown by detailed microscopic imaging that revealed intact fiber networks and proper cell spaces in the preserved tissue. These findings suggest that the antigen removal approach could lead to better tissue transplants for larynx repair that might work without requiring patients to take immune-suppressing medications, though both methods still depleted certain natural tissue components called glycosaminoglycans that future research will need to address.

title: Artificial intelligence in pathology: a framework for preserving brain capital in the diagnostic apex.
abstract: To present a five-criterion calibration framework for evaluating artificial intelligence (AI) tools in pathology centered on preserving "brain capital" - the finite cognitive resources available to clinicians - and stabilizing the "diagnostic apex," the point where histological evidence meets clinical judgment.Using cognitive load theory (CLT) and implementation science, we developed the Pathology AI Diagnostic Balance - a conceptual model mapping the physician-specimen interaction within working memory and IT infrastructure constraints - and examined it in the context of peer-reviewed case studies of implemented pathology AI tools.The framework identifies five criteria: Contextual Literacy (integration of clinical history), Responsibility (preservation of signing authority), Evidence Gap Analysis (closure of diagnostic uncertainty), Verification (feasibility of quality control), and Opportunity Cost (return on cognitive investment). Successful tools, such as Ki-67 quantification and breast cancer screening, reduce cognitive burden by automating routine tasks or enabling rapid verification. Conversely, tools requiring an exhaustive re-review or producing opaque recommendations deplete cognitive bandwidth, causing decision fatigue and diagnostic errors.Pathologists are positioned to exercise evaluative authority over tools that increase extraneous cognitive load. Clinical expertise represents pathologists' most distinctive contribution to AI development: defining which failure modes matter clinically, what context an AI must integrate, and whether a tool serves patient care. By prioritizing cognitive sustainability over purely technical metrics, the profession can ensure AI functions as a genuine enhancement of diagnostic capability rather than an additional burden on diagnostic workflows.

llm_summary: Doctors who read tissue samples under microscopes have limited mental energy to make decisions, and artificial intelligence tools should be designed to help rather than add more work to their thinking process. Researchers created a five-point checklist to evaluate whether new AI tools in pathology actually make doctors' jobs easier by considering factors like whether the tool explains its reasoning, whether doctors still have final say over diagnoses, and whether it solves real diagnostic problems. The study found that successful AI tools are ones that handle routine counting tasks or quickly verify findings, while tools that force doctors to re-examine everything or give unclear recommendations actually make doctors more tired and prone to mistakes. Pathologists should be the ones deciding which AI tools are worth using by thinking about whether the tool truly helps patient care and doesn't just add burden to their already demanding work. By focusing on protecting doctors' mental resources and decision-making authority rather than just measuring technical performance, the medical field can make sure artificial intelligence genuinely improves how diseases are diagnosed instead of making the job harder.

title: Clinicopathologic characteristics of early-onset breast cancer among unselected young Black women.
abstract: Black women are more likely to develop and die from early-onset breast cancer. Hereditary breast cancer (HBC) is strongly associated with early age of onset. Accordingly, HBC characteristics in young Black women were evaluated.Black women diagnosed with invasive breast cancer at age 50 years or younger between 2005 and 2018 were recruited through the state cancer registries in Florida and Tennessee. Participants were asked to complete a questionnaire, sign medical records releases, and donate a saliva sample for free genetic testing to identify HBC germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant (GPV). Women with sporadic versus hereditary breast cancer were compared, based on age distribution, clinical characteristics, and family cancer history.Among 686 participants with confirmed genetic testing, 15.3% had GPVs in breast and/or ovarian cancer predisposition genes, including BRCA1 (7.7%), BRCA2 (4.5%), PALB2 (0.9%), and ATM (0.7%), with 1.5% in other genes. Compared to the sporadic group, triple-negative breast cancers were overrepresented among BRCA1 carriers (23.6% vs. 75.5%; p < .001), and family history of breast cancer was significantly more frequent among BRCA1, BRCA2, and PALB2 carriers (all p < .05). The majority of breast cancers occurred by age 40 years in BRCA1 carriers (52.8%), compared to other genes, where age was more evenly distributed.Among unselected young Black women with breast cancer, our findings demonstrate that the highest frequency of HBC GPVs are in BRCA1, BRCA2, and PALB2, with identification of distinct histopathologic and demographic characteristics across HBC genes, underscoring the critical need for genetic testing in all populations.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Black women develop early-onset breast cancer, which is cancer diagnosed before age 50, at higher rates than other groups, and researchers wanted to understand whether inherited genetic mutations that increase cancer risk play a role in these cases. Scientists recruited 686 young Black women with breast cancer from Florida and Tennessee between 2005 and 2018, asked them to complete surveys about their family history, and tested their saliva samples for genetic mutations known to increase breast cancer risk. The study found that about 15 percent of the women carried inherited genetic mutations in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, and PALB2, which are genes that normally help prevent cancer, and women with BRCA1 mutations were much more likely to have triple-negative breast cancer, a particularly aggressive type that is harder to treat. The results show that genetic testing should be offered to all young Black women diagnosed with breast cancer, not just those with a strong family history, because many women carrying these risky mutations might otherwise go unidentified and miss opportunities for early screening and prevention. These findings highlight the importance of including diverse populations in genetic research and cancer care, since understanding how inherited cancer risk varies across different racial and ethnic.

title: Executive summary of American Radium Society Appropriate Use Criteria for the treatment of locoregionally recurrent rectal cancer.
abstract: This literature-based systematic review and associated guidelines provide evidence-based paradigms for the management of locoregionally recurrent rectal cancer (LRRC). This multispecialty committee included gastrointestinal radiation and medical oncology, gastroenterology, radiology, and colorectal surgery. As is the standard, the previously described American Radium Society Appropriate Use Criteria methodology for this project was followed rigorously, with the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Timing, and Study Design framework and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses methodology to assess the evidence. RAND/University of California Los Angeles consensus methodology (modified Delphi) was used to rate the appropriateness of treatment options. Published between January 1, 2013, and July 16, 2025, 116 peer-reviewed trials provided the evidence: 10 were well-designed randomized phase 2/3 trials, 29 were moderately well designed trials that accounted for most common biases (matched cohort and phase 2), 76 trials had design limitations (retrospective), and one was a meta-analysis. Clinical cases were created as examples to illustrate current acceptable management of LRRC. Treatment and prognosis are influenced by prior therapy and the site(s) and extent of LRRC. The ability to achieve a margin-negative surgical resection is the ultimate determinant of survival and local control. Preoperative systemic therapy, radiation therapy, or a combination of the two can facilitate tumor downsizing and improve the likelihood of a margin-negative resection. An individualized multidisciplinary approach is required to ensure the best outcome. Although this review does not suggest a major alteration of current practice, it provides reassuring evidence of the importance of combined-modality therapy.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: A team of cancer specialists created evidence-based guidelines to help doctors treat locoregionally recurrent rectal cancer, which is cancer that comes back in the same area after initial treatment. The researchers reviewed 116 published studies from 2013 to 2025, including the highest quality randomized trials as well as smaller studies, and used a voting process called the modified Delphi method to determine which treatments were most appropriate. The most important finding was that the ability to surgically remove the cancer with clean margins, meaning no cancer cells are left behind, is the strongest predictor of whether patients will survive and stay cancer-free. Before surgery, doctors can use chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or a combination of both to shrink the tumor and make it easier to remove completely, and the best approach depends on each patient's unique situation including what treatments they received before. Although this review confirms that current medical practices are working well, it emphasizes that treating recurrent rectal cancer successfully requires a team of different specialists working together to create a personalized treatment plan.

title: Heart transplant evaluation in adults with congenital heart disease presenting with advanced heart failure.
abstract: Adults with congenital heart disease (CHD) with stage D heart failure (HF) have 1-year mortality risk of almost 40% without heart transplantation, and as a result, heart transplant evaluation is the logical next step in the management of these patients. The purpose of this study was to describe the clinical characteristics and outcome of adults with CHD referred for heart transplant evaluation.Adults with CHD referred for heart transplant evaluation were divided into 3 treatment pathways after multidisciplinary transplant evaluation. (i) Transplant-listed group (patients with stage D HF and eligible for transplant); (ii) Transplant-declined group (patient with stage D HF but had contraindications for transplant); (iii) Transplant-deferred group (patients without stage D HF).There were 416 patients who underwent transplant evaluation (transplant-listed group [N = 159,38%]; transplant-declined group [N = 101,24%]; transplant-deferred group [N = 156;38%]). Of 159 patients in the transplant-listed group, 110 underwent heart transplant. The patients who received heart transplant had similar survival compared to patients without stage D HF. Among patients with stage D HF (N = 260), heart transplantation was associated with a 9-fold reduction in all-cause mortality. End-organ dysfunction and congestion were common among patients who were declined for transplant listing or died while waiting for transplant and were associated with all-cause mortality.Heart transplantation was associated with improved survival in adults with CHD presenting with stage D HF. End-organ dysfunction and congestion were associated with greater odds of being declined for transplant and waitlist mortality, suggesting need for earlier referral for transplant evaluation to improve outcomes.Among 416 patients referred for heart transplant evaluation, 38% (N = 159) were listed for transplant because of stage D HF of which 110 underwent transplant, 24% (N = 101) were declined for transplant listing because of contraindications to transplant, and 38% (N = 156) were deferred for transplant listing because they did not have stage D HF. Among patients with stage D HF (N = 260), heart transplantation was associated with a 9-fold reduction in all-cause mortality. llm_summary: Adults born with heart defects that worsen over time face a nearly 40 percent risk of death within one year without a heart transplant, making evaluation for transplant a critical step in their care. Researchers examined 416 adults with congenital heart disease, meaning heart problems present from birth, who were referred for heart transplant evaluation and divided them into three groups based on whether they were listed for transplant, declined for transplant due to other health problems, or deferred because their condition had not yet reached the most severe stage. Among the 159 patients who were listed for transplant because of advanced heart failure, 110 actually received a new heart, and these transplant recipients had survival rates similar to patients whose heart disease had not yet reached the most severe stage. Heart transplantation reduced the risk of death by nine times compared to patients with advanced heart failure who did not receive a transplant, and patients who were declined for transplant or died while waiting often had problems with organ function and fluid buildup in their bodies. The findings suggest that doctors should refer patients with congenital heart disease for transplant evaluation earlier in their disease course, before serious complications like organ damage and fluid accumulation develop.

llm_summary: Background:  Major depressive disorder is a serious mental health condition that affects many young people and can significantly impact their daily lives, relationships, and overall well-being. Brain stimulation treatments, which use electrical or magnetic techniques to activate specific areas of the brain, have shown promise as potential therapies for depression, but researchers face significant challenges when testing these treatments in youth populations due to differences in brain development, safety concerns, and the difficulty of conducting rigorous scientific studies with younger participants.

title: Evaluating the impact of SDHAF3 p.F53L genetic variant on clinically significant QTc prolongation in patients prescribed high-risk medications: a retrospective pharmacogenetic study.
abstract: Drug-induced QT prolongation (diQTP) can lead to rare, but potentially fatal adverse effects of many medications, yet individual susceptibility varies due to both clinical and genetic factors. SDHAF3 p.F53L (rs62624461) is a genetic variant that plays a role in mitochondrial function and was previously associated with diQTP in one small prior study. Therefore, the objective of this retrospective pharmacogenetic study was to evaluate whether SDHAF3 p.F53L is associated with clinically significant diQTP. Data were obtained from the Michigan Genomics Initiative, which links genotype information with electronic health records at Michigan Medicine. Adult patients with available genotype and electrocardiogram data who received at least one high-risk QT-prolonging drug between 2001 and 2022 were included. The analysis was limited to 5848 patients of European ancestry, of whom 320 (5.5%) were carriers of the SDHAF3 p.F53L variant. QT prolongation was defined as a QTc greater than or equal to 500 ms or an increase greater than 60 ms from baseline during high-risk QT-prolonging drug prescription. Logistic regression under a dominant genetic model assessed associations between variant carrier status and diQTP, with and without propensity score adjustment. Baseline demographics and comorbidities were similar between carriers and noncarriers. No significant association was observed between SDHAF3 p.F53L and diQTP [unadjusted odds ratio (OR) = 1.06, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.76-1.48, P = 0.742; adjusted OR = 1.05, 95% CI = 0.74-1.51, P = 0.773]. These results suggest that SDHAF3 p.F53L does not meaningfully influence diQTP risk in a large, real-world clinical cohort. Future studies should examine this variant across diverse populations.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Some medications can dangerously slow the heart's electrical rhythm, a condition called QT prolongation, but doctors have noticed that different people react differently to these drugs based on their genes and health conditions. Researchers looked at nearly six thousand patients of European ancestry who took high-risk heart medications between 2001 and 2022, checking whether a specific genetic variant called SDHAF3 p. F53L made them more likely to develop this dangerous heart rhythm problem. The study found no meaningful connection between carrying this genetic variant and developing drug-induced QT prolongation, with the variant carriers showing almost the same risk as those without it. These results suggest that this particular genetic variant does not play an important role in determining who will experience this serious medication side effect, which means doctors cannot use this genetic test to predict this risk in their patients.

title: Adenine base editor for knockout of proteins: A practical guide from design to analysis with updated MultiEditRbatch.
abstract: Adenine base editors (ABEs) are a promising yet underutilized tool for inducing protein knockout compared to Cas9 nuclease, owing in part to a lack of user-friendly platforms for reagent design and implementation. Here, we present a comprehensive workflow to achieve high-efficiency gene knockouts with ABE as an alternative to Cas9 nuclease-based approaches. This includes optimized guide RNA (gRNA) design using SpliceR, a web-based application, followed by genomic and functional validation of ABE-mediated knockouts for several target genes. We validated gRNAs for 14 immunologically relevant targets, using both NGG and NG PAM compatible ABE8e-variants in primary immune cells. To facilitate data analysis, we developed MultiEditRbatch, an updated version of MultiEditR as a user-friendly analysis tool with addition of batch mode for high-throughput analysis of Sanger sequencing data. MultiEditRbatch is available as a web-based application and an R package, enabling robust assessment of base editing outcomes.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Adenine base editors, which are molecular tools that can change the genetic code to turn off disease-causing genes, have been underused compared to other gene-editing methods because scientists lacked easy-to-use software for designing and implementing them. Researchers created a complete step-by-step guide for using adenine base editors to knock out, or disable, proteins in cells, including a web-based tool called SpliceR to design the genetic instructions needed for the editing process. The team tested their approach on fourteen different genes important for immune function in human immune cells and developed an updated analysis tool called MultiEditRbatch that can quickly process and analyze results from many samples at once. These findings suggest that adenine base editors could become a practical and efficient alternative to other gene-editing methods like Cas9 nuclease, potentially making it easier for researchers to develop new treatments for genetic diseases. The user-friendly software tools and detailed workflow presented in this research should help more scientists adopt adenine base editing in their work and accelerate the development of gene-based therapies.

title: Immune responses in aging adults.
abstract: As a widely distributed network of cells, tissues, and organs, the human immune system is profoundly vulnerable to the effects of aging. Intrinsic and extrinsic stressors progressively erode its structural integrity and functional resilience, weakening core protective responses and increasing susceptibility to infection, malignancy, and tissue degeneration. At the same time, aging heightens the risk of chronic inflammation and autoimmune disease. Hematopoietic stem cells become uniquely compromised as aging intensifies metabolic and replicative stress. Their continuous high-volume turnover results in diminished self-renewal capacity, skewed lineage output, and dominance of expanded clones. These changes undermine innate immune competence and amplify inflammatory activity. Adaptive immune function declines with age through coordinated cellular and molecular programs. T and B lymphocytes exhibit a decline in naive cells, progressive loss of stemness, shortened lifespan, and constrained clonal diversity. Aging lymphocytes reconfigure transcriptional networks, undergo widespread organelle dysfunction, develop maladaptive stress responses, and redistribute into noncanonical tissue niches. Collectively, these alterations reduce antigen specificity and precision, promote innate-like immune behavior, and confer resistance to tolerance. These mechanisms result in concurrent immunodeficiency and autoimmunity, exemplified by two autoimmune diseases disproportionately affecting older adults: rheumatoid arthritis and giant cell arteritis.

llm_summary: The human immune system, which is the body's defense network against infection and disease, becomes weaker and less effective as people grow older. As aging occurs, the cells that produce immune cells in the bone marrow become stressed and worn out, leading to fewer protective immune cells and more inflammatory activity that can harm the body. Older adults experience a decline in both types of immune protection: their bodies become worse at fighting off new infections and diseases, while at the same time becoming more likely to attack their own tissues through autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. The immune cells themselves, called T and B lymphocytes, lose their ability to recognize and respond to threats effectively, become less diverse in their responses, and start behaving in ways that promote inflammation rather than protection. Understanding these age-related changes in the immune system is important for developing better treatments to help older adults stay healthy and prevent the serious infections and autoimmune diseases that commonly affect them.

title: Antifibrotic therapy and lung cancer risk in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: a large retrospective propensity-weighted cohort study.
abstract: Antifibrotic (AF) therapy has been shown to potentially reduce the risk of lung cancer (LC) in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Our study further assesses the impact of AF use and LC incidence in a real-world cohort with patient-level data.A retrospective multisite cohort study involving patients with IPF followed at Mayo Clinic between 2005 and 2022 was conducted. We identified individuals with new diagnoses of LC in the pre-AF and post-AF eras and defined AF use as continuous treatment for 6 months or more before LC diagnosis. Given the inclusion of LC cases prior to the wide availability of AF therapy and potential differences in patients exposed and unexposed to treatment, propensity score analysis with inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to balance comparator groups. Fine and Gray modelling was used to explore risk factors for developing LC, reported as parameter subdistribution HRs (SHR).A total of 3313 patients with IPF were included (1161 treated and 2152 non-treated). LC incidence rates were lower for treated patients in the post-AF era (0.34 vs 1.25 per 100 person-years, p<0.001). After IPTW, 2148 treated were compared with 2167 non-treated individuals. AF treatment was independently associated with reduced LC risk (SHR 0.36 (0.16-0.82), p=0.02), while smoking history and higher forced vital capacity were associated with increased risk.AF use appears to be associated with a reduced incidence rate and risk of LC in patients with IPF.© Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether antifibrotic drugs, which slow lung scarring, might lower the chances of developing lung cancer in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a serious lung disease where tissue becomes increasingly scarred and stiff. The study looked back at medical records from over three thousand patients treated at Mayo Clinic between 2005 and 2022, comparing those who received antifibrotic treatment for at least six months with those who did not receive these drugs. Patients who took antifibrotic medications had significantly fewer cases of lung cancer, with rates dropping from 1. 25 cases per one hundred patient-years to just 0. 34 cases per one hundred patient-years.

title: Factors Associated with Aortic Valve Calcification in Type 2 Diabetes - A Steno INTEN-CT substudy.
abstract: This study aimed to identify clinical factors associated with AVC in individuals with T2D.This cross-sectional study is a pre-specified substudy of the multicenter randomized Steno INTEN-CT trial (Clinical Trials - INTEN-CT). Participants were eligible if they had T2D without ischemic heart disease and were aged between 55-69 years (men) or 60-74 years (women). All participants underwent non-contrast cardiac computed tomography. AVC was measured in Agatston Units and categorized as 0, 0-300, ≥ 300.Of the 4570 participants, 46% had AVC > 0. With increasing AVC, patients were older, predominantly males, and with significantly more comorbidities.
