llm_summary: Researchers examined a problem called subsidence, which happens when the bone around a surgical implant in the spine gradually sinks or collapses after a procedure called transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion, a common back surgery where doctors insert a cage-like device between vertebrae to stabilize the spine. The study looked back at medical records and imaging scans from 67 patients who had this surgery between 2017 and 2019, measuring how much subsidence occurred and comparing it to changes in spinal alignment and patient pain or disability scores. The results showed that patients who experienced severe subsidence, defined as sinking of four millimeters or more, ended up with less natural curve in their lower spine compared to those with mild subsidence, even though both groups reported similar improvements in pain and daily function. This finding is important because it suggests that severe subsidence can undo some of the surgical benefits by changing the spine's alignment, which might affect long-term outcomes even if patients feel better in the short term. Future research should follow patients for longer periods to determine whether these alignment changes from severe subsidence eventually lead to worse pain, disability, or the need for additional surgery.

title: Guidelines of care for the primary prevention of atopic dermatitis and awareness of comorbid conditions in pediatric atopic dermatitis.
abstract: Pediatric atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common, chronic inflammatory skin disorder that significantly impacts the quality of life of affected children and their families. In addition to skin-related symptoms, AD in pediatric patients may be associated with a range of comorbid conditions.To provide evidence-based recommendations on primary prevention of AD and to appraise evidence of the association between AD and comorbidities among pediatric patients.A multidisciplinary workgroup conducted a systematic review and applied the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach for assessing the certainty of evidence and formulating and grading recommendations.The workgroup developed 14 evidence-based recommendations on primary prevention of AD and 29 statements on the association between pediatric AD and comorbid conditions.This analysis is based on the best available evidence at the time it was conducted. This guideline does not make recommendations for screening or management of comorbidities in children with AD.We make a conditional recommendation for moisturizing skin care to reduce the occurrence of AD and conditional recommendations against early food introduction, human milk consumption, and probiotic or vitamin D supplementation for the primary prevention of AD. Clinicians should be aware of comorbidities associated with pediatric AD, but further research is needed to optimize screening and/or management of comorbidities.Copyright © 2026 American Academy of Dermatology, Inc. llm_summary: Pediatric atopic dermatitis, a chronic skin condition that causes inflammation and itching in children, significantly affects the quality of life for affected children and their families, and it often occurs alongside other health conditions. A team of dermatologists and medical experts reviewed scientific evidence and used a systematic approach to develop recommendations for preventing atopic dermatitis in children and to identify which other health conditions are associated with the skin disorder. The researchers created fourteen evidence-based recommendations for preventing atopic dermatitis, with the strongest support being for regular skin moisturizing, while they advised against early introduction of foods, exclusive breast milk feeding, and supplements like probiotics or vitamin D for prevention. The study found that while clinicians should be aware of various health conditions that commonly occur with pediatric atopic dermatitis, the guidelines do not yet provide specific recommendations for how to screen for or treat these associated conditions. Further research is needed to better understand how to identify and manage the other health problems that often develop alongside atopic dermatitis in children.

title: Guidelines of care for the management of atopic dermatitis in pediatric patients.
abstract: Pediatric atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common, chronic inflammatory skin disorder that significantly impacts the quality of life of affected children and their families. Multiple therapies were approved to treat AD in children and adolescents since publication of the AAD's 2014 AD guidelines.To provide evidence-based recommendations on the use of topical therapies, phototherapy, and systemic therapies for AD in children and adolescents.A multidisciplinary workgroup conducted a systematic review and applied the GRADE approach for assessing the certainty of evidence and formulating and grading recommendations.The workgroup developed 27 evidence-based recommendations on the medical management of pediatric AD.This analysis is based on the best available evidence at the time it was conducted. Most randomized controlled trials of therapies for AD are of short duration limiting long-term efficacy and safety conclusions.We make strong recommendations for the use of moisturizers, topical calcineurin inhibitors, topical corticosteroids, crisaborole ointment, roflumilast cream, ruxolitinib cream, tapinarof cream, dupilumab, tralokinumab, lebrikizumab, nemolizumab with concomitant topical therapy, upadacitinib, abrocitinib, and baricitinib in the treatment of pediatric AD. We make conditional recommendations in favor of bathing, bleach baths, wet dressings, phototherapy, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, and cyclosporine. We conditionally recommend against the use of topical antimicrobials, PUVA phototherapy, and strongly recommend against systemic corticosteroids.Copyright © 2026 American Academy of Dermatology, Inc. llm_summary: Atopic dermatitis, a chronic skin condition that causes itching and inflammation, is common in children and significantly affects their quality of life and their families' wellbeing. A team of dermatologists and medical experts reviewed scientific evidence and created updated guidelines for treating this condition in children and teenagers, since several new medications have become available since the previous guidelines were published in 2014. The researchers strongly recommend using moisturizers, various topical creams applied directly to the skin, and newer medications like dupilumab and ruxolitinib cream, while they conditionally recommend other treatments like phototherapy (light-based treatment) and certain oral medications for more severe cases. The guidelines advise against using topical antimicrobials (bacteria-killing creams) and strongly warn against systemic corticosteroids, which are oral or injected steroids that affect the whole body. Most studies of these treatments were relatively short in duration, which means doctors still need longer-term research to fully understand how safe and effective these medications are over many years of use.

title: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia According to Chlorhexidine Oral Care Exposure in Patients With New Tracheostomy.
abstract: Chlorhexidine is commonly used in prevention bundles for ventilator-associated pneumonia. Results for use of chlorhexidine in critically ill patients requiring mechanical ventilation via an endotracheal tube are mixed, and data for patients using a tracheostomy are lacking.To assess the risk for ventilator-associated pneumonia according to chlorhexidine exposure in patients requiring a new tracheostomy for mechanical ventilation.This single-center, retrospective cohort study compared the development of ventilator-associated pneumonia according to chlorhexidine exposure in adult intensive care unit patients requiring new tracheostomy at a large academic medical center. Adults who received a new tracheostomy and required ventilator support for at least 48 hours were included. Patients treated for pneumonia at the time of tracheostomy or who met additional exclusion criteria were excluded.Of 235 patients who met the inclusion criteria, 203 received chlorhexidine and 32 did not. The cohort was predominantly White, male, and admitted to a surgical intensive care unit. Incidence of ventilator-associated pneumonia did not differ significantly between patients exposed or not to chlorhexidine (by 30 days, 32.5% vs 35.7%, P = .87). Time to development of ventilator-associated pneumonia also did not differ significantly between patients exposed or not (9 vs 12 days, respectively, P = .34).Chlorhexidine exposure was not associated with a difference in the incidence of or time to ventilator-associated pneumonia after new tracheostomy. Further study is needed on the role of chlorhexidine in preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia after a new tracheostomy.©2026 American Association of Critical-Care Nurses.

title: Computational phosphoproteomic insights into predominant BRAF phosphosites and associated regulatory networks in cancer.
abstract: BRAF, a serine/threonine kinase, functions as a key effector of the MAPK signaling cascade and regulates cell proliferation and survival. Oncogenic BRAF mutations disrupt MAPK pathway homeostasis, contributing significantly to cancer progression and pathogenesis. BRAF phosphorylation is pivotal for modulating downstream signaling events. In this study, we performed a comprehensive analysis of global human phosphoproteomic datasets to elucidate BRAF phosphorylation dynamics and associated regulatory networks. The systematic annotation identified BRAF phosphorylation in 912 qualitative profiles across 166 studies and 234 quantitative differential datasets from 73 studies, revealing 44 and 21 distinct phosphosites, respectively. Class I phosphosites with localization probability ≥75% or A-score > 13 were filtered. A fold-change threshold of ≥1.3 for upregulation and ≤ 0.76 for downregulation was applied. Particularly, six predominant phosphorylation sites, S446, S729, S151, T401, S365, and S447, were frequently observed. Further analysis of melanoma-melanoma-specific phosphoproteomic datasets and correlations with gene expression data from melanoma cell lines revealed several key co-regulated proteins associated with the predominant BRAF phosphosites, including STAT3, BAD, CDK16, ITPKB, NPM1, MDC1, CHEK2, PRKDC, EIF3A, TP53BP1, RB1, and CDK14. These co-regulated proteins highlight the integration of BRAF signaling with critical processes, such as cell cycle control, apoptosis, DNA damage response, and protein synthesis in melanoma. Our analysis suggests that targeting BRAF-interacting proteins may also modulate oncogenic signaling pathways and represent promising biomarkers for melanoma diagnosis and therapy.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. llm_summary: Researchers examined how a cancer-causing protein called BRAF gets modified through a process called phosphorylation, which is when chemical tags are added to proteins to change how they work in cancer cells. The team analyzed data from hundreds of scientific studies involving thousands of patient samples to identify the most common places where these chemical tags attach to BRAF and to understand which other proteins work together with BRAF in melanoma, a deadly form of skin cancer. They discovered six main phosphorylation sites on BRAF that appear most frequently and found that BRAF works together with twelve other important proteins that control cell division, cell death, DNA repair, and protein production. These findings suggest that doctors might be able to develop better treatments for melanoma by targeting not just BRAF itself but also the proteins that work with it, and these discoveries could help identify new ways to diagnose and treat the disease. Future research will need to test these findings in laboratory and animal studies to confirm whether blocking these BRAF-related proteins could actually stop cancer growth in real patients.

title: Platelet factor 4 antibody persistence and long-term pathogenicity in vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia.
abstract: Vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT) is a transient prothrombotic process, although recent data suggest that VITT anti-platelet factor 4 (PF4) antibodies are more persistent than those in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.We sought to interrogate whether anti-PF4 antibody persistence in VITT is related to the continued persistence of antibody clones from the acute phase or to the development of novel anti-PF4 antibodies due to epitope spreading.Samples from 6 patients with Ad26.COV2.S-associated VITT with a median time to follow-up of 244 days from acute presentation (range, 114-664 days) were studied in antigenic/functional assays and by mass spectrometry. One patient with ChAdOx1 nCoV-19-associated VITT was tested >4 years after acute presentation.Upon affinity-enrichment of anti-PF4 antibodies, mono/oligoclonal anti-PF4 antibodies were observed despite negative results in serum protein electrophoresis/"Mass-Fix" testing of native sera. Anti-PF4 antibody abundance decreased over time, with no evidence of novel anti-PF4 antibody production after acute presentation. Although previous studies indicate a stereotypical pairing of VITT antibodies with lambda light chains, 1 patient with VITT produced antibodies with a kappa light chain. Long-term thrombocytopenia/thrombosis was not seen in any of the 6 Ad26.COV2.S-associated VITT patients; however, platelet-activating anti-PF4 antibodies were seen 4 years after the acute event in an additional patient with ChAdOx1 nCoV-19-associated VITT with chronic low-grade thrombocytopenia.VITT, unlike monoclonal gammopathy of thrombotic significance, appears to be a monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance-negative state, but it needs confirmation in larger studies. VITT antibodies can be composed of lambda or kappa light chains, and some patients with VITT exhibit persistent thrombocytopenia many years after the acute event.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether antibodies against a blood protein called platelet factor 4 that develop after certain vaccines persist because they are the same antibodies from the initial immune response or because new antibodies keep forming over time. The team studied blood samples from seven patients who developed vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia, a rare condition where the immune system attacks platelets (blood cells that help with clotting), collecting samples up to four years after their initial illness. They found that the antibodies present months or years later were the same ones from the acute phase rather than newly formed antibodies, and the total amount of these antibodies decreased gradually over time. Most patients did not experience long-term blood clotting problems or low platelet counts, though one patient still had mild low platelet counts four years after infection. The researchers concluded that this vaccine-related condition appears to be a temporary immune response rather than a permanent disease, but they noted that larger studies are needed to confirm these findings and better understand why some patients develop lasting symptoms.

title: Decisional Conflict Among Adolescents and Young Adults Before and After Facilitated Decision-Making About Learning Personal Genomic Information.
abstract: To determine if decisional conflict differed between adolescent (ages 13-17) and young adult (ages 18-21) research participants making decisions about learning actual genomic testing results, and whether decisional conflict changed after a facilitated decision-making (FDM) session.Participants between the ages of 13-21 (n = 483) completed decisional conflict scale (DCS) surveys after using an electronic decision tool to make independent choices about learning genomic testing results (T1) and again following FDM with a study team member and parent if one was involved (T2). Participants had the option to change their choices at T2. We compared DCS scores of adolescents and young adults at T1 and T2.Median total DCS scores were significantly higher for adolescents than young adults at T1 (20.3 vs. 7.8; p < .0001) and T2 (11.7 vs. 1.6; p < .0001). There were significant decreases in median DCS scores from T1 to T2 among adolescents (20.3-11.7; p < .0001) and young adults (7.8-1.6; p < .0001).Although DCS scores were low overall, adolescents experienced higher decisional conflict than young adults. Decisional conflict levels decreased among both cohorts after FDM. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether young people feel uncertain or conflicted when deciding whether to learn their personal genetic test results, and whether talking through the decision with a counselor could help reduce that conflict. The study included 483 teenagers and young adults between ages 13 and 21 who first made their own independent choice about learning genomic information using an electronic tool, then had a guided discussion with a counselor and parent to talk through their decision again. Teenagers reported significantly higher levels of decisional conflict, meaning they felt more uncertain and torn about their choice, compared to young adults both before and after the counseling session. Both age groups experienced a meaningful decrease in their feelings of conflict and uncertainty after having the facilitated discussion with the counselor, suggesting that talking through the decision helped people feel more confident about their choice. Healthcare providers and researchers should make time to have thoughtful conversations with young people about genetic testing that focus on what matters most to them personally, rather than just presenting information alone.

Artificial intelligence technology is now being developed to help doctors more accurately diagnose thyroid nodules by analyzing medical images and data, which could reduce uncertainty and improve patient care by identifying which nodules truly need treatment.

title: Best practices for critically ill patients boarding in the emergency department: A Delphi study.
abstract: Boarding of critically ill patients in the emergency department is common and associated with worse outcomes due to delays in time-sensitive interventions. This study used a Delphi process to develop a checklist of best practices for managing these patients during this vulnerable period.Study personnel recruited a representative Delphi panel of 18 intensivists who are board certified in emergency medicine and critical care. We used a structured literature review to identify candidate items for a best practices checklist. This included a PubMed search of English language articles from 2011 to 2021 using terms like "critical illness," "emergency ward," "ICU," and "boarding." We scrutinized existing best practice checklists and specialty society guidelines. Panel members rated interventions using a seven-point Likert scale via web-based surveys and submitted comments, which were visible to co-panelists in subsequent rounds. Consensus for inclusion was defined a priori as ≥80% of panelists rating the item 5-7 on the Likert scale.An initial list of 92 candidate checklist items was evaluated by 18 expert panelists across three Delphi rounds, with response rates exceeding 85% in each round. The modified Delphi process identified 101 items that achieved consensus for inclusion in the final checklist. Consensus items addressed management of post-cardiac arrest syndrome, increased intracranial pressure, intracerebral hemorrhage, respiratory failure, and shock. Examples of highly rated items included vasopressor selection in shock, lung-protective ventilation strategies for mechanically ventilated patients, and protocolized sedation and analgesia after intubation. Additional consensus items addressed management of gastrointestinal hemorrhage, electrolyte imbalances, renal and liver failure, coagulopathy, endocrine abnormalities, infectious diseases, and considerations for devices and logistics.A Delphi process identified 101 expert consensus items for a checklist designed to support the care of critically ill patients boarding in the ED. Future studies are needed to evaluate implementation and potential effects on care processes and patient outcomes.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Critically ill patients sometimes have to wait in emergency departments before getting admitted to intensive care units, and this delay can lead to worse health outcomes because they miss out on urgent treatments they need. Researchers gathered eighteen expert doctors who specialize in both emergency medicine and critical care to identify the best practices for treating these very sick patients while they wait in the emergency department. Using a structured voting process across three rounds where experts rated different treatment approaches, the team identified one hundred and one specific actions and interventions that doctors should follow, including things like choosing the right blood pressure medications for patients in shock, using gentle breathing machine settings to protect the lungs, and managing pain and sedation after putting patients on breathing tubes. This checklist covers many serious conditions including heart attack recovery, brain swelling, bleeding in the brain, breathing failure, and various organ problems like kidney and liver failure. The next step is for hospitals to test whether using this checklist actually improves how doctors care for these patients and whether it leads to better outcomes for people's health.

title: Topical combined 5-fluorouracil and calcipotriene for actinic keratosis and superficial keratinocyte carcinoma: Modified Delphi expert panel recommendations from ITSCC.
abstract: Evidence on topical combined 5-fluorouracil/calcipotriene (5-FU/C) treatment of actinic keratoses (AKs), squamous cell carcinoma in situ (SCCIS), and superficial basal cell carcinoma is lacking.To develop an expert consensus regarding 5-FU/C treatment of AKs, SCCIS, and superficial basal cell carcinoma.Expert panelists were provided 5-FU/C literature review findings and survey results from International Immunosuppression and Transplant Skin Cancer Collaborative clinician members who prescribe 5-FU/C.Nine dermatologist/dermatologic surgeon International Immunosuppression and Transplant Skin Cancer Collaborative members with >5 years post-training experience or considerable clinical experience prescribing 5-FU/C participated in the panel. A 70% or higher concordance among respondents represented consensus. Key recommendations include: treating AKs with 5-FU/C twice daily for 4 to 5 days on the face/neck and 7 to 10 days on the scalp, trunk, and extremities; treating SCCIS with 5-FU/C twice daily for 7 to 10 days on the face/neck and 10 to 14 days on the scalp, trunk, and extremities; treating actinic cheilitis with 5-FU/C twice daily for 4 to 5 days; and no treatment modifications for patient immunosuppression.Small panel size and literature to date primarily including small, retrospective studies.Dermatologists may consider implementation of expert panel recommendations for treatment of AKs, SCCIS, and sBCC with 5-FU/C while awaiting larger, high-quality studies.Copyright © 2026 American Academy of Dermatology, Inc. llm_summary: Actinic keratosis, which is a rough, scaly patch of skin caused by sun damage, and squamous cell carcinoma in situ, a type of skin cancer that has not spread, are common skin conditions that doctors treat with various medications. A group of nine experienced dermatologists, who are skin specialists, reviewed existing research and surveyed other doctors to develop expert recommendations for using a topical combination treatment made of two medications called 5-fluorouracil and calcipotriene on these skin conditions. The panel agreed that patients with actinic keratosis should apply this combination twice daily for four to five days on the face and neck, or seven to ten days on other body areas, while those with squamous cell carcinoma in situ need longer treatment periods of seven to fourteen days depending on location. These recommendations provide practical guidance for dermatologists treating sun-damaged skin and early skin cancers, though the experts noted that most existing studies on this treatment are small and not as rigorous as researchers would prefer. Doctors can now use these expert guidelines while waiting for larger and more thorough research studies to confirm whether this combination treatment works as well as hoped.

title: Exploring the role of reinforcement learning in vision-language models for cardiovascular disease decision support.
abstract: To explore the role of reinforcement learning (RL) in vision-language models (VLMs) for cardiovascular disease (CVD) decision support and assess whether RL-enhanced multimodal reasoning improves clinical classification performance and interpretability across datasets.We propose CVD-thinking, a multimodal framework that integrates electrocardiogram (ECG) images with textual reports, demographic information, and laboratory results from MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-ECG. The model is trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with Clinical Classification Reward (CCR), a generalizable reward template that combines asymmetric outcome utilities with a soft F1 shaping term to mitigate reward sparsity. We use explicit reasoning prompts (<think>) to elicit step-by-step rationales, compare against supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and a GPT-4o baseline, and evaluate external validity on an independent Mayo Clinic dataset. Ablation studies assess the contributions of reward shaping and explicit reasoning.On the internal test set, GRPO training improved precision compared with baseline approaches (CVD-thinking: 0.716 vs. SFT: 0.662 vs. GPT-4o: 0.625). Explicit reasoning further improved performance relative to a non-reasoning variant (0.716 vs. 0.598) while producing traceable rationales. These gains generalized to the external Mayo Clinic dataset. Ablations suggest that reward shaping and explicit reasoning both contribute to performance and reasoning-format adherence.RL can improve the reliability and transparency of multimodal reasoning for CVD clinical decision support, but its impact on performance depends on the reward formulation. Model scale also matters: smaller backbones (e.g., 3B parameters) show less stable optimization and can experience performance degradation.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how artificial intelligence systems that combine images and text can better help doctors diagnose heart disease by using a training method called reinforcement learning, which rewards the system for making correct decisions. The team created a framework called CVD-thinking that analyzes heart rhythm images called electrocardiograms along with patient reports, personal information, and blood test results from hospital databases to make diagnoses. The reinforcement learning approach improved the system's accuracy compared to standard training methods, with the AI correctly identifying heart disease cases about 72 percent of the time versus 66 percent for traditional methods, and the system could also explain its reasoning step-by-step in a way doctors could understand and verify. These improvements held up when the researchers tested the system on patient data from Mayo Clinic, an independent medical center, suggesting the approach could work reliably in real-world healthcare settings. However, the researchers found that smaller artificial intelligence models with fewer computational parameters struggled with this training approach and sometimes performed worse, indicating that the size and design of the underlying system matters significantly for success.

title: Artificial intelligence in gastroenterology clinical practice: Scoping review of large language model applications.
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence have brought renewed attention to tools that can work with the large amount of written information generated in clinical practice. Among these, large language models (LLMs) stand out for their ability to interpret and generate medical text in a flexible, context-aware way. Gastroenterology, like many specialties, produces a wide range of narrative and semi-structured data, and this has encouraged researchers to explore how LLMs might help clinicians manage everyday tasks. Recent studies have examined their potential contributions to patient education, communication between care teams and patients, decision support, and routine documentation, reflecting a growing interest in how these systems might fit into real-world clinical workflows.This scoping review aimed to map current applications of LLMs in gastroenterology clinical practice, including subspecialty focus, study designs, model types, and reported outcomes.Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between January 2022 and August 2025. Eligible studies included original research assessing LLM applications in gastroenterology clinical practice. Data were extracted on subspecialty, application domain, LLM type, data source, and outcomes. We employed thematic analysis to address our primary research question.73 out of 2895 studies identified in the initial search met the inclusion criteria. Six subspecialties and six application domains emerged from our review. Hepatology (20/73 studies, 27.3%) and endoscopy (17/73 studies, 23.2%) were the most represented subspecialties. The most frequently investigated application domains were patient education and communication (38 studies) and decision support and clinical guidance (24 studies). Most studies were simulation-based or literature-based cases, although an increasing number have used real-world clinical data, particularly in recent years. The majority evaluated general-purpose models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, with some incorporating retrieval augmentation or fine-tuning. Reported outcomes varied by application domain and included measures of accuracy, concordance, completeness, relevance, safety, reliability, usability, user satisfaction, efficiency, time savings, and educational value. Commonly described limitations included variable reliability, incomplete responses, and challenges in generalizing from simulated to clinical settings.Research on LLMs in gastroenterology has expanded across multiple subspecialties and application domains. Current evidence is primarily based on simulation studies, with limited but growing evaluation using real-world clinical data. Further work is needed to assess performance in prospective and applied clinical contexts.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how artificial intelligence systems called large language models, which are computer programs trained to understand and write human language, could help doctors in gastroenterology, the medical specialty focused on the digestive system. The team searched through thousands of published studies between January 2022 and August 2025 and found 73 studies that tested these language models in real gastroenterology work, focusing on areas like liver disease and endoscopy procedures, which are camera examinations of the digestive tract. The studies showed that large language models were most often tested for helping patients understand their conditions and for giving doctors guidance on treatment decisions, with most research using simulated scenarios rather than actual patient data. While these artificial intelligence tools showed promise in areas like accuracy and saving doctors time, the research revealed important concerns including that the systems sometimes gave incomplete or unreliable answers and that results from practice simulations did not always work the same way in real hospitals. Researchers concluded that although large language models show potential for gastroenterology, much more testing in actual clinical settings with real patients is needed before these tools can be trusted for everyday medical care.

title: Housing-Based Socioeconomic Status at Birth and Risk of Mental, Behavioral, and Developmental Disorders in a Population-Based Cohort.
abstract: To evaluate whether the HOUsing-based SocioEconomic Status (HOUSES) index, a validated individual-level proxy derived from property data, predicts the risk of mental, behavioral, and developmental disorders (MBDDs).We performed a retrospective cohort study of live births (2010-2021) using the Rochester Epidemiology Project. The exposure, HOUSES index at birth, was categorized into quartiles (Q1 = lowest; Q4 = highest). The primary outcome was MBDD diagnosis by age 9. We used Cox proportional hazards models to assess risk, adjusting for prematurity.Of 79 444 children (median follow-up 6.2 years), 18 078 (22.8%) received an MBDD diagnosis. Risk increased in a dose-response manner as socioeconomic status decreased: compared with the highest quartile (Q4), adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were 1.11 (Q3), 1.21 (Q2), and 1.35 (95% CI 1.29-1.41) for Q1 (lowest). Comparing Q1 vs Q4, risks were pronounced for autism spectrum disorder (aHR 1.98; 95% CI 1.62-2.41), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (aHR 1.60; 95% CI 1.43-1.80), stress-associated disorders (aHR 1.57; 95% CI 1.24-1.99), and developmental speech or language disorders (aHR 1.20; 95% CI 1.12-1.29). In time-varying analyses accounting for residential mobility, the overall risk for Q1 compared with Q4 increased further (HR 1.69; 95% CI 1.64-1.75). In addition, children in Q1 had higher emergency department utilization rates (incidence rate ratio 1.44; 95% CI 1.41-1.48) compared with Q4. Conversely, no significant difference was observed for inpatient admissions across quartiles.Housing-based socioeconomic status is a robust, independent predictor of MBDD diagnosis. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a housing-based measure of economic status could predict which children would develop mental, behavioral, and developmental disorders, which are common conditions affecting how children think, act, and grow. The study followed nearly eighty thousand children born between 2010 and 2021, tracking whether they received a diagnosis of these disorders by age nine and comparing children from the poorest neighborhoods to those from the wealthiest ones. Children living in the poorest areas at birth were significantly more likely to be diagnosed with conditions like autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and speech or language delays compared to children from wealthy neighborhoods, with the risk increasing steadily as neighborhood wealth decreased. These findings suggest that housing and neighborhood conditions reflect important social factors that affect how children's brains and behavior develop, which could help doctors identify children who need extra support early on. Future research should explore which specific aspects of living conditions matter most and how healthcare providers can use this information to help at-risk children before problems become serious.

Understanding how this cancer affects different groups of people, such as men versus women, and whether its location on the body influences treatment outcomes and survival rates, is important for improving how doctors care for patients with this serious disease.

title: Incidence and outcomes of atrial arrhythmia with cyclin dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors in hormone receptor-positive / human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative breast cancer.
abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors are increasingly used in hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative (HR+/HER2-) breast cancer, yet emerging data suggest potential cardiotoxicity, including atrial arrhythmias (AA). Understanding incidence and outcomes of AA is essential as indications for CDK4/6 inhibitors expand.To evaluate the incidence of new-onset AA and associated outcomes in patients with HR+/HER2- breast cancer treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors.We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients who received CDK4/6 inhibitors for HR+/HER2- breast cancer at Mayo Clinic from 2015 to 2024. The primary outcome was incidence of AA (atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, or atrial tachycardia). Secondary outcomes included cerebrovascular events and all-cause mortality. Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models and Cox regression models were used to assess risk factors for AA and all-cause mortality, respectively.Among 2773 patients, 59% received palbociclib, 28% abemaciclib, and 14% ribociclib. New-onset AA occurred in 42, cumulative incidence at 5 years of 2.1% (95% CI 1.5-2.8%). No significant differences in 5-year AA incidence were observed between agents: 1.5% (95% CI 0.7-2.8%), 2.3 (95% CI 1.6-3.2%), 1.0 (95% CI 0.3-2.6%) (p = 0.49). Multivariable analysis identified age at treatment as the only independent predictor of AA (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.04-1.09, p < 0.001). New-onset AA was associated with increased mortality (HR 1.56, 95% CI 1.10-2.20, p = 0.012).Patients who receive CDK4/6 inhibitors for breast cancer experience a low but measurable risk of new-onset atrial arrhythmias. There was no significant difference in new-onset AA risk between agents. Prospective studies are needed to define mechanisms and guide monitoring strategies.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a group of cancer drugs called cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, which are used to treat a common type of breast cancer, might cause heart rhythm problems like atrial fibrillation, a condition where the heart beats irregularly. The study looked back at medical records from nearly 2,800 patients who received one of three different versions of these drugs between 2015 and 2024 to track how often new heart rhythm problems developed and what happened to these patients afterward. Among all the patients studied, only 42 developed new atrial arrhythmias, meaning the risk was low at about 2. 1 percent over five years, and there was no meaningful difference in risk between the three different drugs tested. The researchers found that older age was the only factor that predicted who would develop these heart rhythm problems, and patients who did develop them had a higher risk of dying during the study period.

title: Finding the etiology of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
abstract: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) has undergone a change in classification that is focused on the etiology of MPGN. Thus, MPGN is classified into immune-complex (IC)-mediated MPGN and complement-mediated MPGN (C3 glomerulopathy) based on immunofluorescence microscopy studies that show positive staining for Igs and/or C3. IC-MPGN typically results from an infection or an autoimmune disease. Deposition of monotypic/monoclonal Ig also results in an MPGN. On the other hand, MPGN with bright C3 and minimal/no Ig is classified as C3 glomerulopathy. On the basis of the absence of any clinical evidence of an infection, autoimmune disease, or monoclonal gammopathy, the IC-MPGN is often labeled as primary/idiopathic MPGN. As such, increasing numbers of primary/idiopathic IC-MPGN are being diagnosed. In my renal biopsy practice, I have rarely seen an MPGN in an adult kidney biopsy in which I could not find an underlying etiology after diligent and careful evaluation of the biopsy. Some of the primary/idiopathic IC-MPGN falls into the monotypic/monoclonal Ig-associated MPGN, some into uncommon diseases, such as fibrillary glomerulonephritis, whereas others represent C3 glomerulopathy to begin with where the Ig is often entrapped in areas of scarring and does not represent true IC-MPGN. On the other hand, infection-related glomerulonephritis may be misclassified into C3 glomerulonephritis when there is sparse IgG on immunofluorescence microscopy. Chronic thrombotic microangiopathies can present with an MPGN pattern of injury and may be mislabeled as IC-MPGN or C3 glomerulonephritis from entrapment of IgM and/or C3. It is thus critical that we perform a thorough clinical and pathologic evaluation before labeling a case as idiopathic/primary IC-MPGN. Kidney biopsy evaluation should include complete immunofluorescence microscopy, including light chains, and electron microscopy. Pronase immunofluorescence microscopy and IgG subclass staining should be available to rule out masked Ig deposits and monotypic/monoclonal Ig-associated MPGN. An accurate diagnosis with identification of the etiology of IC-MPGN will allow for targeted treatment of the MPGN.Copyright © 2026 International Society of Nephrology. Published by Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, which is a kidney disease involving inflammation and abnormal protein deposits, has traditionally been classified in ways that do not always identify what actually caused the disease. Doctors now classify this kidney disease into two main types based on what they see under a microscope: one caused by immune complexes (antibodies and other proteins) and another caused by problems with the complement system (part of the immune system that fights infection). The author argues that many cases labeled as idiopathic or primary, meaning without a known cause, actually do have an identifiable underlying reason such as infection, autoimmune disease, or monoclonal gammopathy (abnormal protein production), but these causes are missed because doctors do not perform thorough enough testing. To properly diagnose these kidney diseases, doctors need to use complete microscopic examination techniques including special staining methods that can reveal hidden antibodies and identify abnormal protein types that are often missed with standard testing. Finding the true cause of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is essential because it allows doctors to provide targeted treatment rather than treating patients for a disease with no known cause.

title: RUNX1 is a mediator of fibrotic activation and epigenetic memory in lung fibroblasts.
abstract: Repetitive injury is hypothesized to lead to progressive tissue fibrosis and end-stage organ failure. Whether tissue-resident mesenchymal cell populations retain epigenetic memory of prior injuries that contribute to this pathological process is unknown. Here we used a genetic lineage labeling approach to mark the lung mesenchyme prior to injury, then performed multimodal analyses on isolated lung mesenchyme during the initiation, progression, and resolution of the fibrotic response. Our results demonstrate the remarkable epigenetic and transcriptional plasticity of the lung mesenchyme during fibrotic activation and de-activation. Despite this plasticity, we also find that the lung mesenchyme exhibits an enhanced fibrotic program upon reinjury. We identify RUNX1 as a critical driver of both fibrotic activation and fibrotic memory. Comparison of fresh isolated and cultured lung mesenchyme demonstrates that RUNX1 is spontaneously activated in standard culture conditions, previously masking these roles of RUNX1. Targeted knockdown of RUNX1 dampens fibrotic mesenchymal cell activation immediately after cell isolation, but with reduced efficacy after only days of culture, confirming its functional importance to both early activation and long-term memory. Collectively, our findings implicate RUNX1 in the initiation and memory of fibrotic mesenchymal cell activation that together prime enhanced mesenchymal cell responses upon repeated injury.© The Author(s) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether lung cells retain a "memory" of previous injuries that makes them more likely to develop scarring, or fibrosis, when injured again. They used genetic labeling to track lung mesenchyme cells, which are connective tissue cells that play a key role in fibrosis, through multiple cycles of injury and healing to understand how these cells change over time. The study found that lung mesenchyme cells show remarkable flexibility in turning their fibrotic programs on and off, yet they still develop an enhanced scarring response when reinjured, and identified a protein called RUNX1 as the critical driver of both the initial fibrotic activation and this long-term memory. The researchers discovered that RUNX1 becomes spontaneously activated when cells are grown in laboratory conditions, which had previously hidden its true role, and that blocking RUNX1 reduces scarring responses in freshly isolated cells but becomes less effective after cells have been cultured for several days. These findings suggest that RUNX1 is a key target for preventing progressive lung fibrosis in patients who experience repeated lung injuries, though further research is needed to develop therapies that can effectively block RUNX1.

title: Results of Two-Stage Exchange for Periprosthetic Joint Infection Following Total Knee Arthroplasty: Low Rates of Failure in 463 Knees at 10 Years.
abstract: Some recent data suggest similar reinfection rates between two- and one-stage exchange arthroplasties for infected total knee arthroplasties (TKAs). However, those data are limited in follow up and analysis of aseptic failure rates. The purpose of this study was to assess the 10-years results of TKA two-stage exchange in one of the largest series to date.We identified 463 infected TKAs treated with two-stage exchange from 1991 to 2021 at a single institution. The mean age at reimplantation was 68 years, 49% were women; mean body mass index was 32 (range, 16 to 64). Diagnosis of periprosthetic joint infection was based on the 2011 Musculoskeletal Infection Society criteria. Cumulative incidences of reinfection and revision with death as a competing risk were calculated. The mean follow-up was eight years (range, two to 30).The cumulative incidence of reinfection was 6% at one year, 14% at five years, and 19% at 10 years. Factors predictive of reinfection included elevated body mass index (hazard ratio (HR) 1.3 for every 5-point increase), McPherson host grade C (HR: 2.3), previous revision surgery (HR: 2.1) and Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute type-3 bone loss (HR: 4.6). The cumulative incidence of aseptic revision was 9% at 10 years. The cumulative incidence of any revision was 26% at 10 years. The most common indications for revision were recurrent periprosthetic joint infection (63%), aseptic loosening (22%), and instability (6%). The mean Knee Society Score improved from 48 to 69 at two years.In this series of 463 two-stage exchanges for infected TKAs, the risk of reinfection was less than 20%, and the risk of aseptic revision was less than 10% at 10 years. Poor host status, obesity, and severe bone loss were predictive of reinfection. These outcomes provide a benchmark against which new management protocols may be compared.Level III.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined a large group of patients who had infected knee replacements treated with a two-stage surgical exchange, which means removing the infected implant, treating the infection, and then placing a new knee replacement in a second surgery. The study followed 463 patients over ten years to see how many experienced reinfection (the infection returning) or needed additional surgery for other reasons like loosening of the new implant. The results showed that about 19 percent of patients had reinfection by ten years, while 9 percent needed revision surgery for aseptic reasons (problems unrelated to infection), and overall 26 percent needed some type of revision surgery. Patients who were overweight, had poor overall health status, or had significant bone loss were at higher risk for reinfection, which helps doctors identify who might need extra precautions. These findings provide important information for doctors to use when deciding on treatment strategies for infected knee replacements and help set realistic expectations for patients undergoing this procedure.

title: Vascular anatomic variant-related venous thromboembolism: what a hematologist needs to know.
abstract: This review will discuss practical aspects pertaining to deep vein thrombosis associated with 3 venous anatomical variants: duplicated femoral vein, May-Thurner syndrome, and Paget-Schroetter syndrome. Each of these conditions presents unique complexities that need to be accurately identified and managed. These conditions are very challenging for hematologists, as the first specialist to evaluate the patient is often not a hematologist but a vascular surgeon or an interventional radiologist. Key aspects from a hematologist's perspective, covering pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic approaches, and treatment strategies, are presented in concise and focused paragraphs, each followed by 3 to 4 clear, practical take-home points. llm_summary: This review examines three uncommon blood vessel shape variations that can cause dangerous blood clots in the legs and lungs, which doctors need to recognize and treat properly. The authors explain the causes, symptoms, and ways to diagnose three specific conditions: duplicated femoral veins (when a major leg vein splits into two), May-Thurner syndrome (when an artery presses on a vein in the pelvis), and Paget-Schroetter syndrome (when a vein in the shoulder area becomes blocked). The paper provides practical guidance for blood specialists by breaking down each condition into clear sections that cover how the problem develops in the body, how patients present with symptoms, the best ways to identify these conditions, and the most effective treatment approaches. Understanding these anatomical variations is important because patients with these conditions often see vascular surgeons or imaging specialists first, so hematologists (blood doctors) need to know how to manage them when they take over care. The authors also highlight common mistakes doctors make when treating these patients and suggest areas where future research could improve outcomes for people with these rare vascular conditions.

title: Admission Acid-Base Status and Mortality in Cardiac Intensive Care Unit Patients.
abstract: BackgroundThere is limited evidence on the epidemiology and prognostic significance of acid-base disorders in the cardiovascular intensive care unit (CICU). This study examines the association of acid-base status at admission with in-hospital mortality among CICU patients.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective analysis of adults admitted to the Mayo Clinic CICU from 2007-2018 with available blood gas data, utilizing values obtained closest to CICU admission. Arterial pH, serum bicarbonate, base excess, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) were examined as predictors of in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess associations, with adjustment for demographics, comorbidities, illness severity, and interventions.ResultsAmong 3229 patients included for analysis, acidemia (pH < 7.35) emerged as the strongest predictor of in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.29-1.98, P < .003). Metabolic acidosis (HCO3 < 20 mEq/L, aOR 1.55, 95% CI 1.24-1.95, P < .001) and respiratory acidosis (PaCO2 > 45 mm Hg, aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14-1.81, P = .002) were associated with higher in-hospital mortality, whereas metabolic and respiratory alkalosis were not. After adjustment, lower pH and more negative base excess were associated with higher in-hospital mortality (both P < .001), whereas HCO3 and PaCO2 were not (P = .053 and P = .051, respectively). Patients with combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis had the highest in-hospital mortality (56.3%).ConclusionsShort-term survival in CICU patients decreases progressively with worse acidemia, especially in the context of combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis. Incorporating metabolic acid-base disorders as key therapeutic targets in randomized cardiogenic shock trials may improve outcomes in this complex population by addressing hemometabolic shock.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether the acid-base status, which refers to how acidic or alkaline a patient's blood is when they arrive at a cardiac intensive care unit, can predict which patients are more likely to die during their hospital stay. The study looked back at records from nearly 3,300 patients admitted to Mayo Clinic's cardiac intensive care unit between 2007 and 2018, measuring their blood acidity levels and other related factors to see if these measurements could predict survival. The results showed that patients with acidemia, meaning their blood was too acidic when admitted, had a significantly higher risk of dying in the hospital, and this risk was even greater when patients had both metabolic and respiratory acidosis, a condition where the blood becomes dangerously acidic from multiple causes. The findings suggest that doctors should pay close attention to acid-base imbalances in cardiac patients and consider treating these imbalances as a priority, since addressing them might help improve survival rates in this very sick population. Future research should test whether actively treating these acid-base problems in randomized clinical trials, where some patients receive the treatment and others do not, can actually improve outcomes for patients with severe heart problems.

title: Cluster Analysis of Fecal Incontinence Symptoms: Associations With Anorectal Physiology and Quality of Life.
abstract: The contributions of bowel disturbances and anorectal dysfunctions to fecal incontinence (FI) remain unclear. Based on defecatory awareness, the classification into urge vs passive FI overlooks other factors (eg, leakage volume). This study examined relationships among FI characteristics (stooling sensation, volume, consistency), bowel movements (BMs), and anorectal neurophysiology; evaluated their effect on quality of life (QoL); and identified clinical phenotypes.Patients completed a 2-week bowel diary, questionnaires, and anorectal manometry. BM and FI characteristics were used for cluster analysis.Over 2 weeks, 268 patients (88% women) had a mean of 28.2 BMs (standard deviation, 15.2) and 19.7 FI episodes (standard deviation, 15.7). Patients >74 years had more frequent FI (P = .01), more solid-FI episodes (P = .008), better FI-QoL scores (P ≤ .02), and lower anorectal pressures (P ≤ .002) than those <58 years. Solid FI was associated with hard (Bristol Stool Form [BSF] 1-2) stools (r = 0.17; P = .006) and normal (BSF 3-4) stools (r = 0.30; P < .001) and inversely with anal resting pressure (r = -0.25; P < .001) and squeeze increment (r = -0.15; P = .02). Loose (BSF 5-7) stools were associated with liquid FI and urge FI (r ≈ 0.3; P < .001). Urge FI was associated with poorer FI-QoL scores (P < .001). Passive FI was associated with the frequency of normal stools (r = 0.16; P = .009) and lower anal resting pressure (r = -0.15; P = .02). Cluster analysis identified 4 distinct phenotypes, 2 characterized by passive and 2 by combined (urge-passive) FI.FI characteristics were weakly but significantly associated with BMs and anorectal functions. Diary-captured stool and FI patterns identified 4 phenotypes associated with FI-based QoL and anorectal function. This stratification will likely facilitate the management of FI. llm_summary: Researchers examined how different types of fecal incontinence, which is the involuntary loss of stool, relate to bowel function and quality of life in order to better understand and treat this common problem. The study involved 268 patients who kept detailed records of their bowel movements and incontinence episodes over two weeks and also underwent testing to measure the strength and function of the muscles around the anus. The researchers found four distinct patterns of fecal incontinence: two types involving passive leakage without warning and two types involving a combination of urge and passive symptoms, with each pattern showing different connections to stool consistency, muscle strength, and how much the condition bothered patients. Older patients experienced more frequent incontinence but reported better quality of life scores, while those with urge-type incontinence reported worse quality of life impacts. These findings suggest that identifying which specific pattern of incontinence a patient has could help doctors choose more targeted and effective treatments tailored to each person's particular symptoms and underlying physical problems.

title: The Weekend Effect on Evidence-Based Care Adherence Before and After Implementation of Checklist-Based Care in the Intensive Care Unit: A Multinational Study.
abstract: BackgroundAdherence to evidence-based care processes and patient outcomes in intensive care units (ICUs) can be influenced by staffing and resource availability. We aimed to evaluate if there is a weekend effect on adherence to evidence-based care processes, and hospitalization outcomes and whether a checklist implementation could mitigate potential differences.MethodsPost hoc analysis of the Checklist for Early Recognition and Treatment of Acute Illness and Injury (CERTAIN) study dataset collected before and after checklist implementation in 34 ICUs across 15 countries (2013-2017). Admission days were classified as 'weekend/holidays' or 'weekdays' according to local work schedules and public holidays. The primary outcome was the omission of 10 evidence-based care processes addressed in the checklist. Mortality and length of stay differences between weekend/holiday and weekday admissions were evaluated as secondary outcomes.Results4256 patients contributed 1141 weekend versus 3501 weekday observation days pre-intervention, and 2014 versus 6507 post-intervention. Pre-intervention, peptic ulcer prophylaxis was omitted more frequently on weekends/holidays than weekdays (adjusted rate ratio [aRR], 0.58 [95%-confidence interval [CI] 0.38-0.88), whereas head-of-bed elevation was omitted more often on weekdays than on weekends/holidays (aRR, 3.17 [1.14-8.86]). Post-intervention, peptic ulcer prophylaxis omission rates became similar (aRR, 1.03 [0.68-1.56], but head-of-bed elevation became omitted more often on weekends than on weekdays (aRR, 0.63 [0.45-0.88]). Post-intervention, oral care was omitted more frequently on weekends/holidays than in weekdays (aRR, 0.63 [0.45-0.9]), and central catheter removal was more frequent on weekdays than in weekends/holidays (aRR, 1.11 [1.02-1.21]). No significant differences in mortality or length of stay were found.ConclusionA weekend effect influenced adherence to some care processes. While checklist implementation improved overall adherence, some disparities diminished, while new ones emerged. Organizational, cultural, and temporal factors should be further studied to optimize care delivery across all times and settings.Clinical Trial Registration NumberNCT01973829.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether patient care in intensive care units follows best practices differently on weekends versus weekdays, and whether using a checklist system could help reduce any gaps in care. The study analyzed data from over 4,200 patients across 34 intensive care units in 15 countries, comparing how often doctors and nurses followed ten important care procedures before and after introducing a checklist tool designed to catch and treat serious illnesses early. Before the checklist was introduced, some care steps like preventing stomach ulcers were skipped more often on weekends, while other steps like elevating the head of the bed were skipped more often on weekdays. After the checklist was put in place, the overall quality of care improved, though some weekend-weekday differences in care disappeared while new ones emerged in different areas. The researchers found no major differences in patient survival rates or hospital stays between weekend and weekday admissions, but they concluded that hospitals should study the organizational and cultural factors that affect care delivery to ensure consistent quality care at all times.

title: A Multicenter Double-blind Randomized Sham-controlled Trial Assessing the EndoBarrier Duodenal-jejunal Bypass Liner for the Treatment of Poorly Controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus With Concomitant Obesity: The ENDO Trial.
abstract: An endoscopically placed duodenal-jejunal bypass liner (DJBL) may provide a safe adjunctive therapy for those with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity.Although some endoscopic therapies have been shown to improve glycemic indices secondary to weight loss, small bowel interventions may have direct metabolic effects. A meta-analysis of observational studies demonstrated reduction in HbA1c by 1.3% at 1 year after DJBL in patients with T2DM and obesity.This was a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, sham-controlled trial comparing DJBL to sham procedure with medical management and lifestyle modification. Primary endpoints included mean difference in changes in HbA1c at 12 months between arms, and device-related serious adverse events (SAEs). Secondary endpoints included percent total weight loss (%TWL) and subjects achieving HbA1c≤7% and TWL≥5% at 12 months.Three hundred twenty subjects were randomized to DJBL (n=212) and sham (n=108). Baseline HbA1c and BMI were 8.79±0.92% and 38.45±5.75 kg/m 2 . On modified intent-to-treat analysis, change in HbA1c at 12 months was -1.10±1.45% and -0.28±1.54% for DJBL and sham groups, respectively ( P =0.0004). Rate of device-related SAEs was 9.4% including intolerance (3.7%), hemorrhage (2.8%), and hepatic abscess (2.3% stopping study early). At 12 months, DJBL group experienced greater weight loss compared with sham (7.7±9.6% TWL and 2.1±5.4% TWL, respectively; P <0.0001), with significantly more patients achieving HbA1c ≤ 7% (28.3% vs. 9.4%; P <0.0003) and TWL ≥ 5% (60.4% vs. 21.3%; P <0.0001).DJBL met primary glycemic control efficacy and primary safety endpoints, while providing clinically significant weight loss, and comorbidity improvement.Copyright © 2025 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. llm_summary: Researchers examined a new treatment called a duodenal-jejunal bypass liner, which is a small tube placed inside the digestive system to help people with type 2 diabetes and obesity control their blood sugar levels. In this double-blind study, which means neither the doctors nor patients knew who received the real device versus a fake procedure, 320 people were randomly assigned to either get the actual device or a sham treatment while also receiving medical care and lifestyle advice. After one year, patients who received the real device had significantly better blood sugar control with a 1. 1 percent drop in their HbA1c test results compared to only a 0. 28 percent drop in the sham group, and they also lost more weight on average.

title: 2025 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Guideline for the Treatment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
abstract: To provide evidence-based and expert guidance for the treatment and management of non-renal systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); treatment and management of lupus nephritis are addressed in a separate guideline.Clinical questions for treatment and management of SLE were developed in the PICO format (population, intervention, comparator, and outcome). Systematic literature reviews were developed for each PICO question, and the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was used to assess evidence quality and formulate recommendations. The Voting Panel achieved a consensus of ≥70% agreement on the direction (for or against) and strength (strong or conditional) of each recommendation.We present recommendations and ungraded, consensus-based good practice statements for the treatment and management of SLE that are applicable to pediatric and adult patients. Recommendations emphasize uniform treatment with hydroxychloroquine, limiting duration of glucocorticoid use, and early introduction of conventional and/or biologic immunosuppressive therapies to achieve and maintain control of SLE inflammation (remission or a low level of disease activity), reduce SLE-related morbidity and mortality, and minimize medication-related toxicities.This guideline presents direction regarding treatment and management of SLE and provides a foundation for well-informed, shared clinician-patient decision-making. These recommendations should not be used to limit or deny access to therapies, as treatment decisions may vary due to the unique clinical situation and personal preferences of each person with SLE.© 2025 American College of Rheumatology.

llm_summary: The American College of Rheumatology created new treatment guidelines for systemic lupus erythematosus, a serious autoimmune disease where the body's immune system attacks its own tissues, because patients need clear direction on how to manage this complex condition. Experts reviewed scientific studies using a rigorous method called GRADE, which evaluates the quality of evidence, and then voted on treatment recommendations until at least seventy percent of the panel agreed on each suggestion. The guidelines strongly recommend that all patients take hydroxychloroquine as a foundation medication, doctors should limit how long patients use steroids, and doctors should start strong immunosuppressive drugs early to control inflammation and prevent long-term damage. These recommendations aim to help doctors and patients make informed decisions together about treatment while reducing harmful side effects and improving survival rates for people with lupus. The guidelines apply to both children and adults with non-kidney forms of lupus, though kidney involvement is covered in a separate guideline, and doctors are reminded that individual patient situations may require different treatment choices.

title: A Qualitative Analysis of Patient Perspectives and Preferences in Lupus Management to Guide Lupus Guidelines Development.
abstract: A patient-centered approach for chronic disease management, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), aligns treatment with patients' values and preferences, leading to improved outcomes. This paper summarizes how patient experiences, perspectives, and priorities informed the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) 2024 Lupus Nephritis (LN) and 2025 SLE screening, treatment guidelines.We completed a cross-sectional qualitative study using content analysis of two Patient Panel meetings for the ACR LN and SLE guidelines. Key themes were presented by Patient Panel representatives during Voting Panel Meetings along with evidence for each recommendation, to ensure comprehensive discussions and align treatment recommendations with patients' priorities and values.Nineteen people (90% women) with diagnoses of SLE and/or LN participated in the Patient Panels and 17 consented to use their feedback for analysis. Thematic analysis of their discussions revealed nine patient-reported key themes in three domains: (1) treatment and monitoring of LN and SLE: medication side effects, daily function, treatment goals, and monitoring and screening; (2) clinical communication: strategies to optimize communication and provider and structural impediments to effective communication; and (3) improving transparency and information sharing: clinical trial participation, and medical costs and insurance coverage. These themes were actively incorporated into discussions during the Voting Panels for the ACR LN and SLE guidelines.This work supported the integration of patient experiences in the clinical practice guideline development process and aligned recommendations with real-world patient experiences and priorities, thereby enhancing the clinical applicability of the ACR LN and SLE guidelines.© 2025 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined how patients with lupus, a serious autoimmune disease where the body attacks its own tissues, want to be treated and managed so that doctors can create better medical guidelines. The study involved nineteen people with lupus who participated in two discussion groups where they shared their experiences and concerns about their condition and treatment. The patients identified nine major themes that mattered most to them, including worries about medication side effects, how their illness affected daily life, the need for better communication with doctors, and concerns about the cost and insurance coverage of their care. The researchers then presented these patient priorities to a voting panel of medical experts who were developing new treatment guidelines for lupus, ensuring that real patient experiences shaped the official recommendations. This approach helped create medical guidelines that better match what patients actually need and value in their real lives, making the guidelines more useful and practical for both doctors and patients.

title: Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty for Isolated Compartment Osteonecrosis: A 20-Year Experience.
abstract: Osteonecrosis of the knee, whether primary (spontaneous) or secondary, can often necessitate surgical intervention. If advanced osteonecrosis is confined to a single compartment, unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is often considered. The purpose of this study was to update and extend our prior series, with specific emphasis on implant survivorship, radiographic results, clinical outcomes, and complications in a concise cohort of UKAs for osteonecrosis.We retrospectively identified 70 consecutive UKAs for osteonecrosis performed at a single tertiary care academic institution from 2002 to 2022. Of these, 64 UKAs (91%) were performed for primary osteonecrosis, and six UKAs (9%) were performed for secondary osteonecrosis. Osteonecrosis was in the medial femoral condyle in 61 UKAs (87%), medial tibial plateau in six UKAs (9%), and lateral femoral condyle in three UKAs (4%). All UKAs were cemented, with 77% utilizing a fixed-bearing design and 23% utilizing a mobile-bearing design. The mean patient age was 66 years, with 59% being women. The mean follow-up was eight years (range, two to 20).The 10-year survivorship free of any revision for the entire cohort was 91%. The predominant indication for revision was the development of osteoarthritis in the lateral compartment in three knees. The 10-year survivorship free of any reoperation was 88%. The secondary osteonecrosis was a significant and substantial risk factor for worse survivorship free of any revision (hazard ratio (HR) = 17; P < 0.001) and any reoperation (HR = 14; P = 0.002). There were no implants that were revised for fracture or wear. Knee society function scores improved from a mean of 54 preoperatively to a mean of 75 postoperatively.A UKA is a durable and reliable option for primary osteonecrosis at eight years of follow-up. However, when performed for secondary osteonecrosis, it has a substantially higher failure rate, primarily related to the progression of osteonecrosis or development of osteoarthritis in the lateral compartment.III, Retrospective Cohort Study.Copyright © 2025 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a surgical procedure called unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, which replaces only the damaged portion of a knee joint, works well for patients with osteonecrosis, a condition where bone tissue dies due to lack of blood supply. The study looked back at 70 patients who had this surgery between 2002 and 2022 at a single hospital, tracking their outcomes over an average of eight years to see how long the implants lasted and how well patients functioned. After ten years, about 91 percent of the implants had not needed to be replaced, and patients' knee function scores improved significantly from an average of 54 before surgery to 75 after surgery. However, patients who had secondary osteonecrosis, meaning the bone death was caused by another condition like steroid use or radiation rather than occurring on its own, had much higher failure rates and were more likely to need additional surgery. The results suggest that this knee replacement surgery is a good long-term option for patients with primary osteonecrosis, but doctors should be cautious when considering it for patients whose bone death stems from other medical causes.

title: The Applications of Photogrammetry in Medical Education: A Review.
abstract: Photogrammetry has emerged as a powerful tool in medical education, offering precise and cost-effective 3D anatomical models that enhance spatial learning and accessibility. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from forty-eight (48) peer-reviewed studies (2000-2025) to evaluate photogrammetry's applications, technical workflows, and educational outcomes in anatomy and surgical training. Findings demonstrate its effectiveness across training levels, with high learner satisfaction (e.g., 96.4% preference over traditional methods) and sub-millimeter accuracy in rendering complex structures like neuroanatomy and musculoskeletal systems. Photogrammetry's adaptability for remote learning and specimen preservation addresses critical gaps in resource-limited settings. However, challenges persist, including the lack of tactile feedback and difficulties in visualizing deep anatomical relationships. Future directions should focus on integrating artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted processing, hybrid digital-physical models, and immersive technologies like virtual reality (VR)/augmented reality (AR) to bridge these gaps. By balancing innovation with evidence-based implementation, photogrammetry can further solidify its role as a transformative adjunct in modern medical curricula.© 2025 American Association of Clinical Anatomists and British Association of Clinical Anatomists.

llm_summary: Photogrammetry, a technique that uses photographs to create three-dimensional digital models, has become an important tool for teaching anatomy and surgical skills in medical schools because it produces accurate models that are affordable and help students learn better. Researchers reviewed forty-eight scientific studies published between 2000 and 2025 to understand how photogrammetry is being used in medical education, how it works technically, and whether it actually helps students learn. The review found that photogrammetry works well for students at all training levels, with over ninety-six percent of learners preferring it to traditional teaching methods, and the models are so precise they can capture tiny details in complex body structures like the brain and muscles. This technology is especially valuable for students in areas with limited resources because it allows remote learning and helps preserve specimens without needing expensive equipment. However, challenges remain because these digital models cannot provide the sense of touch that physical specimens offer, and future improvements should combine artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and augmented reality to make the learning experience even more complete.

llm_summary: Background:  Posterior cerebral artery aneurysms are abnormal bulges in blood vessels at the back of the brain that can be life-threatening if they rupture and bleed. Surgeons use various specialized approaches and techniques to access and repair these aneurysms safely, sometimes requiring creative solutions like moving important blood vessel structures to reach the aneurysm and clip it closed.

title: Outcomes Associated With SGLT2 Inhibitor Use Following Acute Myocardial Infarction Without Heart Failure: A Propensity-Matched Study.
abstract: This retrospective propensity-matched cohort study assessed the association between sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) use and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) without a history of heart failure. Using the TriNetX U.S. Collaborative Network, we identified 1440 matched patients (720 SGLT2i+ vs 720 SGLT2i-) with preserved ejection fraction and no prior heart failure. Nearly 90% of patients had diabetes. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as a composite of MI, stroke, heart failure, and all-cause mortality. At 1 year, MACE occurred in 17.4% of SGLT2i+ versus 22.0% of SGLT2i- patients (odds ratio [OR] 0.746, 95% CI 0.574-0.969; P = .028), and all-cause mortality occurred in 3.1% versus 7.6%, respectively (OR 0.389, 95% CI 0.234-0.645; P < .001). SGLT2i use was also associated with lower risks of major bleeding. Findings were consistent over long-term follow-up. While the observed associations suggest potential cardioprotective effects of SGLT2i post-MI in patients without heart failure, residual confounding cannot be excluded. The observed reduction in bleeding events is novel and warrants further investigation in prospective studies.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a type of diabetes medication called SGLT2 inhibitors could help patients who had suffered a heart attack and did not have heart failure, a condition where the heart cannot pump blood effectively. The study used medical records from a large U. S. network to compare 720 patients who took SGLT2 inhibitors with 720 similar patients who did not take the medication, following them for one year to track serious heart problems, strokes, and deaths. Patients taking SGLT2 inhibitors had significantly better outcomes, with fewer major adverse cardiovascular events (a combined measure of heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, and death) and notably lower death rates compared to those who did not take the medication.

title: The use of artificial intelligence to improve detection of acute incidental pulmonary emboli.
abstract: Incidental pulmonary emboli (IPE) are frequently overlooked by radiologists. Artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms have been developed to aid detection of pulmonary emboli.To measure diagnostic performance of AI compared with prospective interpretation by radiologists.A commercially available AI algorithm was used to retrospectively review 14 453 contrast-enhanced outpatient computed tomography examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis in 9171 patients, where pulmonary embolism was not clinically suspected. Natural language processing searches of reports identified IPE detected prospectively. Thoracic radiologists reviewed all cases read as positive by AI or natural language processing to confirm IPE and assess the most proximal level of clot and overall clot burden. A total of 1400 cases read as negative by both the initial radiologist and AI were rereviewed to assess for additional IPE.Radiologists prospectively detected 218 IPE, and AI detected an additional 36 unreported cases. AI missed 30 cases of IPE detected by the radiologists and had 94 false positives. For 36 IPE missed by the radiologists, median clot burden was 1, and 19 were solitary segmental or subsegmental. For 30 IPE missed by AI, 1 case had large central emboli, and the others were small with 23 solitary subsegmental emboli. Radiologist rereview of 1400 examinations interpreted as negative found 8 additional cases of IPE.Compared with radiologists, AI had similar sensitivity but reduced positive predictive value. Our experience indicates that the AI tool is not ready to be used autonomously without human oversight, but a human observer plus AI is better than either alone for detection of IPE.Copyright © 2025 International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis.
