llm_summary: Microsurgery, which involves operating on very small structures like blood vessels using a microscope, is an important surgical skill that is rarely taught in poorer countries due to lack of resources and training programs. Researchers created and ran a multi-day training course in four countries (South Africa, Rwanda, Vietnam, and Egypt) from 2022 to 2025 to teach surgical residents basic and advanced microsurgical techniques, and they measured how much participants improved by giving them surveys before and after the course. Sixty surgical residents completed the course, and most had performed very few microsurgical procedures before; during the training, they each completed an average of seven practice procedures, and all participants showed significant improvements in their confidence and skills with microscope operation, instrument handling, vessel preparation, and connecting blood vessels together. The participants also reported feeling less anxious about performing microsurgery and became more confident in their ability to evaluate whether their work was successful, and they increasingly believed that learning these skills would help their future careers. These results suggest that offering international microsurgery training courses could help address the shortage of surgeons trained in these techniques in lower-income countries and improve access to reconstructive surgical care for patients who need.

title: Perioperative management of Evans Syndrome for free tissue transfer: Case report and recommendations.
abstract: Evans syndrome (ES) is a rare autoimmune disorder characterized by autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenic purpura, conferring an increased risk of postoperative bleeding, thrombosis, and infection. Limited guidance for perioperative management is available for patients with ES undergoing free flap reconstruction.A 21-year-old female presented with a six-month history of progressive forearm pain, a palpable tender mass in the right volar forearm, paresthesias in the ulnar nerve distribution, and limited forearm rotation from neutral to 30 degrees supination. Imaging revealed an expansile lytic lesion in the midshaft of the ulna, and biopsy diagnosed an aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC). Medical history was significant for ES, stable on daily sirolimus and hydroxychloroquine with weekly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) infusions. Preoperative labs were within normal limits. She underwent wide local excision of the ABC, resulting in an 8.5 cm bony defect within the midshaft of the ulna. A vascularized free fibula flap was performed to reconstruct the ulna. Sirolimus and hydroxychloroquine were held for one week pre- and post-operatively and IVIG continued peri‑operatively. While hospitalized, she received Aspirin 325 mg and Lovenox 40 mg daily for deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis. Daily labs confirmed stable blood counts. At 4 months post-operatively, CT scans confirmed bony union of the proximal and distal osteotomy. She regained near full supination and pronation range of motion, and all her incisions were well-healed.In patients with ES undergoing free tissue transfer, perioperative management of immunosuppression and anticoagulation must balance the risks of bleeding, anastomotic thrombosis, and wound healing complications. Our patient was safely treated with prophylactic anticoagulation while hospitalized and immunosuppressive medications were held one week pre- and post-operatively. Overall, we report successful vascularized free tissue transfer in a patient with ES on chronic sirolimus without incidence of hematoma, thrombosis, or infection.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Evans syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease where the body's immune system attacks its own blood cells, causing both anemia (low red blood cells) and low platelet counts (cells that help blood clot), which makes surgery risky because patients can bleed excessively or develop dangerous blood clots. Doctors had limited guidance on how to safely manage patients with Evans syndrome who needed complex reconstructive surgery, so researchers documented the case of a 21-year-old woman who had a bone tumor in her forearm and required a free tissue transfer, which is a surgical procedure where healthy bone from another part of the body is transplanted to repair the defect. The surgical team carefully managed her condition by continuing her immune-suppressing medications during the operation while temporarily stopping two of her regular medications for one week before and after surgery, and they also gave her blood-thinning medications to prevent clots while she was in the hospital. The patient recovered successfully with no serious bleeding, blood clots, or infections, and her bone healed completely within four months with excellent restoration of her arm's range of motion. This case demonstrates that patients with Evans syndrome can safely undergo major reconstructive surgery when doctors thoughtfully balance.

title: Variant classification for mucopolysaccharidosis type I; ACMG/AMP specification for IDUA from the ClinGen lysosomal diseases variant curation expert panel.
abstract: With the increasing use of DNA sequencing technologies in healthcare, an accurate understanding of the clinical relevance of genetic variants is vital for the appropriate integration of these results into personalized care. To address this need, the NIH-funded Clinical Genome Resource (ClinGen) Lysosomal Diseases Variant Curation Expert Panel (VCEP) has developed variant classification guidance for IDUA, the gene encoding alpha-L-iduronidase. Deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase activity causes mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I). IDUA variant interpretation was prioritized by the VCEP following the 2016 inclusion of MPS I in the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) for newborns in the USA, reflecting the critical role of IDUA sequencing in therapeutic decision-making and care of individuals identified through either newborn screening or diagnostic platforms. Furthermore, as genetic testing is increasingly used as a first line test in the diagnosis of lysosomal diseases, accurate variant classification is vital. The LD VCEP's IDUA-specific variant classification guidance is based on the American College of Medical Genetics & Genomics and Association for Molecular Pathology's (ACMG/AMP) variation classification guidelines [1], with criteria tailored specifically to IDUA and MPS I. To date, the LD VCEP has submitted classifications and supporting data for 131 IDUA variants to ClinVar and to the ClinGen Evidence Repository, where this data is publicly available. Here, we discuss the development of the ClinGen LD VCEP's IDUA-specific ACMG/AMP criteria, our results to date, challenges, and plans for future work.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Researchers created a detailed guide for understanding genetic changes in the IDUA gene, which when faulty causes a rare inherited disease called mucopolysaccharidosis type I that affects how the body breaks down certain molecules. The team, called the Lysosomal Diseases Variant Curation Expert Panel, developed this classification system because genetic testing is now commonly used to diagnose this disease early in newborns and to help doctors decide on the best treatments. The experts reviewed and classified 131 different genetic variants in the IDUA gene using established medical guidelines, then shared all their findings publicly so other doctors and researchers could access this information. This work is important because accurate classification of genetic changes helps ensure that patients receive correct diagnoses and appropriate medical care based on their specific genetic makeup. The team plans to continue expanding their classifications and refining their criteria as they encounter new genetic variants and learn more about how different changes in the IDUA gene affect disease severity.

llm_summary: Background:  Prone positioning, which means placing a patient face-down on their stomach, became a widely used treatment strategy during the COVID-19 pandemic to help patients with severe respiratory failure breathe more easily by improving oxygen levels in their blood. This technique experienced a dramatic increase in use early in the pandemic but then declined as doctors learned more about its effectiveness and as new treatments became available.

title: International expert consensus on definitions and management of weight recurrence and suboptimal response after metabolic and bariatric surgery: a Delphi study.
abstract: Weight recurrence and suboptimal response after metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) lack standardized definitions and management approaches, creating barriers to evidence-based treatment decisions and coordinated care across multiple specialties.To establish international expert consensus on terminology, diagnostic approaches, and management strategies for suboptimal response and weight recurrence after MBS.International Delphi study across multiple countries and health care systems.A two-round modified Delphi study was conducted with 66 international experts across five specialties (MBS, obesity medicine, gastroenterology, endocrinology, dietetics and nutrition, and psychology). A 164-item questionnaire was developed, spanning seven dimensions: conservative management, diagnostic methods, endoscopic interventions, quantitative thresholds, risk factors, surgical interventions, and terminology. Consensus was defined a priori as ≥70% agreement. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using Gwet's AC1 coefficient.Response rates were 54.5% (Round 1) and 57.6% (Round 2). Consensus achievement improved significantly between rounds (26.2% to 40.9% of items). Experts reached unanimous agreement on core management principles including individualized patient care (100%) and the appropriateness of specialists prescribing antiobesity medications (100%). Strong consensus emerged on standardized terminology with "suboptimal" as the preferred term (89.5%) and %TWL as the optimal measurement approach (94.6). For quantitative thresholds, consensus was achieved on surgical nonresponse defined as <10% TWL at 12 months (73.0%), recurrent weight gain as >25% of lost weight from nadir (70.3%), and a 10% change in %EWL from nadir as normal physiologic response (83.8%). Conservative management items achieved the highest consensus rates (80.9%) while quantitative threshold items require additional research (28.1%). Inter-rater reliability improved across all domains, with conservative management achieving substantial agreement (AC1 = .70).Expert consensus was achieved on fundamental principles of postbariatric care, including preferred terminology, measurement metrics, and provider roles. These recommendations address important gaps in clinical practice standardization.Copyright © 2026 American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery. Published by Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Weight loss surgery patients sometimes regain weight or don't lose as much weight as expected, but doctors and specialists have not agreed on standard definitions or treatment plans for these problems, making it difficult to provide consistent care across different hospitals and countries. Researchers gathered 66 international experts from different medical fields including surgeons, obesity specialists, and nutritionists to create a survey asking about the best ways to define, diagnose, and treat weight regain and poor weight loss results after surgery. The experts reached strong agreement on several important points, including that patients need personalized care plans, that doctors should be able to prescribe weight loss medications, and that weight loss should be measured using a specific calculation called percent total weight loss. The study established clear definitions such as calling poor initial results "suboptimal response" when patients lose less than ten percent of their body weight in the first year, and defining weight regain as gaining back more than twenty-five percent of the weight they had lost. These agreed-upon standards will help doctors across different specialties and countries communicate better and make more consistent treatment decisions for patients struggling with weight after bariatric surgery.

title: What is the Utility of Point-of-care Ultrasound for Diagnosing Retinal Detachment?
abstract: Retinal detachment is an important condition for emergency physicians to be aware of, as it can be challenging to diagnose on physical examination alone and, if it is missed, can lead to vision loss. Ultrasound has demonstrated utility in diagnosis.What is the utility of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for diagnosing retinal detachment?Studies retrieved included three systematic reviews and meta-analyses evaluating the use of POCUS for diagnosing retinal detachment. These studies provide estimates of the potential utility of POCUS, with a sensitivity of 94-100% and specificity of 83-100%, positive likelihood ratios ranging from approximately 12-25, and negative likelihood ratios ranging from 0.06-0.25.Based upon the available literature, POCUS by emergency clinicians can reliably diagnose retinal detachment.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Retinal detachment, a serious eye condition where the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye separates from its supporting layer, is difficult for emergency doctors to diagnose through physical examination alone and can cause permanent vision loss if missed. Researchers reviewed three major studies that examined whether point-of-care ultrasound, a portable imaging tool that uses sound waves to create pictures inside the body, could help emergency doctors quickly identify retinal detachment. The studies found that ultrasound was highly effective at detecting retinal detachment, with the ability to correctly identify the condition between 94 and 100 percent of the time and correctly rule it out between 83 and 100 percent of the time. These results suggest that emergency doctors trained in ultrasound can reliably use this quick bedside imaging technique to diagnose retinal detachment without needing to wait for specialized eye doctor consultations. This finding is important because it gives emergency physicians a practical tool to catch this vision-threatening condition early and get patients the urgent care they need.

title: Criteria for Hidradenitis Suppurativa Competence Centers.
abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic, systemic, immune-mediated disease requiring multimodal care, which is crucial for raising awareness and advancing treatment. This project aimed to establish consensus among HS experts to define HS Competence Centers (HSCC) criteria using the Delphi consensus method.Overall, 22 global HS experts (3 patient representatives and 19 healthcare professionals [HCPs]) from 16 countries across 5 continents were invited to participate. Subsequently, a three-step Delphi polling was conducted among the HS experts from 20 May 2024 to 8 July 2024. A 50% agreement was required to reach consensus. Consensus levels included strong consensus (≥ 95%), consensus (≥ 75%), majority agreement (≥ 50%) and no majority agreement (< 50%).In the prepolling step, 22 participants proposed 26 criteria. In step 1, 23 criteria were selected, of which 6 (23.1%) reached strong consensus, 11 (42.3%) reached consensus, and 6 (23.1%) majority agreement. The remaining 3 (11.5%) criteria proposed were rejected. In step 2, 13 of the 23 criteria (56.5%) were proposed for wording modifications. Of these, four (30.8%) retained initial wording and nine (69.2%) were modified. In step 3, 21 of the 23 criteria were identified as very important (91.3%), while 2 (8.7%) were considered less important. Among the 21 very important criteria, 2 (9.5%) reached strong consensus, i.e., essential, 12 (57.1%) reached consensus, and 7 (33.4%) had majority agreement. Overall, a set of 23 criteria (2 essential, 12 required-1st grade, 7 required-2nd grade, and 2 potential) was recommended to establish HSCC.This article reveals a consensus among an international group of HCPs and patients on a series of evidence-based criteria for HSCC. Standardized care, a hub and spoke model, multidisciplinary teams, specialized treatments, well-defined protocols, patient education, medical training, and robust referral systems were identified as essential/very important criteria for HSCC.© 2026. llm_summary: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a serious long-term skin disease that affects the immune system and requires care from multiple types of doctors working together, which is why experts wanted to create standards for specialized treatment centers. An international group of twenty-two specialists, including doctors and patients from sixteen countries, used a voting method called the Delphi consensus to agree on what makes a good hidradenitis suppurativa competence center. Through three rounds of voting between May and July 2024, the group identified twenty-three criteria that should define these specialized centers, with two criteria considered absolutely essential, twelve considered required as first priority, seven as required second priority, and two as potential additions. The essential and highly important standards include having standardized care practices, a team of different medical specialists working together, specialized treatments, clear treatment plans, patient education programs, doctor training, and strong systems for referring patients to these centers. These agreed-upon criteria now provide a clear roadmap for hospitals and clinics around the world to establish centers that can properly diagnose and treat hidradenitis suppurativa patients with the highest quality of care.

title: Constructive Conversations: Mastering the Exchange of Feedback.
abstract: Feedback is the transfer of information about an action back to the performing individual in order that the individual can adjust the performance on subsequent actions, allowing for informed learning. In his landmark article, Ende explained that feedback exposes the gap between the actual and intended outcomes. By increasing the learner's awareness of his/her weaknesses and strengths, feedback supports the development of strategies for performance improvement. The focus of this article is on formative feedback in the context of surgical education and practice. As trainees progress through a competency-based curriculum, they observe, participate, and gradually gain independence. The importance of prompt and specific feedback cannot be overstated as it helps trainees track progress, adapt performance and behaviors, and ultimately achieve required competencies. This discussion will explore established feedback models, barriers to giving and receiving feedback, and the unique considerations of feedback to trainees and surgeons.Thieme. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Feedback, which is information given back to someone about how well they performed so they can improve next time, plays a crucial role in helping surgical trainees learn and develop their skills. This article examines how feedback works in surgical education, explaining that good feedback helps trainees understand the difference between what they actually did and what they were supposed to do. The author discusses established models for giving feedback, identifies common obstacles that prevent people from sharing or accepting feedback, and explores special considerations when giving feedback to both trainees and experienced surgeons. Prompt and specific feedback is essential because it allows trainees to track their progress, adjust their behaviors, and eventually master the skills needed to become competent surgeons. The article emphasizes that understanding how to give and receive constructive feedback is a key part of improving surgical training and helping surgeons continue to develop throughout their careers.

title: Outcomes of liver resections for neuroendocrine tumor liver metastases in carcinoid heart disease.
abstract: Carcinoid heart disease (CHD) is associated with advanced neuroendocrine tumor liver metastases (NETLM) and may preclude surgical cytoreduction. We assessed perioperative and long-term outcomes of hepatectomy in patients with CHD. We retrospectively analyzed 311 patients undergoing cytoreductive hepatectomy for intestinal NETLM: non-functional (n = 163), carcinoid syndrome (CS) without CHD (n = 110), and CHD (n = 38), including patients undergoing pre-hepatectomy valve replacement. CHD patients more frequently had >10 liver metastases (78%) and larger lesions (median 9.5 cm) and required major hepatectomy more often (58%). Major morbidity was higher in CHD (up to 47%), yet 90-day mortality remained low (≤4%). Median overall survival after hepatectomy was comparable across groups (12.5 vs. 9.1 vs. 11.4 years; p = .19), including matched analyses. With optimal cardiac management, cytoreductive hepatectomy in CHD is feasible and provides long-term survival comparable to patients without CHD.© 2026 British Society for Neuroendocrinology.

llm_summary: Carcinoid heart disease, a serious heart condition that develops in patients with advanced neuroendocrine tumors that have spread to the liver, has traditionally made surgery risky or impossible for these patients. Researchers examined medical records from 311 patients who underwent liver surgery to remove tumors, comparing outcomes between those with carcinoid heart disease and those without the heart condition. Patients with carcinoid heart disease had more extensive liver tumors and required more extensive surgery, and they experienced higher rates of serious complications after surgery, though very few died within 90 days of the operation. Despite these challenges, patients with carcinoid heart disease who underwent surgery lived just as long after the procedure as patients without the heart condition, with survival times around 11 to 12 years. These findings suggest that with proper heart care before and after surgery, patients with carcinoid heart disease can safely undergo liver surgery and achieve long-term survival benefits comparable to those without the heart condition.

title: Amputation Following Oncologic Endoprosthetic Limb Salvage.
abstract: Endoprosthetic reconstruction has become a primary means of limb salvage for oncologic resection of primary or metastatic disease to avoid amputation. The purpose of this study was to determine the rate at which limb salvage procedures using endoprosthesis ultimately required amputation.The total joint registry from a single institution was queried for patients who underwent primary endoprosthesis placement for oncologic indications.A total of 586 implants in 561 patients were included for analysis. Amputations occurred in 14 patients, and in 9 amputations were the only reoperation following reconstruction. The indication for amputation was most commonly infection (n=7, 50%) and recurrence (n=5, 35%). Mean time to amputation was 71 months for all indications, with a 10-year cumulative incidence of amputation of 2.9%. Distal femoral and proximal tibial endoprostheses were associated with higher rates of amputation (p<0.001).Overall, the rate of amputation following endoprosthetic reconstruction was low with proximal tibia and distal femoral replacements associated with a higher risk of amputation. Amputation for infection tended to occur as late, whereas amputation for local recurrence typically occurred early.Copyright © 2026 International Institute of Anticancer Research (Dr. George J. llm_summary: Researchers examined how often patients who received artificial joint replacements to save their limbs from cancer ultimately needed amputation, which is the surgical removal of a limb. The study looked at 586 artificial joint implants placed in 561 patients at a single hospital for cancer-related reasons and tracked how many of these patients eventually had their limbs amputated. Out of all the patients studied, only 14 needed amputation, with infection being the most common reason for amputation followed by cancer returning in the treated area. The overall rate of amputation was quite low at about 3 percent over ten years, though artificial joints placed in the upper shin bone and lower thighbone had higher amputation rates than other locations. These results suggest that artificial joint replacement is generally a successful way to save limbs from cancer, though certain locations in the leg carry greater risks and require closer monitoring.

title: Coronal Tibio-Femoral Subluxation Leads to Inferior 15-Year Survival After Mobile-Bearing Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract: The impact of coronal tibiofemoral subluxation (CTFS) on 15-year outcomes after unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) remains unclear. This study evaluated whether preoperative CTFS influences implant survivorship.A total of 175 patients (219 knees) underwent medial UKA between 2007 and 2017 and were prospectively followed; the mean age was 64 years (range, 20 to 92), and CTFS was 4.1 ± 2.8 mm. Patients were stratified by preoperative CTFS: ≥ five mm (subluxation group, n = 87) and less than five mm (non-subluxation group, n = 132). Outcomes were assessed with Kaplan-Meier survival, competing risk analyses, and multivariate Cox regressions.The 10- and 15-year survivorships for the entire cohort were 94.7 and 92.2%, respectively, after a minimum of eight years of follow-up (mean, 11.8 ± 3.8). Kaplan-Meier analyses demonstrated lower survivorship in the subluxation group, with 95.4, 90.5, and 88.3%, respectively, at five, 10, and 15 years compared with 99.2, 97.6, and 95.0% in the nonsubluxation group (P = 0.020). Competing risk analyses confirmed this difference (P = 0.020). Preoperative CTFS ≥ five mm was independently associated with an increased conversion risk (hazard ratio 3.9, P = 0.029), whereas the hip-knee-ankle angle was not. Neither preoperative correctability on postero-anterior flexion radiographs nor residual postoperative subluxation significantly altered the risk of conversion. The most common indications for conversion were progression of osteoarthritis (n = seven) and aseptic loosening (n = six). All cases of aseptic loosening occurred exclusively in the subluxation group (P = 0.002).Both groups exhibited survivorship higher than 90% at 15 years; however, preoperative CTFS ≥ five mm was associated with a higher risk of conversion to TKA due to aseptic loosening after mobile-bearing UKA. CTFS should be incorporated into preoperative evaluation and counseling before UKA.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a specific knee alignment problem before surgery affects how well a partial knee replacement works over time. The study followed 219 knees in 175 patients who had a type of partial knee replacement called mobile-bearing unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, dividing them into groups based on whether they had significant coronal tibiofemoral subluxation, which means the upper and lower leg bones were shifted sideways relative to each other by five millimeters or more. After fifteen years, patients without the alignment problem had better results, with ninety-five percent of their implants still working compared to eighty-eight percent in the group with the alignment issue. The main reason for failure in the misaligned group was aseptic loosening, meaning the implant became loose without infection, and this problem did not occur at all in the well-aligned group. Doctors should now measure this specific alignment problem before surgery and use this information when discussing risks and benefits with patients considering this type of knee replacement.

title: Telisotuzumab Vedotin Monotherapy in Patients With Previously Treated c-Met Protein Overexpressing, Nonsquamous, EGFR Wild-type Advanced NSCLC: Updated Analysis of the LUMINOSITY Trial.
abstract: Telisotuzumab vedotin (Teliso-V) is a c-Met-directed antibody-drug conjugate comprising the monoclonal antibody telisotuzumab and the monomethyl auristatin E payload. Primary analysis of the phase 2 LUMINOSITY trial (NCT03539536) revealed Teliso-V monotherapy 1.9 mg/kg elicited durable responses and had generally manageable safety in patients with locally advanced or metastatic c-Met protein overexpressing, EGFR wild-type, nonsquamous NSCLC. We present updated outcomes with approximately 6 months longer follow-up and explore the impact of previous therapies.Patients (≥18 y; had previous therapy including ≤1 chemotherapy) received 1.9 mg/kg Teliso-V every 2 weeks. c-Met protein overexpression (clinical trial assay for MET [SP44] [Roche]) was defined as greater than or equal to 25% tumor cells with 3+ staining intensity (c-Met high: ≥50% 3+; c-Met intermediate: 25 to <50% 3+). Primary end point was the overall response rate by independent central review per the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1.As of February 21, 2024, 172 patients received at least one dose of Teliso-V; 168 patients (c-Met high, n = 84; c-Met intermediate, n = 84) were evaluable for efficacy. The overall response rate was 29.2% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 22.4-36.7; c-Met high, 34.5% [24.5-45.7]; c-Met intermediate, 23.8% [15.2-34.3]). Median duration of response was 7.2 months (95% CI: 5.5-11.0; c-Met high, 7.2 [95% CI: 4.2-12.0]; c-Met intermediate, 7.2 [95% CI: 4.7-11.5]). Previous therapy (platinum, immune checkpoint inhibitors, or both) did not impact efficacy outcomes. The most common treatment-related adverse event was peripheral sensory neuropathy (any-grade: 31%; grade ≥3: 7%).Teliso-V monotherapy 1.9 mg/kg elicited durable responses, irrespective of the type of previous therapy received, and maintained a manageable safety profile in patients with c-Met protein overexpressing EGFR wild-type, nonsquamous NSCLC.NCT03539536.© 2026 The Authors.

In this trial called LUMINOSITY, 172 patients with advanced nonsquamous lung cancer that had not responded to previous treatments received injections of this drug every two weeks. The main side effect was a nerve-related tingling or numbness in the hands and feet, which occurred in about one-third of patients but was usually manageable.

title: Distal Agrin (AGRN) Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome With Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
abstract: Agrin-congenital myasthenic syndrome (AGRN-CMS) is a rare, heterogeneous genetic disorder of the neuromuscular transmission that can present from infancy to adulthood. The clinical phenotype includes distal weakness mimicking distal myopathies. Additionally, electromyography and muscle biopsy may demonstrate myopathic features, increasing the diagnostic challenge. Mitochondrial dysfunction has not been reported in the muscle of AGRN-CMS patients.We report the clinical, electrophysiological, radiological, myopathological, and genetic findings of a patient with AGRN-CMS.A 47-year-old male presented at age 18 with sudden onset of eyelid ptosis, weakness, and fatigue, followed by dysphagia, dyspnea on exertion, exercise intolerance, and myalgias. Three sisters had similar symptoms. Neurological examination showed lower limb weakness, predominantly affecting the calf muscles with associated atrophy. Tendon reflexes were normal but absent at the ankles. Creatine kinase levels were normal. Electromyography demonstrated myopathic changes in distal muscles with fibrillation potentials in the gastrocnemius. 2 Hz-Repetitive nerve stimulation of the fibular nerve revealed a 32% decrement in the extensor digitorum brevis without facilitation. Tibialis anterior biopsy showed non-specific myopathic changes, neurogenic features, and histological evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction, as suggested by the scattered cytochrome c oxidase-negative fibers. Whole exome sequencing detected a homozygous pathogenic AGRN variant (c.5012G>A, p.Arg1671Gln). No pathogenic or suspected pathogenic variants were detected in muscle mitochondrial DNA or in nuclear genes affecting mitochondrial function.This patient expands the pathological spectrum of AGRN-CMS to include mitochondrial dysfunction and highlights the importance of low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation in the assessment of patients with distal weakness for differentiating myopathies from CMS.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Agrin-congenital myasthenic syndrome is a rare genetic disorder affecting how muscles and nerves communicate, and it can cause weakness that looks similar to other muscle diseases, making it difficult to diagnose correctly. Researchers documented the case of a 47-year-old man who developed drooping eyelids, weakness, and difficulty swallowing starting at age 18, along with three sisters who had similar symptoms, and they performed various tests including nerve stimulation studies, muscle biopsies, and genetic testing to understand his condition. The patient's muscle biopsy showed unusual patterns suggesting that his mitochondria, which are the energy-producing structures inside cells, were not working properly, which had never been reported before in patients with this particular genetic disorder. This case is important because it expands our understanding of how agrin-congenital myasthenic syndrome can affect the body and shows that doctors should use specific nerve stimulation tests when evaluating patients with weakness in their lower legs to distinguish between muscle diseases and nerve-muscle communication problems. Future research should investigate whether mitochondrial dysfunction is a common feature of this syndrome and whether understanding this connection could lead to better treatments for affected patients.

title: Inpatient Outcomes and Complications After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion in Rural Versus Urban Hospitals in the United States.
abstract: Disparities in management of atrial fibrillation in rural and urban hospitals across the U.S. have been reported. However, studies investigating disparities regarding outcomes and complications after left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) based on hospital location are lacking.To evaluate differences in outcomes and complications related to LAAO among rural and urban hospitals.The National Inpatient Sample was used to identify patients who underwent LAAO implantations in the U.S. from 2016-2020. Study endpoints assessed included inpatient complications, outcomes, and resource utilization after LAAO procedures among rural and urban hospitals.From 2016-2020, there were a total of 87 315 and 1985 LAAO device placements in urban and rural hospitals, respectively. Baseline characteristics were similar among both groups, with a few exceptions. After multivariable adjustment for confounders, odds of inpatient complications and mortality were similar among both groups. However, rural LAAO recipients experienced greater rates of discharge to an acute care facility (3.3% vs 2.4%, p = 0.01), as well as lower costs (aOR: 0.58, 95% CI: 0.49-0.69) and length of stay (aOR: 0.89, 95% CI: 0.81-0.98).A majority of LAAO implantations occurred in urban hospitals in the U.S. Baseline characteristics and adjusted odds of inpatient complications and mortality were similar in rural and urban recipients. However, important differences were described regarding resource utilization and disposition. Further investigation into the specific factors driving these inequities is encouraged to promote improved access to and outcomes of cardiovascular care for rural residents.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined whether patients who received left atrial appendage occlusion devices, which are small implants that help prevent blood clots in people with irregular heartbeats, had different outcomes depending on whether they were treated at rural or urban hospitals across the United States. The study looked at data from over 89,000 patients who received these devices between 2016 and 2020, comparing complication rates, deaths, and hospital costs between the two types of hospitals. The results showed that patients at rural and urban hospitals experienced similar rates of complications and death after the procedure, but rural patients were more likely to be transferred to another acute care facility after leaving the hospital and had shorter hospital stays with lower costs. These findings suggest that while the safety and effectiveness of the procedure itself were comparable between rural and urban settings, differences existed in how patients were discharged and how much the treatment cost. The researchers called for further investigation into why these differences occurred so that rural residents can have better access to this type of heart care and achieve the same quality outcomes as urban patients.

llm_summary: Researchers identified and confirmed a new genetic variant called HLA-B*15:591, which is part of the human leukocyte antigen system that helps the body recognize and fight infections. The team used next generation sequencing, a modern DNA reading technology that can identify tiny changes in genetic code, to study this variant in detail. They discovered that HLA-B*15:591 is defined by a single letter change in the genetic instructions at position 219 in a specific section of the HLA-B gene. This genomic confirmation, meaning they proved the exact genetic makeup using advanced sequencing methods, adds to the growing catalog of known HLA variants that doctors and researchers use for organ transplant matching and understanding immune responses. The findings contribute to a more complete understanding of human genetic diversity and may help improve the accuracy of medical tests used in transplantation and disease research.

title: Facial feature removal in magnetic resonance imaging scans of adults with Down syndrome: A de-facing methodological study.
abstract: Face identification algorithms have increased the risk of study participants being identified through different neuroimaging modalities. De-facing algorithms can de-identify neuroimages; however, none are validated in individuals with Down syndrome (DS) - a population at high risk of Alzheimer's disease and the focus of numerous Alzheimer's disease cohort studies.Overall, 37 adults with DS were parcellated using FreeSurfer before and after de-facing with mri_reface. The study compared 37 adults with Down syndrome to a similar group of people without Down syndrome, measuring brain structure and thickness before and after the facial removal process was applied to their magnetic resonance imaging scans. The results showed that removing facial features had no meaningful impact on the brain measurements that researchers typically use to track brain health and changes over time. This finding is important because it means scientists can safely remove faces from brain scans to protect people's privacy without worrying that it will ruin their research data. The researchers recommend that studies involving adults with Down syndrome should use this de-facing technique before sharing brain scan images to keep participants' identities private and secure.

title: Clinical Vignette: Delayed Loss of Hand Dexterity in a Young Woman With Stroke.
abstract: A 38-year-old woman presented with progressive loss of hand dexterity 2 years after achieving full functional recovery from a prior ischemic stroke. Despite preserved strength, the impairment significantly disrupted her ability to perform activities of daily living. This case highlights a comprehensive clinical approach to late-onset upper limb motor dysfunction after stroke. We explore diagnostic considerations, outline standard-of-care management strategies, and review emerging adjunctive therapies for cases where conventional treatment proves insufficient.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. llm_summary: A 38-year-old woman experienced an unusual problem where she gradually lost the ability to use her hands skillfully, even though she had fully recovered from a stroke two years earlier. Doctors examined her case carefully to understand why her hand dexterity, or ability to perform precise movements, was declining despite her arm strength remaining normal. The woman's loss of hand control made it very difficult for her to do everyday tasks like cooking, writing, and getting dressed, even though her muscles were still strong. This case study shows doctors how to approach and diagnose late-onset problems with upper limb movement that happen long after a stroke, and it reviews both standard treatments and newer experimental therapies that might help when regular treatment does not work. Understanding cases like this one helps medical professionals recognize that stroke recovery can be complicated and that patients may develop new movement problems months or years after their initial stroke.

title: Cancer treatment-related cognitive impairment.
abstract: There is a growing number of cancer survivors given improvement in early cancer diagnosis, therapeutics, and supportive care strategies. Cognitive impairment is among the most common and clinically significant symptoms managed by cancer survivors, which negatively impacts quality of life, functional and occupational status for patients and their care partners. Cancer-related cognitive impairment is often multifactorial-impacted by patient and cancer-specific factors. For systemic (non-CNS) malignancies, cognitive impairment has been identified in up to 75%, depending on cohort, which persists in up to 35% of patients in the years following initial treatment. The most common areas of impairment include memory and processing speed, and executive function. These adverse effects of cancer treatment have been reported after chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. This review will summarize existing knowledge regarding the nature and pattern of cognitive changes, mechanisms and risk factors underlying these changes, and biomarkers to support identification of this adverse consequence of cancer therapies.© The Author(s) 2026. llm_summary: As more people survive cancer thanks to better detection and treatment methods, doctors are noticing that many survivors struggle with thinking and memory problems that hurt their quality of life and ability to work. Researchers reviewed existing studies to understand how cancer treatments affect the brain and cause cognitive impairment, which means difficulty with thinking, remembering, and processing information. They found that up to 75 percent of cancer survivors experience some cognitive problems, with the most common issues being trouble with memory, processing speed (how quickly the brain handles information), and executive function (planning and decision-making skills). These thinking problems can happen after various cancer treatments including chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, and they can last for years even after treatment ends. The review highlights the need for better ways to identify which patients are at risk and to find biological markers, or measurable signs in the body, that could help doctors predict and prevent these cognitive side effects in cancer survivors.

title: Biomimetic model for the identification of distinctive microenvironmental factors in glioblastoma radiosensitivity.
abstract: Radiation therapy (RT) has long been included in the treatment of glioblastoma (GBM). However, radioresistance in cancer cells as well as toxicity in normal tissues are major obstacles to clinical efficacy. Improved understanding of the mechanisms of tumor microenvironment-induced radioresistance during and after radiation therapy can provide fundamental insights to improve clinical outcomes in GBM. Here, using three-dimensional engineered hydrogel models in vitro, we report the influence of extracellular matrix, hypoxia, and adjacent neuronal cells in radiotherapeutic sensitivity. We find that mechanical cues and oxygen availability regulate cellular response to radiation, with softer matrices allowing for more DNA damage. Hyaluronan fragments from the extracellular matrix also modulate rapid metabolic response to radiation, especially in hypoxic environments. We show that neuronal networks influence tumor metabolic activity and the inflammatory response. Overall, we demonstrate here that alternative radiation strategies, such as low dose rate radiation therapy and microenvironmental regulation, have the potential to be more effective in a specific subset of radiosensitive GBM tumors.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Radiation therapy is a common treatment for glioblastoma, a serious type of brain cancer, but many tumors become resistant to radiation and the treatment can damage healthy tissue, making it important to understand why some tumors resist radiation better than others. Researchers created three-dimensional gel-based models in the laboratory that mimicked the tumor environment, including the supportive tissue around cancer cells, low oxygen conditions, and nearby nerve cells, to study how these factors affect how cancer cells respond to radiation. The study found that softer supportive tissue allowed cancer cells to take more damage from radiation, while low oxygen levels and fragments of a natural substance called hyaluronan changed how quickly cancer cells used energy after radiation exposure. The presence of nerve cell networks nearby also influenced how active the tumor cells remained and how the body's immune system responded to the radiation treatment. These findings suggest that doctors might improve radiation therapy results by using different radiation approaches, such as giving lower doses over longer periods, or by changing the tumor's environment to make it more sensitive to treatment in certain types of glioblastoma.

title: Anisometropia at Age 7 After Bilateral Secondary Intraocular Lens Implantation at 2 to Younger than 6 Years for Pediatric Aphakia: The CCPMOH Report.
abstract: To evaluate anisometropia at age 7 years after bilateral secondary intraocular lens (IOL) implantation in children with pediatric aphakia and to identify factors associated with long-term refractive symmetry.A prospective observational cohort study.This study was conducted from 2014 to 2023 at a single center. Of 251 eligible children, 158 (316 eyes) who underwent lensectomy before age 2 and secondary IOL implantation between ages 2 and 6 were included.Participants were grouped by age at secondary IOL implantation: 2 to <3 years, 3 to <4 years, 4 to <5 years, and 5 to <6 years. Demographic and clinical data were collected, and refractive outcomes at postoperative 1 month and age 7 years were analyzed. All refractive outcomes were expressed as spherical equivalent (SE), calculated as the sphere plus half of the cylinder (SE = sphere + ½ cylinder).Interocular anisometropia at age 7 years, defined as the absolute interocular difference in SE.At postoperative month 1, 77.2% of children had anisometropia <1.0 D. By age 7 years, this proportion decreased to 52.5%, and significant differences in anisometropia distribution were observed among age-at-implantation groups (P = 0.035). In multivariable analyses, earlier age at secondary IOL implantation (β = -0.260; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.386 to -0.134; P < 0.001), greater interocular axial length difference at implantation (β = 0.330; 95% CI, 0.033-0.628; P = 0.030), and greater early postoperative anisometropia (β = 0.355; 95% CI, 0.079-0.631; P = 0.012) were independently associated with greater anisometropia at age 7 years.Interocular anisometropia tends to increase during childhood after bilateral secondary IOL implantation and is influenced by implantation timing, interocular axial length asymmetry, and early postoperative refractive status. llm_summary: Researchers examined how children's eyes develop after receiving artificial lenses implanted to replace cloudy natural lenses removed early in life, a condition called pediatric aphakia. The study followed 158 children who had surgery between ages two and six years old, tracking their eye measurements and vision development until age seven to see if their two eyes remained balanced in focusing power. At one month after surgery, most children had well-matched eyes, but by age seven years, the balance between their two eyes had worsened in many cases, with differences in focusing power becoming more noticeable. The researchers found that children who received their artificial lenses earlier in life, those with greater differences in eye size between their two eyes at the time of surgery, and those with unbalanced focusing power right after surgery were more likely to develop mismatched eyes by age seven. These findings suggest that doctors should try to minimize focusing imbalances immediately after surgery and may want to wait longer before implanting lenses in children whose two eyes are very different sizes.

title: From microtissues to macro solutions - The future of scalable and automated cartilage tissue engineering.
abstract: The burden of articular cartilage damage on society continues to rise. Suitable treatment is necessary to reduce pain, improve quality of life, and avoid progression into osteoarthritis. Current regenerative cartilage repair strategies remain limited in clinical practice due to high costs, complex logistics, patient burden, and poor reimbursement. To ensure that treatment innovations effectively reach the patient, the focus during development should be on automated and scalable solutions. A promising concept is using cartilage microtissues as building blocks in a modular approach to create larger cartilage constructs. By enabling controlled microtissue assembly and reproducible, scalable manufacturing, this could lead to the efficient production of tissue-engineered cartilage implants. Several automated, scalable steps have been described in literature, ranging from cell isolation and expansion to microtissue formation and harvesting, and finally to macrotissue assembly and maturation. However, integrating all these steps into a single, cost-effective, and automated process remains a conceptual idea. This review focuses on potential routes and key choices that should be considered in the early design process of future ready-to-implant tissue-engineered cartilage implants. Furthermore, the added value of investigating and implementing automatic quality measures and cleaning protocols, as well as the recommended regulatory checks and cost-effectiveness implications, are discussed. The translational potential of this article: Leveraging microtissues for cartilage tissue engineering in a scalable, automated, and GMP-compliant manner could address the growing burden of articular cartilage damage. This review shows the translational potential of this approach by focusing on the early implementation of these concepts in the design process of cartilage tissue-engineered solutions, ensuring compatibility and viability within current healthcare systems.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Cartilage damage in joints is a growing health problem that causes pain and can lead to arthritis, a condition where joints become stiff and painful over time. Researchers reviewed current methods for growing replacement cartilage in laboratories and identified ways to make the process faster, cheaper, and more automated so it could help more patients. The key idea they explored is building larger cartilage pieces from tiny tissue building blocks called microtissues, which could be assembled together in a controlled way to create implants ready for surgery. This approach could reduce costs and make cartilage treatments available to more people by streamlining every step from growing cells to final assembly and quality checking. While this modular building-block method shows promise, scientists still need to develop a single complete system that combines all these steps automatically and meets medical safety standards before it can be used in hospitals.

title: Long-term cryopreservation reanimation success of pancreatobiliary patient-derived xenograft models.
abstract: Patient-derived xenografts are cancer models where patient tumor tissue is implanted into immunocompromised mice for preclinical research. Patient-derived xenografts recapitulate the original patient tumor with high fidelity and highly correlate with treatment efficacy compared with cell lines or genetically engineered mice. Maintaining validated patient-derived xenograft libraries requires effective cryopreservation and reanimation techniques. While we previously demonstrated success using specialized cryoprotectant techniques after short-term preservation (<3 years), optimal long-term methods remain unclear. We investigated successful reanimation of validated pancreatobiliary patient-derived xenografts following long-term (>5 years) cryopreservation.From our patient-derived xenograft library of over 760 prospectively collected unique patient tumors, we utilized 32 random histopathologically confirmed pancreatic adenocarcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma tumors from validated second-generation patient-derived xenograft models that were cryopreserved >5 years. Growth was assessed up to 6 months. Upon reaching a volume of 500-1,000 mm3, tumors were harvested and histologically compared with the original patient tumor and first-generation patient-derived xenograft. The primary outcome was successful growth of long-term cryopreserved patient-derived xenograft tumors.Of the 14 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and 18 cholangiocarcinoma patient-derived xenografts, 31 (96%) were successfully reanimated and validated after long-term cryopreservation with a 2-month median time to harvest. One model (3%) was unsuccessful. The original patient-derived xenograft models were derived from cancer tissue obtained at surgical resection 28 (87%) or biopsy 4 (13%). The median duration of cryopreservation was 8 years (range 6-11 years).Previously validated cryopreserved pancreatobiliary patient-derived xenograft tumor models were effectively reanimated from long-term (>5 years) cryopreservation at -80°C with a high success rate (>95%). Optimized protocols enable maintaining a cryoinventory of patient-derived xenograft models for future translational applications.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether tumor samples from cancer patients that had been frozen and stored for many years could be successfully thawed and grown again in laboratory mice, which is important because these mouse models help doctors test new cancer treatments before trying them on actual patients. The team took 32 previously validated tumor samples from pancreatic cancer and bile duct cancer patients that had been frozen for more than five years at very cold temperatures and attempted to revive them by implanting them into immunocompromised mice, which are mice whose immune systems have been weakened so they do not reject human tissue. Out of the 32 frozen tumor samples, 31 were successfully brought back to life and grew properly in the mice within about two months, with a success rate of 96 percent, and the revived tumors matched the original patient tumors and earlier mouse versions very closely. This high success rate means that hospitals and research centers can safely store large collections of these patient-derived tumor models in freezers for many years without losing their usefulness, allowing researchers to conduct cancer studies and drug testing whenever needed in the future. The findings suggest that long-term frozen storage of these tumor models is a reliable way to maintain valuable research resources.

title: The role of microRNAs and competing endogenous RNA regulatory networks in mesothelioma response to immunotherapy.
abstract: Assessing the contributions of microRNAs to gene expression regulation and treatment outcomes in malignancies is challenging. Traditional analyses focus on individual microRNAs, overlooking competitive binding among RNA species sharing common microRNAs. We evaluated the impact of microRNA's impact on the survival of patients with mesothelioma in response to treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) within the context of competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) networks. Using two large public mesothelioma datasets, we constructed ceRNA networks (ceRNETs) and analyzed differentially expressed microRNAs in patients with favorable versus unfavorable survival outcomes from two ICI mesothelioma trials. ceRNETs from public and trial cohorts were largely consistent. Notably, tumors with favorable survival outcomes exhibited overexpressed microRNAs targeting ceRNETs with co-regulated gene expression profiles. These downregulated profiles are often linked to ICI resistance. Crosstalk among ceRNETs appeared coordinated, forming part of an existing mesothelioma regulatory network. Furthermore, in response to ICI this regulatory network was tipped towards downregulation of immune suppressive pathways in patients with the favorable outcomes. Our findings suggest that ceRNET-based analysis elucidates the immunologic context of cancers and may have prognostic significance for patients who receive ICI. These findings may also uncover novel therapeutic strategies, including delivery of immunoregulatory microRNAs frequently lost in mesothelioma.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how tiny pieces of genetic material called microRNAs affect how mesothelioma, a deadly cancer linked to asbestos exposure, responds to immunotherapy drugs that help the immune system fight cancer. They studied two large groups of mesothelioma patients and created detailed maps showing how different microRNAs work together in networks to control gene expression, which is the process of turning genes on and off. Patients who survived longer and responded well to immunotherapy had higher levels of specific microRNAs that shut down genes associated with immune resistance, meaning their bodies were better able to fight the cancer. The findings suggest that analyzing these microRNA networks could help doctors predict which patients will benefit most from immunotherapy and potentially identify new treatments involving delivering protective microRNAs that are often lost in mesothelioma tumors. Future research will need to test whether these microRNA-based predictions work in new patient groups and whether delivering these genetic molecules could improve treatment outcomes for people with this serious disease.

title: Semaglutide 2.4 mg Cardiometabolic Long-Term Effects in Patients With Obesity or Overweight in a Real-World Setting: A Retrospective Cohort Study in the United States (SMILE).
abstract: To evaluate the real-world associations between semaglutide 2.4 mg and cardiometabolic comorbidities, biomarkers and cardiovascular risk among adults with overweight or obesity.This retrospective cohort study used US claims data and laboratory measurements from the Komodo Research Database (2016-2024). Adults with obesity or with overweight and ≥ 1 obesity-related comorbidity were included. Patients on semaglutide 2.4 mg for ≥ 12 months were compared with non-users (including users of other obesity medications) using propensity score weighting with residual imbalances adjusted in regression model. Outcomes included time to onset of cardiometabolic comorbidities, change in cardiometabolic biomarkers and changes in 10-year ASCVD risk score at 12 months.25 783 semaglutide 2.4 mg users and 8 948 913 non-users were identified. Semaglutide 2.4 mg was associated with significantly lower risks for incident prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, type 2 diabetes only, hypertension, ASCVD, heart failure and CVD (HRs 0.45-0.75; all p < 0.05), as well as greater improvements in BMI (-4.1 kg/m2), SBP (-6.2 mmHg), HbA1c (-0.4%), LDL cholesterol (-7.7 mg/dL), triglycerides (-28.6 mg/dL) and HDL cholesterol (+1.9 mg/dL; all p < 0.001). They looked at real-world medical records and test results from over 25,000 people taking semaglutide compared to nearly 9 million people not taking it, tracking their health outcomes over several years. title: Clinical document metadata extraction: A scoping review.
abstract: Clinical document metadata, such as document type, structure, author role, medical specialty, and encounter setting, is essential for accurate interpretation of information captured in clinical documents. However, vast documentation heterogeneity and drift over time challenge harmonization of document metadata. Automated extraction methods have emerged to coalesce metadata from disparate practices into target schema. This scoping review aims to catalog research on clinical document metadata extraction, identify methodological trends and applications, and highlight gaps warranting further investigation.We followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines to identify articles from Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science and external sources that perform clinical document metadata extraction, either primarily as a methodology study, secondarily as a feature for a downstream application, or for analysis. We initially identified and screened 342 articles published between 2011 and 2025, then comprehensively reviewed 77 we deemed relevant to our study.Among the 77 articles included in our full text review, 49 were methodological, 22 used document metadata as features in a downstream application, and 6 analyzed document metadata composition. We observe myriad purposes for methodological study and application types. Available labelled public data remains sparse except for structural section datasets. Methods for extracting document metadata have progressed from largely rule-based and traditional machine learning with ample feature engineering to transformer-based architectures with minimal feature engineering.Clinical document metadata extraction research has accelerated over recent years. The emergence of large language models has enabled broader exploration of generalizability across tasks and datasets, allowing the possibility of advanced clinical text processing systems. We anticipate that research will continue to expand into richer document metadata representations and integrate further into clinical applications and workflows.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Clinical documents like patient records contain important information such as document type, author role, and medical specialty, but this information is often scattered across different healthcare systems in different formats, making it hard to use consistently. Researchers reviewed 77 studies published between 2011 and 2025 to understand how computers can automatically pull out and organize this metadata, or descriptive information, from clinical documents. They found that extraction methods have evolved from simple rule-based systems to more advanced artificial intelligence approaches called transformers that require less manual setup. The research shows that newer large language models, which are powerful artificial intelligence systems trained on vast amounts of text, are making it easier to extract this metadata across different documents and healthcare settings. Future work will likely focus on capturing more detailed information from documents and building these extraction tools directly into healthcare workflows so they can be used in real clinical practice.

title: A case report of malignant catatonia in a patient with apparent intoxication.
abstract: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by motor and behavioral abnormalities, such as mutism and stupor. Delay in recognition and treatment can lead to progression of a life-threatening condition, malignant catatonia. Benzodiazepines are typically used as first-line treatment, but electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) may be required in cases refractory to benzodiazepines. We present a 24-year-old male presented to the emergency department (ED) with altered mental status and demonstrated several features of catatonia, including immobility, staring, posturing, grimacing, verbigeration, rigidity, negativism, and impulsivity. Despite multiple doses of lorazepam, the patient deteriorated, developing autonomic instability and requiring intubation. He was admitted to the intensive care unit and underwent two sessions of electroconvulsive therapy. Mental status improved on hospital day seven and he was discharged in stable condition on hospital day 8. Catatonia can mimic other conditions such as psychosis, intoxication, or delirium, making diagnosis challenging in the ED. Failure to recognize malignant catatonia can lead to rapid deterioration and even death. Emergency physicians should consider catatonia in patients with altered mental status with motor and behavioral abnormalities. llm_summary: Catatonia is a serious brain condition that causes people to stop moving or speaking and can become life-threatening if not treated quickly, which is why doctors need to recognize it early. A 24-year-old man came to the emergency room appearing confused and showing signs of catatonia, including being unable to move, staring blankly, and making repetitive movements, but his condition looked similar to drug intoxication which made it harder to diagnose correctly. Even after receiving multiple doses of lorazepam, a sedative medication typically used to treat catatonia, the patient got worse and developed dangerous changes in heart rate and blood pressure that required him to be put on a breathing machine. The doctors admitted him to the intensive care unit and gave him electroconvulsive therapy, which is a medical treatment that uses controlled electrical currents to help the brain, and after two sessions his mental condition improved enough for him to go home on the eighth day. Emergency room doctors should consider catatonia as a possible diagnosis when patients have confused thinking along with unusual movements or behaviors, because recognizing and treating it quickly can prevent serious complications and even death.

title: Outcomes of stereotactic body radiotherapy for supraclavicular lymph node metastasis among patients with metastatic prostate cancer.
abstract: Metastasis directed therapy (MDT) with stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) has demonstrated clinical benefit among select oligometastatic prostate cancer (PCa) patients. The outcomes of SBRT to the left supraclavicular lymph nodes (SCLNs) are examined.Between 2017 and 2024, 16 (3.8%) of 419 patients with PCa metastatic to lymph nodes were found by prostate-specific PET to have SCLN involvement. Survival, relapse patterns, and toxicity are analyzed.At initial PCa diagnosis, median PSA was 6.7 ng/mL (range 2.1-315) with 50% of patients having Gleason score of 8-10. Mean time from initial diagnosis to SCLN metastasis was 10.4 years with median PSA of 2.0 ng/mL and median number of involved SCLNs of 1.5 (range 1-10). The most common fractionation scheme was 35 Gy in 5 fractions daily (44%) with 81% of patients receiving concurrent hormonal therapy. No grade ≥ 2 toxicities were reported. Local relapse-free survival at 5 years was 90.9%. Mean distant progression-free survival was 16.7 months (95% CI: 7.9-25.5). Mean prostate cancer-specific survival (PCSS) and overall survival were 4.6 years (95% CI: 3.6-5.6) and 4.0 years (95% CI: 2.8-5.1), respectively. Patients with castration-sensitive disease had 100% 5-year PCSS, and 58.3% for those with mCRPC.SBRT to SCLNs was well tolerated with no significant toxicity. Durable local control was satisfactory. The presence of SCLN metastases is frequently a harbinger of additional metastatic progression which suggests that patients require close monitoring and could benefit from the addition or intensification of systemic therapy.© 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V. on behalf of European Society for Radiotherapy and Oncology.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a focused radiation treatment called stereotactic body radiotherapy could effectively treat cancer that had spread to lymph nodes in the neck area of men with advanced prostate cancer. Between 2017 and 2024, they studied 16 patients who received this targeted radiation therapy, tracking how well the treatment worked, whether the cancer came back, and what side effects occurred. The treatment was very well tolerated with no serious side effects, and about 91 percent of patients had no cancer returning in those treated areas after five years, though cancer did spread to other parts of the body in many cases. The findings suggest that while this radiation treatment successfully controls cancer in the neck lymph nodes, patients still need close monitoring and stronger systemic treatments throughout their body because the presence of cancer in these neck nodes often signals that cancer will develop elsewhere. These results indicate that this radiation approach could be a helpful option for select patients, but it works best when combined with other cancer-fighting treatments rather than used alone.

title: Procedure-dependent cardiovascular risk reduction after metabolic and bariatric surgery: a large cohort study.
abstract: Obesity is a major contributor to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) through adverse effects on blood pressure, lipid metabolism, and glucose regulation. Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) produces durable cardiometabolic improvement, but procedures differ in their metabolic effects. Whether these differences translate into meaningful variation in integrated cardiovascular risk reduction remains uncertain. We compared changes in estimated cardiovascular risk after sleeve gastrectomy (SG), Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB), and biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD-DS).We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing primary MBS at a tertiary academic center. Patients were required to have complete clinical and laboratory data at baseline and 1 year after surgery. Ten-year and lifetime ASCVD risk estimates were calculated using pooled cohort equations. Primary outcomes were absolute changes in estimated 10-year and lifetime cardiovascular risk at 1 year. Secondary outcomes included percent total body weight loss (TBWL%) and changes in blood pressure and lipid parameters.The cohort included 2642 patients (699 SG, 1813 RYGB, and 130 BPD-DS). At 1 year, the mean 10-year cardiovascular risk decreased by 0.33 after SG, 0.93 after RYGB, and 1.58 after BPD-DS (P = .006). The mean lifetime cardiovascular risk decreased by 3.24, 7.67, and 10.49, respectively (P < .001). TBWL% was 23.6%, 31.0%, and 36.8%, respectively (P < .001).MBS is associated with significant cardiovascular risk reduction, with greater benefit observed after more metabolically intensive procedures.Copyright © 2026 Society for Surgery of the Alimentary Tract. llm_summary: Obesity increases the risk of heart disease and stroke by harming blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and blood sugar control, but weight loss surgery can help reverse these problems. Researchers studied nearly 2,700 patients who had one of three different types of weight loss surgery to see which procedure was most effective at reducing heart disease risk over ten years and a lifetime. After one year, patients who had the most intensive surgery, called biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch, showed the greatest improvement in heart disease risk scores, followed by those who had gastric bypass surgery, and then those who had sleeve gastrectomy. The study found that all three surgical procedures significantly reduced cardiovascular risk, but the more complex surgeries that change how the body processes food and absorbs nutrients produced better results than simpler procedures. These findings suggest that doctors and patients should consider not just weight loss alone when choosing a bariatric surgery, but also the specific heart disease risk reduction benefits that each procedure offers.

title: The Society of Thoracic Surgeons 2026 Expert Consensus on the Multimodal Treatment of Pleural Mesothelioma.
abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is a rare and complex thoracic malignancy for which treatment regimens continue to evolve. The role of surgery in the management of PM is controversial. We reviewed contemporary literature to provide consensus recommendations from an expert multidisciplinary panel on the multimodal treatment of PM with an emphasis on surgical intervention to update management pathways.An international, multidisciplinary panel developed Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes (PICO)-based questions and conducted a comprehensive literature review to identify relevant literature. Consensus statements were developed using a modified Delphi process with at least 75% agreement over three voting rounds.The panel developed 13 PICO questions, and detailed summary statements were provided for each PICO subtopic based on systematic literature review and multidisciplinary expert panel discussion. There was strong consensus that accurate diagnosis depends on adequate pleural biopsy specimens and that clinical evaluation should include, at a minimum, computed tomographic and positron emission tomographic imaging. Therapeutic decisions should be discussed by a multidisciplinary tumor board, including thoracic surgeons with expertise in PM treatment. If surgical resection is deemed appropriate, it should be part of a multimodal treatment plan. Pleurectomy/decortication or extended pleurectomy/decortication is strongly favored over extrapleural pneumonectomy as the approach to resection.This Society of Thoracic Surgeons Expert Consensus Document includes contemporary treatment recommendations for PM based on systematic literature review and multidisciplinary expert panel discussion and provides a management framework for practicing thoracic surgeons.Copyright © 2026 The Society of Thoracic Surgeons. llm_summary: Pleural mesothelioma is a rare and serious cancer of the lung lining that affects people exposed to asbestos, and doctors have been debating the best way to treat it for years. An international team of thoracic surgeons and cancer specialists reviewed all the latest medical research and used a voting process to reach agreement on the best treatment approaches for this disease. The experts strongly agreed that accurate diagnosis requires proper tissue samples, that imaging scans should be used to evaluate patients, and that treatment decisions must involve a team of specialists including experienced surgeons. The panel concluded that when surgery is appropriate, it should be combined with other treatments like chemotherapy and radiation, and that a less invasive procedure called pleurectomy or decortication is preferable to more extensive surgical removal of the lung lining and lung. This new guidance document provides thoracic surgeons with a clear framework for treating pleural mesothelioma patients based on current evidence and expert consensus.

title: PAK1 inhibition synergistically enhances the anti-tumor efficacy of PARP inhibitors in ovarian cancers.
abstract: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) demonstrate effective treatment outcomes in ovarian cancer patients with BRCA1/2 mutations or homologous recombination (HR) repair deficiencies, leveraging the principle of synthetic lethality. However, PARPi resistance and HR proficiency remain significant challenges in the clinical management of PARPi, necessitating the development of novel strategies for PARPi therapy in ovarian cancer. Our previous research identified PAK1's involvement in replication stress-induced cytotoxicity. Nonetheless, whether PAK1 also affects HR repair and PARPi sensitivity in ovarian cancer remains unresolved. In this research, we found that the expression of PAK1 correlated with an unfavorable prognosis in ovarian cancer. Depletion of PAK1, introduction of a kinase-dead mutation, or treatment with the inhibitor IPA-3 could reduce HR repair efficiency and increase ovarian cancer cell sensitivity to the PARP inhibitor olaparib. The combination of olaparib and IPA-3 synergistically increased olaparib-induced DNA replication stress and double-stranded breaks. Using cell line-derived xenograft, patient-derived organoid, and patient-derived xenograft models, we discovered that IPA-3 potentiated the therapeutic efficacy of olaparib both in vivo and ex vivo. Collectively, our findings suggest that targeting PAK1 might offer a new avenue for increasing the sensitivity of olaparib and improving the outcomes of ovarian cancer patients.© 2025 The Authors.
