llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a procedure called genicular nerve radiofrequency treatment, which uses heat to reduce pain signals from the knee, actually works for people suffering from chronic knee osteoarthritis, a common condition where the protective cartilage in the knee wears down over time. The team reviewed eleven high-quality studies involving 868 patients total, comparing those who received the radiofrequency treatment to those who received other treatments like injections, fake procedures, or oral medications. The results showed that the radiofrequency treatment did reduce pain for the first three months after the procedure, but this benefit disappeared by six months and did not improve patients' overall function or quality of life at any point. Importantly, studies funded by companies that make or sell these devices reported better results than studies without such funding, which raises questions about whether the treatment is truly as effective as some claim. Based on these findings, the researchers concluded that while genicular nerve radiofrequency treatment may provide temporary pain relief, it should not be routinely recommended for long-term treatment of knee osteoarthritis pain because the benefits do not last and do not meaningfully improve how well patients can function.

title: A Cost-Effective High Task Alignment Model for Ultrasound-Guided Central Venous Catheterization Training.
abstract: Central venous catheterization (CVC) is a fundamental procedural competency in pulmonary and critical care medicine (PCCM). Although commercially available task trainers are effective for teaching CVC placement, their high cost and logistical requirements can limit access to repeated practice.To evaluate learner and faculty perceptions and usability of a newly developed CVC simulation model compared with a standard commercial task trainer and detail the technical report of the novel model's construction.We conducted a prospective educational evaluation during the PCCM CVC workshop. Participants practiced CVC placement with both the standard commercial trainer and a locally constructed simulation model developed at our institution. Teaching faculty were asked to evaluate both models from an instructional standpoint.Eighteen participants (15 PCCM 1st year fellows and 3 faculty instructors) evaluated the novel CVC simulation model. All fellows (n = 15, 100%) preferred the new model over a standard commercial model, with 14 (93%) reporting improved understanding of CVC insertion steps and 11 (73%) noting ease of ultrasound landmark identification. All fellows (n = 15, 100%) endorsed inclusion of the model in future workshops. Additionally, faculty instructors preferred the novel model for teaching (n = 3, 100%). All faculty supported future use of the model. The initial model development cost was approximately $288.96 with most materials' reusable.The novel task-aligned CVC simulation model offers a realistic, reusable, and cost-effective alternative to commercial simulators, with high learner and faculty preference and strong educational value. Its functional alignment supports integration into fellowship training, with future studies needed to assess objective skill acquisition and retention.© The Author(s) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined a new, affordable training model for teaching doctors how to place central venous catheters, which are tubes inserted into large veins to deliver medications and fluids in critically ill patients. The study involved eighteen medical trainees and instructors who practiced the catheter placement procedure using both a commercially available expensive simulator and a newly designed low-cost model that the researchers built themselves for less than three hundred dollars. All fifteen trainee doctors preferred the new homemade model over the expensive commercial version, with most reporting that it helped them better understand the procedure steps and made it easier to identify landmarks using ultrasound imaging. Both the trainee doctors and faculty instructors strongly supported using this new model in future training workshops because it provided realistic practice at a fraction of the cost while using materials that could be reused many times. The researchers concluded that this cost-effective training model could be integrated into fellowship training programs, though they noted that additional studies are needed to measure whether doctors actually develop better skills and retain what they learn over time.

title: Comprehensive Isomer-Resolved Ganglioside Profiling by HILIC-nanoESI-MS/MS.
abstract: Gangliosides are structurally complex glycosphingolipids that regulate cellular signaling via interactions with extracellular binding partners and by influencing protein function within the membrane. Their comprehensive analysis remains analytically challenging, in part due to low endogenous abundance, extensive structural diversity, and the frequent occurrence of isomeric species arising from both glycan and ceramide moieties. Here, we present a hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) nanoelectrospray ionization tandem mass spectrometry (nanoESI-MS/MS) method specifically designed to achieve isomer-resolved analysis and molecular species-level quantification of gangliosides. To improve characterization of low-abundance fatty acyl fragments, the workflow was extended by combining nanoESI with online fraction collection and subsequent direct infusion. The method demonstrated stable chromatographic performance, high sensitivity, and reproducible quantitative results across ten mouse tissues. Application of the workflow enabled quantification of 80 ganglioside molecular species belonging to 18 subclasses and revealed pronounced tissue-specific differences in subclass distribution and ceramide composition. Overall, this study establishes a robust and sensitive platform for comprehensive ganglioside analysis, providing new opportunities to investigate ganglioside diversity, regulation, and function in complex biological systems.

llm_summary: Gangliosides are fatty molecules found in cell membranes that help control how cells communicate with each other, but studying them has been difficult because they exist in very small amounts and come in many similar forms that are hard to tell apart. Researchers developed a new laboratory technique using specialized equipment called HILIC-nanoESI-MS/MS that can separate and identify these ganglioside molecules with much greater precision than previous methods, even when they are nearly identical in structure. When they tested this new method on ten different mouse tissues, they were able to identify and measure eighty different ganglioside molecules belonging to eighteen different groups, and they discovered that different tissues had very different patterns of these molecules. The findings show that gangliosides vary significantly depending on which part of the body you look at, which suggests these molecules play important and specific roles in different tissues. This new technique gives scientists a powerful tool to study how gangliosides work in healthy bodies and could help researchers understand what goes wrong in diseases where these molecules are not functioning properly.

title: Circadian Pattern of Ventricular Fibrillation-Terminating Shocks among Patients with Diagnosed and Treated Congenital Long QT Syndrome.
abstract: Episodes of ventricular fibrillation (VF) from coronary artery disease cluster in the early morning hours. The circadian pattern of VF in congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS) is less defined.To assess the circadian pattern of VF episodes in LQTS focusing on activity-specific timing.A retrospective study of LQTS patients with an implanted cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) evaluated from 1999 to 2025 in the Mayo Clinic Windland Smith Rice Genetic Heart Rhythm Clinic. Events were VF-terminating shocks with the exact time recorded; for ICD electrical storm, the time of first shock was recorded. Statistical analysis used Rayleigh- and two-harmonic regression tests.Among 321 LQTS patients with an ICD (224 female, mean implant age 21+15 years, 96 LQT1, 161 LQT2, and 64 LQT3), 85 patients (26%) experienced 199 VF-terminating shocks. Per-event and per-patient analysis (correcting for patients with many events) demonstrated clustering in the midafternoon. Two-harmonic regression showed a predominance of events at 15:01 (LRT=30.6; p<0.001), strengthened by the bin-free Rayleigh test with a clustering at 14:58 (Z=14.1; p<0.001). This was driven mainly by LQT1 (Z=10.9; p<0.001) rather than LQT2 (Z=1.2; p=0.3) or LQT3 (Z=7; p<0.001 not maintained by per-patient analysis). Activity analysis showed similar clustering for times of events for daily and exercise/stress-related activities.VF in LQTS, mainly driven by LQT1, is not uniformly distributed throughout the day but concentrates in a mid-afternoon "torsadogenic window". These results align with a previously published "QT clock" and circadian activity of ion channel expression and may influence future management.Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: Researchers examined when dangerous heart rhythms called ventricular fibrillation occur in patients with congenital long QT syndrome, a genetic condition that affects how the heart's electrical system works. The study looked back at records from 321 patients who had received implanted heart devices called defibrillators between 1999 and 2025, tracking exactly when 199 dangerous heart rhythm episodes happened throughout the day. The results showed that these dangerous heart rhythms clustered in the mid-afternoon around 3 p. m. , particularly in patients with the LQT1 type of the condition, rather than being spread evenly across all hours of the day.

title: SINGLE-BLINDED RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL COMPARING THE EFFECT OF UNDERWATER VERSUS CARBON DIOXIDE INSUFFLATION DURING PERORAL ENDOSCOPIC MYOTOMY ON POST-PROCEDURAL PAIN (U-POEM TRIAL).
abstract: "Underwater" endoscopic techniques have gained traction given its potential advantages. The aim of this multicenter randomized trial was to compare the effect of saline immersion (U-POEM) vs. carbon dioxide insufflation during peroral endoscopic myotomy (CO2-POEM) on post-procedural pain.Consecutive patients with achalasia subtype I and II were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to U-POEM or CO2-POEM during the study period between February 2025 to November 2025. Pain was assessed using the validated numeric pain rating (NPRS) on a scale of 0 (none) to 10 (most severe). Primary outcome was immediate post-procedure pain. Secondary outcomes included: post-procedure pain at different time periods, requirement of analgesics, and clinical response (defined as a post-POEM Eckardt score <3).Thirty-six patients were randomized to U-POEM (n=18) and CO2-POEM (n=18). Technical and clinical success were 100% in both groups with no immediate and delayed adverse events. There were no differences in dissection speed or procedural time between the two groups. The immediate post-POEM mean NPRS score was significantly lower in the U-POEM vs. CO2-POEM group (1.6 ± 1.6 vs. 3.3 ± 2.6; 95% CI: 0.23-3.16; p=0.02). When compared to CO2-POEM, patients who underwent U-POEM reported less moderate-severe pain (16.7% vs. 55.5%; 95% CI: 0.04-0.64; p=0.04) and a lower number required opioids for post-operative pain management (5.5% vs. 50%; 95% CI: 0.11-0.68; p=0.007). Mean NPRS score remained lower in the U-POEM vs. CO2-POEM group at 72-hours after the procedure (1.13±1.36 vs. 2.26±1.78; 95% CI: 0.06-2.20; p=0.04).U-POEM was safe, effective, and associated with lower post-procedure pain scores when compared to CO2-POEM (U-POEM trial:NCT06918730).Copyright © 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined a condition called achalasia, where the throat muscle fails to relax properly and makes swallowing difficult, to find the best way to perform a minimally invasive procedure that cuts the muscle to improve swallowing. In this randomized controlled trial, which is a type of study where patients are randomly assigned to different treatment groups, thirty-six patients received either the underwater technique using saline solution or the traditional carbon dioxide gas method during the procedure called peroral endoscopic myotomy. The underwater technique resulted in significantly less pain immediately after the procedure and at seventy-two hours later, with patients in that group experiencing lower pain scores and fewer needing strong pain medications like opioids. Both techniques were equally safe and effective at treating the condition, but the underwater method offered a clear advantage in reducing patient discomfort during recovery. These findings suggest that doctors should consider using the underwater technique when performing this procedure, though larger studies may be needed to confirm these results in more diverse patient populations.

title: Sequential transcatheter closure of sinus venosus and secundum atrial septal defects using covered stents and a septal occluder, a two-step strategy: a case report.
abstract: Superior sinus venosus atrial septal defect (SVASD) is an uncommon congenital anomaly frequently associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD). Surgical repair has traditionally been the standard treatment; however, transcatheter strategies have recently emerged as viable alternatives in selected patients.We describe a 22-year-old Persian male with SVASD and PAPVD who underwent a staged transcatheter intervention. Initially, two PTFE-covered stents were deployed at the superior vena cava-right atrial junction to redirect pulmonary venous flow and exclude the defect. Due to residual shunting and persistent symptoms, a second procedure was performed, during which a septal occluder device was implanted to close the residual SVASD and a concomitant secundum ASD. The combined approach achieved effective defect closure and symptomatic improvement.This case illustrates the feasibility of a minimally invasive, staged endovascular strategy for complex SVASD with PAPVD. Instead of having open surgery, doctors tried a new approach using minimally invasive procedures, meaning they used catheters (thin tubes) inserted through blood vessels rather than opening the chest. In the first procedure, doctors placed two special covered stents (small mesh tubes) to redirect the blood flow and block part of the defect, but some leaking remained and the patient still had symptoms. During a second procedure a few weeks later, doctors implanted an additional device specifically designed to close the remaining heart opening and another hole that was also present. This two-step approach successfully closed the heart defects and improved the patient's symptoms, suggesting that carefully selected patients with this complex condition might avoid traditional open-heart surgery in the future.

title: Use and safety of corticosteroid injections in joints and musculoskeletal soft tissue: guidelines from the American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine, the American Academy of Pain Medicine, the American Society of Interventional Pain Physicians, and the International Pain and Spine Intervention Society.
abstract: Intra-articular corticosteroid (IACS) injection and peri-articular corticosteroid injection are commonly used to treat musculoskeletal conditions. Results vary by musculoskeletal region, but most studies report short-term benefit with mixed results on long-term relief. Publications showed adverse events from single corticosteroid injections. Recommended effective doses were lower than those currently used by clinicians.Development of the practice guideline for joint injections was approved by the Board of Directors of the American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine and the participating societies. A Corticosteroid Safety Work Group coordinated the development of three guidelines: peripheral nerve blocks and trigger points; joints; and neuraxial, facet, and sacroiliac joint injections. The topics included safety of the technique in relation to landmark-guided, ultrasound-guided, or radiology-aided injections; effect of the addition of the corticosteroid on the efficacy of the injectate; and adverse events related to the injection. Experts on the topics were assigned to extensively review the literature and initially develop consensus statements and recommendations. A modified version of the US Preventive Services Task Force grading of evidence and strength of recommendation was followed. A modified Delphi process was adhered to in arriving at a consensus.This guideline focuses on the safety and efficacy of corticosteroid joint injections for managing joint chronic pain in adults. The joints that were addressed included the shoulder, elbow, hand, wrist, hip, knee, and small joints of the hands and feet. All the statements and recommendations were approved by all participants and the Board of Directors of the participating societies after four rounds of discussion. There is little evidence to guide the selection of one corticosteroid over another. Ultrasound guidance increases the accuracy of injections and reduces procedural pain. A dose of 20 mg triamcinolone is as effective as 40 mg for both shoulder IACS and subacromial subdeltoid bursa corticosteroid injections. The commonly used dose for hip IACS is 40 mg triamcinolone or methylprednisolone. Triamcinolone 40 mg is as effective as 80 mg for knee IACS. Overall, IACS injections result in short-term pain relief from a few weeks to a few months. llm_summary: Multiple medical organizations created guidelines to help doctors safely and effectively use steroid injections in joints and soft tissues around joints to treat chronic pain in adults. The expert teams reviewed extensive medical research on injections in the shoulder, elbow, hand, wrist, hip, knee, and small joints of the hands and feet, then used a structured voting process to reach agreement on best practices. The guidelines found that ultrasound imaging helps doctors place injections more accurately and causes less pain during the procedure, and that lower doses of steroids like 20 to 40 milligrams work just as well as higher doses of 40 to 80 milligrams. While steroid joint injections provide short-term pain relief lasting from a few weeks to a few months, they can cause side effects including increased blood sugar, weakened bones, damage to cartilage in the joint, and increased risk of infection after procedures. These recommendations give doctors specific guidance on how to use steroid injections safely and effectively for musculoskeletal pain while minimizing potential harms to patients.

title: Sex- and experience-dependent regulation of synaptic protein turnover.
abstract: Synaptic transmission can be tuned through plasticity mechanisms that regulate synaptic strength, structure, and number. In vivo measurements demonstrate remarkable spine dynamics, with subsets of synapses persisting for months. This correlates with the longevity of certain memories, which can persist for an organism's lifetime. The molecular basis supporting the long-term stability of specific synapses and the long-term durability of memories remains unknown. At the protein level, most proteins persist for a relatively short amount of time before they are degraded and replaced with new molecules. However, recent work has identified a population of proteins, including those present at the synapse, that are exceptionally long-lived. It has been speculated that long-lived proteins (LLPs) could contribute to long-term synapse stability, function, and memory. Here, we used stable isotope labeling in mammals to first identify LLPs in the post synaptic density (PSD) of the hippocampus and subsequently determine if protein turnover rates varied by sex or following learning. We identified synaptic LLPs and found that both sex and experience can regulate synaptic protein turnover rates. We identified sex-dependent changes in protein turnover rates in autism spectrum disorder risk genes, including increased stability of Gabrg2, a GABA-A receptor subunit, in male mice. Furthermore, we observed stabilization of a subset of PSD proteins, such as Shank3, following contextual fear conditioning. We propose that sex- and experience-dependent changes in protein turnover rates could help explain sex-differences in psychiatric risk and aid our understanding of the molecular mechanisms that support learning and memory.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how proteins at synapses, which are the connection points between brain cells, stay stable over long periods and how this stability might support lasting memories and brain function. They used a special labeling technique to track protein turnover, meaning how quickly proteins are broken down and replaced, in the hippocampus, which is the brain region involved in learning and memory, and they compared these rates between male and female mice and between mice that had learned something new and those that had not. The study found that both sex and learning experiences can change how quickly synaptic proteins are replaced, with some proteins becoming more stable in males and others becoming more stable after mice learned to fear a specific situation. These findings suggest that differences in how quickly proteins are replaced between males and females might help explain why certain mental health conditions like autism affect people differently based on sex, and that learning may work by making certain brain proteins last longer. Future research should investigate whether these protein stability changes are the actual cause of memory formation and whether targeting protein turnover could lead to new treatments for memory problems or psychiatric conditions.

title: Microbial Detection in Community-Acquired Pleural Space Infections Using the BIOFIRE Joint Infection Panel and Individual Polymerase Chain Reaction Assays.
abstract: New insights into community-acquired pleural infection microbiology may enable development of more rapid and accessible diagnostics that can streamline treatment. This study systematically compared molecular approaches for pathogen detection in pleural fluid from patients with such infections. Considering the need for rapid results with minimum hands-on time and test complexity, off-label use of the cassette-based, random-access BIOFIRE Joint Infection Panel (BF-JIP, bioMérieux) with and without supplementary in-house polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays was evaluated.Pleural fluids from 162 subjects from the Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota) and Haukeland University Hospital (Bergen, Norway), where molecular tests are routinely used for analyzing pleural fluid, were studied. The performance of the BF-JIP was compared to 16S rRNA gene PCR followed by Sanger and/or next-generation sequencing (16S rRNA gene PCR/sequencing), an in-house PCR panel specifically designed for pleural space infections, and culture.The BF-JIP supplemented with 3 in-house PCR assays targeting Fusobacterium nucleatum group, Streptococcus intermedius/constellatus, and Aggregatibacter aphrophilus detected 96.8% of pleural infections, providing complete microbial profiles in 70.1%. In comparison, the detection rate of 16S rRNA gene PCR/sequencing was 92.2%, providing complete microbial profiles in 87.0%. Culture detected bacteria in only 31.9% of pleural fluids, providing complete microbial profiles in 15.3%.These results underscore the importance of molecular approaches in diagnosing pleural space infections and demonstrate the feasibility of panel-based PCR-based diagnostics for these sometimes-complex infections. The BF-JIP, designed for testing synovial fluid, could be modified to provide a useful diagnostic for testing pleural fluid.© The Author(s) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a rapid molecular test called the BIOFIRE Joint Infection Panel, which detects bacteria using genetic material rather than growing cultures, could help doctors quickly identify infections in the fluid around the lungs. The study compared this panel test, sometimes combined with additional genetic tests, against traditional culture methods and other molecular approaches in fluid samples from 162 patients with lung infections at two hospitals in the United States and Norway. The BIOFIRE panel combined with three extra genetic tests successfully detected nearly 97 percent of infections, though it only identified the complete mix of bacteria present in about 70 percent of cases, while traditional culture methods found bacteria in only about 32 percent of samples. These results show that genetic testing methods are much better than old-fashioned culture techniques at finding the bacteria causing these infections, and suggest that the BIOFIRE panel could be adapted and improved to become a useful tool for diagnosing lung infections more quickly in clinical practice. The researchers concluded that modifying this panel specifically for lung fluid testing could help doctors start treatment faster, though further development and validation would be needed before it could be used routinely in hospitals.

title: Proteomic markers enhance mortality prediction in heart failure.
abstract: Clinical models incompletely capture the molecular pathways driving heart failure (HF) progression. This study evaluated whether molecular risk stratification provides incremental prognostic information beyond established clinical predictors in patients with HF.A total of 2432 patients from the Global Congestive Heart Failure (G-CHF) registry with available genotyping, DNA methylation, and proteomic profiling were analysed. Three molecular scores were assessed: a composite cardiovascular polygenic risk score (PRS) from DNA sequence polymorphisms, a methylation risk score (MRS) derived from epigenome-wide associations, and a 23-protein-based score (ProteomicDeath23). Each score was tested individually and in combination with the clinical Meta-Analysis Global Group in Chronic Heart Failure (MAGGIC) risk score and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels for mortality prediction. Validation was performed in an HF subset of the UK Biobank (UKB).Over a median follow-up of 3.0 years in G-CHF, 523 patients died from any cause (7.64 per 100 person-years [PY]). In multivariable analyses, ProteomicDeath23 was the strongest independent predictor of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR] per 1 standard deviation, 2.23), outperforming NT-proBNP (HR 2.00), MRSMortality (HR 1.66), PRSmetaCVD (HR 1.10), and the MAGGIC score (HR 1.70). A model combining ProteomicDeath23 with MAGGIC and NT-proBNP achieved the highest discrimination for mortality (C-index, 0.77). Addition of MRSMortality to this proteomic-clinical model resulted in only small improvements in discrimination (ΔC-index, +0.004, P = .0039), while the PRSmetaCVD provided no incremental benefit. Among patients with low NT-proBNP/MAGGIC score, mortality rates increased from 1.71 to 8.12 per 100 PY across ProteomicDeath23 tertiles. Consistent results were observed in the UKB-HF validation cohort.A proteomic score was the strongest molecular predictor of mortality in HF. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether measuring proteins in the blood could better predict which heart failure patients might die, beyond what doctors already know from standard clinical tests. The study analyzed blood samples from over 2,400 heart failure patients, measuring their genes, chemical markers in their DNA, and 23 specific proteins to create risk scores that could forecast death rates. A protein-based score proved to be the strongest predictor of death, performing better than existing measures like a common heart failure risk calculator and a standard blood test called NT-proBNP. When doctors combined the protein score with traditional clinical information and the standard blood test, they achieved the best ability to identify which patients faced the highest risk of dying, even among patients who appeared low-risk by conventional measures. These findings suggest that adding protein measurements to routine heart failure care could help doctors more accurately predict patient outcomes and potentially guide treatment decisions.

title: Loss of the kinases TBK1 and IKKε sensitizes target cancer cells to T cell killing through an IFN-γ-mediated inflammatory death program.
abstract: Cytotoxic T cells produce the cytokine interferon-γ (IFN-γ). We sought to determine whether IFN-γ directly kills target cells and found that T cells used IFN-γ to kill murine melanoma cells lacking the kinases TBK1 and IKKε. In the absence of both kinases, IFN-γ induced the production of TNF receptor 1 (TNFR1) and the sensor Z-DNA binding protein 1 (ZBP1) in the tumor cells to stimulate receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)-dependent apoptosis in a cell-autonomous manner. IFN-γ also enhanced the activation of nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) signaling in a TNFR1-dependent manner in cells deficient in both TBK1 and IKKε. Because IFN-γ-induced apoptosis occurred in a transcription-dependent manner with slow kinetics, STAT1 and NF-κB cooperated to activate the expression of inflammatory genes in the dying cells. Thus, IFN-γ-induced cell death was accompanied by an inflammatory signature in the absence of TBK1 and IKKε. TBK1 and IKKε not only mediated the induction of type I IFN but also inhibited RIPK1-dependent death and NF-κB-dependent inflammation. Therefore, we propose that these kinases may have gained these intertwined functions so that cells infected by pathogens that produce antagonists of TBK1 and IKKε are eliminated by IFN-γ-secreting T cells in an inflammatory manner to compensate for the inhibition of type I IFN production.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how immune cells called T cells kill cancer cells, specifically looking at whether a signaling molecule called interferon-gamma plays a direct role in this process. They discovered that when melanoma cancer cells lacked two specific proteins called TBK1 and IKKε, the interferon-gamma produced by T cells could trigger a death program in those cancer cells by activating other proteins that cause cell death and inflammation. The cancer cells that were missing these two proteins responded to interferon-gamma by producing death-triggering molecules and inflammatory signals that worked together to kill the cells in a coordinated way. This finding suggests that these two proteins normally protect cells from being killed by immune signals, and cancer cells may use them to hide from the immune system. Understanding this mechanism could help researchers develop new cancer treatments that either block these protective proteins or enhance the immune system's ability to recognize and kill cancer cells through this inflammatory death pathway.

title: Host site experiences with resident and fellow global health electives: a qualitative study.
abstract: Global health electives (GHEs) are increasingly integrated into residency and fellow training programs within the United States, offering benefits for trainees and institutions. However, limited data exists on the investment host institutions make to provide these experiences. This study aimed to explore the costs, benefits, and contextual factors that influence whether hosting visiting physician trainees is viewed as a worthwhile investment by GHE host sites.We conducted a qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with 11 physician educators from nine designated Mayo International Health Program (MIHP) global partner sites across Africa, Asia, and Central and South America. Participants included both national and expatriate physicians with longstanding institutional partnerships with Mayo Clinic. Interviews were transcribed, coded, and analyzed to identify key themes related to host experiences.All participants acknowledged both the costs and benefits of hosting physician trainees on GHEs. Costs included time spent coordinating logistics, orienting and supervising trainees, and providing housing and resources, often within resource-constrained settings. Benefits included clinical workload support, educational contributions, staff morale enhancement, and institutional capacity strengthening. Perceptions of reciprocity varied where some felt their institution and the visiting trainee benefited equally, while others believed the visiting trainee gained more. Hosts identified strategies to improve reciprocity, such as stronger institutional partnerships, provision of relevant supplies, and bi-directional exchange programs. Three contextual factors strongly influenced whether hosts viewed their investment as worthwhile: trainees' language proficiency, level of training and engagement, and rotation duration. Despite costs noted, many hosts described GHE experiences as a meaningful investment when trainees were well-prepared, engaged, and stayed for at least one month.Host institutions recognize value in hosting GHEs, yet this value is contingent upon thoughtful elective design. Trainee characteristics and rotation logistics significantly impact perceived reciprocity and institutional benefit. To ensure GHEs are ethical and sustainable, sending institutions should prioritize longer rotations, match trainees' experience to host capacity, direct pre-departure planning, and foster ongoing, reciprocal partnerships. Continuing to explore host perspectives is critical to developing more equitable and impactful global health training programs for all parties.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Researchers examined how host institutions in Africa, Asia, and Central and South America experience welcoming American medical trainees for short-term global health learning rotations, since these programs are becoming more common but little is known about the actual costs and benefits to the host sites. The study involved interviews with eleven experienced doctors from nine partner institutions who work with Mayo Clinic, asking them about their experiences hosting visiting trainees and what they gained or lost from the arrangement. The doctors reported that hosting trainees required significant time and resources like housing and supervision, but also brought benefits such as extra help with patient care, opportunities to teach, improved staff morale, and strengthening of their institution's abilities. The doctors felt the experience was worthwhile when visiting trainees spoke the local language well, had appropriate training levels, stayed for at least a month, and were actively engaged in their work. To make these global health training programs fairer and more sustainable for everyone involved, sending institutions should plan longer rotations, prepare trainees thoroughly before they arrive, match trainees to what the host site can actually support, and build lasting partnerships based on mutual benefit rather than one-sided advantage.

title: POEMS Syndrome: 2026 Update on Diagnosis, Risk-Stratification, and Management.
abstract: POEMS syndrome is a life-threatening syndrome due to an underlying plasma cell neoplasm. The major criteria for the syndrome are polyneuropathy, clonal plasma cell disorder (PCD), sclerotic bone lesions, elevated vascular endothelial growth factor, and the presence of Castleman disease. Minor features include organomegaly, endocrinopathy, characteristic skin changes, papilledema, extravascular volume overload, and thrombocytosis.The diagnosis of POEMS syndrome is made with three of the major criteria, two of which must include polyneuropathy and clonal plasma cell disorder, and at least one of the minor criteria.Because the pathogenesis of the syndrome is not well understood, risk stratification is limited to clinical phenotype rather than specific molecular markers. Risk factors include low serum albumin, age, pleural effusion, pulmonary hypertension, and reduced eGFR.For those patients with a dominant plasmacytoma, first line therapy is irradiation. Patients with diffuse sclerotic lesions or disseminated bone marrow involvement should receive systemic therapy. Corticosteroids are temporizing, but alkylators and lenalidomide are the mainstays of treatment, the former either in the form of low dose conventional therapy or as high-dose conditioning for stem cell transplantation. Thalidomide and bortezomib also have activity, but their benefit needs to be weighed against their risk of exacerbating the peripheral neuropathy. Daratumumab combinations also appear promising based on case series. Prompt recognition and institution of both supportive care measures and therapy directed against the plasma cell result in the best outcomes.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: POEMS syndrome is a serious disease caused by cancer of plasma cells, which are a type of white blood cell that normally helps fight infection, and it affects multiple body systems including nerves, bones, and blood vessels. The diagnosis requires doctors to identify at least three major signs from a specific list, with polyneuropathy (weakness and damage to nerves in the arms and legs) and a clonal plasma cell disorder (abnormal growth of identical cancer cells) being mandatory, plus at least one minor sign like enlarged organs or skin changes. Because scientists do not fully understand what causes POEMS syndrome, doctors cannot use genetic tests to predict how severe a patient's disease will be and must instead rely on clinical warning signs such as low protein levels in the blood, fluid around the lungs, and reduced kidney function. Treatment depends on the pattern of bone involvement, with radiation therapy used for patients with a single tumor and chemotherapy drugs like alkylators and lenalidomide used for patients with widespread disease, though doctors must be careful because some drugs can worsen nerve damage. Early recognition of POEMS syndrome combined with prompt treatment targeting the cancer cells and supportive care measures gives patients the best chance of recovery and improved outcomes.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Nephrology Education.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models are increasingly reshaping nephrology education. This review advances a hierarchical framework for understanding AI in nephrology education. At the primary level, AI may represent a scalable educational infrastructure that helps address the mismatch between educational demand and delivery capacity. At the secondary level, 3 mechanisms enable this infrastructure: workflow integration, continuous adaptation, and scalability. At the tertiary level, downstream outcomes include enhanced clinical reasoning, curriculum acceleration, burden reduction, improved patient education, and equitable access. However, safe and effective implementation requires addressing limitations related to accuracy, hallucinations, bias, transparency, privacy, and alignment with evolving clinical guidelines. Emerging innovations, including adaptive tutors, digital twins, and AI-orchestrated curricula, highlight a rapidly evolving educational ecosystem. Overall, AI and large language models hold substantial promise to modernize nephrology education and patient engagement, provided they are integrated with rigorous governance, continuous expert oversight, and ethical safeguards.Copyright © 2026 National Kidney Foundation, Inc. llm_summary: Artificial intelligence and large language models, which are computer systems that can understand and generate human language, are increasingly being used to improve how kidney doctors are trained and educated. Researchers created a framework with three levels to explain how artificial intelligence works in kidney disease education, starting with how it can provide more educational resources to meet growing demand, then showing the three ways it does this through integrating into daily workflows, adapting to individual learners, and expanding to reach more people. The study found that artificial intelligence could improve how doctors think through medical problems, speed up training programs, reduce workload burden, help patients understand their conditions better, and make quality education available to people in underserved areas. However, the researchers emphasized that safely using artificial intelligence in kidney education requires careful attention to accuracy, preventing the system from making up false information, removing biases, being transparent about how decisions are made, protecting patient privacy, and keeping up with changing medical guidelines. Moving forward, new tools like personalized tutoring systems, computer models that mimic real patients, and artificial intelligence that organizes entire educational programs show promise for modernizing kidney disease education, but only if they are used with strong oversight by human experts and ethical safeguards.

title: Perceptions of the Acceptability of Community-Based Breast Cancer Risk Assessment among Underserved Latinas in Maricopa County, Arizona.
abstract: Latinas are more likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer at later stages than Non-Hispanic White women. Risk-based breast cancer screening offers a promising alternative to age-based approaches by prioritizing women at highest risk and reducing harms. Understanding the acceptability of a breast cancer risk assessment tool is essential for promoting uptake among Latinas.To explore the acceptability of performing a breast cancer risk assessment in community settings among Latinas residing in Maricopa County, Arizona.Twenty-three Latinas aged 45 to 65 years old, and residing in Maricopa County in Arizona, participated in focus groups and individual interviews between November 2022 and May 2023. Qualitative findings were analyzed by a deductive-inductive approach.Participants stated no experience using the risk assessment yet overwhelmingly expressed acceptability. Participants reported that early detection of breast cancer was a strong motivator but acknowledged how community acceptability would depend on the implementation of the tool. Latinas indicated that the tool would be best received if offered by word of mouth, social networks, and by aid of trusted health providers, including Community Health Workers.Latinas in Maricopa County portray an acceptability towards the risk assessment tool. Themes identified include the acceptability of breast cancer risk assessment and effective breast cancer risk assessment delivery in community settings. llm_summary: Latinas in Arizona are more likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer at advanced stages compared to white women, which is why researchers wanted to test a new approach that identifies which women are at highest risk rather than screening all women based on age alone. The study team talked with twenty-three Latina women between ages forty-five and sixty-five living in Maricopa County through focus groups and one-on-one interviews between November 2022 and May 2023 to understand whether they would accept using a breast cancer risk assessment tool in their communities. The women had never used such a tool before, but they overwhelmingly said they would be willing to try it, especially because they understood that catching breast cancer early could save lives. The women explained that the tool would work best if trusted people in their community, like health workers they already know and their social networks, told them about it through word of mouth and social media rather than through formal medical channels. These findings suggest that offering breast cancer risk assessment tools through trusted community members and digital platforms could help more Latina women get screened and potentially catch cancer earlier.

title: Motivation and perceived learning in serious games: Reflexive thematic analysis of educational escape room experiences.
abstract: Serious games represent an innovative and engaging method for teaching procedural skills, but educators lack sufficient data on optimal design and implementation strategies for enhancing learning and motivation. The purpose of this study was to explore learners' perceptions of how core design features of an educational escape room affected their motivation and learning during procedural skills training.We conducted individual interviews in 2023 with anesthesia residents and student nurse anesthetists who concurrently participated in a randomized controlled trial examining the effects of time pressure in a procedural skills escape room. We analyzed interview transcripts using reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist paradigm.We reached thematic sufficiency after interviewing 13 participants across 13 escape room sessions. We identified 7 themes: 1) competition with self and others is motivating and improves cognitive engagement, 2) time pressure enhances simulation fidelity and affects participants' goals, 3) group dynamics impact participants' motivation and learning, 4) psychological safety within teams enhances motivation and learning, 5) pre- and post-escape room activities enhance participant motivation, 6) struggling in a task promotes learning, and 7) relevant and memorable tasks enhance motivation and learning.Competition, time pressure, social dynamics (e.g. social cues, team learning), and active effort contributed to the educational success of serious games. Immediate feedback embedded in the design of escape room puzzles may benefit learners by improving their self-efficacy. Findings suggest productive avenues for advancing understanding of how motivation and performance intersect in other types of serious games and for identifying effective ways to incorporate struggle or failure.

llm_summary: Educators have been looking for better ways to teach medical skills using games and interactive activities, but they need more information about what design features actually help students learn and stay motivated. Researchers interviewed anesthesia residents and student nurse anesthetists who participated in an escape room training exercise, which is a type of puzzle-solving game where participants work together to solve problems under time pressure, and they analyzed the interviews to find patterns in what helped or hurt learning. The study found seven important factors that affected how well students learned, including friendly competition that kept people engaged, time limits that made the training feel more realistic, good teamwork and trust among group members, and tasks that were meaningful and easy to remember. These findings suggest that when serious games include elements like competition, time pressure, strong team dynamics, and immediate feedback on performance, they help students learn procedural skills more effectively. Future research should explore how these same motivating factors could improve learning in other types of educational games and investigate whether letting students struggle or fail during training actually helps them learn better in the long run.

title: Barrier restoration as a therapeutic strategy for disorders of gut-brain interaction.
abstract: Disorders of gut-brain interaction, such as irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia, are increasingly linked to defects in gut barrier function. Mucosal disruption, encompassing alterations in the epithelial and mucus layers, leads to enhanced intestinal permeability, microbial translocation, and aberrant immune and neuronal signalling, potentially contributing to symptom severity. Despite growing recognition of barrier dysfunction in disorders of gut-brain interaction, clinical interventions remain largely symptom-based, with few therapies designed to directly restore epithelial integrity. In this Review, we examine the cellular and molecular pathways underpinning gut barrier function and highlight evidence supporting the role of diet, microbiome-targeted interventions, stress modulation, and pharmacological agents in maintaining or restoring intestinal permeability. Mechanistic insights reveal that short-chain fatty acids, amino acids (glutamine and tryptophan), and targeted probiotics can enhance tight junction integrity and mucin secretion, whereas psychological stress, low-fibre diets, and high-fat diets disrupt these pathways. We also discuss novel therapeutics, including antihistamines, mast cell stabilisers, protease inhibitors, secretagogues, and guanylate cyclase C agonists, and emerging technologies, such as vagal nerve stimulation and barrier-protective hydrogel delivery systems. Although promising, these strategies require validation in well designed clinical trials with targeted endpoints, and patient stratification based on microbial and immune phenotypes. By integrating advances in molecular biology with translational therapeutics, interventions targeting intestinal permeability could shift the treatment paradigm for disorders of gut-brain interaction from general symptom management to personalised disease modification.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. llm_summary: Disorders that affect how the gut and brain communicate, such as irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia, are increasingly understood to involve damage to the protective barrier lining the intestines. Researchers reviewed scientific evidence about how the intestinal barrier works and examined various approaches that might repair it, including dietary changes, modifications to gut bacteria through targeted supplements, stress reduction, and new medications. The review found that certain nutrients like short-chain fatty acids and amino acids can strengthen the tight connections between intestinal cells and increase protective mucus production, while stress, low-fiber diets, and high-fat diets damage these same protective mechanisms. The findings suggest that future treatments could move away from simply managing symptoms toward actually fixing the underlying intestinal damage by personalizing therapy based on each patient's unique bacterial and immune characteristics. However, these promising approaches still need to be tested in well-designed clinical trials to confirm their effectiveness and determine which patients would benefit most from each type of treatment.

title: Availability and Use of Social Determinants of Health Data in Alliance Gastrointestinal Cancer Clinical Trials.
abstract: Social determinants of health (SDOH) shape cancer treatment access, adherence, and outcomes, yet their collection and use within National Clinical Trials Network (NCTN) studies remain poorly defined. This study examined how demographic and SDOH-related variables were historically collected and published to identify gaps that constrain the study of social context within NCTN trials.Participant-level data from completed phase III trials for gastrointestinal (GI) cancers conducted by the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology (Alliance) or its legacy groups from 1999 to 2018 were pooled. Thirteen measures were assessed: four demographic and nine SDOH-related. The proportion of individual participants with data collected for each measure was evaluated. Data utilization was evaluated for all primary articles and via targeted review of related publications using the number either reporting subgroups or publishing analyses for each measure.A total of 12,701 participants across 11 trials were included. All trials collected demographic measures (<2% of patients missing), insurance status (1% missing), and ZIP code (3% missing). Education level was collected in two trials (28% missing) with marital and employment status collected in one trial (41% missing for both). No trials collected data on other SDOH-related measures. Education level was the only SDOH-related measure reported in primary articles, and none reported analysis of SDOH-related measures. Of the 149 related publications, <2% reported or analyzed any SDOH-related measure.Across Alliance and NCTN legacy group phase III trials for GI cancers, demographic variables have been consistently collected and frequently reported or analyzed, whereas SDOH-related measures are inconsistently collected and rarely published in the literature. These findings demonstrate a historical absence of routine SDOH data capture and utilization within NCTN trials.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how well cancer clinical trials collect information about social factors that affect patient health, such as income level, education, and access to transportation, because these factors significantly influence whether patients can receive treatment and whether that treatment works. The study looked at data from eleven completed cancer trials involving over twelve thousand patients with gastrointestinal cancers, which are cancers of the stomach, colon, and related organs, conducted between 1999 and 2018 to see what information was gathered and how often it was reported in published results. The researchers found that basic information like age and race was collected from nearly all patients, but important social factors like education level were only collected from a small number of trials, and other social factors like employment status and housing stability were almost never recorded. When researchers published their findings about these trials, they almost never included analysis of the social factors that had been collected, meaning doctors and patients were missing important information about how life circumstances affect cancer treatment outcomes. These findings show that cancer clinical trials have historically ignored social determinants of health, which represents a significant gap that future trials should address by routinely collecting and analyzing this information to better understand how patients' life situations influence their ability to benefit from cancer.

title: Temporal changes in cortisol secretion and their association with long-term outcomes in benign adrenal incidentalomas: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS), the most common hormonal abnormality in adrenal incidentalomas, is associated with increased cardiometabolic risk. MACS is defined by cortisol concentrations higher than 50 nmol/L after a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (1-mg DST). The prognostic value of a single test remains uncertain. We examined longitudinal changes in 1-mg DST results, cumulative cortisol exposure, and their associations with cardiometabolic outcomes and mortality.In this retrospective cohort study conducted in 25 adrenal centres that are part of the European Network for the Study of Adrenal Tumours consortium across 14 countries with adults (aged ≥18 years) with benign adrenal incidentalomas diagnosed from Jan 1, 2000, to Dec 1, 2020, two or more 1-mg DSTs, and follow-up of at least 36 months, we used multivariable Cox models to assess associations between longitudinal 1-mg DST results and all-cause mortality and cardiovascular and thrombotic events. Patients with Cushing's syndrome, primary aldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, or androgen-secreting tumour at baseline; active malignancy within 36 months of incidentaloma diagnosis; or suspicion of unreliable 1-mg DST results were excluded, along with patients taking oral glucocorticoids, strong CYP3A4 modulators, adrenal enzyme inhibitors, oral oestrogen, or selective oestrogen receptor modulators. Cumulative cortisol exposure was estimated from serial 1-mg DSTs. Restricted mean survival time (RMST) quantified differences in event-free time. Data were collected from the electronic health records of all eligible patients at each participating centre.Among 2525 patients (median follow-up 80 months [IQR 49-122]), 563 (22·3%) had changes in 1-mg DST results leading to a change in diagnosis, most within 3 years of their baseline 1-mg DST. Patients with persistently abnormal 1-mg DST results (ie, MACS-to-MACS patients; n=839) were older and had a greater cardiometabolic burden than those with persistently normal results (ie, non-functioning adrenal tumours [NFAT]-to-NFAT patients; n=1103). MACS-to-MACS patients had a higher rate of worsening hypertension (adjusted hazard ratio 1·34 [95% CI 1·03-1·73]) and a shorter event-free time for worsening hypertension (10-year RMST 60·4 months [56·8-75·5] vs 86·1 months [79·1-93·4]) than NFAT-to-NFAT patients. In crude analyses, patients with higher baseline post-1-mg DST cortisol, patients with greater cumulative cortisol exposure, and MACS-to-MACS patients had shorter survival and event-free time; however, these associations were not independent of age and baseline cardiometabolic risk factors after multivariable adjustment.Longitudinal 1-mg DST changes are common. MACS-to-MACS patients had worsening hypertension, but rates of mortality and cardiovascular or thrombotic events were not significantly associated with 1-mg DST trajectories after adjustment for age and cardiovascular risk factors. These findings identify patients with persistently abnormal 1-mg DST results as a group with high cardiometabolic risk that warrants closer attention to modifiable risk factors. llm_summary: Researchers examined how changes in a hormone test called the dexamethasone suppression test could predict health problems in patients with benign adrenal tumors, which are growths on glands that produce hormones. This retrospective cohort study followed 2,525 patients across 25 medical centers in 14 countries for an average of about six and a half years, tracking their test results over time and recording any heart problems, blood clots, high blood pressure, or deaths that occurred. Patients whose test results stayed abnormal over time had worse high blood pressure outcomes compared to those with consistently normal results, but surprisingly, the researchers found that cortisol levels alone did not independently predict heart problems or death after accounting for age and existing health conditions. The findings suggest that patients with persistently abnormal test results represent a high-risk group who need careful monitoring and management of modifiable risk factors like blood pressure and cholesterol, but a single test result may not be reliable for predicting serious health events. Future studies using a prospective design, where patients are followed forward in time rather than looking back at past records, are needed to determine whether repeating this hormone test helps doctors better identify which patients.

title: Distinct Attentional Control Profiles during Language Comprehension in Major Mental Health Disorders.
abstract: The current study combined behavioral and EEG measures to investigate variations in attentional state during comprehension of spoken stories in a clinical sample that included participants with several major mental health disorders that often feature attentional control difficulties.Participants with schizophrenia (N=62), bipolar disorder (N=44), major depressive disorder (N=51) and psychiatrically healthy controls (N=82) completed a story-listening task and were periodically interrupted by attention probes. Attention probes assessed three different states of engagement via self-reports: on-task attention, partially off-task split-attention, and fully off-task lapsed attention. EEG was recorded to examine corresponding changes in periodic alpha-band (8-13 Hz) power.We found that all patient groups reported significantly less time fully on-task during story listening than did control participants, but that individual patient groups reported distinct patterns of off-task attention. Whereas reports of fully-lapsed attention dominated off-task reports for participants with schizophrenia, participants with major depressive disorder reported a higher incidence of experiencing a distracted or split attentional state. The EEG results provided additional evidence that the three self-report attention probe categories tapped into biologically distinguishable attentional states, with split attention and fully lapsed attention associated with distinct neural signatures relative to on-task attention. Periodic alpha power was modulated by attentional state in all groups, although there were significant group differences.Our results demonstrate distinct behavioral and neurophysiological attentional control profiles in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder compared to control participants during language comprehension.Copyright © 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined how people with serious mental health conditions like schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depression pay attention differently than healthy people when listening to stories. The study had participants listen to recorded stories while occasionally stopping them to ask whether they were fully focused, partially distracted, or completely zoned out, and the researchers also measured brain activity using electrodes placed on the scalp to detect electrical patterns associated with attention. All three patient groups reported spending significantly less time fully focused on the stories compared to healthy controls, but each disorder showed its own unique pattern of attention problems, with people with schizophrenia tending to completely zone out while people with depression more often experienced split attention where their mind was partially on the story and partially elsewhere. The brain activity measurements confirmed that these three different attention states produced distinct electrical signatures in the brain, and while all groups showed changes in brain wave patterns based on their attention level, the patient groups differed from healthy controls in how their brains responded. These findings suggest that schizophrenia and depression affect attention control in different ways during language comprehension, which could help doctors better understand and potentially treat attention problems in people with these conditions.

The Rome criteria are internationally recognized guidelines that doctors use to diagnose functional gastrointestinal disorders, including those affecting the anorectal region, by establishing consistent definitions and diagnostic standards across different medical centers and countries.

title: Age- and Region-Stratified Growth in Emergency Department Neuroimaging Utilization within Epic Cosmos, 2016-2025.
abstract: Emergency department (ED) neuroimaging utilization has reportedly increased over the past decade, but whether this growth is concentrated among a specific age range or specific geographic regions remains less well characterized. The present study aimed to address this gap using the data from participating Epic Cosmos healthcare organizations across the United States.We analyzed deidentified aggregate data for ED encounters captured within participating healthcare organizations between January 2016 and December 2025. Annual aggregate volumes were extracted for 16 neuroimaging examination categories. Encounter-adjusted utilization rates per 1,000 ED encounters were calculated and stratified by age and U.S. Census region with temporal trends assessed using Poisson log-linear regression.Total neuroimaging utilization increased across all age groups from 2016 to 2025, from 21.9 to 33.5 examinations per 1,000 ED encounters in children younger than 5 years and from 377.5 to 592.6 per 1,000 ED encounters in adults aged 65 years or older. The absolute rate difference was largest among adults aged 65 years or older (+215.1 per 1,000 ED encounters) and smallest among children younger than 5 years (+11.7 per 1,000 ED encounters). Utilization also increased across all U.S. Census regions, from 174.1 to 313.4 in the South, 167.5 to 318.4 in the Midwest, 159.7 to 322.0 in the Northeast, and 193.8 to 304.0 per 1,000 ED encounters in the West. Regional absolute rate differences ranged from +110.2 per 1,000 ED encounters in the West to +162.3 in the Northeast. Formal temporal trend analysis confirmed increasing encounter-adjusted utilization across all age groups and regions, with annual incidence rate ratios ranging from 1.048 to 1.059 across age strata and from 1.050 to 1.071 across regions; all p-values for trend were <.001.Within the evolving Epic Cosmos network, ED neuroimaging utilization varied by patient age and region from 2016 to 2025, but increased consistently across all evaluated age and geographic strata rather than being limited to older adults or a specific region. However, the magnitude of increase was greater among older adults and varied modestly by region. These utilization patterns may inform neuroradiology staffing, training, scanner allocation, and imaging stewardship initiatives.© 2026 by American Journal of Neuroradiology.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether the increased use of brain and spine imaging scans in emergency departments over the past decade was happening equally across all age groups and different regions of the United States. The study analyzed data from hundreds of hospitals using the same electronic health record system between 2016 and 2025, tracking how many imaging scans were performed for every thousand emergency room visits. Brain and spine imaging use grew significantly across all age groups and all regions of the country, but the biggest increases happened among older adults aged sixty-five and over, whose imaging rates jumped from about 378 scans per thousand visits to nearly 593 scans per thousand visits. The Northeast region saw the largest overall increase in imaging use, while younger children had the smallest increases, suggesting that aging populations and regional differences are important factors driving the growth in emergency imaging. These findings could help hospitals plan how many imaging machines they need, train enough radiologists to read the scans, and develop better strategies to use imaging wisely without ordering unnecessary tests.

title: Effects of fentanyl on diaphragm muscle force in patients undergoing knee arthroplasty: a randomised double-blind clinical trial.
abstract: Opioids exert important negative effects on respiration, evident across a range of behaviours. The present study evaluated whether fentanyl administration decreases diaphragm muscle forces across levels of inspiratory loading in adult patients undergoing elective knee arthroplasty surgery.Adult patients undergoing elective knee arthroplasty with no pulmonary pathology were randomly assigned to a fentanyl dose (25, 50, or 100 μg) in a double-blind, single-institution clinical trial. Ultrasound-based shear wave elastography was used to measure diaphragm Young's modulus (E). The primary outcome was change in the difference in E achieved across levels of inspiratory loading (E range) before randomisation and 10 min post-fentanyl (ΔE range) as a measure of fentanyl-induced changes in diaphragm force-generating capacity.Sixty-nine patients (average age 69 yr) were randomised, with final data analysis in 22, 22, and 19 patients from the 25, 50, and 100 μg groups, respectively. The ΔE range was compared across dose groups using analysis of covariance, with the pretreatment E range included as the covariate. The estimated treatment effect (95% confidence interval) for 50 μg vs 25 μg, and for 100 μg vs 25 μg was -0.7 (-9.5, 8.1) and -5.3 (-14.1, 3.6), respectively. There was no statistically significant effect of fentanyl on ΔE range (P=0.432).Fentanyl did not reduce the E range generated by the diaphragm muscle during inspiratory pressure-threshold loading, possibly reflecting relatively low levels of inspiratory loading or the presence of a fentanyl effect even at the lowest dose used (25 μg) in this older patient population.NCT05856136.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers examined whether fentanyl, a powerful painkiller commonly used during surgery, weakens the diaphragm muscle that controls breathing in older patients undergoing knee replacement surgery. The study randomly assigned 63 patients to receive different doses of fentanyl (25, 50, or 100 micrograms) and used ultrasound technology to measure how well their diaphragm muscle could generate force before and after the medication was given. The results showed that fentanyl did not significantly reduce the diaphragm's ability to create force across different levels of breathing effort, which was surprising given that opioids are known to affect breathing in other ways. The researchers suggested that their findings might be explained by the relatively mild breathing challenges the patients faced during the test or because even the lowest fentanyl dose used may have already affected the diaphragm in this older population. This study highlights the need for further research to better understand how fentanyl affects breathing muscles under different conditions and in different patient groups.

title: Prospective evaluation of hepatic steatosis and fibrosis after one anastomosis gastric bypass using transient elastography.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is highly prevalent among individuals with severe obesity and is closely associated with insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction. Although metabolic and bariatric surgery has demonstrated favorable hepatic effects, prospective data evaluating liver-related outcomes following one-anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB) remain limited. This prospective cohort study included adults with severe obesity undergoing OAGB between February 2024 and January 2025 at a tertiary academic center. Hepatic steatosis and fibrosis were assessed preoperatively and 6 months postoperatively using ultrasonography and transient elastography, including liver stiffness measurement (LSM) and controlled attenuation parameter (CAP). Metabolic, biochemical, and anthropometric parameters were also evaluated using paired comparisons. A total of 85 patients were included, of whom 82 completed the 6-month transient elastography assessment. The mean age was 44.34 ± 10.23 years, and 82.4% were female. At 6 months, patients achieved a mean total body weight loss of 29.64%. Significant improvements were observed in liver-related parameters, including reductions in ALT (P < 0.01), AST (P = 0.02), LSM (P < 0.01), and CAP (P < 0.01). Significant improvements were also observed in fasting blood glucose (P < 0.01), HbA1c (P < 0.01), triglycerides (P < 0.01), total cholesterol (P < 0.01), and LDL cholesterol (P = 0.01). OAGB was associated with significant short-term improvement in hepatic steatosis, liver stiffness, liver enzymes, glycemic control, and lipid profile among patients with severe obesity. These findings support the potential role of OAGB as a metabolic and hepatic therapeutic intervention for MASLD.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Fatty liver disease linked to obesity and poor metabolism is very common in people with severe weight problems and often leads to serious health complications. Researchers studied 82 adults with severe obesity who had a weight loss surgery called one-anastomosis gastric bypass, measuring their liver health before surgery and six months afterward using ultrasound technology that checks for fat buildup and scarring in the liver. After six months, patients lost an average of nearly 30 percent of their body weight and showed major improvements in liver health, including lower liver enzymes, less fat in the liver, and reduced scarring, along with better blood sugar control and healthier cholesterol levels. These results suggest that this particular weight loss surgery can help improve fatty liver disease and related metabolic problems in people with severe obesity, offering a potential treatment option beyond just diet and exercise. Future research should track patients for longer periods to confirm these benefits last over time and to understand exactly how the surgery improves liver health.

title: Co-exposure to cannabinoids and nicotine increases senescence in prenatal human lung development.
abstract: Tandem use of cigarettes and cannabis is increasing, particularly where recreational marijuana is legalized, posing a serious risk to fetal development. This study investigates the impact of cannabinoids (THC and CBD) and nicotine on fetal lung development using human lung explants from 10-16 weeks of gestation. Our results show that THC promotes epithelial cysting RESULTS: Our data revealed decreased proliferation (Ki-67) following treatment with CBD and CBD + THC+nicotine, whereas smooth muscle cell differentiation decreased across all conditions. Furthermore, the combination treatments induced a senescence-like phenotype as demonstrated by increased CDKN1A and CDKN2A expression and a strong reduction in LAMIN B1 staining. Additionally, DNA damage response markers ɣH2A.X and 53BP1 were significantly upregulated in the combination treatments. This was accompanied by an activation of the interferon pathway with increased expression of the downstream targets MX1 and IFI2. The addition of senolytics, Dasatinib and Quercetin (D + Q), reduced the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), such as IL-6, IL-8, M-CSF, MCP-3, MIP-1β, TNFα, MIP-3β, and TSLP, the senescence gene expressions, and reversed interferon pathway activation CONCLUSION: Our results demonstrate that co-exposure to nicotine and cannabis alters cellular proliferation and differentiation, induces a senescence-like phenotype and DNA damage response in human fetal lung cultures, which may be partially rescued using senolytics.This study aims to assess the effect of cannabis and nicotine use during pregnancy on fetal human lung development. The combinatorial exposure to CBD, THC, and nicotine during pregnancy increases senescence-like phenotype, DNA damage response, and senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASP) secretion. The use of senolytics (D + Q) may prove to be a promising therapeutic option, alleviating several of the adverse effects induced by the different substances.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Researchers examined how smoking cigarettes and cannabis together during pregnancy might harm a developing baby's lungs, since more pregnant people are using both substances in places where marijuana is legal. The scientists studied human lung tissue from early pregnancies between ten and sixteen weeks of development and exposed samples to the active chemicals in cannabis (THC and CBD) combined with nicotine from cigarettes. The results showed that this combination exposure caused the lung cells to age prematurely, develop DNA damage similar to what happens in aging cells, and release harmful inflammatory chemicals that can injure developing tissue. The team discovered that a type of medicine called senolytics, which removes aged cells, could reduce some of the damage caused by the combined exposure and decrease the harmful inflammatory response. This research suggests that pregnant people who use both cigarettes and cannabis may put their babies' lung development at serious risk, but that new treatments might help prevent some of this damage.

title: Comparing those Most Satisfied Versus Least Satisfied Following Surgery for Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy: Are there Differences in Baseline Characteristics?
abstract: Post hoc analysis of prospectively-collected data.To identify factors predicting the most (and least) satisfaction following surgery for cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM).Patient satisfaction affects long-term outcomes after surgery but the preoperative factors that influence postoperative satisfaction have not been well studied in patients with CSM.We conducted a post hoc analysis of prospectively-collected data from the Quality Outcomes Database (QOD) CSM registry cohort. Baseline and surgical characteristics were compared for patients with CSM reporting the most [North American Spine Society Satisfaction Score (NASS) 1] and least (NASS 4) satisfaction 24 months postoperatively. A multivariable logistic regression model was constructed using backward stepwise elimination to determine significant predictors of most versus least satisfaction. Twenty-four-month patient-reported outcomes (PROs) were compared.Overall, 1141 patients were prospectively enrolled with 948 (83.1%) reaching 24-month follow-up. Of these, 699 met prespecified inclusion criteria: 610 (87.3%) were most satisfied and 89 (12.7%) were least satisfied. Though there were mean improvements in all 24-month PROs for the most satisfied cohort ( P <0.001), there were no significant improvements in 24-month PROs for the least satisfied cohort ( P >0.05). Using multivariable logistic regression modeling, a preoperative symptom of upper extremity weakness (OR=2.5, P =0.003), subjective myelopathy (OR=2.0, P =0.04), absence of numbness complaints (OR=2.2, P =0.003), symptom duration under 12 months (OR=1.6, P =0.047), Caucasian race (OR=2.3, P =0.001), participation in activities outside of the home (OR=2.0, P =0.04), anterior approach (OR=2.3, P <0.001), and higher baseline quality of life (OR=4.0, P =0.01) were predictive of the most satisfaction.Compared with the least satisfied, those most satisfied following surgery for CSM more often had a preoperative symptom of arm weakness, subjective myelopathy, the absence of numbness complaints, symptom duration under 12 months, higher baseline quality of life, and participation in activities outside of the home. Compared with a posterior approach, an anterior approach was associated with the most satisfaction. Taken together, early surgical treatment--before myelopathic symptoms significantly impact one's quality of life--may be considered to optimize patient satisfaction following CSM surgery.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. llm_summary: Researchers examined what factors help predict whether patients feel satisfied after surgery for cervical spondylotic myelopathy, a condition where the spinal cord in the neck becomes compressed and causes weakness or numbness. The study analyzed information from nearly 1,000 patients who had surgery for this condition and were followed for two years, comparing those who reported the highest satisfaction with those who reported the lowest satisfaction. Patients who were most satisfied tended to have had arm weakness before surgery, shorter symptom duration of less than one year, no numbness complaints, better quality of life before surgery, and had received an anterior approach surgery (entering from the front of the neck rather than the back). In contrast, patients who were least satisfied showed no meaningful improvement in their symptoms or quality of life two years after surgery, suggesting their expectations or baseline health status may have differed significantly. The findings suggest that operating on patients earlier in their disease, before symptoms severely damage their quality of life, may lead to better satisfaction with surgical outcomes.
